q: You run kubeadm init on a fresh VM and the cluster comes up. A teammate asks where the cluster's state — every Deployment, Secret, and ConfigMap — is actually persisted. Which component holds it?
options: etcd, the distributed key-value store backing the control plane
The kube-scheduler, which caches cluster state in memory
kube-proxy, which replicates objects to every node
The kube-apiserver, which writes objects to its local disk under /etc/kubernetes
explain: etcd is the single source of truth for all Kubernetes objects; the API server is stateless and fronts etcd. That is why etcd backup and restore is a core CKA skill — lose etcd and you lose the cluster definition. The scheduler only caches, and kube-proxy handles networking, not state.

q: You need to join a second control-plane node to an existing kubeadm cluster. You already ran kubeadm token create --print-join-command on the first control-plane node, but the new node must run control-plane components too. What must you add to the join command?
options: --worker-only=false to promote the node after joining
--apiserver-advertise-address 10.0.0.5 to register the new API server
Nothing — the printed join command works for control-plane nodes as-is
--control-plane --certificate-key CERT-KEY so the new node gets the control-plane certificates
explain: Joining an additional control-plane node requires --control-plane plus the certificate key (from kubeadm init phase upload-certs or a fresh kubeadm init phase upload-certs run) so the new node can decrypt and install the control-plane certs. The plain printed join command only adds a worker node. There is no --worker-only flag, and the advertise address alone does not install control-plane components.

q: Your cluster runs Kubernetes v1.33 and you must upgrade to v1.34 with kubeadm. Which sequence is correct?
options: apt-get upgrade kubelet on all nodes, then kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34 on the control plane
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34 on every node simultaneously, then reboot the cluster
Edit the kube-apiserver manifest image tag to v1.34 and let the cluster self-upgrade

kubeadm upgrade plan, kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34 on the first control-plane node, upgrade kubeadm on other control-plane nodes and run kubeadm upgrade node, then drain/upgrade kubelet and kubectl on every node one at a time
explain: The supported order is: plan, apply on the first control-plane node, upgrade the kubeadm binary and run kubeadm upgrade node on remaining control-plane nodes, then per node: drain, upgrade kubelet/kubectl, uncordon. Upgrading kubelet first or applying everywhere at once breaks version skew policy and risks an inconsistent control plane. Editing the manifest tag by hand bypasses kubeadm's upgrade logic and is unsupported.

q: Before upgrading the kubelet on worker node node-3, you must move its pods elsewhere safely. Which command does this correctly, and what is the key difference from merely marking the node unschedulable?
options: kubectl delete node node-3 — it removes the node and reschedules its pods
kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets — it evicts pods AND marks the node unschedulable, while cordon only marks it unschedulable without moving anything
kubectl taint node-3 upgrade=true:NoSchedule — it evicts running pods immediately
kubectl cordon node-3 — it evicts running pods to other nodes
explain: drain cordons the node and evicts pods (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets; --ignore-daemonsets is needed because DaemonSet pods cannot be evicted). cordon alone only prevents new scheduling — existing pods keep running, which is not enough before a kubelet upgrade. Deleting the node is destructive and unnecessary, and a NoSchedule taint does not evict pods already running.

q: Company policy requires a nightly backup of etcd on the stacked-etcd control-plane node cp-1. Which command performs a consistent snapshot?
options: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db
kubectl cp kube-system/etcd-cp-1:/var/lib/etcd /backup/etcd
kubectl backup etcd --all-namespaces -o /backup/etcd.db
cp /var/lib/etcd/member/snap/db /backup/etcd-snapshot.db while etcd is running
explain: etcdctl snapshot save with ETCDCTL_API=3 and the etcd PKI certs (ca.crt, server.crt, server.key under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd) takes a consistent point-in-time snapshot against the secured endpoint. There is no kubectl backup command, copying the live data dir risks corruption, and kubectl cp of the data directory is not a supported backup method.

q: etcd on cp-1 is corrupted. You have /backup/etcd-snapshot.db. After running etcdctl snapshot restore --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored, what must you do before the API server will work again?
options: Run kubeadm init --restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db to rebuild the cluster
Delete and recreate every Deployment so they re-register in the fresh etcd
Update the etcd static pod manifest (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml) so its hostPath volume points at /var/lib/etcd-restored, then wait for the kubelet to restart the pod
Nothing — the API server detects the new data directory automatically
explain: snapshot restore writes to a NEW data directory (it never overwrites the live one). The etcd static pod manifest must be edited so its --data-dir and mounted hostPath volume point at the restored directory; the kubelet then restarts the pod from the manifest. The API server does not auto-detect anything, kubeadm init would create a brand-new cluster, and workloads are stored in etcd itself so they reappear once etcd is healthy.

q: A developer needs permission to list and delete pods, but ONLY in the dev namespace. Which RBAC approach follows least privilege?
options: Editing the kube-apiserver manifest to add the developer as a superuser
A ClusterRole with pods delete/list verbs bound with a RoleBinding in the dev namespace
A ClusterRole with * verbs bound with a ClusterRoleBinding to the developer
A Role with pods get/list/delete verbs in the dev namespace, bound with a RoleBinding to the developer
explain: A namespaced Role granting only the needed verbs, bound via a RoleBinding in that namespace, is least privilege. A ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding in one namespace technically scopes to that namespace, but a ClusterRole is reusable cluster-wide and over-broad here; a ClusterRoleBinding would grant access everywhere. The API server has no superuser list to edit.

q: A monitoring ServiceAccount in the monitoring namespace must read nodes and pods cluster-wide. Which binding is correct?
options: A ClusterRoleBinding referencing a Role in the monitoring namespace
A Role in the monitoring namespace bound with a RoleBinding
A ClusterRole with nodes and pods get/list/watch verbs, bound with a ClusterRoleBinding to the ServiceAccount
A Role in the kube-system namespace bound with a ClusterRoleBinding
explain: Nodes are cluster-scoped, so only a ClusterRole can grant access to them, and it must be bound with a ClusterRoleBinding to apply cluster-wide. A namespaced Role cannot cover nodes at all, a ClusterRoleBinding cannot reference a namespaced Role, and binding in kube-system does not magically widen scope.

q: A CI ServiceAccount gets Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User cannot create resource pods in API group in the namespace ci. The Role exists and lists pods with create. What is the most likely cause?
options: The ServiceAccount token expired and must be recreated by hand
The API server is down
The pods are in CrashLoopBackOff
No RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding connects that ServiceAccount to the Role
explain: A Role alone grants nothing until a binding attaches it to a subject — the classic forgotten RoleBinding. Forbidden with an existing Role almost always means the binding is missing or references the wrong subject/namespace. An API server outage would produce connection errors, pod health is irrelevant to authorization, and ServiceAccount tokens are auto-managed.

q: The exam task says: use context cluster-east for all work. You create the Deployment, but the grader says it is missing. kubectl config get-contexts shows you are on cluster-west. What is the exam-day lesson?
options: Delete the cluster-west context so kubectl defaults to the right one
Graders sometimes check the wrong cluster; recreate it and hope
Always run kubectl config use-context cluster-east as the first command of every task — resources created in the wrong context score zero
Contexts are just labels; the resources replicate to all clusters automatically
explain: Each task is graded in the named context, and work done in the wrong cluster earns zero even if perfect. The guide's rule stands: read the task, switch context, then act. Contexts do not replicate anything, and deleting contexts risks destroying the config you need.

q: You are designing a 3-node control plane with kubeadm. The requirement is that the loss of any single control-plane node must not lose cluster state. Which etcd topology satisfies this with the least operational overhead?
options: Running etcd as a Deployment with 3 replicas
External etcd on dedicated hosts, one member per control-plane node
Stacked etcd (default kubeadm), giving 3 etcd members so quorum (2 of 3) survives one failure
A single etcd member with hourly snapshots to S3
explain: Stacked etcd — the kubeadm default — colocates an etcd member on each control-plane node; with 3 members, quorum needs 2, so one node can fail safely. External etcd also works but adds dedicated hosts and operational overhead. A single member has no quorum at all, and etcd must never run as a regular Deployment (it needs stable identity and the control plane depends on it at boot).

q: You install the metrics-server with helm install metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system. The chart's default image tag is too old. Which command upgrades the release to a new image tag without uninstalling?
options: helm install metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system --set image.tag=v0.7.2 --replace
kubectl set image deployment/metrics-server metrics-server=newtag -n kube-system
helm upgrade metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system --set image.tag=v0.7.2
helm rollback metrics-server --to v0.7.2
explain: helm upgrade with --set overrides the value and performs an in-place release upgrade — the standard Helm workflow. Re-installing over an existing release fails (use upgrade), kubectl set image would be overwritten by the next Helm operation and breaks Helm's state tracking, and helm rollback reverts to a previous release revision rather than applying a new value.

q: A Helm release is failing after an upgrade. You want to see the release history and return to the previous working revision. Which commands do this?
options: helm list --failed and helm delete --purge
helm status webshop and helm uninstall webshop --keep-history
helm history webshop -n prod, then helm rollback webshop 2 -n prod
kubectl rollout undo deployment/webshop
explain: helm history shows per-revision status, and helm rollback returns the release to a chosen revision — Helm's native undo. list/delete destroys the release, status alone shows only the current state, and kubectl rollout undo operates on the Deployment but leaves Helm's release state inconsistent with reality.

q: Your team manages 40 nearly-identical Deployments with Kustomize. You need to add the same securityContext to every Deployment without editing 40 files. What is the idiomatic Kustomize approach?
options: Use helm template to regenerate everything
Copy the securityContext into each base file — Kustomize requires explicit per-file edits
Write a bash loop that sed-edits all 40 YAML files
Add a strategic merge patch or JSON patch in the kustomization.yaml patches section targeting kind: Deployment
explain: Kustomize patches (strategic merge or JSON 6902) in kustomization.yaml apply one change across all matching resources — exactly the DRY workflow Kustomize exists for. Sed loops are fragile and untracked, per-file edits defeat the purpose of overlays, and Helm is a different templating tool, not a Kustomize feature.

q: You install a database operator with kubectl apply -f operator.yaml, but the operator crashes with no matches for kind Database, Kind=Database. What did you miss?
options: The operator image tag is wrong
The operator needs cluster-admin RBAC before anything else
Custom resources must be created in the kube-system namespace
The CustomResourceDefinition for kind Database was never installed — CRDs must exist before custom resources or the operator can use them
explain: no matches for kind means the API server knows no such type: the CRD was not installed. Operators ship CRD manifests that must be applied first (often a separate crds/ directory). RBAC and image tags produce different errors, and custom resources can live in any namespace.

q: A pod needs storage from a new vendor that ships a CSI driver. Which Kubernetes extension interface is involved, and what must be true for dynamic provisioning to work?
options: CRI — containerd must be rebuilt with the vendor's plugin
CRD — the vendor must define a Volume custom resource
CSI — the vendor's external-provisioner sidecar must be deployed so PVCs referencing its StorageClass get volumes provisioned automatically
CNI — the driver must be listed in /etc/cni/net.d
explain: Storage drivers integrate through the Container Storage Interface (CSI); dynamic provisioning requires the vendor's CSI external-provisioner sidecar watching for PVCs on its StorageClass. CNI is networking, CRI is the container runtime interface (no rebuild needed for storage), and no custom Volume kind is required.

q: After a reboot, worker node w-2 shows NotReady. systemctl status kubelet shows it failing with an error about /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. What is the fastest correct recovery path?
options: Fix or restore /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (the kubelet's config file), then systemctl restart kubelet
Delete the node object; the kubelet will recreate its own config
Reinstall Kubernetes on the node from scratch
Run kubeadm init again on w-2 to regenerate all config
explain: The kubelet reads /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml at startup; a corrupt or missing file prevents it from starting, so restoring a known-good copy and restarting the service is the fix. Reinstalling or re-running kubeadm init is destructive overkill, and deleting the Node object does not recreate kubelet configuration.

q: Your monitoring warns that the Kubernetes API server certificate expires in 5 days. Which kubeadm commands check and fix this?
options: Certificates auto-renew; no action is needed
openssl check on /etc/kubernetes/pki, then kubeadm init --renew-certs
kubeadm certs check-expiration, then kubeadm certs renew apiserver
kubectl get certificates --all-namespaces, then kubectl renew apiserver
explain: kubeadm certs check-expiration reports all control-plane cert expiries, and kubeadm certs renew apiserver (or all) rotates them. There is no kubectl renew command, re-running kubeadm init would clobber the cluster, and while the kubelet client certs can auto-rotate, the PKI certs do not renew themselves.

q: The bootstrap token printed during kubeadm init expired after 24 hours and you must join three more worker nodes today. What do you do?
options: Join commands never expire; reuse the original output
Run kubeadm token create --print-join-command to mint a fresh token and join command
Re-run kubeadm init to generate a new token
Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to the workers — tokens are unnecessary
explain: kubeadm token create mints a new bootstrap token on demand; --print-join-command gives the full join line including the CA cert hash. Tokens default to a 24h TTL, re-running init would destroy the cluster, admin.conf grants cluster-admin (never distribute it to workers), and the original command's token is genuinely expired.

q: Node old-worker is being decommissioned. Which sequence removes it cleanly so its pods are rescheduled and the API server forgets it?
options: kubectl drain old-worker --ignore-daemonsets, then kubectl delete node old-worker
kubectl cordon old-worker, then power off the VM
kubectl taint nodes old-worker retired=true:NoExecute, then delete the VM
kubectl delete node old-worker — pods reschedule automatically
explain: Drain first (evict pods safely, honoring disruption budgets), then delete the Node object so the API server drops it. Deleting the node without draining orphans pod objects, cordon alone leaves pods running on a dead node, and a taint plus power-off leaves a NotReady node object lingering in the cluster.

q: You find a file /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml on a control-plane node. You edit its --v log level and save. What happens, and why?
options: The kubelet, which watches the manifest directory, kills and recreates the API server static pod with the new flags automatically
The change applies only after the next node reboot
The API server must be restarted with systemctl restart kube-apiserver
Nothing — manifest changes require kubeadm upgrade to take effect
explain: Files in /etc/kubernetes/manifests define static pods; the kubelet watches that directory and recreates any pod whose manifest changes — no systemctl involved (control-plane components are not systemd services in kubeadm clusters). That is why editing manifests is the standard way to reconfigure the API server, scheduler, and controller-manager.

q: kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows kube-apiserver-cp-1, etcd-cp-1, and kube-scheduler-cp-1, but kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -l tier=control-plane on another cluster shows nothing. What explains the first cluster's control-plane pods?
options: They were created by a Deployment in kube-system
They are static pods created by the kubelet from manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests — they exist only on that node and are not visible via the API as normal pods in some listings
The API server creates its own pod as a self-hosted cluster
They are DaemonSet pods scheduled to control-plane nodes
explain: kubeadm runs the control plane as static pods from /etc/kubernetes/manifests; the kubelet creates them directly, which is why the control plane can bootstrap itself before the API is up. They do appear via the API once it is running, but they are not owned by any Deployment or DaemonSet — deleting their manifest file is what removes them.

q: For a highly available cluster, clients must reach the API servers through a single stable endpoint even if one control-plane node dies. Which component provides this, and where is it configured at install time?
options: A load balancer (or virtual IP such as kube-vip) in front of the API servers, set as --control-plane-endpoint during kubeadm init
CoreDNS — configured with an A record for the API
kube-proxy in IPVS mode, configured on each worker
An Ingress resource pointing at the API server Service
explain: --control-plane-endpoint is the stable DNS name or IP (backed by an external LB or a virtual IP like kube-vip) that kubeadm bakes into kubeconfigs and certs; if a control-plane node dies, traffic fails over. CoreDNS serves in-cluster service DNS, not external API access; Ingress routes HTTP workloads, not the API; kube-proxy handles Service IPs on nodes.

q: You need to install the same cluster add-ons (metrics-server, ingress-nginx) on five clusters with environment-specific tweaks per cluster, and the team refuses templating. Which tool fits, and what does its per-environment unit look like?
options: Helm — each environment gets its own chart
kubectl apply with 5 hand-maintained copies of every manifest
Kustomize — a base plus one overlay directory per environment, each with its own kustomization.yaml applying patches
etcd — store the variants as keys
explain: Kustomize's base-plus-overlays model is built for exactly this: one base, one overlay directory per environment containing a kustomization.yaml with patches and configMapGenerators. Helm is the templating the team refused, hand-maintained copies drift, and etcd is cluster state, not a config management tool.

q: After upgrading the control-plane to v1.34, kubectl get nodes shows the control-plane node at v1.34 but workers still at v1.33, and everything works. Is this supported, and what remains?
options: Supported and complete — mixed versions are the desired end state
Unsupported — all nodes must be upgraded atomically
The workers auto-upgrade within 24 hours; no action needed

Supported: kubeadm allows the kubelet to lag up to two minor versions behind the API server; you still must upgrade each worker's kubeadm, run kubeadm upgrade node, then drain and upgrade its kubelet one node at a time
explain: Kubernetes version skew policy permits kubelets up to two minor versions older than the API server, so the mixed state is valid temporarily. The remaining work per worker: install the new kubeadm, kubeadm upgrade node, drain, upgrade kubelet/kubectl, uncordon. Nothing auto-upgrades, and leaving workers behind permanently is not the goal.

q: You update a Deployment's image and want the rollout to keep at least 70% of pods available while allowing up to 30% extra pods during the update (10 replicas). Which strategy block expresses this?
options: strategy: {type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: {maxUnavailable: 3, maxSurge: 3}}
strategy: {type: BlueGreen, activeService: web}
strategy: {type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: {maxUnavailable: 30%, maxSurge: 30%}}
strategy: {type: Recreate}
explain: maxUnavailable: 30% keeps at least 70% available; maxSurge: 30% caps extra pods at 30% above desired. With 10 replicas both compute to 3 pods, but the percentage form documents intent and scales with replica changes. Recreate causes full downtime, absolute numbers work but are less expressive, and BlueGreen is not a native Deployment strategy.

q: A rollout of image api:2.0 is crashing. api:1.9 was healthy. Which single command returns the Deployment to 1.9, and what should you check first?
options: kubectl edit deployment/api and change the tag, then wait
kubectl rollout restart deployment/api — restarts pull a fresh image automatically
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api — first confirm the previous revision with kubectl rollout history deployment/api
kubectl delete deployment api, then recreate it with 1.9 — check nothing, just redeploy
explain: rollout undo reverts to the previous ReplicaSet revision in one command; checking rollout history first confirms which revision holds 1.9. Deleting and recreating loses rollout history and causes downtime, restart re-pulls the same broken 2.0 image, and editing works but undo is the purpose-built rollback.

q: You run kubectl rollout status deployment/web and it hangs at Waiting for deployment spec update to be observed. Which command shows whether new pods are failing, and what is the most common cause of a stuck rollout?
options: kubectl describe node — the cause is usually disk pressure
kubectl logs deployment/web — the cause is usually RBAC
kubectl get events — the cause is usually the new pods failing (bad image, CrashLoopBackOff) so the rollout can never complete
kubectl top pods — the cause is usually high CPU
explain: A stuck rollout almost always means the new ReplicaSet's pods never became ready — describe the ReplicaSet or check events to see ImagePullBackOff/CrashLoopBackOff. top shows usage not rollout state, logs on a deployment name needs a pod target, and node describe is for node-level issues rather than the typical bad-image rollout.

q: An application reads 12 settings from environment variables. You want them in a ConfigMap created imperatively and injected in bulk. Which commands do this?
options: kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=KEY1=v1 --from-literal=KEY2=v2 ... then envFrom: configMapRef in the pod spec
kubectl create secret app-config --from-env-file=settings.env
kubectl apply -f settings.env — Kubernetes parses env files directly
Environment variables cannot come from ConfigMaps, only from Secrets
explain: create configmap --from-literal (or --from-env-file for bulk) builds the ConfigMap imperatively, and envFrom with configMapRef injects every key as an env var. Secrets are for sensitive data, kubectl cannot apply a raw env file as a resource, and ConfigMaps absolutely support env injection.

q: You edit a ConfigMap that a running Deployment consumes via env vars. The pods keep the old values. Why, and what is the standard fix?
options: Edits to ConfigMaps apply only to volumes, never to env vars, so the design is broken
ConfigMaps are immutable — you must delete and recreate it
Env-var injection happens only at pod creation; existing pods never see the update. Run kubectl rollout restart deployment/web to recreate pods with the new values
The kubelet caches ConfigMaps for 24 hours; wait it out
explain: Environment variables are resolved once when the container starts, so live pods never pick up ConfigMap edits. rollout restart triggers a rolling recreation that injects the new values. ConfigMaps are mutable by default (immutable is opt-in), there is no 24h cache for env injection, and the volume-vs-env distinction is about update propagation, not editability.

q: A pod needs a database password. The team debates Secret vs ConfigMap. Which statement is correct, and what is the minimal secure pattern?
options: Secrets are encrypted with AES-256 automatically in every cluster
No difference — use a ConfigMap, it is simpler
Passwords must be baked into the container image

Secrets are base64-encoded (not encrypted by default, but treated as sensitive: not shown in logs, can be encrypted at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration); create with kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=password=S3cret and reference it via env or volume
explain: Secrets are the correct primitive: base64-encoded, excluded from logs and describe output, and encryptable at rest via EncryptionConfiguration. They are NOT encrypted by default in stock etcd (a classic exam trap). Baking credentials into images is never acceptable.

q: Traffic to the web Deployment spikes daily at 9am. You want pods to scale 3-10 based on CPU. Which command sets this up, and what cluster component must exist for it to function?
options: HPAs only work on StatefulSets, so convert the Deployment first
kubectl create hpa web --min=3 --max=10 — needs Prometheus installed
kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=10 — needs the cluster-autoscaler
kubectl autoscale deployment/web --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70 — needs metrics-server providing CPU metrics to the metrics API
explain: kubectl autoscale creates the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, which reads CPU utilization from the metrics API — served by metrics-server. Without metrics-server the HPA cannot get metrics and will not scale. cluster-autoscaler scales nodes, not pods; Prometheus is optional for custom metrics; HPAs work fine on Deployments.

q: A log-collector agent must run on every node, including nodes added next month. Which workload type guarantees this, and what must its pods tolerate?
options: A Job with completions equal to the node count
A DaemonSet — it places one pod per node (including new ones); its pods typically need tolerations for the control-plane and other taints
A Deployment with 100 replicas — it covers future nodes automatically
A StatefulSet with podManagementPolicy Parallel
explain: DaemonSets exist for per-node agents: the controller adds a pod to every matching node, including future ones. Deployments do not track node count, StatefulSets give stable identity not per-node coverage, and Jobs run to completion rather than persisting. DaemonSet pods usually tolerate node taints (e.g. node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane) via default or explicit tolerations.

q: You taint a node: kubectl taint nodes gpu-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule. A pod without any toleration is already running on gpu-1. What happens to it, and what taint effect WOULD evict it?
options: It is evicted immediately — all taints evict
The pod is evicted but rescheduled onto gpu-1 in a loop
It keeps running forever and NoExecute would do the same — taints are advisory only
It keeps running — NoSchedule only blocks NEW scheduling. NoExecute would evict running pods lacking a matching toleration
explain: NoSchedule affects only future scheduling decisions; existing pods are untouched. NoExecute evicts running pods that do not tolerate the taint (optionally after tolerationSeconds). PreferNoSchedule is a soft preference. This distinction is one of the most-tested scheduling facts on the CKA.

q: Pods must run only on nodes with SSDs, labeled disktype=ssd. The requirement may later grow to complex rules (ssd OR nvme, but never on spot nodes). Which mechanism should you use today to stay future-proof?
options: Pod anti-affinity against non-SSD nodes
nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd} — it supports OR and NOT operators
nodeAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution — it supports matchExpressions (In, NotIn, Exists) for complex rules, unlike nodeSelector
A taint on all non-SSD nodes
explain: nodeAffinity's matchExpressions support In/NotIn/Exists/Gt/Lt, covering the future OR/NOT requirements; nodeSelector only does exact-match AND. Taints invert the model awkwardly, and anti-affinity is about pod colocation, not node attributes.

q: A cache Deployment with 3 replicas must spread across zones for fault tolerance: no two replicas in the same zone. Which scheduling feature expresses this?
options: podAntiAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution, labelSelector matching the cache app, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
nodeAffinity with topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
podAffinity with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
A PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable: 1
explain: Required pod anti-affinity on the zone topology key forces the scheduler to place each replica in a different zone. podAffinity would attract pods together (the opposite), nodeAffinity constrains nodes not pod spread, and a PDB limits voluntary disruptions but does not spread replicas.

q: A critical monitoring pod must preempt less important workloads when the cluster is full. Which objects make this happen, and where is the priority assigned?
options: A LimitRange with a high default
ResourceQuotas on the monitoring namespace
A PriorityClass with a high value, referenced by priorityClassName in the pod spec — the scheduler preempts lower-priority pods to make room
Taints on all nodes with matching tolerations only on the monitoring pod
explain: PriorityClasses assign integer priorities via the pod's priorityClassName field; the scheduler preempts lower-priority pods when a higher-priority pod cannot schedule. Quotas cap namespace usage, LimitRanges set defaults, and taints control placement rather than preemption order.

q: A pod spec sets requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi} and limits: {cpu: 2000m, memory: 1Gi}. Which statement about scheduling and runtime is true?
options: Requests are ignored; only limits matter for both scheduling and runtime
The scheduler places the pod using the requests (it needs a node with 500m CPU and 512Mi free); at runtime the pod may burst to the limits but is throttled/killed beyond them
The pod gets exactly 500m CPU and 512Mi RAM, never more
The scheduler places the pod using the limits; the pod is guaranteed 2000m CPU at all times
explain: Scheduling is bin-packing on requests; limits are runtime ceilings enforced by the kubelet (CPU throttling, memory OOM-kill past the limit). CPU is compressible (throttled), memory is not (killed). Guaranteed QoS only comes from requests == limits.

q: A pod must run a database migration script to completion BEFORE the application container starts. Which construct does this, and what happens if the script fails?
options: An initContainer — it runs to completion before app containers start; if it fails, the pod restarts it (per restartPolicy) and the app never starts
An HPA — it delays app start until metrics are available
A postStart lifecycle hook — it blocks container start until it succeeds
A sidecar container — the app starts anyway and retries the migration
explain: initContainers run sequentially to completion before any app container starts; a failed init container blocks app startup and is retried according to the pod's restartPolicy. Sidecars start alongside the app, postStart hooks run asynchronously after start, and HPAs are unrelated to startup ordering.

q: A web pod passes its liveness probe but a Service still sends it traffic while it is still warming up, causing 500s. Which probe is misconfigured, and what is the correct behavior?
options: The readiness probe — it is missing or misconfigured; readiness gates Service endpoints, so a proper readiness probe keeps the pod out of endpoints until it can serve
The startup probe — it should be removed
The liveness probe — it should delay traffic until warmup finishes
Probes cannot affect Service traffic; the Service is misconfigured
explain: Readiness probes control membership in Service endpoints: a failing readiness probe removes the pod from the endpoints so it gets no traffic while warming up. Liveness restarts containers (wrong tool here — it would just restartloop a slow starter), startup probes gate liveness during slow starts, and probes absolutely do affect endpoint membership.

q: You create a Service of type ClusterIP for a database that only in-cluster apps should reach. A teammate suggests NodePort so they can test from their laptop. Why is ClusterIP the right call here?
options: ClusterIP automatically encrypts traffic; NodePort does not
NodePort does not work for databases
ClusterIP is faster because it bypasses kube-proxy
ClusterIP exposes the service only on an internal virtual IP reachable within the cluster; NodePort would open a port on every node's public interface, widening exposure unnecessarily
explain: ClusterIP allocates a virtual IP routable only inside the cluster — the correct scope for an internal database. NodePort opens a high port on ALL nodes' interfaces, which is both a security widening and unnecessary for in-cluster consumers. Neither type encrypts traffic, and both work for any TCP/UDP workload.

q: A StatefulSet of 3 Cassandra pods needs each pod reachable by its stable DNS name (cass-0.db, cass-1.db...). Which Service configuration enables this?
options: A headless Service (clusterIP: None) with a selector matching the StatefulSet — it creates individual A records for each pod instead of one virtual IP
An ExternalName Service pointing at each pod
A normal ClusterIP Service — stable DNS per pod is automatic
A NodePort Service with sessionAffinity: ClientIP
explain: Headless services (clusterIP: None) skip the virtual IP and publish DNS A records for each backing pod, which is exactly how StatefulSet members get stable per-pod DNS. A regular ClusterIP gives one IP for the whole set, NodePort is about external access, and ExternalName aliases an external DNS name.

q: kubectl get endpoints web-svc shows no addresses, though the Deployment's pods are Running. curl to the ClusterIP times out. What is the most likely cause and the confirming command?
options: kube-proxy is down — check systemctl status kube-proxy on the node
The Service selector does not match the pods' labels — confirm with kubectl get pods --show-labels and compare to the Service's selector
The ClusterIP is exhausted — create a new Service
CoreDNS is down — check kubectl get pods -n kube-system
explain: Empty endpoints with healthy pods is the signature of a selector/label mismatch — the Service finds no pods to send traffic to, so the ClusterIP blackholes. Comparing pod labels against the Service selector confirms it in seconds. kube-proxy or CoreDNS failures produce different symptoms (no proxying at all, or DNS failures), and ClusterIPs do not get exhausted per-service.

q: A Service manifest sets port: 80 and targetPort: 8080. A pod in the Deployment listens on 8080. Which statement is correct?
options: The Service will listen on 8080 and forward to 80
targetPort refers to the node port opened by NodePort services
Clients connect to port 80 on the Service; kube-proxy forwards to port 8080 on the pods. Mismatching them is normal when the container listens on a non-standard port
port and targetPort must always be identical or traffic is dropped
explain: port is the Service's frontend port; targetPort is where the pod actually listens — they are independent by design, so an 80-to-8080 mapping is routine. NodePort adds a third field (nodePort). Reversing them would forward pod-8080-bound expectations to port 80 on the container, which nothing listens on.

q: You need shop.example.com to route /api to the api Service and everything else to the web Service, over HTTPS. Which Ingress structure does this, and what TLS prerequisite exists?
options: TLS is automatic; no Secret is needed
An Ingress with defaultBackend only — path routing is not supported
Two Ingress objects cannot share a host; use a LoadBalancer Service instead
One Ingress with host shop.example.com, two path rules (/api and /), plus a tls section referencing a kubernetes.io/tls Secret containing the certificate for that host
explain: A single Ingress rule supports multiple path entries under one host, and the tls list binds hosts to a kubernetes.io/tls Secret holding tls.crt/tls.key. Multiple Ingresses can share a host (controllers merge them), defaultBackend only catches unmatched traffic, and TLS always needs a certificate from somewhere.

q: Your Ingress serves HTTPS but browsers warn about an untrusted certificate. kubectl describe ingress shows the tls secret is referenced correctly. What is the most likely problem with the Secret itself?
options: The Secret is in the wrong namespace — Ingress requires tls Secrets cluster-wide
HTTPS on Ingress requires a Gateway API Gateway instead
The Secret is type Opaque instead of kubernetes.io/tls, or its tls.crt is self-signed/expired — the Ingress controller serves exactly what is in tls.crt/tls.key
Ingress TLS Secrets must be named tls-secret exactly
explain: The controller terminates TLS with the bytes in the Secret: a self-signed or expired cert, or an Opaque secret the controller ignores, produces exactly this browser warning. The Secret must live in the Ingress's namespace (not cluster-wide), any name works if referenced correctly, and Ingress TLS is fully supported without Gateway API.

q: Two teams share one ingress-nginx controller. Team A installs its own second ingress-nginx for canary testing. How do you prevent the two controllers from fighting over the same Ingress objects?
options: Put each controller in a different namespace — namespaces isolate Ingress processing automatically
Give each controller a distinct IngressClass and set ingressClassName on each Ingress so each controller only processes its own class
They cannot coexist — only one Ingress controller per cluster is allowed
Label the Ingress objects; controllers ignore labels
explain: IngressClass plus ingressClassName is the multiplexing mechanism: each controller watches only Ingresses naming its class. Multiple controllers coexist fine, namespaces do not isolate Ingress processing, and controllers do not filter by arbitrary labels.

q: Security requires that pods in the payments namespace accept traffic ONLY from pods in the frontend namespace, and initiate no outbound connections except DNS. Which NetworkPolicy design enforces this?
options: A policy with only an ingress rule — egress defaults to deny once any policy selects the pod

A policy selecting payments pods with policyTypes [Ingress, Egress], an ingress from rule with namespaceSelector matching frontend, and an egress rule allowing UDP port 53 to kube-system plus no other egress
NetworkPolicies cannot restrict egress; use a Service mesh instead
Two separate policies cannot select the same pods; use one policy with ingress only
explain: Selecting a pod with any NetworkPolicy makes it isolated for the listed policyTypes, so both Ingress and Egress must be specified with explicit allows: ingress from the frontend namespace, egress only DNS (UDP/TCP 53, typically to kube-system's DNS). An ingress-only policy would leave egress wide open, multiple policies CAN select the same pods (rules are additive), and egress restriction is core NetworkPolicy functionality.

q: You apply a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress] but no ingress rules, in namespace api. What is the effect on pods in api?
options: No effect — a policy with no rules is ignored
All pods in the namespace are now denied all ingress traffic (default deny), because an empty podSelector selects every pod and the empty rule list allows nothing
All ingress is allowed — empty rules mean allow-all
Only new pods are affected; existing pods keep their connections
explain: This is the canonical default-deny pattern: empty podSelector matches all pods in the namespace, and with Ingress in policyTypes but zero ingress rules, nothing is allowed in. It applies to all selected pods immediately. Allow-all requires an ingress rule with an empty from, which is a different (dangerous) construct.

q: After applying a default-deny Ingress policy in namespace db, the application's pods can no longer resolve Service names, though pod-to-pod IPs work. What egress allowance is missing?
options: TCP 443 to the API server
TCP 80 to the internet
No egress allowance can fix DNS; DNS bypasses NetworkPolicy
UDP (and TCP) port 53 to the DNS pods (usually in kube-system) — DNS was cut off by the deny policy
explain: DNS is just UDP/TCP traffic to port 53 (CoreDNS in kube-system); a default-deny egress policy blocks it like anything else, so name resolution dies while raw IPs still work — the classic symptom. The fix is an egress rule to port 53 on the kube-dns Service/pods. API server and internet access are separate concerns.

q: A pod must reach the payments API at payments.prod.svc.cluster.local. Which correctly expands this name, and what does each segment mean?
options: The segments are namespace.service.svc.cluster.local — namespace comes first
Pod payments in namespace prod — pods cannot be addressed by DNS
It is an external name that requires an ExternalName service
Service payments, namespace prod, svc cluster suffix — the full in-cluster FQDN is payments.prod.svc.cluster.local
explain: The canonical form is service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Short names (payments, or payments.prod) also resolve thanks to the pod's resolv.conf search domains, but the FQDN is unambiguous. Pods do get DNS names too (pod-ip.namespace.pod.cluster.local), ExternalName is for aliasing external domains, and namespace comes second, not first.

q: CoreDNS pods are CrashLoopBackOff after you edited its ConfigMap. Cluster DNS is down. What is the fastest recovery, and what guardrail should you have used?
options: Delete the CoreDNS Deployment — it recreates with defaults
Restart kubelet on every node
DNS recovers automatically in 10 minutes; wait

Restore the previous ConfigMap (kubectl rollout is unavailable for it; re-apply the known-good ConfigMap from backup or version control) and the CoreDNS pods will reload; the guardrail is backing up or versioning the ConfigMap before editing
explain: CoreDNS reads its Corefile from a ConfigMap; restoring the good ConfigMap lets the pods start and reload. Deleting the Deployment does not restore the ConfigMap, kubelet restarts are irrelevant to CoreDNS config, and nothing self-heals a bad Corefile. The exam lesson: never hand-edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap without a backup.

q: The team is migrating from Ingress to Gateway API. Which object replaces the Ingress resource's routing rules, and what must exist first?
options: Gateway API uses the same Ingress objects with a new annotation
An HTTPRoute holds the routing rules; it attaches to a Gateway, which itself references a GatewayClass managed by the Gateway controller — GatewayClass comes first
A Gateway holds the rules directly; no other objects are needed
The IngressClass becomes the GatewayClass automatically on upgrade
explain: Gateway API splits concerns: GatewayClass (installed by the controller/provider) → Gateway (listener config) → HTTPRoute (host/path routing attached to the Gateway). HTTPRoute cannot function without a Gateway to attach to, Ingress objects are not auto-converted, and annotations are not the migration path.

q: You need to reach a database pod's port 5432 from your laptop for five minutes of debugging, without exposing anything. Which command does this with the least blast radius?
options: kubectl port-forward pod/db-0 5432:5432 — it tunnels one pod's port to localhost with no cluster changes
Change the Service to type LoadBalancer temporarily
kubectl expose pod db-0 --type=NodePort
Edit the NetworkPolicy to allow your laptop's IP
explain: port-forward creates a temporary localhost tunnel to a single pod — zero cluster mutation, zero exposure. Changing Service types or exposing NodePorts alters cluster state and widens access, and NetworkPolicy edits for a laptop IP are clumsy and persistent.

q: An ExternalName Service named legacy-db points to db.internal.example.com. A pod queries legacy-db and gets the external IP. What did the Service actually do?
options: It created Endpoints pointing at the external IP
It created a DNS CNAME record: legacy-db resolves to db.internal.example.com via CoreDNS; no proxying or endpoints are involved
It proxied the connection through kube-proxy to the external address
ExternalName only works for IPs, not DNS names
explain: ExternalName is pure DNS: CoreDNS returns a CNAME to the configured external name, and the pod connects directly. There is no kube-proxy involvement and no Endpoints object. It accepts DNS names (that is its purpose); for raw external IPs you would use a headless Service with manual Endpoints.

q: Ingress path /app must strip the /app prefix before reaching the backend (the app serves at /). With ingress-nginx, how is this done?
options: Create a second Ingress for the stripped path
Change the Service's targetPort to /
Set pathType: Prefix — prefix stripping is automatic
Add the annotation nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: / — the controller rewrites the URI before proxying
explain: The rewrite-target annotation tells ingress-nginx to rewrite the request URI (here to /) before forwarding. pathType: Prefix only controls matching, not rewriting. Services route by port, not URI, and a second Ingress would not strip anything either.

q: kubectl get svc shows the api Service with CLUSTER-IP 10.96.5.20 but a pod curling that IP hangs. Endpoints exist. What component should you suspect, and what does it do?
options: The CNI plugin — it assigns ClusterIPs
etcd — it stores the ClusterIP allocation
kube-proxy — it programs iptables/IPVS rules on each node that implement the ClusterIP virtual IP; if it is down or misconfigured, the VIP is unroutable
CoreDNS — it resolves the ClusterIP to pod IPs
explain: ClusterIP is a virtual IP with no network interface — kube-proxy's iptables/IPVS rules on every node are what actually route it to endpoints. If kube-proxy is down, the IP exists in the API but no node knows how to forward it. CoreDNS only resolves names, the CNI handles pod networking not Services, and etcd just stores the allocation.

q: A NetworkPolicy in namespace web has an ingress rule with from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}}] but no namespaceSelector. Which pods can reach the selected pods?
options: Only pods labeled app=api in the SAME namespace (web) — a lone podSelector is namespace-scoped
Pods labeled app=api in ANY namespace
All pods in the web namespace
No pods — the rule is invalid without namespaceSelector
explain: In a NetworkPolicy peer, podSelector alone matches pods in the policy's own namespace; adding namespaceSelector (optionally combined with podSelector) widens it cross-namespace. The rule is perfectly valid as written — it is simply namespace-scoped, a frequent source of cross-namespace connectivity surprises.

q: You must expose an app to the internet on bare metal with no cloud load balancer. Which Service type gives you a stable external IP:port per Service, and what opens on every node?
options: NodePort — a static port (30000-32767 by default) opens on every node's IP; clients reach NODE-IP:NODE-PORT
LoadBalancer — works without any cloud provider
ClusterIP — nothing opens on nodes
Headless — each pod gets a public IP
explain: NodePort allocates a cluster-wide static port on every node, so any node's IP plus that port reaches the Service — the standard bare-metal exposure path (often fronted by an external LB or MetalLB later). LoadBalancer needs a cloud controller (or MetalLB) to provision anything, ClusterIP is internal-only, and headless affects DNS, not external reachability.

q: A Gateway API HTTPRoute must send /v2 traffic to the v2 Service and all other traffic to v1. Which rule structure does this, and how are conflicts ordered?
options: Path matching is not supported; use header matches only
Two Gateways, one per version — routes cannot share a Gateway
One rule with two backendRefs — traffic splits 50/50 automatically
Two rules with path matches (/v2 with PathPrefix, / with PathPrefix); the more specific /v2 match wins for its paths, with rules evaluated in order
explain: HTTPRoute rules support multiple path matches; the longest/most-specific match takes precedence, so /v2 routes to v2 while / catches the rest. Multiple routes can attach to one Gateway, multiple backendRefs in one rule split (with optional weights, not automatic 50/50), and path matching is core functionality.

q: A Deployment with 3 replicas mounts a PVC with accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]. Two pods schedule to node-a and one to node-b. The node-b pod stays in ContainerCreating with a failed mount event. What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?
options: ReadWriteOnce allows only ONE node to mount the volume read-write at a time; the node-b pod can never attach it. Fix: use ReadWriteMany (with a supporting provisioner) or run the workload as a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates giving each pod its own volume
The PVC is too small — increase the storage request
The StorageClass provisioner is down — restart the external-provisioner pod
The kubelet on node-b needs a restart to discover the volume
explain: EXAM TRAP: access modes are about which nodes can attach the volume, not how many pods. ReadWriteOnce means a single node may mount it read-write — the second node's attach will fail forever, which is exactly the stuck ContainerCreating you see. The fix depends on intent: shared storage across nodes needs ReadWriteMany (and a provisioner that supports it, like NFS or EFS), while per-pod storage for replicated workloads is the StatefulSet plus volumeClaimTemplates pattern. Bumping PVC size or restarting kubelets cannot change attach semantics.

q: You create a PVC with storageClassName: fast-ssd. kubectl get pvc shows it Pending for 20 minutes. kubectl get storageclass shows only standard. Describe the PVC shows no events from a provisioner. What happened, and how do you confirm the next step?
options: The cluster is out of disk — add nodes
PVCs take 30 minutes to bind on first creation; wait longer

The PVC references a StorageClass that does not exist, so no provisioner ever sees the claim. Confirm with kubectl get storageclass and either create the fast-ssd StorageClass or change the PVC to an existing class
The access mode is wrong — change it to ReadOnlyMany
explain: A PVC naming a nonexistent StorageClass sits Pending forever with no provisioner events — the API accepts the object but nothing acts on it. This is a silent failure: no error, just Pending. Confirm with kubectl get storageclass, then fix the name or create the class. Disk pressure and access modes produce different symptoms (or would still attempt provisioning), and there is no 30-minute bind delay in Kubernetes.

q: A PVC with reclaimPolicy: Retain (via its StorageClass) is deleted after a migration. The underlying cloud disk still exists and still holds data. A teammate says the data is gone. Who is right, and what must you do to reuse or release the disk?
options: The data is kept but the PV rebinds automatically to the next matching PVC

You are right: Retain keeps the provisioned volume after PVC deletion, but the PV goes to Released and cannot auto-rebind. To reuse it you must manually clear pv.spec.claimRef and recreate a PV/PVC pair (or delete the PV to let the cloud disk be cleaned up)
The teammate is right — deleting the PVC deletes the data regardless of reclaim policy
Retain only applies to hostPath volumes
explain: EXAM TRAP: Retain vs Delete is one of the most-tested storage facts. Retain preserves the volume and its data, but the PV transitions to Released — and a Released PV never rebinds automatically (a safety feature so a new claim cannot accidentally adopt someone else's data). Reuse requires manually editing the PV to remove spec.claimRef. Delete (the default on most dynamic provisioners) would have destroyed the cloud disk with the PVC. Retain applies to any PV type, not just hostPath.

q: A StorageClass sets volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer. A PVC using it stays Pending even though the provisioner is healthy. The moment a pod using the PVC is created, binding proceeds. Explain why, and name the problem this mode solves.
options: The provisioner was stuck and the pod creation restarted it

WaitForFirstConsumer deliberately delays binding AND provisioning until a pod is scheduled, so the volume is provisioned in the pod's zone/topology. It solves the classic failure where Immediate binding provisions a volume in zone-a while the pod schedules to zone-b and can never attach it
The PVC was waiting for a manual pv create
Pending is a bug in WaitForFirstConsumer; use Immediate instead
explain: With Immediate binding, the provisioner picks a zone at claim time — if the pod later schedules elsewhere, the volume is unreachable and the pod hangs in ContainerCreating. WaitForFirstConsumer flips the order: schedule first, then provision in the pod's topology. The Pending state before any pod exists is correct behavior, not a bug. On the exam, any scenario mentioning zones/regions plus stuck volume mounts is pointing at this setting.

q: A database PVC is at 90% capacity. The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true. Which sequence grows the PVC from 20Gi to 40Gi, and what is the common gotcha?
options: Delete and recreate the PVC with 40Gi — data is preserved automatically

kubectl edit pvc db-data (or patch) changing spec.resources.requests.storage to 40Gi — the controller expands the volume; the gotcha is that shrinking is never allowed and some drivers need a pod restart or support only online expansion of mounted volumes
Edit the PV's capacity directly — PVCs follow automatically
Expansion requires recreating the StorageClass with a larger default size
explain: Volume expansion is a PVC edit: raise spec.resources.requests.storage and the external-resizer/controller grows the volume (filesystem resize follows, online or at next mount depending on driver). EXAM TRAPS: you can only ever grow, never shrink; and allowVolumeExpansion must be true on the StorageClass or the edit is rejected. Deleting the PVC risks the reclaim policy destroying the volume, and editing the PV directly does nothing.

q: A PV of type local declares nodeAffinity requiring node-ssd-1. A pod with a PVC bound to this PV is scheduled by chance to node-ssd-2 and fails to start. What is the structural lesson about local volumes?
options: The PV should have used hostPath instead
Local volumes are broken and should never be used

Local volumes are tied to a specific node via nodeAffinity; the scheduler does not know this unless the pod also constrains itself to that node. The fix is to give the pod a matching nodeSelector/nodeAffinity (or let WaitForFirstConsumer-style delayed binding handle topology) so pod and volume land together
Delete the nodeAffinity from the PV — it is optional metadata
explain: A local PV's nodeAffinity is a hard constraint on where the data lives, but nothing forces the pod to that node — scheduling and volume topology are separate decisions. The pod must carry its own node constraint (or the StorageClass must use WaitForFirstConsumer so provisioning follows the pod). hostPath has the same node-coupling with even fewer guarantees, and removing the affinity would let the scheduler assume the volume is reachable anywhere, making things worse.

q: Two sidecar patterns are proposed: (a) share a scratch directory between two containers in one pod via emptyDir, (b) persist a cache across pod restarts on the same node via hostPath. Which statement about their lifetimes is correct?
options: emptyDir lives and dies with the POD (deleted on pod removal, survives container restarts); hostPath survives the pod and ties data to a specific node's filesystem — which is why hostPath is a security and portability risk and rarely the right answer on the exam
Both survive pod deletion as long as the node stays up
emptyDir is backed by network storage; hostPath is memory-only
Neither survives a container restart
explain: EXAM TRAP: the lifetimes are the whole point. emptyDir is pod-scoped scratch — perfect for sidecar communication, gone when the pod is gone. hostPath exposes the node's filesystem into the pod: data persists, but the pod is now pinned to that node and a compromised path can expose the host — the exam treats hostPath as a red flag unless the scenario explicitly demands node-local files (like reading node logs). Container restarts do not wipe either; pod deletion wipes emptyDir only.

q: A pod must mount a single file, app.conf, from a ConfigMap — not the whole ConfigMap directory, because the app's config dir contains other files the mount would hide. Which volume syntax achieves this, and what breaks if you forget the second field?
options: configMap with items: [{key: app.conf, path: app.conf}] plus subPath: app.conf on the volumeMount — without subPath the entire ConfigMap directory mounts over the target dir and hides its existing files
volumes from the ConfigMap directly — single-file mounts are automatic
Mount the ConfigMap as env vars — files cannot be selective
Use a Secret instead — Secrets support single-file mounts, ConfigMaps do not
explain: subPath mounts one file (or subdir) from the volume at the mount point instead of overlaying the whole volume contents. The classic failure: mounting a ConfigMap volume at /etc/app hides every existing file in /etc/app except the ConfigMap keys — subPath: app.conf avoids that. items selects which keys materialize, but only subPath controls the mount granularity. Secrets behave identically here.

q: A PVC manifest omits storageClassName entirely. The cluster has a default StorageClass (standard) and a second class (fast). What happens at bind time?
options: The cluster's default StorageClass (standard) is applied automatically — omitting the field is not the same as setting it to empty string, which would request statically-provisioned storage with no class
It binds to the fast class because it sorts first alphabetically
The PVC stays Pending until you specify a class
The PVC binds to any available PV regardless of class
explain: EXAM TRAP with two layers. Omitted storageClassName means 'use the default StorageClass' — dynamic provisioning proceeds on standard. But storageClassName: '' (explicit empty string) means 'no class: bind only to a pre-created static PV with no class'. Mixing these up is a favorite exam distractor. Binding still requires access-mode and capacity compatibility — class matching is necessary, not sufficient.

q: A Deployment's pods each need RWO storage, and the team proposes one shared PVC mounted by all 5 replicas. The storage backend only supports ReadWriteOnce. What breaks, and what is the idiomatic workload for per-pod volumes?
options: Nothing breaks — RWO allows unlimited pods on different nodes
Deployments cannot use PVCs at all — only StatefulSets can
The fix is to set accessModes to ReadWriteMany on the same backend

Only one node can attach the RWO volume, so replicas on other nodes fail to start. The idiomatic fix is a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates, which provisions one dedicated PVC per pod automatically
explain: This is the RWO multi-attach trap in workload form: one volume, one node, so spreading replicas across nodes guarantees mount failures. volumeClaimTemplates is the purpose-built answer — the StatefulSet controller creates pvc-name-0, pvc-name-1, etc., each bound to its pod for life (and they survive pod rescheduling). You cannot wish ReadWriteMany onto a backend that does not support it, and Deployments use PVCs fine — they just share one.

q: A pod has restarted 47 times and sits in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs web-0 shows nothing useful because the container just died again. Which command sequence actually reveals the crash reason?
options: kubectl logs web-0 --previous — shows the last terminated container's logs; then kubectl describe pod web-0 for the exit code and last state
Delete the pod and watch the new one — the history is unrecoverable
kubectl logs web-0 -f — follow the live logs until it crashes again
kubectl top pod web-0 — check whether it is CPU-starved
explain: EXAM TRAP: plain kubectl logs reads the CURRENT container, which in CrashLoopBackOff may have just started and printed nothing. --previous reads the last dead container — where the actual error lives. Pair it with describe to get the exit code (137 means OOMKilled, 1/2 often config errors) and the Last State block. Following live logs wastes exam minutes watching backoff delays, and history is absolutely recoverable via --previous.

q: A pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. kubectl describe pod shows Failed to pull image registry.internal:5000/api:v9: unauthorized. The registry needs authentication. What is the complete fix?
options: Restart containerd on the node
Add the credentials to the container's environment variables
Create a docker-registry Secret (kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...) and reference it via imagePullSecrets in the pod spec
Switch the image to :latest — latest is always public
explain: Private registries need an imagePullSecret: a docker-registry-type Secret holding the registry credentials, referenced in the pod spec's imagePullSecrets list. Env vars never authenticate pulls, :latest is just a tag with no bearing on auth, and the node runtime is fine — the API server simply never presented credentials. On the exam, build this imperatively: kubectl create secret docker-registry ... --dry-run=client -o yaml, then patch it into the pod spec.

q: Two pods show different statuses: pod-a is ErrImagePull, pod-b is ImagePullBackOff. A teammate treats them as the same problem. What is the real distinction, and why does it matter?
options: There is no distinction — both mean the image does not exist
ErrImagePull is for public registries, ImagePullBackOff for private ones
ErrImagePull resolves itself; ImagePullBackOff never does

ErrImagePull is the FIRST failed pull attempt; ImagePullBackOff means kubelet has retried and is now in exponential backoff between attempts. It matters because BackOff tells you the failure is persistent (bad name, bad tag, auth), not transient — stop waiting and investigate
explain: The statuses are a timeline, not two diseases: every pull failure starts as ErrImagePull and escalates to ImagePullBackOff as the kubelet backs off. Seeing BackOff means retries have already failed repeatedly — waiting longer will not help. Diagnose immediately with describe (the exact pull error is in the events). Neither is registry-type-specific, and neither self-heals.

q: A pod has been Pending for 10 minutes. kubectl describe pod shows 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu. The Deployment requests 2 CPUs per pod and the nodes have 4 CPUs with system pods running. What are your two realistic options?
options: Increase the CPU limit — limits control scheduling
Delete the system pods to free CPU
Wait — the scheduler retries every 10 minutes and will eventually fit it

Lower the CPU request to match reality, or add node capacity (cluster-autoscaler or a new node). The scheduler cannot oversubscribe requests — Pending with Insufficient cpu is a capacity fact, not a glitch
explain: Insufficient cpu in the events is the scheduler telling you the truth: requests are reservations, and no node has 2 free CPUs after system reservations. Your levers are smaller requests (if the app truly needs less) or more capacity. The scheduler will retry forever and never succeed — waiting is not a strategy. Deleting system pods destabilizes the node, and limits do not affect scheduling at all (another exam trap: scheduling uses requests, always).

q: A new pod stays Pending with 0/5 nodes available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu}. No GPU workload is involved. What is the fastest fix, and what should you check before applying it?
options: Add a matching toleration to the pod — but first check WHY the taint exists (kubectl describe node): if the node is genuinely reserved (GPU drivers, spot isolation), the right fix may be scheduling elsewhere, not tolerating your way onto special hardware
Cordon the node so the scheduler stops considering it
Taints cannot be tolerated by pods — recreate the cluster
Remove the taint from the node immediately — taints are never legitimate
explain: The mechanics are simple: pod tolerates the taint or it never schedules there. The judgment call is the exam point — taints encode intent (this node is special). Blindly tolerating onto a GPU node wastes expensive hardware and can break the pod (no GPU drivers for its needs). Read the node's taints and labels first, then decide: tolerate deliberately, or constrain the pod to general nodes with nodeAffinity. Cordoning makes it worse, and pods tolerate taints routinely.

q: A pod using a PVC is Pending with no CPU/memory complaints in the events. kubectl get pvc shows the claim Pending too. Which investigation order is correct?
options: Follow the dependency chain: describe the PVC (is the StorageClass right? does a matching PV exist? is the provisioner healthy?) — a pod cannot schedule until its volumes bind, and PVC Pending is upstream of pod Pending
Check the Deployment's image tag first — Pending is usually an image problem
Restart the kube-scheduler — it is stuck
Delete the PVC so the pod can start without storage
explain: Troubleshoot dependency chains upstream-first: the pod is Pending BECAUSE the PVC is Pending, so the PVC is the actual patient. Describe it and check class existence, provisioner health, access-mode/capacity matching. Images cause ImagePullBackOff, not Pending; the scheduler is correctly refusing to place a pod whose volumes cannot bind; and deleting the PVC orphans the pod's storage requirement rather than fixing it.

q: kubectl get nodes shows worker-2 NotReady for 15 minutes. Pods on it are being evicted. Which commands diagnose the root cause, in order?
options: kubectl describe node worker-2 (conditions and events), then SSH to the node and check systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet — NotReady almost always means the kubelet stopped reporting (crashed, bad config, disk pressure, expired certs)
kubectl delete node worker-2 — a fresh node object fixes reporting
kubectl drain worker-2 — draining restores readiness
Restart the API server — it is not receiving heartbeats
explain: NotReady means kubelet heartbeats stopped arriving. Diagnose outside-in: describe the node (conditions like DiskPressure/MemoryPressure show in the status), then go to the node itself — systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet reveal crashes, config errors, or certificate expiry. Deleting the Node object hides the symptom, draining a NotReady node changes nothing about the kubelet, and the API server is fine (other nodes report normally).

q: A node reports DiskPressure and the kubelet starts evicting pods. df on the node shows /var/lib/docker at 96%. What is the proper remediation sequence?
options: Delete random pods to free space
Increase the pods' memory limits
Cordon the node — cordoning clears DiskPressure

Free disk: prune unused images (crictl rmi / docker system prune), clear dead container logs, expand the disk; then address the cause (log rotation, image GC thresholds in kubelet config). Eviction is the kubelet protecting the node — fighting it without freeing disk just repeats the cycle
explain: DiskPressure is a node condition with a physical cause: the kubelet evicts to protect the node, and it will keep evicting until space is actually freed. Prune images, rotate/truncate runaway logs, and fix the root cause (kubelet image-gc and log rotation settings). Cordoning only stops new scheduling — pressure remains. Memory limits are irrelevant to disk pressure, and deleting random pods is not a remediation plan.

q: A Java pod is OOMKilled repeatedly (describe shows Exit Code 137, Reason: OOMKilled). The pod has NO memory limit set. How can it be OOMKilled with no limit, and what are the two fixes?
options: Impossible — without a limit the pod cannot be OOMKilled; the exit code is a coincidence
Set the memory request higher — requests prevent OOM kills

The NODE ran out of memory, so the kernel OOM-killer (or kubelet eviction) killed the biggest consumer. Fixes: set a proper memory limit AND request so the pod is accounted for and gets predictable QoS, and/or add node memory. Exit 137 is the signature to memorize
Increase the CPU limit — CPU starvation manifests as OOMKilled
explain: EXAM TRAP: OOMKilled without a limit confuses everyone. Container-level OOM comes from exceeding a limit; node-level OOM comes from the host running dry, and the kernel kills the fattest process — your JVM. Memorize 137 = SIGKILL = OOM. The fix is sizing honesty: real requests/limits (limits trigger orderly container OOM instead of node chaos) plus enough node capacity. CPU settings never cause OOM, and requests alone do not cap usage.

q: A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating for 20 minutes. describe shows FailedMount: unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[data], timed out waiting for the condition. The PVC is Bound. What do you check next?
options: Delete the pod — ContainerCreating always clears on recreation

The volume's attachability: is it an RWO volume already attached to another node? Check where the PV is attached and whether any pod on another node holds it (the multi-attach trap), plus StorageClass/node topology mismatches
The pod's CPU request — increase it
The image — ContainerCreating is always an image pull problem
explain: Bound PVC plus FailedMount means the claim is fine but the attach/mount is not — the signature of the RWO multi-attach trap (another node's pod holds the volume) or a topology mismatch (volume in zone-a, pod in zone-b). Describe the PV for its attachments, check which node holds it. Images produce ImagePullBackOff, not FailedMount; recreating the pod re-triggers the same failed attach; CPU is unrelated to mounts.

q: A pod with an initContainer has been in Init:0/1 for an hour. The app container never starts. kubectl logs myapp -c init-db returns a connection refused error. What is the diagnosis and the correct mental model?
options: The init container itself is failing (it cannot reach the database), so the pod is correctly blocked: initContainers must ALL complete before app containers start. Fix the init container's target (wrong DB host/port, DB not ready, missing Secret) — the app is innocent
Delete the initContainer from the spec — they are optional decorations
Init containers run in parallel with app containers; the app will start once the backoff ends
The app container is crashing and taking the init container down with it
explain: Init:0/1 means zero of one init containers have completed — and app containers NEVER start until all init containers succeed. The logs already told you the story: connection refused from init-db. The exam trap is blaming the app container, which has not even started yet. Debug init containers with -c init-db logs; fix the dependency (DB address, credentials, startup ordering), not the app.

q: curl from a debug pod to http://orders:80 times out. kubectl get endpoints orders returns NO endpoints, but the orders Deployment shows 3/3 pods Running. What is broken and what is the one-line verification?
options: CoreDNS is down — verify with nslookup orders
Port 80 is blocked by the cloud firewall — open it
The pods are Running but their containers are crashed — verify with kubectl logs
The Service selector does not match the pods' labels — verify with kubectl get pods --show-labels and compare labels against the Service's selector; fix the selector or the pod labels
explain: Running pods plus empty endpoints is the selector/label mismatch signature — the Service is looking for pods that do not exist. The verification is mechanical: print the Service's selector, list pods with those labels, observe zero matches. DNS would fail name resolution (not time out on a direct ClusterIP), crashed containers would show in pod status, and cloud firewalls do not affect in-cluster ClusterIP traffic.

q: Every pod in the cluster suddenly fails DNS lookups (nslookup kubernetes.default returns SERVFAIL), but pod-to-pod IP traffic works. kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows both CoreDNS pods in CrashLoopBackOff. What is the recovery priority, and what caused the blast radius?
options: Restart each application's pods — they cache DNS negatively
The applications must be reconfigured to use IPs instead of names

Fix CoreDNS FIRST (check its logs and ConfigMap — a bad Corefile edit is the usual cause), because cluster DNS is a single shared dependency: one broken CoreDNS breaks name resolution for every pod simultaneously. Restore the known-good ConfigMap and the pods will reload
DNS is per-node; reboot all nodes
explain: The symptom pattern is the giveaway: IPs work, names fail, EVERYWHERE — that is a shared-dependency outage, and CoreDNS is the shared dependency. CrashLoopBackOff on both CoreDNS pods plus a recent ConfigMap edit points at a bad Corefile. Recovery is restoring the ConfigMap, not touching workloads. Negative DNS caching is a minor concern compared to the outage, reboots do not fix config, and hardcoding IPs is never the answer.

q: A deploy pipeline's ServiceAccount gets Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden: User system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer cannot create resource deployments in API group apps in the namespace prod. The Role in prod already allows create on deployments. What is wrong, and what is the precise fix?
options: The ServiceAccount needs cluster-admin — bind it to cluster-admin

The Role exists but nothing binds it to system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer — create a RoleBinding in namespace prod with subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: deployer, namespace: ci}] and roleRef to the Role. A Role without a binding grants zero permissions
The API server is misconfigured — restart it
The namespace prod does not exist
explain: Forbidden naming the exact user, verb, resource, and namespace is RBAC doing its job: the Role is unbound. The fix is the RoleBinding, and the exam-critical detail is the subject's NAMESPACE: the ServiceAccount lives in ci while the binding lives in prod — cross-namespace subjects are normal but the namespace field must be right or the binding silently matches nobody. Granting cluster-admin for a deploy pipeline violates least privilege and would fail any sane review.

q: Monday morning, kubectl fails on all control-plane operations with Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid. Workloads keep running. Which commands confirm and fix this?
options: Wait 24 hours — certificates self-renew on Sundays
The cluster is unrecoverable — rebuild with kubeadm init

kubeadm certs check-expiration (confirms which PKI certs lapsed), then kubeadm certs renew all (or apiserver) and restart the affected static pods — workloads survive because the data plane does not need the API certs to keep running
kubectl get certificates — then renew them with kubectl certificate renew
explain: The x509 expired error against the API server is the control-plane PKI lapsing (default 1-year validity — a classic 'worked for a year then died Monday' story). kubeadm certs check-expiration lists every cert's expiry; renew rotates them. Static pods pick up renewed certs on restart. Workloads keep running because kubelet-to-pod traffic never touches these certs. There is no kubectl certificate renew for the PKI, rebuilds are for quitters, and nothing self-renews.

q: A 3-node stacked-etcd cluster loses control-plane node cp-2 permanently (hardware dead). What is the cluster's state, and what MUST you do before the next failure?
options: The cluster survives: 2 of 3 etcd members maintain quorum, and the API servers on cp-1/cp-3 keep serving. But you MUST remove the dead member (etcdctl member remove) and add a replacement, because with only 2 members the loss of ONE more kills quorum and the cluster
Restore etcd from snapshot on the remaining nodes
Quorum is 2 of 3, so nothing needs doing — 2 members are fine permanently
The cluster is down — etcd needs all members
explain: EXAM TRAP: surviving is not the same as healthy. Quorum math (floor(n/2)+1) means 3 members tolerate 1 failure — you just spent your one failure. Running on 2 members is a ticking clock: the next failure takes the cluster down. The dead member must be removed from the member list (a ghost member can block quorum decisions) and replaced. No restore is needed — the surviving members hold the full dataset.

q: Pods can reach each other by IP, but every ClusterIP Service times out from every node. kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows kube-proxy DaemonSet pods CrashLoopBackOff on all nodes. What is the relationship, and what do you check?
options: CoreDNS is down — Services need DNS to route
Unrelated — Services do not need kube-proxy when pods can talk directly

kube-proxy programs the iptables/IPVS rules that IMPLEMENT ClusterIPs on each node; with it dead everywhere, the virtual IPs are unroutable even though pod networking (CNI) is fine. Check the kube-proxy logs and its ConfigMap (a bad config push is the usual cause)
The CNI is broken — reinstall it
explain: This is the cleanest isolation test in Kubernetes networking: pod IPs work (CNI healthy), ClusterIPs do not (kube-proxy dead). ClusterIP is not a real interface — it exists only as packet-filter rules kube-proxy writes. All nodes' kube-proxy failing together screams bad shared config (the kube-proxy ConfigMap) or a bad DaemonSet image rollout. DNS affects names, not VIP routing, and the CNI is demonstrably fine.

q: After applying a new NetworkPolicy, the frontend pods cannot reach the API pods (connection timed out), though both are Running. What is the fastest way to confirm the policy is the culprit, and what is the permanent fix pattern?
