options: Temporarily delete (or scale down) the suspect policy and retest: if traffic flows, the policy's selectors or ports are wrong. The permanent fix is correcting the ingress from rules (right podSelector/namespaceSelector, right ports) — never 'fix' it by deleting policy enforcement
Restart the API pods — they need to re-register with the policy
The timeout proves it is a DNS issue, not a policy issue
Delete all NetworkPolicies in the cluster — policies are too dangerous to use
explain: Isolate by removal: policies are declarative, so deleting the suspect and retesting is a 30-second experiment with zero side effects (you re-apply the corrected version after). Timeouts (not refused) are the NetworkPolicy signature — packets dropped silently. The fix is surgical: correct the from selectors and ports. Deleting all policies 'fixes' connectivity by abandoning security, restarts do not re-evaluate policy, and DNS failures look different (name resolution errors, not timeouts).

q: An Ingress returns 503 Service Temporarily Unavailable for host shop.example.com. The backend pods are Running and the Service has endpoints. kubectl describe ingress shows the rule and backend correctly. What are the two most likely causes, in order?
options: The DNS record is wrong — fix the A record

The Ingress controller is down, or the backend Service's targetPort does not match the container's listening port — 503 from the controller means it accepted the request but could not get a healthy response from any backend
The TLS secret is missing — that always produces 503
503 means the cluster is out of memory — add nodes
explain: Read the status code's story: the controller IS running (it answered 503 itself) but has no working backend. Causes in order: the controller's own pods failing (then nothing would answer at all — so check controller health first), or the classic targetPort mismatch where the Service forwards to a port nothing listens on (endpoints exist because pods are Running, but the app is not on that port). Missing TLS gives handshake errors, DNS failures never reach the controller, and 503 is not a capacity signal.

q: After maintenance, new pods never schedule to node db-1 though it is Ready and has free resources. kubectl describe node db-1 shows Unschedulable: true. What happened and what is the one-command fix?
options: The node is tainted — remove all taints
The scheduler is broken — restart kube-scheduler
Ready with Unschedulable means the kubelet is lying — reboot the node
Someone left the node cordoned (kubectl cordon) during maintenance and never uncordoned it. Fix: kubectl uncordon db-1
explain: EXAM TRAP: Ready and Unschedulable are independent flags. Ready = kubelet healthy; Unschedulable = cordoned (usually left over from a drain during maintenance). The scheduler skips cordoned nodes entirely — no events, no errors, just silence, which is why it is missed. One command reverses it: uncordon. Taints show separately in describe output, and the scheduler is fine.

q: An exam task says: in cluster-prod, delete the broken Deployment. You run the delete, it succeeds, but the grader marks it wrong. kubectl config get-contexts shows your current context is cluster-staging. What is the lesson, and is there any recovery?
options: Delete your kubeconfig and let the exam rebuild it
Contexts are advisory; kubectl figures out the right cluster from the task

You operated in the wrong cluster: always run kubectl config use-context cluster-prod FIRST in every task. Recovery: switch to cluster-prod and redo the task — but the wrongly-deleted staging Deployment may need restoring, which is why the habit matters
The grader is wrong — a delete is a delete
explain: The single most expensive unforced error on the CKA: doing perfect work in the wrong context scores zero AND can destroy the wrong cluster's resources. The discipline is mechanical — read task, use-context, then act — because under time pressure your hands will run commands before your brain checks the prompt. Recovery is redoing the work in the right context; the staging damage is a painful reminder, not a grading technicality.

q: Creating a pod fails with: exceeded quota: dev-quota, requested: requests.memory=1Gi, used: requests.memory=9Gi, limited: requests.memory=10Gi. The node has 30Gi free. What is blocking creation, and what are the legitimate fixes?
options: Increase the pod's memory limit — limits bypass quotas
The node is lying about free memory — reboot it

A ResourceQuota on the namespace caps total requests at 10Gi and the namespace already uses 9Gi. Fixes: raise the quota (if justified), lower the pod's requests, or delete unused workloads in the namespace — the node having free RAM is irrelevant because quotas are admission-time accounting, not capacity checks
Quotas only apply to CPU; this error is spurious
explain: EXAM TRAP: the node has room but the NAMESPACE does not — ResourceQuota is admission control, evaluated before scheduling ever happens. The error message does the accounting for you: 9 used plus 1 requested exceeds the 10 limit. Legitimate fixes are quota increase (with approval), smaller requests, or namespace cleanup. Limits do not bypass quotas (quotas count requests by default), and quotas cover both CPU and memory.

q: An admin applies taint node-1维护=true:NoExecute (a taint with an invalid-effect typo that kubectl actually rejected — instead they apply node-1 spot=true:NoExecute). Within a minute, running pods without that toleration start terminating on node-1. What is happening, and what is the critical difference from NoSchedule?
options: The node is being drained automatically — wait for it to finish
Taints cannot affect running pods — the terminations are a coincidence

NoExecute EVICTS running pods that do not tolerate the taint (unlike NoSchedule, which only blocks new pods). This is how you forcefully clear a node class — and how you accidentally nuke workloads if you taint the wrong nodes. Check tolerationSeconds for graceful variants
The pods are crashing because of the taint's value
explain: NoExecute is the evicting taint: the node controller actively kills non-tolerating pods, with optional tolerationSeconds grace. This is the number-one 'I tainted one node and half my fleet restarted' incident pattern. NoSchedule would have left everything running. The value (spot=true) is irrelevant to the eviction — only the key/effect matching against tolerations matters.

q: A Deployment's pods are Running and passing liveness probes, but the Service sends no traffic to them and kubectl get endpoints shows the pods missing. The app takes 90 seconds to warm up. What is misconfigured, and why is liveness the wrong probe to blame?
options: The liveness probe is too aggressive — tune its timeout

The readiness probe is missing or failing: only readiness gates endpoint membership. Liveness only restarts containers — a passing liveness probe says nothing about whether the pod should receive traffic. Add a proper readiness probe (or a startup probe guarding the 90s warmup) so the pod joins endpoints only when it can serve
90-second warmups are unsupported in Kubernetes
Services ignore probes entirely — the Service selector is wrong
explain: EXAM TRAP: liveness vs readiness is THE probe question. Liveness = 'restart me if broken'. Readiness = 'send me traffic if capable'. Endpoints are built from readiness alone. A slow-starting app with only liveness looks healthy while serving 500s — the fix is a readiness probe reflecting true servability, optionally with a startupProbe disabling liveness during the 90s warmup so slow starts are not kill-looped. Services absolutely honor readiness.

q: etcd lost all members (disk failure on a single-node test cluster). You have yesterday's snapshot /backup/etcd.db. Walk the correct restore sequence.
options: Run kubeadm init --restore=/backup/etcd.db

etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored (writes to a NEW dir, never in place) → point the etcd static pod manifest's --data-dir and volume hostPath at the new dir → kubelet restarts etcd → verify with etcdctl endpoint health. In-place overwrite of a live data dir corrupts it
Snapshots cannot restore a fully dead etcd — rebuild the cluster and reapply all manifests
Copy the snapshot over /var/lib/etcd and restart the node
explain: The restore ritual has three non-negotiable steps: restore to a fresh directory (etcd refuses to overwrite live data for good reason), repoint the static pod manifest (the kubelet only watches the manifest — it knows nothing about your restore until the flags change), and verify health before declaring victory. Copying over the live dir risks torn writes; kubeadm init builds a new cluster (new identity, empty); and snapshots are exactly the supported path for dead-etcd recovery — that is why the exam tests it.

q: After editing /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml on a worker, the kubelet will not start: journalctl -u kubelet shows Error: failed to load Kubelet config file. The node is NotReady. What is the recovery, and what safety habit prevents this?
options: Restore the known-good config (from backup, /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf-adjacent copies, or a sibling node's file adjusted for hostname) and systemctl restart kubelet. Safety habit: cp config.yaml config.yaml.bak before EVERY hand edit — a single YAML indentation error takes down the node
Reinstall the kubelet package — the binary is corrupted
The node must be rejoined with kubeadm join
Delete the config file — the kubelet regenerates it
explain: The kubelet is unforgiving about its config: one bad indent and it refuses to start, taking the node NotReady with it. Recovery is restoring a good copy — sibling nodes' configs are nearly identical (adjust hostname-specific fields). The kubelet never regenerates the file, reinstalls do not fix config, and rejoining is pointless when the binary and certs are fine. The .bak habit is the cheapest insurance in cluster administration.

q: kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows kube-apiserver-cp-1 in CrashLoopBackOff. The API is flapping. Where do you look FIRST, and why is this different from debugging a normal pod?
options: Delete the pod — the Deployment will recreate it
The API server cannot fail — this status is impossible
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-cp-1 — same as any pod

The static pod manifest (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml) and the kubelet's logs on cp-1 — because with the API flapping, kubectl itself is unreliable; the manifest is the pod's source of truth and a bad flag edit there is the usual cause. Also check disk space and cert validity on the node directly
explain: EXAM TRAP: you cannot rely on the API to debug the API. When the apiserver flaps, kubectl becomes untrustworthy — go to the node. Static pods come from manifests, so a recent manifest edit (bad --advertise-address, bad etcd endpoints, typo'd flag) is suspect number one; kubelet logs show the crash reason. There is no Deployment to recreate it (static pods are manifest-bound), and API servers fail in very ordinary ways.

q: A NodePort Service (port 31080) is reachable via curl localhost:31080 ON the node, but times out from outside the cluster. Pods and ClusterIP work fine. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Service selector is wrong — but then localhost would fail too

kube-proxy is fine (localhost works, so rules exist) — the block is upstream: cloud security group / host firewall (firewalld/iptables INPUT) dropping external traffic to the 30000-32767 range. Open the NodePort range on the firewall
NodePort only works from localhost by design
The NodePort range is exhausted — pick a lower port
explain: Localhost success isolates the fault beautifully: kube-proxy rules exist and the app answers, so everything inside Kubernetes works. The failure is at the host/cloud boundary — security groups or host firewalls that nobody opened for the NodePort range. This inside/outside bisection is the general troubleshooting move: find the layer where behavior changes, and the culprit lives there. NodePorts are reachable externally by design; the range is not exhausted by one Service.

q: A pod with required nodeAffinity (disktype in [nvme]) stays Pending: 0/4 nodes available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity. The nodes ARE labeled disktype=ssd. The team insists the labels are 'close enough'. What is the scheduler telling you, and what is the decision?
options: The scheduler is exact: requiredDuringScheduling means ALL terms must match, and nvme != ssd. Decision: either relabel/reprovision nodes to nvme, or change the pod to accept ssd (preferredDuringScheduling if it is a soft wish). 'Close enough' is not a scheduling concept
The scheduler is buggy — affinity should fuzzy-match
Delete the affinity — labels do not matter
The pod will schedule after the affinity cache expires in an hour
explain: Required affinity is a hard predicate: match or Pending, forever. The scheduler does not negotiate, and there is no cache expiry that fixes a mismatch. The real decision is a requirements question — does the workload truly need nvme, or was the affinity aspirational? If soft, preferredDuringScheduling expresses 'want, not need'. This exactness is why the exam loves affinity questions: one wrong label value, permanent Pending.

q: You inherit a broken cluster with five simultaneous symptoms: some pods Pending, one node NotReady, a Service with no endpoints, DNS failures, and a CrashLoopBackOff deployment. Where do you start, and what is the underlying method?
options: Fix the CrashLoopBackOff first — application errors are always the priority

Start with the shared dependencies, bottom-up: node NotReady (capacity affects Pending), then DNS (breaks everything name-based), then endpoints/selectors, then app crashes. Method: isolate layers (node → network/DNS → workload), verify each fix before moving up, and never change two things at once
Rebuild the cluster — multi-symptom breakage is unrecoverable
Fix all five in parallel — speed matters most
explain: The CKA troubleshooting meta-skill: order faults by dependency. A NotReady node explains Pending pods (lost capacity); dead DNS explains cascading name failures; only then do app-level issues (endpoints, crashloops) get attention — many 'app bugs' evaporate once the platform is healthy. Change one thing, verify, move on: parallel changes make it impossible to know what fixed what. Rebuilds are the admission of defeat the exam never rewards — every one of these symptoms is diagnosable with describe, logs, and systemctl.

q: You run kubeadm init on a fresh VM, then kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows both CoreDNS pods stuck in Pending, and every pod you create also stays Pending. The node itself is Ready. What did you skip?
options: Running kubeadm init --upload-certs so the certificates replicate
Installing kubectl on the worker nodes
Installing a CNI network plugin (e.g. kubectl apply -f calico.yaml) — kubeadm ships no pod network, so no pod gets networking until a CNI is installed
Starting the kube-scheduler, which kubeadm leaves stopped by default
explain: kubeadm deliberately installs no pod network: until a CNI plugin is applied, the node has no podCIDR networking and every pod (including CoreDNS) stays Pending. This is the single most common fresh-cluster gotcha. --upload-certs matters only for multi-control-plane joins, kubectl is not needed on workers, and the scheduler starts automatically as a static pod.

q: A contractor needs read-only kubectl access to the staging namespace for two weeks. A teammate suggests copying /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to the contractor's laptop. Why is this wrong, and what is the correct approach?
options: admin.conf expires after 24 hours, so it would stop working mid-contract
Contractors are not allowed to use kubectl under any circumstances

admin.conf grants cluster-admin on every namespace — wildly over-privileged. The correct path is least privilege: generate a private key and CSR, approve it via the certificates.k8s.io API, build a kubeconfig with the signed client cert, and bind it with a Role/RoleBinding limited to staging
Copying admin.conf is fine — it is the standard onboarding method
explain: admin.conf embeds the cluster-admin client certificate: handing it out gives total control of the cluster, and you cannot scope or easily revoke it. The exam-correct onboarding is the CSR flow (openssl req, kubectl certificate approve) plus a namespaced RoleBinding — real identity, real scoping, revocable by deleting the binding. Nothing about contractors bans kubectl; the issue is purely privilege.

q: You carefully craft Roles and Bindings, but a junior engineer deletes a production Deployment despite having no binding that allows it. The audit shows the API server was started with --authorization-mode=Node,AlwaysAllow. What happened?
options: AlwaysAllow authorizes every request no matter what RBAC says — your Roles were evaluated and then ignored. The fix is --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC so RBAC decisions actually gate requests
Roles are advisory documentation; they never enforced anything
RoleBindings take 24 hours to take effect, so the delete slipped through the window
Every authenticated user is cluster-admin by default
explain: Authorization modes are a chain, and AlwaysAllow at the end grants anything earlier modes did not decide — including RBAC denials. With AlwaysAllow present, RBAC is theater. The kubeadm default is Node,RBAC, which is why this usually appears only on hand-rolled clusters. Bindings take effect immediately, and no user is cluster-admin by default.

q: etcd starts logging 'etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded' and all writes fail, though reads still work. The cluster is otherwise healthy. What is the recovery?
options: Delete old Deployments to free space — the API objects are the bulk of etcd
Restart the etcd static pod; the alarm clears on restart
Restore from the last snapshot immediately

The backend hit its quota (default 2GB) and raised a NOSPACE alarm. Recover with etcdctl defrag (after compaction) to reclaim space from old MVCC revisions, and raise --quota-backend-bytes if legitimate growth demands it
explain: etcd's MVCC keeps old revisions until compacted, so deleting API objects alone does not shrink the backend file — only compaction plus defrag reclaims it. The NOSPACE alarm specifically guards the quota-backend-bytes limit (2GB default); a restart does not clear it, and restoring a snapshot is for corruption, not a full disk. Monitor etcd db size: this alarm is the 'worked fine for a year, died Monday' of etcd.

q: On a single-node kubeadm dev cluster (one control-plane node, no workers), your test Deployment's pods stay Pending with '0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: }'. What is the right call?
options: Add a matching toleration to every pod spec — the only supported method

Remove the taint with kubectl taint nodes <node> node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule- (trailing dash removes it). Fine for dev/single-node; in production you would keep the taint and tolerate selectively
Delete the node object and rejoin it as a worker
Taints are permanent and cannot be removed
explain: kubeadm taints control-plane nodes NoSchedule by default to keep workloads off them. On a single-node dev cluster that taint strands everything, so removing it (note the trailing '-' syntax) is the pragmatic fix. Per-pod tolerations also work and are the right answer when only SOME workloads should run on control-plane nodes in a real cluster. Taints are fully removable.

q: You ran kubeadm init --upload-certs three hours ago. Joining the second control-plane node now fails with certificate errors suggesting the certificate key is rejected. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: The join command's bootstrap token expired — mint a new token
Re-run kubeadm init to generate fresh certificates

Uploaded control-plane certificates expire from the cluster after 2 hours by design. Re-run kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs on the first control-plane node, then join with the newly printed certificate key
Certificate keys never expire — this must be a network issue
explain: kubeadm stores uploaded certs in the cluster for only 2 hours (a security measure so the key is not lying around). After that, joins fail until you re-upload. The bootstrap token is a separate 24h TTL — do not confuse the two expiries. Re-running init would destroy the cluster, and the failure is by design, not a network fault.

q: After enabling the PodSecurity admission plugin, a Deployment's pods are rejected: 'violates PodSecurity "restricted": runAsNonRoot != true'. The image runs as root. What are the legitimate options?
options: Comply or consciously scope: set securityContext runAsNonRoot/runAsUser (and seccompProfile) so the pod meets restricted, or set the namespace's enforce label to baseline (or audit/warn) if the workload genuinely needs more privilege — a deliberate policy decision, not a bypass
Delete the admission configuration so the check goes away
PodSecurity cannot be adjusted per namespace — it is cluster-wide or nothing
Add privileged: true to the pod to override the policy
explain: PodSecurity is enforced per namespace via the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce|audit|warn labels, each pinning a standard (privileged, baseline, restricted). The exam-correct response is either fix the pod's securityContext to satisfy the policy or deliberately lower the namespace's enforce level with sign-off. Deleting admission config or slapping privileged: true on the workload defeats the control you just installed.

q: A pod specifies schedulerName: gpu-scheduler and sits Pending forever. Pods using the default scheduler schedule fine. What is wrong?
options: schedulerName is not a valid pod field
The scheduler is selected with a node label, not schedulerName
Pending for an hour is normal for custom schedulers

No scheduler named gpu-scheduler is running — custom schedulers are separate processes (usually Deployments) the cluster must actually run. Check its pods and logs, or remove schedulerName to use the default scheduler
explain: schedulerName just names the scheduler the pod waits for; Kubernetes does not create it for you. A typo'd or never-deployed custom scheduler means the pod waits forever with zero scheduler events — the signature is Pending with no 'failed scheduling' events at all. The field is valid, selection is by name, and there is no warm-up period.

q: Your cluster is v1.31 and you need v1.33. kubeadm upgrade plan only offers v1.32 as a target. The team wants to jump straight to v1.33 to save a maintenance window. What is the rule?
options: Jumping two minor versions is fine if you use --force
kubeadm only supports upgrading one minor version at a time: complete the full 1.31 to 1.32 cycle (control plane, then every node's kubelet), then repeat for 1.32 to 1.33
Edit the version string in the kubeadm config and apply
Minor versions are cosmetic; just upgrade the kubelets to v1.33
explain: One minor version per upgrade cycle is a hard kubeadm rule, mirroring the Kubernetes version-skew policy. Skipping (even with --force) strands components across unsupported skew and is exactly how clusters end up with a v1.33 API server talking to v1.31 etcd manifests. Two windows is the price; there is no shortcut flag.

q: kubectl top nodes returns 'Metrics not available' and the HPA shows <unknown> for CPU. All pods are healthy. Where is the break?
options: Metrics require Prometheus — install it
The kubelet is broken on every node
The metrics API has no provider: metrics-server is not installed (or its APIService v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io is failing). Check kubectl get apiservice and the metrics-server deployment
kubectl top was removed in recent versions
explain: kubectl top and HPA CPU both read the metrics.k8s.io API, which is served by metrics-server through an APIService registration — it is an aggregated API, not built into the API server. 'Metrics not available' with healthy pods points at the missing/broken provider, not the kubelets. Prometheus is optional (custom metrics); top is alive and well.

q: A pod curls https://kubernetes.default from inside the cluster and gets 403 Forbidden. DNS resolves fine and the API server is up. The pod needs to list ConfigMaps. What is the most likely cause?
options: The request authenticated as the pod's ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:default:default) but nothing grants it permission — no Role/RoleBinding covers listing ConfigMaps. Create the binding; 403 means authenticated-but-unauthorized
CoreDNS is misconfigured
The API server is down
Pods must mount /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to call the API
explain: In-cluster API auth comes from the mounted ServiceAccount token; a 403 (not a connection failure, not a 401) says the identity was accepted but RBAC denied the verb. The fix is the missing binding, not networking. Pods never use admin.conf — that file is for humans and would be a grotesque privilege leak inside a workload.

q: kubeadm join fails with 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority'. The bootstrap token is fresh and the API server is reachable. What is the likely cause?
options: The token expired — create another one
The node's clock is wrong — check NTP first
The API server certificate expired

The --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash does not match the cluster CA. The hash pins the CA for TLS verification; recompute it from /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt (openssl x509 -pubkey ...) or reprint the join command with kubeadm token create --print-join-command
explain: The CA cert hash is how the joining node verifies it is talking to YOUR cluster and not an impostor. A stale or hand-copied hash fails TLS verification with exactly this x509 error — token freshness is irrelevant to it. Clock skew and expired API certs produce different errors, and the fix is the correct hash, not a new token.

q: With 4,000 Services, kube-proxy in iptables mode is slow to program rules. You want IPVS mode on a kubeadm cluster. What is the procedure?
options: Reinstall the cluster with --proxy-mode=ipvs
Edit the kube-proxy ConfigMap (mode: "ipvs"), ensure the ip_vs kernel modules are loaded on every node, then delete the kube-proxy DaemonSet pods so they restart with the new config
kubectl set image on the kube-proxy DaemonSet
IPVS is selected automatically when iptables gets slow
explain: kube-proxy reads its mode from the kube-proxy ConfigMap in kube-system; changing it and rolling the DaemonSet pods applies it — no reinstall. The classic miss is the kernel modules (ip_vs, ip_vs_rr, nf_conntrack): without them the pods CrashLoop. Nothing auto-switches modes, and the image has nothing to do with the proxy mode.

q: A pod has nodeName: old-node-2 hardcoded in its spec. That node was decommissioned last week. The pod is Pending forever and the scheduler logs show nothing about it. Why?
options: The scheduler ignores nodeName
Pending is expected until the scheduler's cache expires

nodeName bypasses the scheduler entirely and pins the pod to that exact node — which no longer exists, so nothing will ever place it. Remove nodeName (or point it at a live node) and let the scheduler decide
A taint on the new nodes is blocking it
explain: nodeName is a scheduler bypass, not a hint: the pod is assigned directly to the named node, and if that node is gone the pod waits forever with no scheduling events — the silence is the signature. It exists for corner cases (like bringing up a pod before the scheduler runs), not for normal placement. Taints would produce 'untolerated taint' events, which are absent here.

q: Compliance requires logging every API write with who did what and when. How do you enable audit logging on a kubeadm cluster?
options: kubectl logs -n kube-system covers all API activity
Etcd logs already record every write
Audit logging is on by default
Write an audit Policy file, then add --audit-policy-file and --audit-log-path (plus rotation flags like --audit-log-maxage) to the kube-apiserver static pod manifest
explain: Audit is opt-in: a Policy file selects which requests to record at what level (None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse), and the API server flags turn on the log sink. Editing the static pod manifest is the kubeadm-native way to add flags. kubectl logs shows stdout, etcd logs show storage operations without user identity, and nothing is audited by default.

q: Exactly one year after joining, a worker node goes NotReady. journalctl -u kubelet shows 'x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid'. What is the recovery?
options: The kubelet's client certificate expired (1-year validity). Trigger a fresh CSR: remove the stale client cert so the kubelet requests a new one on restart, then approve it with kubectl certificate approve — or enable --rotate-certificates so this never happens again
Rebuild the node from scratch
Restart the API server — it issues kubelet certificates on demand
Kubelet certificates last forever; this error must be a clock issue
explain: Kubelet client certs are 1-year by default, and this 'worked for a year then died' pattern is the tell. The kubelet can mint a new CSR automatically once the expired cert is out of the way; a human (or an auto-approver) approves it. --rotate-certificates automates renewal going forward. The API server does not reissue kubelet certs spontaneously, and rebuilds are overkill for a cert rotation.

q: You passed --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 to kubeadm init, then installed a CNI configured for 192.168.0.0/16. Pods get IPs but cross-node traffic fails. What is wrong?
options: The CIDRs are cosmetic labels; the problem must be the firewall

The pod CIDR given to kubeadm must match the CNI's expected range — the controller-manager carves per-node CIDRs from --cluster-cidr, and a CNI programmed for a different range sets up wrong routes/IPAM. Align them: reinstall the CNI with matching config or re-init with the CNI's CIDR
You need two CNIs, one per CIDR
Cross-node traffic always fails on kubeadm; use a managed cluster
explain: The --pod-network-cidr is a contract with the CNI, not a suggestion: Flannel/Calico/Weave read it (or their own config) to program routes and IPAM. When the two disagree, pods get addresses from one range while the overlay routes another, and cross-node traffic blackholes. Same-node traffic may still work, which makes this extra confusing. Pick one CIDR and make both sides agree.

q: You ran kubeadm reset on a worker to rejoin it, but kubeadm join now fails with leftover CNI state and 'port 10250 is in use' style errors. What did reset miss?
options: kubeadm reset is broken and should not be used
Just reboot the node and retry
Nothing — reset cleans everything

kubeadm reset does not clean everything: stop the kubelet, flush iptables/IPVS rules, and remove /etc/cni/net.d (and $HOME/.kube/config remnants as documented) before rejoining. Reset reverses init/join; host network state needs manual cleanup
explain: kubeadm reset removes the cluster state but deliberately leaves host networking artifacts: iptables rules, CNI configs, and sometimes the kubelet still running. The documented cleanup (iptables -F/-X, ipvsadm --clear, rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d) is part of the rejoin ritual. Skipping it produces exactly these ghost-state join failures. A reboot alone does not flush persisted CNI config.

q: Nodes each receive a /24 from the cluster CIDR, but you need ~400 pods per node. Past ~110 pods, new pods stay Pending with no free IPs. Which setting controls per-node pod IP capacity?
options: --max-pods on the API server
Per-node IP capacity cannot be changed after init

The controller-manager's --node-cidr-mask-size (default /24 = 254 addresses): set a larger block like /22 or /21 at cluster creation, and raise the kubelet's --max-pods to match. A /24 physically cannot address 400 pods
Just add more nodes — pod density is fixed
explain: Each node gets one CIDR block of --node-cidr-mask-size, and a /24 yields 254 IPs — the ~110-pod ceiling you hit is that block minus system reservations, and no scheduler trickery creates more addresses. This is an init-time decision: changing it later means re-creating nodes. --max-pods on the kubelet is the companion knob, but the CIDR mask is the hard ceiling.

q: A cron job snapshots etcd nightly and reports success. How do you prove a snapshot is actually restorable BEFORE disaster strikes?
options: Run etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd.db --write-out=table — it validates the snapshot's integrity and shows its revision and size; plus periodically test-restore to a scratch directory. A cron exit code only proves the command ran
Check that the file is non-empty
Trust the cron success — etcdctl never lies
Snapshots cannot be verified without restoring over the live cluster
explain: snapshot status reads the bbolt integrity and reports the revision — catching truncated or corrupt files that a 'success' exit code would miss. The gold standard is a trial restore into a temp --data-dir (never over live data), which exercises the full path you will use at 3 AM. File size proves nothing, and verification never touches the running cluster.

q: You need to change a Deployment's image AND add two environment variables as a single atomic rollout — not two separate rolling updates back to back. How?
options: Apply the image change, wait, then apply the env change — two rollouts is the only way
kubectl rollout pause, make both edits (they accumulate as one pending revision), then kubectl rollout resume — pause batches multiple changes into a single rollout
Delete and recreate the Deployment with everything at once
Rollout pause is permanent and cannot be resumed
explain: rollout pause freezes the rollout controller so successive edits coalesce into one new ReplicaSet revision; resume then rolls it out once. Without pause, each kubectl apply triggers its own rolling update — wasteful and, for coupled changes, briefly inconsistent. Pause is fully reversible with resume.

q: A bad config shipped four revisions ago. You try kubectl rollout undo --to-revision, but only the last two revisions exist. Why did the older ones vanish?
options: rollout undo is broken for old revisions
Revisions are stored in git, not in the cluster
Use kubectl rollout history with --revision=1 to recover them

revisionHistoryLimit (default 10, set to 2 here) caps how many old ReplicaSets the Deployment keeps — older revisions are garbage-collected and unrecoverable via undo. Raise the limit if you need deeper history
explain: Each revision is a retained ReplicaSet; revisionHistoryLimit bounds how many are kept, and the collector deletes the rest. Undo can only travel within retained history. The default 10 is usually fine, but teams that lower it for tidiness lose their rollback runway. Git holds your manifests, not the cluster's revision chain.

q: A legacy app uses a file lock: two copies running simultaneously corrupt its data. A rolling update briefly runs old and new pods side by side. Which strategy is safe?
options: strategy: type: Recreate — all old pods are killed before any new pod starts. Downtime, but zero overlap, which is what the lock requires
RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 — keeps full capacity, guaranteeing overlap
Run two Deployments and switch the Service between them
Recreate still overlaps briefly during the swap
explain: Recreate is the purpose-built strategy for workloads that cannot tolerate two versions alive at once: scale old to zero, then start new. RollingUpdate (even tuned) is designed around overlap — maxUnavailable: 0 maximizes it. The blue-green-via-two-Deployments pattern works but is manual; Recreate is declarative and honest about the downtime tradeoff.

q: A Job's pod fails and the Job controller keeps creating new pods for hours — hundreds of attempts. You expected it to give up. Which fields control this?
options: restartPolicy: Always — the kubelet keeps restarting it
Jobs never give up; this is by design

backoffLimit (default 6) caps the number of retries — this Job must have it set sky-high. Also note restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure for Jobs (Always is rejected), and activeDeadlineSeconds sets a hard wall-clock cap on the whole Job
completions: 100 — it is trying to reach 100 completions
explain: A Job retries failed pods until backoffLimit is hit — the default 6 is sane, but someone raised it (or set it absurdly high) here. Two knobs, two jobs: backoffLimit counts attempts, activeDeadlineSeconds bounds total time (kills runaway Jobs even if attempts remain). restartPolicy: Always is invalid on Jobs, and completions counts successes, not retries.

q: A CronJob's data import takes 25 minutes but the schedule fires every 15 minutes. Overlapping runs corrupt the import. What is the fix?
options: Run a second CronJob to serialize them
concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — skips a scheduled start while the previous run is still active. Pair it with startingDeadlineSeconds so missed starts do not pile up silently
concurrencyPolicy: Allow — the default, which is the problem
CronJobs never overlap, so the corruption must come from elsewhere
explain: CronJobs absolutely overlap by default (Allow): each schedule tick starts a Job regardless of the last. Forbid makes the controller skip ticks while a run is active — exactly the mutual-exclusion this import needs. Replace (kill the old, start the new) is the third option, right for 'latest wins' workloads but wrong here.

q: A CronJob with schedule '0 2 * * *' runs at 2 AM UTC, but the business wants 2 AM America/New_York. All nodes are UTC. How do you fix this (v1.27+)?
options: Change every node's timezone to America/New_York
Cron syntax supports timezones inline — use '0 2 * * * America/New_York'
It is impossible — CronJobs always use UTC
Set spec.timeZone: America/New_York — the controller schedules in that zone, DST-aware, independent of node timezones
explain: spec.timeZone (GA since 1.27) decouples the schedule from node clocks — the CronJob controller interprets the cron expression in the named zone, handling DST transitions. Changing node timezones is fragile and affects everything; cron syntax has no zone field. Before 1.27 the answer was 'compute the UTC equivalent and accept DST drift twice a year.'

q: A distroless production pod is crash-looping and the image has no shell. You need to inspect its filesystem and running processes live. What works?
options: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> — attaches an ephemeral debug container sharing the target's process namespace (and view of its filesystem), no image rebuild needed
kubectl exec — there is no shell to exec into
SSH to the node and docker exec — bypasses the API and assumes a docker runtime
It is impossible without rebuilding the image with busybox
explain: Ephemeral containers (kubectl debug) are the designed answer for distroless/scratch debugging: a temporary container joins the pod's namespaces, so you get a shell with visibility into the crashing container's filesystem and processes. exec cannot conjure a shell that is not in the image, and node SSH breaks the Kubernetes-native workflow (and containerd nodes have no docker).

q: Replicas keep piling onto nodes in a single zone despite your anti-affinity preferences. You want a HARD guarantee: spread evenly across 3 zones, max skew 1. Which field?
options: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution pod anti-affinity — it is only a soft preference
nodeSelector with the zone label

topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule — the scheduler computes skew per topology domain and refuses placements that would exceed it
A PodDisruptionBudget
explain: topologySpreadConstraints are the purpose-built even-spread mechanism: maxSkew bounds the difference in pod counts between zones, and DoNotSchedule makes it a hard rule (ScheduleAnyway makes it soft). Anti-affinity expresses 'not together' pairwise; spread constraints express 'evenly distributed' globally — different math, and the exam tests knowing which to reach for. PDBs limit disruptions, not placement.

q: Applying a pod fails: 'pods "x" is forbidden: minimum cpu limit 100m not specified'. You DID set cpu requests. What is going on?
options: Requests are invalid — only limits count

A LimitRange in the namespace enforces minimum (and possibly default) limits — your pod violates its min. Set limits satisfying it, or let the LimitRange inject its defaults by omitting the fields it defaults
A ResourceQuota is blocking it
Kubernetes always requires limits on every pod
explain: LimitRange is the namespace-level policy that sets min/max/defaults for requests and limits — and it rejects pods outright that violate its minimums. This is distinct from ResourceQuota (which caps namespace totals at admission). Kubernetes itself does not require limits; the requirement here comes from the namespace's LimitRange. Read the namespace's LimitRanges when a pod is rejected for missing fields you thought were optional.

q: During node upgrades you apply a NoExecute taint, but pods die instantly and drop connections. You want a 5-minute grace period before eviction. How?
options: Taints cannot be delayed — eviction is immediate
A PodDisruptionBudget alone delays eviction
terminationGracePeriodSeconds alone — that only controls shutdown AFTER SIGTERM; it does not delay the eviction decision

Add tolerationSeconds: 300 to the pods' toleration for that taint — the pod tolerates the NoExecute taint for 5 minutes, then is evicted. Combine with a PDB and a preStop hook for a truly graceful drain
explain: tolerationSeconds is the delayed-evict knob: 'tolerate this taint for N seconds, then leave.' It is how rolling node maintenance drains gracefully instead of massacring connections. PDBs cap how many may go down at once (a different axis), and terminationGracePeriodSeconds only governs the kill sequence once eviction starts — without tolerationSeconds there is no delay to be graceful during.

q: You used preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution pod anti-affinity, but during a busy hour two replicas still landed on the same node. Is this a bug?
options: No — 'preferred' is best-effort scoring, not a rule. Under resource pressure the scheduler still places them together and the pod stays Pending nowhere; it just scores co-location lower. Use requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution for a hard guarantee
Yes — file a bug against the scheduler
Anti-affinity does not work across nodes
You need taints instead — affinity is deprecated
explain: The name says it: preferredDuringScheduling is a weighted hint. The scheduler tries to honor it, but if honoring it means leaving the pod Pending while capacity exists elsewhere, it will co-locate and move on. Required affinity is the hard predicate (Pending beats violating it). The exam loves this soft-vs-hard distinction — 'IgnoredDuringExecution' further means it never evicts already-running pods.

q: An HPA flaps: a 1-minute CPU spike scales the Deployment up, then it scales straight back down, thrashing pods all day. Which tuning calms the scale-down?
options: Raise maxReplicas so it has headroom
Lower the target CPU so it stays scaled up
behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds (e.g. 300) — the autoscaler considers the highest desired replica count over the window before scaling down, ignoring transient dips
Delete the HPA and scale manually
explain: The behavior block (scaleUp/scaleDown with stabilizationWindowSeconds, policies, selectPolicy) is the anti-flap toolkit. The default scale-down stabilization is already 300s, but teams often need to tune it (or the scale-up window, default 0) for spiky workloads. Changing targets or replica bounds treats the symptom; the stabilization window treats the oscillation.

q: A sidecar must send SIGHUP to the main container's process when config changes. By default it cannot even see the process. What enables this with least privilege?
options: privileged: true on the sidecar
shareProcessNamespace: true on the pod — both containers share one PID namespace, so the sidecar can see and signal the main container's processes
hostPID: true — shares the node's PID namespace
It is impossible — containers are fully isolated
explain: shareProcessNamespace merges the pod's containers into one PID namespace: the sidecar sees the main container's PID 1 and can signal it. It is pod-scoped (unlike hostPID, which exposes every host process) and needs no privilege escalation. This is the standard pattern for config-reload and debug sidecars.

q: Every deploy drops in-flight requests: pods get SIGTERM and die instantly. The app needs 30 seconds to drain connections. What is the complete graceful-shutdown setup?
options: Nothing — Kubernetes drains connections automatically
A preStop hook alone is enough
terminationGracePeriodSeconds alone — without a preStop the app still gets SIGTERM immediately and dies on its own speed

lifecycle.preStop.exec.command: ["sleep", "30"] (or a real drain script) AND terminationGracePeriodSeconds comfortably above 30 — preStop runs BEFORE SIGTERM is sent, and the grace period must exceed the hook or the kubelet SIGKILLs mid-drain
explain: The shutdown sequence is: preStop hook runs, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds. A sleep (or better, a drain endpoint call) in preStop buys the drain time; the grace period must cover hook + drain or the KILL lands early. Either field alone fails: preStop without enough grace gets cut off, grace without preStop just delays the same instant death.

q: An app needs its own pod name and namespace as environment variables for structured logging. Hardcoding them per pod is wrong. How?
options: Downward API: env with valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath: metadata.name and metadata.namespace — the kubelet injects the pod's own fields at container start
One ConfigMap per pod with hardcoded values
The hostname is the pod name, so nothing is needed
Pod fields cannot be exposed to containers
explain: The Downward API exists precisely for this: fieldRef exposes metadata.name, metadata.namespace, pod IP, node name, and resource requests/limits as env vars or files. Hostname gives the pod name but not the namespace, per-pod ConfigMaps are toil, and the API is a first-class, documented feature.

q: Every app in the cluster uses the default ServiceAccount, which was granted broad read access years ago. You are deploying a new payments app. What is the least-privilege fix?
options: Keep using default — it already works
Delete the default ServiceAccount from the namespace

Create a dedicated ServiceAccount for the app (serviceAccountName in the pod spec) and grant it ONLY what it needs via a Role/RoleBinding — a compromise or bug in one app no longer inherits every other app's permissions
Bind the app to cluster-admin so it never hits a permission error
explain: The default ServiceAccount is shared ambient authority: every permission ever granted to it accrues to every pod that never bothered to set serviceAccountName. A dedicated SA per app (or per tier) contains blast radius and makes audit meaningful. Deleting default breaks system expectations; cluster-admin for an app is the opposite of least privilege.

q: kubectl drain hangs with 'cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget'. The PDB sets maxUnavailable: 0. What is the right move?
options: drain --force — it bypasses the PDB

Recognize the PDB is doing its job: maxUnavailable: 0 forbids ALL voluntary disruptions, so the drain is correctly blocked. Coordinate a temporary PDB relaxation (change control, off-peak) rather than force-deleting pods and defeating the availability guarantee
Delete the PDB permanently — it is blocking maintenance
cordon instead of drain and leave the pods running
explain: PDBs distinguish voluntary disruptions (drains, voluntary evictions) from involuntary ones (node death). maxUnavailable: 0 is a deliberate 'never voluntarily disrupt me' stance — the drain hanging is the system working. --force does not override PDB eviction blocking (it overrides other safeguards); the legitimate paths are adjusting the PDB with approval or accepting the node cannot be drained now. Deleting the PDB 'fixes' maintenance by abandoning the guarantee.

q: A DaemonSet rolling update restarts the log collector on ALL nodes simultaneously — cluster-wide log loss during every update. How do you serialize the update?
options: DaemonSets cannot roll — delete and recreate them
Delete the pods by hand one node at a time
Set updateStrategy to OnDelete and delete pods manually forever
updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 1 — the DaemonSet controller updates one node's pod at a time, keeping collectors running everywhere else
explain: DaemonSets support RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable, exactly like Deployments — one unavailable pod per step keeps per-node agents continuously running. The default maxUnavailable: 1 is usually already serial; someone likely raised it (or the DaemonSet predates the default). OnDelete is the manual alternative, right only when you want human-gated updates.

q: A 60-replica StatefulSet takes forever to roll: pods update strictly one at a time, in ordinal order. The app has no ordering requirements. How do you speed this up?
options: podManagementPolicy: Parallel — pods start, update, and scale concurrently instead of strictly ordered 0..N. OrderedReady is the default and the bottleneck here
Add more replicas to parallelize
OrderedReady is mandatory for StatefulSets
Convert it to a Deployment
explain: OrderedReady (create/update/delete in ordinal sequence, each waiting for its predecessor) is the StatefulSet default and the safe choice for ordered systems (quorums, primaries). When the app does not need ordering, Parallel removes the serialization. Converting to a Deployment would forfeit stable identity and per-pod storage — the reasons it is a StatefulSet.

q: You want to canary a StatefulSet: update ONLY the highest-ordinal pod (web-9 of web-0..web-9) first and watch it before rolling the rest. How?
options: It is impossible — StatefulSets update all or nothing
Set partition: 0 — that updates everything
updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: 9 — only pods with ordinal >= 9 get the new revision; the rest stay pinned. Lower the partition to roll forward, raise it to hold back
Delete web-9 and let it recreate on the new image
explain: partition is the StatefulSet canary knob: ordinals at or above the partition update, below it stay. partition: 9 canaries exactly web-9; partition: 0 rolls everything. Deleting web-9 recreates it at the CURRENT revision (no canary), and StatefulSets never do all-or-nothing — the rolling update is ordinal-ordered by design.

q: A legacy web app keeps session state in process memory. Behind a Service, users bounce between pods and get logged out on every other click. What is the fix, and what is its limit?
options: sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service — kube-proxy routes the same client IP to the same pod (best-effort). It is not a substitute for a shared session store: it breaks behind NATs and on pod restarts
A headless Service — removes load balancing, making it worse
sessionAffinity: None — the default, which is the problem
Sticky sessions require an Ingress; Services cannot do this
explain: ClientIP session affinity makes kube-proxy hash the source IP to a stable backend — the standard fix for in-memory sessions. Its limits are the exam point: many clients behind one NAT IP all pin to one pod (hotspotting), and pod death still loses sessions. Services absolutely support this; Ingress-cookie affinity is the fancier alternative, not a requirement.

q: Cross-AZ network bills are spiking because Service traffic hops availability zones. You want traffic to stay on the client's own node whenever a local endpoint exists. Which field, and what is the catch?
options: externalTrafficPolicy: Local — that only affects external traffic
Nothing can constrain internal Service routing
internalTrafficPolicy: Local — only node-local endpoints receive traffic. The catch: if a node has NO local endpoint, traffic to the Service from that node is DROPPED, not rerouted
sessionAffinity: ClientIP
explain: internalTrafficPolicy: Local (default Cluster) restricts routing to endpoints on the originating node — cutting cross-zone hops and their cost. The exam trap is the failure mode: unlike Cluster, there is no fallback, so a node without a local pod gets connection failures. externalTrafficPolicy is the external-traffic sibling with the same tradeoff.

q: A 3-node etcd cluster runs as a StatefulSet behind a headless Service. New members cannot bootstrap: they cannot resolve peer DNS names because those peers are not Ready yet. What is missing?
options: Fix the readiness probes so peers become Ready faster
publishNotReadyAddresses: true on the headless Service — DNS must return pod addresses BEFORE they pass readiness, because quorum bootstrap requires reaching peers that are not yet 'ready'
Switch to a ClusterIP Service
Add more replicas
explain: Headless Services normally publish only Ready addresses — correct for steady state, fatal for bootstrapping distributed systems where members must discover each other before anyone is ready. publishNotReadyAddresses flips this: DNS returns all pod IPs regardless of readiness. Readiness probes are not the problem (the peers genuinely are not ready yet), and a ClusterIP would give one VIP instead of per-pod DNS.

q: Pods must reach a managed database at 10.20.30.40 (no DNS name for it) via the in-cluster name db.prod.svc.cluster.local. There is no selector that can match it. How?
options: An ExternalName Service — it requires a DNS name target, which does not exist here
A headless Service — it only changes DNS for selected pods
A NodePort Service — that exposes cluster workloads outward, the wrong direction
A Service with NO selector plus a manually created Endpoints object listing 10.20.30.40:5432 — the Service gets its ClusterIP/DNS name, and kube-proxy routes to your hand-written endpoints
explain: Selector-less Services are the integration pattern for anything outside the cluster's label world: you supply the Endpoints object by hand and get full Service semantics (ClusterIP, DNS name, kube-proxy routing) for an external IP. ExternalName only aliases DNS names to DNS names — with a bare IP there is nothing to CNAME to. NodePort is for inbound exposure, not outbound integration.

q: A Service fronts 300 pods, but some pods never receive traffic. kubectl get endpoints shows a confusing, seemingly incomplete list. Where is the full picture?
options: EndpointSlices — the endpoint controller mirrors Endpoints into EndpointSlice objects (capped at ~100 addresses each, more scalable); inspect them with kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<name>
The endpoints list is always complete; the missing pods must be unready
kube-proxy is dropping backends — restart it
Delete and recreate the Service to rebuild the list
explain: At scale, the Endpoints object becomes a bottleneck, so the controller shards addresses across EndpointSlices — the Endpoints resource you are reading may be a legacy mirror. Debugging large Services means reading the slices (check their addresses and conditions, including terminating/hints). Unready pods are excluded by design, but 'never receives traffic while Ready' points at the slice contents, not kube-proxy.

q: Unknown hosts hitting your Ingress get the controller's blank default 404 page. Marketing wants a branded catch-all page. How?
options: Impossible — the controller's 404 is hardcoded
Create a second Ingress with host '*'
Set defaultBackend on the Ingress (or configure the controller's custom default backend) — requests matching no host/path rule go there instead of the controller's stock 404
Add a DNS wildcard record
explain: defaultBackend is the Ingress catch-all: any request not matching a rule routes to it. (Separately, most controllers let you replace their global default backend Deployment for a cluster-wide branded 404.) A second Ingress cannot match 'no host' — rules are additive, not fallback. DNS only gets the client to the controller; it does not choose the page.

q: You want 5% of production traffic on the new v2 Deployment for canary analysis, using ingress-nginx, without a service mesh. How?
options: Two Ingresses with the same host — they conflict and the result is undefined
Canary annotations on the v2 Ingress: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true" plus nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "5" — the controller splits 5% of traffic to the canary backend
An HPA on v2 — that scales pods, not traffic share
Split it in the Service — Services do not weight backends
explain: ingress-nginx's canary annotations implement weighted traffic splitting natively: the canary Ingress (same host, canary: 'true') receives the configured weight percentage. This is the mesh-free canary path the exam expects you to know. Two plain Ingresses on one host merge/conflict rather than split, and Services distribute evenly across endpoints with no weights.

q: The app must see the ORIGINAL TLS client certificate (mutual TLS all the way to the pod). Terminating TLS at the Ingress breaks this. What enables end-to-end TLS with ingress-nginx?
options: The rewrite-target annotation
Setting the backend protocol to HTTPS — the Ingress still terminates the client connection first
Migrating to Gateway API

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: "true" — the controller routes the encrypted stream by SNI without decrypting it, so the pod terminates TLS itself (requires --enable-ssl-passthrough on the controller)
explain: SSL passthrough keeps the TLS session intact end to end: nginx never sees plaintext, and the pod sees the real client certificate. The tradeoffs are the exam point: routing is SNI-only (no L7 path/header routing on the encrypted stream) and the controller needs the passthrough flag enabled. Backend-protocol HTTPS is TLS re-encryption, not passthrough — the client cert still terminates at the edge.

q: After applying a default-deny Ingress NetworkPolicy in namespace api, the Ingress controller returns 503 for the api app, though direct pod-to-pod IPs work. What is missing?
options: An ingress from rule allowing the Ingress controller — the controller's pods are the actual clients, and the deny policy blocks them. Allow from the controller's namespace/pod labels (e.g. ingress-nginx) to the app's port
Delete the policy — Ingress is incompatible with NetworkPolicy
The Ingress controller is broken — reinstall it
This is a DNS problem — check CoreDNS
explain: Default-deny means default-deny, including for your own Ingress controller: its pods live in another namespace and match no allow rule, so traffic dies at the policy. The fix is an ingress from entry selecting the controller (namespaceSelector and/or podSelector) on the backend port. Pod IPs work because policy enforcement is about the destination pod's selectors — direct tests from unlabeled debug pods would fail the same way.

q: After applying default-deny egress, an operator pod cannot reach the Kubernetes API at https://kubernetes.default. Cluster DNS works fine. What egress allowance is missing?
options: UDP port 53 — DNS already works, so this is covered
TCP 80 to the internet

TCP 443 to the API server endpoints — and note the trap: a namespaceSelector for kube-system does NOT cover the API server (it is not a pod in kube-system). Allow the control-plane IPs or the kubernetes Endpoints addresses on 443
Egress policies cannot allow API access — the API bypasses policy
explain: In-cluster API traffic is just HTTPS to the control-plane IPs (via the kubernetes Service). Default-deny egress blocks it like anything else — the operator's watch/list calls die. The classic mistake is allowing 'kube-system' and wondering why it still fails: the API servers are not pods in kube-system, so namespaceSelector misses them. Allow the actual endpoint IPs on 443.

q: Pod-to-pod traffic works between pods on the SAME node but fails across nodes. Services fail cross-node too. Node-to-node ping works fine. Which layer is broken?
options: kube-proxy — Service VIPs would fail but pod IPs would still route

The CNI overlay — same-node traffic uses the local bridge/veth pair, but cross-node needs the overlay encapsulation (VXLAN etc.) or the routes the CNI programs. Check the CNI pods (DaemonSet) and their logs
CoreDNS — name resolution is not involved in IP tests
etcd — it does not forward packets
explain: This is layer bisection: node underlay works (ping), local pod networking works (bridge), cross-node pod networking fails — the fault sits exactly at the overlay the CNI builds between nodes. A dead CNI agent on a node (or mismatched encapsulation config) produces precisely this pattern. kube-proxy failure would leave pod IPs working everywhere while VIPs fail — the inverse symptom.

q: At 6,000 Services, every Service change spikes CPU on all nodes as kube-proxy rewrites thousands of iptables rules. What is the architectural fix, and why does it help?
options: Run fewer Services — not an option
Restart kube-proxy on a schedule
Switch to IPVS — it is slower but more compatible

Switch kube-proxy to IPVS mode — iptables is O(n) linear chain traversal per packet and full rule rewrites per change; IPVS uses O(1) hash-table dispatch and incremental updates, so scale stops hurting
explain: iptables mode degrades linearly: each packet walks chains and each Service change rewrites the whole ruleset. IPVS (kernel-level load balancing) dispatches via hash tables in constant time with incremental sync — the standard answer for large Service counts. This is the 'why' behind the mode switch: same kube-proxy, fundamentally different data plane.

q: External DNS lookups from pods are slow — about 5 seconds of delay — but always succeed. In-cluster names resolve instantly. What is the classic cause?
options: ndots:5 plus the pod's search domains — short external names are tried against every search domain first (each NXDOMAIN costs a round trip). Use the FQDN with a trailing dot (example.com.) to skip search expansion
CoreDNS is down
The cluster network is slow
Increase the resolver timeout
explain: With ndots:5, any name with fewer than 5 dots (i.e. every normal external name) is first expanded through all search domains — 'example.com' becomes 'example.com.default.svc.cluster.local' etc., each failing slowly before the real lookup happens. The trailing dot marks the name absolute and skips the whole dance. This 5-second delay pattern is unmistakable once you have seen it.

q: Pods must resolve corp.internal names via the company DNS at 10.0.0.53; all other names use the normal upstream. How do you configure this?
options: Edit /etc/resolv.conf inside each pod — it is managed and gets overwritten
hostAliases — only for static entries, not a whole zone

Add a server block to the CoreDNS Corefile forwarding corp.internal to 10.0.0.53 (.:53 { forward . /etc/resolv.conf } plus corp.internal:53 { forward . 10.0.0.53 }) — and back up the ConfigMap before touching it, per the hard-learned lesson
NodeLocal DNSCache alone does this
explain: CoreDNS's Corefile supports per-zone server blocks: a dedicated block for corp.internal with a forward plugin sends just that zone to the corporate DNS while everything else follows the default path. Pod resolv.conf is kubelet-managed, hostAliases cannot cover a zone, and NodeLocal DNSCache is a performance daemon, not a zone-routing mechanism.

q: A node-monitoring agent must sniff the host's network interfaces. As a normal pod it sees only its own network namespace. What grants host visibility, and what is the cost?
options: privileged: true — that is about capabilities, a different axis

hostNetwork: true — the pod shares the host's network namespace: it sees host interfaces and can bind host ports. The cost is total loss of network isolation — port conflicts with the host and a much larger blast radius, so reserve it for node agents
hostPID: true — that shares process visibility, not networking
A NodePort Service
explain: hostNetwork drops the pod into the host's netns — the standard (and intended) pattern for CNI-adjacent agents, node exporters, and network monitors. The exam wants the cost stated plainly: no port isolation (collisions with host services), host-visible traffic, and elevated risk — which is why it is wrong for application pods. privileged and hostPID solve different problems.

q: Your app logs show every client IP as a node internal IP instead of the real client address. The Service is type NodePort (later LoadBalancer). Why, and what is the fix?
options: The app is misreading the X-Forwarded-For header
kube-proxy is broken — reinstall it
Source IP preservation is impossible in Kubernetes

The default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster routes through kube-proxy with SNAT, masking the client IP. Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local so traffic goes only to node-local pods without SNAT — accepting the tradeoff that nodes without local endpoints will not serve external traffic
explain: Cluster (the default) load-balances across all nodes, and the extra hop requires source NAT — hence node IPs in your logs. Local preserves the client IP by skipping the SNAT hop, but only nodes actually running the pod can answer, which can skew distribution. This same tradeoff appears on cloud LoadBalancers; the field is the lever in both cases.

q: On bare metal with no cloud provider, a Service of type LoadBalancer stays <pending> for its EXTERNAL-IP forever. What provides the external IP?
options: MetalLB — a bare-metal load-balancer implementation that claims IPs from a configured pool via BGP or Layer-2 (ARP/NDP) and assigns them to LoadBalancer Services
Change to NodePort — that gives no EXTERNAL-IP
Wait longer — the cloud controller will eventually respond
LoadBalancer works on bare metal natively — nothing is needed
explain: The LoadBalancer type is just an API contract: some controller must fulfill it. In the cloud that is the provider's controller; on bare metal it is MetalLB (or alternatives like kube-vip in LB mode). Nothing in stock Kubernetes assigns external IPs — Pending forever is the signature of the missing controller. NodePort is the no-controller exposure path, but it never fills EXTERNAL-IP.

q: You want an Ingress rule to match ONLY the literal path /api — but /api/users is also routing there. The rule uses pathType: Prefix. What is the subtlety?
options: This is a controller bug — Prefix should be exact
Use a regular expression instead
Prefix matches on path ELEMENT boundaries: /api matches /api, /api/, and /api/users (but not /apiv2). For a literal-only match, use pathType: Exact
Add a trailing slash to the path
explain: Prefix is element-wise, not string-prefix: /api covers everything beneath that element, which surprises people expecting either exact matching or naive string prefixing (note /apiv2 does NOT match — a favorite exam detail). Exact matches the path and only the path. ImplementationSpecific is the escape hatch for controller-specific regex behavior.

q: Migrating to Gateway API: you need an HTTPS listener terminating TLS for shop.example.com. Where does the certificate attach?
options: On the HTTPRoute — routes do not own TLS config
On the Gateway listener: protocol HTTPS with tls.certificateRefs pointing at the kubernetes.io/tls Secret — listeners own the TLS termination config, routes attach to listeners
On the GatewayClass — that selects the controller implementation
Via an Ingress annotation — that is the old API
explain: Gateway API separates concerns: the Gateway's listeners define ports, protocols, hostnames, and TLS (certificateRefs); HTTPRoutes bind to listeners and supply routing rules. Putting certs on the route or the class are both category errors the exam will offer. The Secret itself is the same kubernetes.io/tls type Ingress used.

q: You run kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80 and share your laptop's IP with a teammate. They cannot connect, though it works on your own localhost. Why?
options: port-forward is broken for Services — use a pod target
The Service selector is wrong
The office firewall is blocking it
port-forward binds 127.0.0.1 by default — only your own machine can connect. Use --address 0.0.0.0 to listen on all interfaces (and consider the security implication of exposing it to the LAN)
explain: The default bind is localhost-only, a deliberate safety choice: port-forward is a debugging tunnel, not a sharing mechanism. --address 0.0.0.0 opens it to the network — useful for a quick teammate check, but it bypasses every NetworkPolicy and access control, so treat it as temporary. Forwarding to a Service name (vs a pod) is fully supported.

q: Staging needs a full copy of the production database volume for realistic load tests. The CSI driver supports cloning. How do you create the copy?
options: Create a PVC with dataSource: {name: prod-db, kind: PersistentVolumeClaim} — the driver clones the source volume's contents into the new volume. Note: the source PVC must be in the SAME namespace
Copy the data with a temporary pod and kubectl cp
Clone the etcd snapshot — it contains volume data
CSI drivers cannot clone volumes
explain: PVC-to-PVC cloning is the native copy primitive: dataSource referencing a PersistentVolumeClaim asks the provisioner to duplicate the volume. The exam traps are the limits: same-namespace only, and the driver must actually implement cloning (check its docs — not all do). Copying via pods works but is slow and manual; etcd never holds volume bytes.

q: The database is corrupted at 3 PM. You have a VolumeSnapshot taken at 2 PM. How do you get a working volume back?
options: Edit the VolumeSnapshot to mark it writable

Create a NEW PVC with dataSource: {name: db-snap-2pm, kind: VolumeSnapshot, apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io} — the provisioner creates a fresh volume pre-populated from the snapshot; then point the workload at the new PVC
kubectl restore the snapshot in place
Mount the VolumeSnapshot directly as a volume
explain: Snapshots are restore POINTS, not usable volumes: you always materialize a new PVC from them via dataSource, then repoint the workload (update the StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplate reference or the pod's claimName). There is no in-place restore and snapshots are not mountable. The apiGroup field is the detail people forget in the YAML.

q: VolumeSnapshot objects are created but stay not-ready forever; no snapshot content appears. The PVC and driver are healthy. What is the usual missing piece?
options: Snapshots are not supported on any CSI driver
etcd is too slow to record the snapshot

No VolumeSnapshotClass exists for the driver (or the external-snapshotter sidecar is not deployed) — the snapshot controller needs a class to know HOW to snapshot. Create the class or install the sidecar, matching the driver's documented setup
The PVC is too large to snapshot
explain: Volume snapshots need the same triangle as provisioning: the CRDs, the external-snapshotter sidecar, and a VolumeSnapshotClass naming the driver — miss any one and snapshots sit pending silently. This mirrors the 'PVC Pending with no provisioner events' failure from dynamic provisioning: the API accepts the object, nothing acts on it. Size is irrelevant to the mechanism.

q: Two pods on the SAME node both mount an RWO volume read-write and corrupt the filesystem. The scheduler allowed it because RWO only constrains node attach, not pod count. Which access mode prevents even single-node multi-writer attach?
options: ReadWriteMany — that allows MORE writers, not fewer
ReadOnlyMany — that is for read-only sharing
RWO is sufficient — the corruption must have another cause
ReadWriteOncePod — restricts the volume to exactly ONE pod in the whole cluster, enforced at attach time
explain: EXAM TRAP: RWO = one NODE may mount read-write, but every pod on that node can then mount it — the 'Once' never meant one pod. ReadWriteOncePod (GA since 1.29) is the stricter mode: a single pod cluster-wide, which is what databases-with-local-disks actually want. If your scenario says 'exactly one writer, guaranteed,' RWOP is the answer, not RWO.

q: NFS-backed PVCs mount with NFSv3 by default, but the app needs NFSv4 locking semantics. Where do you set the NFS version?
options: In the StorageClass mountOptions: ["nfsvers=4.1"] — mount options are passed to the mount syscall for every volume provisioned from the class
In the pod spec's volumeMount
It cannot be changed — the server dictates the version
In the kubelet config on every node
explain: mountOptions on the StorageClass is the lever for mount-time flags (nfsvers, hard/soft, rsize/wsize) — it applies uniformly to every dynamic volume from that class. Pod specs cannot inject mount flags, and while the server negotiates, the client proposes: nfsvers=4.1 makes the client insist on v4. This is also where you would set options like nosuid for hardening.

q: A pod mounts a healthy, empty PVC, but the app gets 'permission denied' writing to it. ls shows the mount owned by root:root. What is the standard fix?
options: chmod 777 from a debug pod — works once, breaks on every reprovision
Set securityContext.fsGroup on the pod — the kubelet recursively chowns the volume to the fsGroup (and applies group read/write), so the app's user can write
Run the container as root
Delete and recreate the PVC — ownership is set at provision time only
explain: Fresh provisioned volumes are root-owned; fsGroup is the designed fix — kubelet chowns/chmods the volume at mount to the given group. The exam trap is reaching for runAsUser: root or 777, which 'works' by abandoning the security model. fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch is the performance-tuned variant for huge volumes (skips the recursive chown when already correct).

q: An app reads config from a ConfigMap mounted as a volume. After you edit the ConfigMap, the file updates within a minute — EXCEPT for one key mounted with subPath, which stays stale forever. What explains the asymmetry?
options: Restart the kubelet to pick up subPath changes
ConfigMaps are immutable once mounted

subPath mounts are bind-mounts of a single file taken at container start — they NEVER receive ConfigMap updates, while whole-volume mounts sync via the kubelet's eventual consistency (~1 min). Drop subPath or roll the pod to refresh
Volume-mounted ConfigMaps never update — the first observation was a fluke
explain: EXAM TRAP, and a brutal one in production: the kubelet syncs whole ConfigMap/Secret volume mounts automatically, but subPath is implemented as a bind mount resolved once at container creation — updates never propagate. If you need live config AND single-file granularity, you must roll the pods (or use a reloader sidecar). Knowing which mount style updates is exactly the kind of detail the CKA probes.

q: A pod needs three things in ONE directory: a TLS cert (Secret), app config (ConfigMap), and its own pod name (downward API). Three separate mounts is clumsy. What is the single-volume answer?
options: An emptyDir with an initContainer that copies everything in
A hostPath combining the sources
Three subPath mounts from three volumes
A projected volume — it projects secret, configMap, downwardAPI, (and serviceAccountToken) sources into a single directory, each with optional items/path mapping
explain: Projected volumes exist to merge multiple volume sources into one mount — the canonical answer for 'cert + config + metadata in one dir.' Each source keeps its own update semantics (secret/configMap refresh, downwardAPI static). The initContainer-copy pattern freezes values at start and triples the moving parts; subPath triples the mounts without merging anything.

q: Each replica needs 10Gi of real provisioned scratch space that is created automatically with the pod, counts against storage quota, and is garbage-collected when the pod dies. No PV admin allowed. Which volume type?
options: ephemeral with a volumeClaimTemplate — the ephemeral controller creates a real PVC per pod (quota-enforced, StorageClass-provisioned) and deletes it with the pod. This is generic ephemeral volumes, distinct from emptyDir
emptyDir — pod-scoped and auto-cleaned, but not quota-tracked as storage and not StorageClass-provisioned
hostPath — ties data to a node and never cleans up
One hand-made PVC per replica
explain: Generic ephemeral volumes are PVCs with pod lifetime: full StorageClass features (provisioning, quota accounting, snapshots) without manual claim management. emptyDir is the lightweight alternative but lives outside the storage subsystem — no quotas, no snapshots, node-disk backed. The exam distinction: 'needs real storage semantics per pod, zero admin' is ephemeral; 'throwaway scratch' is emptyDir.

q: Your StorageClass still uses provisioner: kubernetes.io/aws-ebs. New clusters warn that in-tree provisioners are deprecated. What is the migration?
options: Ignore the warning — in-tree provisioners work forever
Install the EBS CSI driver and move the StorageClass to provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com — CSI is the supported path; CSI migration transparently translates old in-tree volume references
Switch to NFS to avoid the issue
Provisioner names are cosmetic — any string works
explain: In-tree storage plugins were extracted to CSI drivers years ago; the kubernetes.io/* provisioners are deprecated shims. The migration is mechanical: deploy the vendor's CSI driver (with its sidecars) and point the StorageClass at the CSI provisioner name. CSI migration handles existing volumes' translation. Ignoring deprecation warnings is how you end up surprised on upgrade day.

q: Every new PVC stays Pending with the event 'multiple default StorageClasses found'. The provisioners are healthy. What happened?
options: The provisioner is misconfigured
The default StorageClass concept is broken — specify a class on every PVC forever
Two StorageClasses carry the storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class annotation — the defaulting admission cannot choose between them. Remove the annotation from one so exactly one default exists
Delete both StorageClasses and recreate one
explain: Exactly one StorageClass may be the default; the annotation on two of them makes 'omitted storageClassName' ambiguous, so the admission controller refuses to default anything. The fix is removing the annotation from one (kubectl patch storageclass ... -p '{"metadata": {"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"false"}}}'). The provisioner is innocent — this fails before provisioning is even attempted.

q: A pod uses hostPath: /data/cache. It works on old nodes but fails on fresh nodes with the path missing. What is the robust fix, and what is the caveat?
options: SSH to every new node and mkdir — toil that never ends
hostPath always exists — the error must be elsewhere
Use a DaemonSet to create the directory ahead of time

Set hostPath.type: DirectoryOrCreate — the kubelet creates the directory if absent. Caveat: it is created as root with restrictive perms, so pair it with appropriate ownership handling — and remember hostPath remains a portability red flag
explain: DirectoryOrCreate is the self-healing hostPath type (siblings: Directory, File, Socket, CharDevice for strict existence checks). It removes the fresh-node failure, but the created dir is root-owned — combine with fsGroup or initContainer chown as needed.
