The trap is assuming 'omitted means Ingress-only' — the default follows the rules you wrote, and it applies to all selected pods immediately.

q: A StatefulSet named db with a headless Service named db-svc should give each pod a stable DNS name like db-0.db-svc.default.svc.cluster.local, but nslookup db-0.db-svc fails. The Service and StatefulSet exist. What field wires the pod's DNS subdomain?
options: spec.subdomain: db-svc on the pod template — the pod's hostname plus subdomain forms its DNS name; without it the pod gets no such record
The StatefulSet's serviceName already does this — the failure must be CoreDNS
Pods never get DNS names, only Services do
Set hostname: db-0 on the pod — hostnames alone create no DNS records
explain: Stable per-pod DNS needs two halves: the headless Service (which publishes the records) and spec.subdomain matching the Service name on the pod template (which tells DNS under which domain to publish the pod's hostname). serviceName on the StatefulSet governs which Service owns the pods, not DNS publication. Hostname without subdomain yields no record.

q: Corporate networking demands ClusterIPs come from 172.30.0.0/16 instead of the default 10.96.0.0/12. Where is the ClusterIP range set?
options: kubectl edit the kubernetes Service — the range follows the edited IP
A NetworkPolicy — policies filter, they do not allocate
It is fixed at 10.96.0.0/12 and cannot be changed
The API server's --service-cluster-ip-range flag (set at cluster build time via the kubeadm ClusterConfiguration networking.serviceSubnet) — it is init-time configuration, not editable in place
explain: --service-cluster-ip-range is an API server startup flag, configured in kubeadm via networking.serviceSubnet; like the pod CIDR it is an init-time decision. Editing the kubernetes Service changes one IP, not the allocator's range, and there is no in-place renumbering — the range is chosen at build time.

q: You want canary routing by request header (X-Canary: always goes to v2) rather than by weight, using ingress-nginx. Which annotations do this?
options: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: '100' — weight splits by percentage, not by header
A second Ingress with the same host — the two conflict instead of splitting

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: 'true' with nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: 'X-Canary' (and canary-by-header-value) — matching requests route to the canary backend, everything else to primary
Header-based routing requires a service mesh; ingress-nginx cannot do it
explain: ingress-nginx's canary-by-header (optionally pinned to a header value) routes only matching requests to the canary — the standard header-gated canary without a mesh. Weight-based canary is the percentage sibling, a duplicate host Ingress merges/conflicts rather than conditionally routing, and no mesh is required.

q: A NetworkPolicy ingress rule has one from entry containing BOTH a namespaceSelector (team: blue) and a podSelector (app: api). Another rule has two from entries: one with the namespaceSelector, one with the podSelector. How do the two rules differ?
options: They are identical — selectors always OR together

The single entry ANDs them (pods labeled app: api IN namespaces labeled team: blue); the two entries OR them (pods in blue namespaces, plus api pods in ANY namespace) — selectors combine with AND inside one entry, OR across entries
The single entry is invalid — a from entry may hold only one selector
namespaceSelector and podSelector cannot appear in the same policy
explain: Boolean logic of NetworkPolicy peers: within one from/to entry, selectors are ANDed; across entries, they are ORed. The single-entry form is the tight 'api pods of team blue'; the two-entry form is far broader. A from entry may freely combine namespaceSelector, podSelector, and ipBlock — the exam tests whether you know which connective applies where.

q: Pods resolve myservice.myns.svc.cluster.local fine, but myservice.myns.svc.cluster.local:8080 fails from a debug tool while the port is correct. Meanwhile CoreDNS logs show no errors. Which CoreDNS plugin actually serves the cluster.local zone, and what should you check first?
options: The forward plugin serves cluster.local — check the upstream DNS

The kubernetes plugin serves cluster.local — check that the Service's port is actually named/declared and that endpoints exist; DNS only resolves names, never ports, so a 'port resolution' failure is really a connectivity or Service-definition problem
The hosts plugin serves cluster.local — check the Corefile hosts entries
The proxy plugin — check its upstream list
explain: The kubernetes plugin owns the cluster.local zone (forward handles everything else upstream). The deeper lesson: DNS never resolves ports — SRV records aside, 'name:port fails' means the name resolved and the connection failed, so the investigation is endpoints, selectors, and the Service's port declaration, not CoreDNS. The plugin list matters because editing the wrong stanza (forward vs kubernetes) fixes nothing.

q: A legacy single-writer application must never have two pods mount its volume — not even on different nodes, where plain ReadWriteOnce would technically allow a second mount. Which access mode enforces single-pod mounting cluster-wide?
options: ReadWriteOncePod — it restricts the volume to exactly one pod in the whole cluster, closing the multi-node RWO loophole
ReadWriteOnce — that already guarantees one pod; the extra mode is redundant
ReadOnlyMany — that allows many readers, the opposite of what is needed
ReadWriteMany — that allows many writers, the opposite of what is needed
explain: ReadWriteOnce limits writers to one NODE, but two pods on different nodes can each mount the same RWO volume (the classic split-brain corruption). ReadWriteOncePod tightens this to one POD cluster-wide — the mode designed for applications that cannot tolerate any concurrent access. ReadOnlyMany/ReadWriteMany widen access instead of narrowing it.

q: A high-performance database wants the raw block device (/dev/xvdf) rather than a formatted filesystem, to manage its own storage layout. Which volumeMode and mount style does the pod use?
options: volumeMode: Filesystem with a mount — the database gets a directory, not a device
volumeMode: Block is not supported by Kubernetes; databases must use filesystems
volumeMode: Block on the PV/PVC, consumed via volumeDevices (devicePath: /dev/xvdf) instead of volumeMounts — the container sees the raw device
hostPath to /dev/xvdf — the only way to reach raw devices
explain: volumeMode: Block provisions the volume as a raw block device, and the pod consumes it through volumeDevices with a devicePath — no filesystem, no mount. Filesystem mode always formats and mounts. Block volumes are a first-class CSI feature, and hostPath is a node-local hack that bypasses dynamic provisioning entirely.

q: You scale a StatefulSet from 5 replicas to 2 for the weekend. On Monday you scale back to 5 — and the old PVCs (with Friday's data) are gone, deleted during the scale-down. Which StatefulSet field controls whether scaled-down PVCs are kept?
options: reclaimPolicy on the StorageClass — that governs PV deletion when the PVC is deleted, not whether the PVC is deleted

persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy (whenDeleted: Retain / whenScaled: Retain) — it decides whether the StatefulSet controller deletes the PVCs on scale-down or on StatefulSet deletion; the default deletes them
volumeClaimTemplates cannot be retained; this data loss is unavoidable
The reclaimPolicy of the PV — same as the StorageClass option, wrong layer
explain: persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy (GA since 1.27) separates the two deletion events: whenScaled and whenDeleted, each Retain or Delete. The default deletes PVCs on scale-down — the 'weekend scale-down ate my data' surprise. StorageClass reclaimPolicy only decides what happens to the PV after its PVC is gone; it cannot save a PVC the controller already deleted.

q: A Deployment mounts an optional feature-flag ConfigMap. In clusters where the ConfigMap does not exist, the pods must still start (running without the flags) instead of blocking in ContainerCreating. Which volume field allows the missing ConfigMap?
options: No field — a missing ConfigMap always blocks pod startup
Delete the volume when the ConfigMap is absent — that requires a second manifest
Mount it as an environment variable instead — env injection from a missing ConfigMap fails the same way
optional: true on the configMap volume source — the kubelet skips a missing optional ConfigMap (or Secret) instead of failing the mount
explain: optional: true makes the volume source lenient: if the ConfigMap/Secret does not exist, the pod starts without it (env vars from it are simply unset). Without it, the kubelet blocks container creation waiting for the object — the 'pod stuck in ContainerCreating because someone deleted the ConfigMap' outage. It applies to both configMap and secret volumes and env sources.

q: A pod uses emptyDir with medium: Memory for a fast tmpfs cache. Under load the node starts evicting the pod, and describe shows the emptyDir grew to 4 GB. Which field caps a tmpfs emptyDir, and what happens at the cap?
options: resources.limits.memory on the container — that caps the container, not the tmpfs volume
emptyDir volumes cannot be capped; tmpfs always grows to RAM size
The kubelet evicts based on node pressure only; per-volume caps do not exist
sizeLimit on the emptyDir — for medium: Memory it caps the tmpfs; exceeding it triggers pod eviction, just like exceeding a container's memory limit
explain: sizeLimit bounds the emptyDir (and for tmpfs, exceeding it evicts the pod — the kubelet treats it like a memory limit). Without it, a tmpfs emptyDir grows until node memory pressure evicts something, usually your pod. Container memory limits do not cover tmpfs volumes, which is exactly how the cache escaped accounting.

q: Each replica of a Deployment must write its logs to a per-pod subdirectory of a shared volume: /logs/<pod-name>/. The pod name is not known when you write the manifest. How do you template the path?
options: subPathExpr: logs-$(POD_NAME) with env POD_NAME from the downward API (fieldRef: metadata.name) — subPathExpr expands environment variables, unlike plain subPath
subPath: logs-$(POD_NAME) — plain subPath does no variable expansion
One PVC per pod with the name hardcoded — that defeats the Deployment model
hostPath with the pod name — the name is still unknown at manifest time
explain: subPathExpr is the expanding variant of subPath: it resolves $(VAR) references against the container's environment, so pairing it with a downward-API POD_NAME yields per-pod directories from one shared volume. Plain subPath takes the literal string (creating a directory literally named '$(POD_NAME)'), and per-pod PVCs abandon the Deployment abstraction.

q: A pod mounts its ServiceAccount token via a projected volume. Months later the token is rotated by the cluster, and the pod keeps working with the new credentials without a restart. Why did the projected volume pick up the rotation while an old-style Secret volume would not?
options: Projected volumes poll the API continuously; Secret volumes are write-once

The projected serviceAccountToken volume is refreshed by the kubelet on the token's rotation schedule — projected tokens are short-lived and auto-renewed, while legacy long-lived Secret tokens never rotated at all
The pod was restarted by the deployment controller
Tokens never rotate; the pod is using a cached copy
explain: Projected ServiceAccount tokens are bound, audience-scoped, and short-lived: the kubelet refreshes the projected file before expiry, so rotation is transparent. The legacy auto-generated Secret tokens were effectively immortal (and are being phased out) — 'rotation' was never a thing for them. No polling magic and no restart: the kubelet owns the refresh.

q: You mount a ConfigMap with 50 keys, but the app needs only two of them as specifically-named files: db.host and db.port (the keys are named database_hostname and database_port). How do you control the file names?
options: Rename the ConfigMap keys — that breaks the other 48 consumers
The file names always equal the key names; selective renaming is impossible
Use the volume's items list: [{key: database_hostname, path: db.host}, {key: database_port, path: db.port}] — items maps chosen keys to arbitrary file paths and excludes everything else
Mount the ConfigMap twice — mounts cannot rename keys
explain: The items array on configMap/secret volumes is the key-to-path mapper: each entry selects one key and the filename it appears as, and unlisted keys are not mounted at all. Default behavior (no items) mounts every key under its own name — fine until you need renaming or subsetting. Renaming keys is a breaking change for other consumers, and double mounts do not rename.

q: A developer dynamically provisions a PVC, deletes it after testing, and is shocked that the 500 GB cloud disk — and its data — vanished with it. Which default caused this, and where is it set?
options: PVs are always deleted with their PVC; data loss on delete is unavoidable
The developer should have used a Retain StorageClass — but nothing is Retain by default

reclaimPolicy: Delete is the default for dynamically provisioned volumes, set on the StorageClass — the provisioner deletes the backing disk when the PVC is deleted. Set reclaimPolicy: Retain on the StorageClass to keep disks after PVC deletion
The CSI driver has a bug; reclaim should default to Retain
explain: Dynamic provisioning defaults to Delete: PVC deletion cascades to the PV and the cloud disk. It is the StorageClass's reclaimPolicy that sets this, and Retain must be chosen deliberately per class. The 'test PVC ate the disk' story is the canonical lesson — for anything precious, the class should Retain and a human should delete the disk.

q: You edit a PVC from 50Gi to 100Gi. The API accepts it, the StorageClass allows expansion, but the driver documentation says shrinking is not supported. A teammate asks to shrink a different PVC from 100Gi to 50Gi to save money. What happens?
options: The shrink succeeds — expansion support implies shrink support
The API accepts the edit and the filesystem shrinks on next pod restart
The shrink is rejected: Kubernetes does not support shrinking volumes at all — the PVC edit will be denied or ignored, and the only path is creating a smaller PVC and migrating data
Shrinking works if you delete the pod first
explain: Volume shrinking is unsupported by design: filesystems cannot reliably give back capacity, so the API will not shrink a PVC regardless of pod state. The supported path is a new smaller PVC plus data migration (or a snapshot-restore to a smaller size where the driver allows). Expansion is one-way — size your initial claims with that in mind.

q: A shared NFS volume must be writable by containers running as different UIDs, all members of group 2000. fsGroup: 2000 sets the group on the mount, but files created by one container are not group-writable for the others. Which supplemental setting fixes group collaboration?
options: runAsUser: 2000 — that changes the user, not group write access
supplementalGroups: [2000] on the pod securityContext — every container process gains the group, so group-permissioned files are accessible across containers
fsGroupChangePolicy — that only controls how fast group ownership is applied
chmod 777 the mount in an initContainer — it works until the next file is created with a restrictive umask
explain: supplementalGroups adds the group to every container process's group set: with the volume group-owned and group-writable, all containers collaborate regardless of their runAsUser. fsGroup fixes the mount's group ownership but not the processes' membership. chmod 777 is a recurring toil and a security smell, and runAsUser changes identity rather than group access.

q: A team puts a database on local persistent volumes for speed. A node dies permanently. What is the state of the data, and what architectural assumption did the team get wrong?
options: The data fails over to another node automatically — local volumes replicate
The data is intact on the dead node's disk and Kubernetes reattaches it elsewhere — it does not; the disk is gone with the node

The data is lost with the node: local volumes are tied to one machine with no replication — the team assumed storage failover that local volumes never provide. Databases on local PVs need application-level replication
A snapshot restores it automatically — snapshots are not automatic
explain: Local volumes are exactly what the name says: a directory or disk on one node, with zero replication and zero failover. Node death is data death unless the application replicates (or you snapshot elsewhere). Teams choose local PVs for latency and then rediscover the durability tradeoff at the worst moment — the exam wants you to name it upfront.

q: You restore a VolumeSnapshot into a new PVC in namespace reporting, but the snapshot lives in namespace prod. The PVC stays Pending with a complaint about the data source. What is the rule?
options: Snapshots are cluster-scoped and usable from any namespace — the Pending state must be a driver bug

dataSource must reference a snapshot in the SAME namespace as the new PVC — cross-namespace restore needs dataSourceRef (the newer field) with explicit namespace permission, not the classic dataSource
Copy the snapshot object YAML to the reporting namespace — snapshots are portable manifests
Snapshots can only be restored in the namespace where the driver runs
explain: The classic dataSource field is namespace-local: the referenced VolumeSnapshot must live in the PVC's namespace. Cross-namespace restore is the job of dataSourceRef, which carries its own authorization rules. Copying the snapshot manifest does not copy the snapshotted data, and driver-namespace placement is irrelevant to the API rule.

q: Two CSI drivers both claim to support volume expansion. Driver A grows the volume while the pod keeps running; Driver B requires the pod to be stopped first. Which Kubernetes concept distinguishes these, and where is it declared?
options: There is no distinction — all expansion is online
The StorageClass declares it with allowVolumeExpansion: true — that flag only permits expansion, it says nothing about online vs offline

The CSIDriver object's spec (requires online vs offline expansion is a driver capability the cluster discovers) — but practically, the exam point is: online expansion needs filesystem support and the driver to handle it; offline expansion needs the pod stopped so the node can resize before remount
Pods must always be deleted for any resize
explain: allowVolumeExpansion merely authorizes resizing; whether it happens online or requires pod downtime is a driver/filesystem capability. Online expansion resizes the mounted filesystem live; offline needs the volume unmounted (pod stopped) first. Assuming every driver does online expansion is how you schedule a resize that never completes until someone kills the pod.

q: Compliance wants the TLS key file at 0400 but the rest of the Secret volume's files at the default 0644. Where do you set per-file permissions on a Secret volume?
options: defaultMode on the volume — that sets one mode for every file, not per-file
The mode field on individual items entries: items: [{key: tls.key, path: tls.key, mode: 0400}] — per-item modes override defaultMode for that file
chmod in a postStart hook — racy and reverted on volume refresh
Secret file modes are fixed at 0644 and cannot be changed
explain: Each items entry accepts its own mode, overriding the volume's defaultMode for that file — the precise tool for 'key file locked down, rest default.' defaultMode is the blunt instrument for the whole volume, postStart chmod races the kubelet's periodic volume refresh, and modes are fully configurable.

q: A monitoring agent needs to read the node's /etc/machine-id file (a single file, not a directory) from a DaemonSet pod. Which hostPath configuration does this correctly?
options: hostPath: {path: /etc/machine-id} with no type — it works until the file is missing, when the mount behaves unexpectedly
hostPath: {path: /etc/machine-id, type: File} — the type check fails the mount clearly if the path is not a file, instead of silently mounting whatever is there
hostPath: {path: /etc, type: Directory} and read machine-id inside — it over-mounts the whole directory for one file
hostPath cannot mount single files, only directories
explain: The hostPath type field (File, Directory, Socket, CharDevice, BlockDevice, and the OrCreate variants) validates the target before mounting: type: File refuses to mount if /etc/machine-id is missing or a directory, failing fast instead of surprising you. Omitting type mounts blindly, and mounting all of /etc for one file widens the pod's host access for no reason.

q: On AWS, the team needs EBS volumes as gp3 with encryption enabled, provisioned dynamically. Where do these driver-specific settings live?
options: In the PVC spec — PVCs stay portable and driver-agnostic
As annotations on the pod — the driver does not read pod annotations
In the StorageClass parameters (e.g. type: gp3, encrypted: 'true') — parameters are the driver's configuration surface; the PVC only names the class
In the CSIDriver object — that registers capabilities, not per-volume settings
explain: StorageClass parameters are the per-driver settings channel: type, iops, encrypted, and friends are interpreted by the provisioner named in provisioner. PVCs remain portable by referencing only the class name. Pod annotations are invisible to the provisioner, and the CSIDriver object describes capabilities (like expansion support), not volume configuration.

q: You pre-provisioned a special high-IOPS PV (labeled tier: platinum) and need one specific PVC to bind to it — not to any dynamically provisioned volume. How do you steer the binding?
options: Name the PV in the PVC spec — PVCs cannot name a PV directly
Put a selector on the PVC: selector: {matchLabels: {tier: platinum}} — the binder matches the PVC only to PVs with those labels
Label the PVC tier: platinum — labels on the claim do not influence binding
Binding is random; create the PVC and hope
explain: PVC selector.matchLabels is the directed-binding mechanism: the controller binds the claim only to an available PV carrying those labels. PVCs cannot name PVs, claim labels are cosmetic for binding, and binding is deterministic — label selectors are the steering wheel.

q: A PV was manually created with claimRef pointing at PVC data-0. That PVC was deleted long ago, but the PV still shows as Bound and no new PVC will take it. What is wrong and how do you free it?
options: The PV is permanently stuck; delete and recreate it
The stale claimRef still binds the PV to the deleted claim's identity — clear it (kubectl edit pv and remove the claimRef, or recycle/delete per reclaimPolicy) so the PV returns to Available
PVs bind by name automatically once the old PVC is gone — just wait
Change the new PVC's name to data-0 — names must match claimRef
explain: claimRef is a one-way reservation: once set (manually or by binding), the PV stays Bound to that claim UID even after the PVC is deleted. Clearing the claimRef releases the PV back to Available for new claims. Waiting fixes nothing, renaming the new PVC to match a stale UID cannot work, and recreating the PV is unnecessary surgery.

q: A cache needs disk space that must survive container restarts (so a crash does not cold-start the cache) but must NOT survive pod deletion (stale cache on reschedule causes bugs). Which volume type matches this lifecycle exactly?
options: A PVC — it survives pod deletion, violating the second requirement
hostPath — it survives pod deletion AND node reuse, and leaks across pods
emptyDir — its lifetime is the pod's: it survives container crashes/restarts but is deleted with the pod
A ConfigMap volume — it is read-only and config-sized
explain: emptyDir's lifecycle is precisely 'the pod': created with the pod, shared across its containers and restarts, destroyed with the pod. That matches 'survive crash, die with pod' exactly. PVCs outlive the pod (stale cache bug), hostPath outlives it and is node-scoped (worse), and ConfigMaps are not writable scratch space.

q: After a containerd upgrade, the kubelet will not start: 'failed to run Kubelet: failed to get the container runtime endpoint: rpc error'. The containerd service itself is running. Where is the disconnect?
options: The kubelet's --container-runtime-endpoint still points at the old socket path (e.g. unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock moved or the config was reset) — verify the socket exists and the kubelet flag/config matches the runtime's actual socket
The API server is down — that would break kubectl, not the kubelet's local startup
The CNI plugin is missing — that blocks pods, not kubelet startup
Reinstall Kubernetes — the runtime upgrade corrupted the cluster
explain: The kubelet dials the runtime over a socket; an upgrade that moves or resets the socket path breaks that dial with an rpc error at startup. Checking the socket file and the kubelet's configured endpoint is the two-minute diagnosis. A down API server, a missing CNI, or a full reinstall are all the wrong layer — the error is local IPC, not cluster state.

q: After a security tool's validating webhook went down, EVERY pod creation in the cluster fails — including in kube-system. Deleting the webhook configuration is proposed. What is the mechanism, and what is the safer immediate fix?
options: Webhooks are advisory; the failures must come from elsewhere
Delete the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration — the only fix, and safe
The webhook's failurePolicy: Fail blocks admission when the webhook is unreachable — set failurePolicy: Ignore (or fix/scale the webhook) so a down webhook fails open instead of bricking the cluster
Restart the API server — it caches webhook failures permanently
explain: failurePolicy: Fail means 'if you cannot ask the webhook, deny the request' — a down webhook then vetoes all matching admissions cluster-wide. Ignore fails open: admissions proceed unvalidated until the webhook recovers. Deleting the configuration works but discards the policy; the exam-correct framing is Fail-closed vs Fail-open, chosen deliberately per webhook's criticality.

q: You try to change a Deployment's selector (app: web to app: web-v2) via kubectl apply, and the API rejects it: field is immutable. The pods need the new selector. What is the required procedure?
options: kubectl edit and force it — the API will accept with --force

Delete and recreate the Deployment with the new selector (pausing/ deleting with --cascade=orphan first if you want zero pod churn, then adopting) — selectors are immutable because changing them would orphan or steal pods unpredictably
Selectors are advisory; the change applies on the next rollout automatically
Scale to zero first — scaling unlocks the selector field
explain: Pod-template selectors are immutable by design: allowing changes would let a Deployment silently adopt or abandon live pods. The supported path is recreating the object (with --cascade=orphan to keep pods running, then deleting the orphan ReplicaSet, for a zero-downtime variant). --force does not override immutability, and scaling never unlocks the field.

q: A pod referencing Secret api-keys is stuck: 'CreateContainerConfigError: secret "api-keys" not found'. The Deployment applied cleanly yesterday and nobody touched the Secret. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: Secrets are namespaced — the pod is in a different namespace than the Secret, or the Secret was deleted. Recreate the Secret in the pod's namespace (or fix the namespace)
The kubelet caches Secrets for 24h; wait for the cache to clear
CreateContainerConfigError is always an image problem — check the image tag
Secrets replicate across namespaces automatically after a delay; just wait
explain: CreateContainerConfigError on a Secret means the kubelet cannot fetch it: wrong namespace (Secrets do not cross namespaces) or deleted. The fix is the Secret existing in the pod's namespace — recreate it or correct the deployment's namespace. There is no 24h cache for missing Secrets, no cross-namespace replication, and the image is irrelevant to config errors.

q: Two pods died. Pod A shows exit code 137, pod B shows exit code 143. A teammate treats both as OOMKills. What do the codes actually mean?
options: Both are OOMKills — 143 is just the newer code

137 means the container was SIGKILLed (OOMKill is the common cause, but so is exceeding a deadline or manual kill); 143 means SIGTERM followed by exit — the graceful-shutdown path (scale-down, rolling update, eviction with grace). Conflating them misdiagnoses normal terminations as memory problems
143 is worse than 137 — it means the node itself died
Exit codes are random; neither is diagnostic
explain: 137 = 128+9 (SIGKILL): OOMKill is the usual suspect but any SIGKILL lands here. 143 = 128+15 (SIGTERM): the container received SIGTERM and exited — the normal, graceful path during rollouts and scale-downs. Reading every 143 as an OOMKill sends you tuning memory limits for a pod that was simply updated. The codes are 128+signal, fully deterministic.

q: A pod stays Pending: '0/4 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient ephemeral-storage'. CPU and memory are plentiful. What is ephemeral-storage, and where is the pressure?
options: Ephemeral-storage is node-local disk used for container writable layers, logs, and emptyDir volumes — the nodes' disks (or the kubelet's reserved thresholds) are exhausted. Free disk, raise eviction thresholds, or set ephemeral-storage requests/limits so the scheduler accounts for it
It is the same as RAM — add memory to the nodes
It refers to etcd storage — compact etcd
The message is cosmetic; the real problem is CPU
explain: Ephemeral storage is the node's local disk as the kubelet sees it: image layers, container overlays, logs, emptyDir. 'Insufficient ephemeral-storage' with free CPU/RAM is a disk problem — full /var/lib/kubelet or /var/log, often from unbounded logs or huge emptyDirs. It is schedulable like CPU/memory (requests/limits supported), and etcd is unrelated to pod scheduling.

q: A pod runs a backup script as its main container. It completes successfully in 40 seconds — then the pod goes CrashLoopBackOff, rerunning the backup endlessly. The script is fine. What is the design error?
options: The script needs restartPolicy: Never — but bare pods do not run to completion and stay done

The pod's restartPolicy: Always restarts the container even after clean exit code 0 — a run-to-completion workload in a bare pod with Always restarts forever. Use a Job (or restartPolicy: Never/OnFailure) for finite work
CrashLoopBackOff only happens on errors; exit 0 cannot cause it
The image is corrupted — repull it
explain: restartPolicy: Always means 'keep this container running forever' — a clean exit is still an exit, so the kubelet restarts it, producing the CrashLoopBackOff on a healthy script. Finite work belongs in a Job (which tracks completions) or at minimum restartPolicy: Never/OnFailure. The script succeeding is exactly why the loop is confusing: the failure is in the workload type, not the code.

q: Pods fail with ErrImagePull: 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority' against the company's private registry, which uses an internal CA. A manual curl from the node works after the CA was added to the OS trust store. Why does the kubelet still fail, and where does containerd need the CA?
options: The imagePullSecret is missing — but this is a TLS trust failure, not an auth failure
The nodes need a reboot — trust stores reload without one

containerd does not use the OS trust store for registry TLS by default: configure the registry's CA under the containerd certs directory (e.g. /etc/containerd/certs.d/<registry>/hosts.toml with ca = ...) or the registry TLS config, then restart containerd
The registry must use a public CA — internal CAs are unsupported
explain: x509 'unknown authority' is TLS trust, not credentials: containerd validates the registry's certificate against its own configured CAs, not the host OS bundle. The fix is registering the internal CA in containerd's per-registry TLS config (certs.d/hosts.toml). imagePullSecrets carry auth credentials — a different failure with a different message — and internal CAs work fine once trusted.

q: From a pod in namespace frontend, curl http://api:8080 fails with 'Could not resolve host: api', but curl http://api.backend:8080 works. The Service api exists. What is the resolution rule you tripped over?
options: Short names only resolve in the pod's OWN namespace — api lives in backend, so the pod must use api.backend (or the FQDN). The search domains cover the pod's namespace, not every namespace
CoreDNS is down — but then the FQDN would fail too
Services are only reachable by FQDN; short names never work
The Service needs an ExternalName for cross-namespace access
explain: Unqualified names resolve against the pod's own namespace via the resolv.conf search list — api means api.frontend here, which does not exist. Cross-namespace traffic needs the namespace-qualified name (api.backend) or FQDN. CoreDNS is healthy (the qualified name works), short names work fine within the namespace, and ExternalName is for external targets, not cross-namespace Services.

q: A deploy pipeline's ServiceAccount gets 'Forbidden' creating Deployments in namespace staging. The Role and RoleBinding look correct to your eyes. Which command definitively tests what the ServiceAccount is allowed to do?
options: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:staging:deployer -n staging — it evaluates the effective RBAC for that identity, no guessing from YAML
kubectl describe role — that shows the Role, not the effective permission
kubectl get rolebinding -o yaml — bindings are only half the picture
Ask the cluster admin — the tooling cannot answer this
explain: kubectl auth can-i --as impersonates the ServiceAccount and asks the API server for the authoritative answer, cutting through YAML-eyeballing (wrong subject name, wrong namespace, missing apiGroup — the usual suspects). describe/get show the declared pieces; can-i shows the evaluated result. It is the fastest RBAC debugger in the toolbox.

q: The API becomes intermittently unresponsive, and kubectl hangs. On the control-plane node, df shows /var/lib/etcd at 100%. What is the failure chain?
options: A full etcd disk blocks writes: etcd raises NOSPACE, the API server cannot persist anything, and all mutating calls hang or fail — free disk (or defrag after compaction), then the API recovers. Reads may still work while writes are dead
The API server needs more CPU; disk is irrelevant to API latency
etcd automatically compacts when full; just wait
Delete the API server pod — it will reschedule with a fresh disk
explain: etcd is the API server's storage: a full backend disk halts all writes (NOSPACE alarm), so creates/updates/deletes hang while reads limp along — the classic 'kubectl get works, kubectl apply hangs' split. Recovery is disk space plus defrag after compaction (deleting API objects alone does not shrink the backend file). CPU is not the constraint, nothing auto-compacts to zero, and the API pod shares the same full disk.

q: A node's disk fills every few weeks. Investigation shows /var/log/containers holding gigabytes of JSON log files from a chatty app. What is the durable fix at the runtime layer?
options: Delete the logs in a cron job — toil that races the next fill-up

Configure container log rotation in the runtime (containerd: max_container_log_line_size / max_log_size via the CRI plugin config, or Docker's json-file log-opts max-size/max-file) — the runtime then rotates logs automatically instead of growing them unbounded
Reduce the app's log verbosity — you do not control the vendor's app
Add a bigger disk — it only postpones the same outage
explain: Container runtimes support log rotation natively (containerd CRI plugin or Docker log-opts): capped file sizes with a kept-file count, enforced at write time. Cron-deletion races the fill and risks deleting a file the runtime holds open; a bigger disk is a slower fuse; and while fixing the app's verbosity is nice, the platform should bound log growth regardless of what apps do.

q: A node shows plenty of free CPU and memory, but new pods will not schedule to it: '0/1 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods'. What limit did you hit?
options: The scheduler is broken — free resources mean it should schedule
A ResourceQuota on pods — that is namespace-scoped, but this message is node-scoped

The kubelet's --max-pods (default 110) — the node hit its pod-count ceiling, which is independent of CPU/memory. Raise it (and ensure the pod CIDR has addresses) if the workload genuinely needs denser packing
The CNI ran out of IPs — that surfaces as IPAM errors, not this message
explain: 'Too many pods' is the max-pods ceiling: the kubelet refuses more pods per node regardless of free CPU/RAM (default 110). It is commonly hit on small nodes or dense batch workloads. The fix is raising --max-pods (with a pod CIDR mask that can address them) — not more RAM, not quota changes, which live at the wrong scope.

q: CoreDNS pods enter CrashLoopBackOff with logs saying 'plugin/loop: Loop detected'. No config change was made recently. What causes the loop plugin to fire?
options: Two CoreDNS replicas querying each other — the loop plugin detects forwarding loops, usually because the node's /etc/resolv.conf points back at the cluster DNS (e.g. systemd-resolved stub pointing at CoreDNS), so queries cycle
The loop plugin is deprecated and fires randomly
Too many Services — DNS cannot scale past 1,000 records
CoreDNS needs more memory; the loop message is a red herring
explain: The loop plugin detects queries returning to CoreDNS itself: the classic cause is the host's resolv.conf forwarding to the cluster DNS IP, which forwards upstream to the host resolver, which forwards back — a cycle. It commonly appears after node DNS changes (systemd-resolved reconfigurations) with no CoreDNS edit at all. The fix is breaking the cycle in host DNS config, not scaling CoreDNS.

q: After enabling TLS on the Ingress, browsers spin with 'too many redirects'. The backend app also redirects HTTP to HTTPS itself. The Ingress terminates TLS and talks HTTP to the backend. What is the loop?
options: The certificate is invalid — browsers redirect on cert errors, they do not; they show warnings

The app sees plain HTTP from the Ingress (TLS was terminated at the edge) and redirects to HTTPS; the Ingress terminates again and re-sends HTTP — an infinite HTTP→HTTPS→HTTP cycle. Fix: make the app trust X-Forwarded-Proto (or terminate TLS at one layer only)
Ingress TLS always causes redirect loops; disable TLS
The redirect comes from the DNS provider, not the cluster
explain: Double termination logic: the app does not know the client used HTTPS because the Ingress stripped TLS, so it 'helpfully' redirects to HTTPS forever. The standard fixes are honoring X-Forwarded-Proto in the app (it already IS https from the client's view) or moving the HTTP→HTTPS redirect solely to the Ingress. Disabling TLS 'fixes' the loop by abandoning security, and browsers do not redirect on cert errors.

q: You applied a default-deny NetworkPolicy, but pods in namespace prod still reach everything. The YAML is valid and kubectl shows the policy exists. What is the most embarrassing — and common — cause?
options: The policy was created in the wrong namespace (e.g. default instead of prod) — NetworkPolicies only select pods in their own namespace, so a misplaced policy enforces nothing where it matters
NetworkPolicies apply cluster-wide regardless of namespace — they do not
The policy needs a ClusterRoleBinding to take effect — policies are not RBAC
Deny policies are not supported; only allow-lists work — default-deny IS the standard pattern
explain: NetworkPolicy is namespaced: podSelector and policyTypes only touch pods in the policy's own namespace. A valid policy in the wrong namespace is silently inert — kubectl shows it, nothing enforces it. The CNI-enforcement question is the deeper cause when the namespace IS right; the wrong namespace is the face-palm cause to check first. Policies need no RBAC binding, and default-deny is fully supported.

q: Pods on node-a reach a ClusterIP Service fine; pods on node-b time out. Pod-to-pod networking works from node-b, and the Service has endpoints. What is node-local and worth checking on node-b?
options: CoreDNS — DNS failures look different (name errors, not timeouts)
The endpoints — they exist, and node-a proves the backends serve
The API server — a down API would break kubectl everywhere, not one node's traffic

kube-proxy on node-b (its pods/logs, iptables/IPVS rules) — ClusterIP routing is programmed per node; a dead or wedged kube-proxy on node-b blackholes that node's Service traffic while everything else works
explain: kube-proxy programs Service routing on every node independently: if node-b's kube-proxy is down or its rules are stale, node-b's pods cannot reach ClusterIPs while node-a is unaffected — the single-node blast radius is the signature. Pod-to-pod traffic bypasses Service IPs (it uses the CNI), which is why it still works. Endpoints existing proves the control plane is fine; the data plane on node-b is the suspect.

q: A node shows NotReady. You SSH in: kubelet is running, containerd is healthy, disk and memory are fine, and the node can curl the API server's /healthz. But kubectl get node still says NotReady. What component renews node readiness, and where is it stuck?
options: The scheduler — it does not set node readiness

The node lease: the kubelet renews its Lease object every ~10s; NotReady with a healthy local kubelet means status updates are not landing — check kubelet logs for update failures (auth, API throttling, or network asymmetry where curl works but the watch/update path does not)
etcd — node status lives in the API, not etcd directly
The CNI — networking affects pods, not the node's Ready condition directly
explain: Node Ready is the kubelet's heartbeat: it renews its Lease and posts status, and the node controller marks NotReady when updates stop arriving. A locally-healthy kubelet with a NotReady node means the updates are failing — kubelet logs will show the rejected writes (expired certs, throttling, or asymmetric network paths where a curl probe succeeds but the API write path fails). The scheduler, etcd, and CNI do not own this signal.

q: A PVC manifest omits storageClassName entirely and stays Pending forever with no provisioner events. kubectl get storageclass shows two classes, but neither is marked default. What is the binding rule, and what are the two fixes?
options: A PVC without storageClassName binds using the cluster's default StorageClass — with no default marked (storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class annotation), nothing provisions it. Fix: set storageClassName explicitly, or annotate one class as the default
PVCs without a class always use the first StorageClass alphabetically — rename a class
The provisioner is down — but a down provisioner would still emit events
Wait — binding without a class takes up to an hour
explain: An empty storageClassName means 'use the default class' — and the default is whichever class carries the is-default-class annotation. With no default, the PVC waits forever with zero provisioner activity (nothing claims it). The two fixes are naming a class on the PVC or designating a default. Provisioner health is irrelevant when no provisioner is ever selected.

q: It is exam day. You need a Deployment manifest fast, but hand-writing YAML from memory risks indentation errors under time pressure. What is the recommended generation workflow?
options: Write it from scratch — memorized YAML is the exam skill being tested
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml — generate the skeleton imperatively, then edit in the probes, resources, and fields the generator does not cover
Copy YAML from the Kubernetes docs website — no browser in the exam
kubectl run --generator — the generator flag was removed years ago
explain: The exam-sanctioned speed workflow is generate-then-edit: --dry-run=client -o yaml produces valid boilerplate (apiVersion, kind, selector, template) that you extend with the task's specifics. Hand-writing everything wastes the clock and invites indentation bugs; the docs site is unavailable in the exam environment; and --generator is long gone. Know the imperative generators cold — they are half the exam's time management.

q: Your team rebuilds dev clusters weekly and the kubeadm init command has grown to a 14-flag monster. Someone mistypes a flag every time. How do you make installs repeatable?
options: Keep the long flag chain in a runbook — flags are the only way to configure kubeadm
Write a config file with kind: ClusterConfiguration (and InitConfiguration) and run kubeadm init --config cluster.yaml — version-controlled, reviewable, and typo-proof
Run kubeadm init with no arguments, then hand-edit the static pod manifests afterward to fix networking and certificates
Use kubeadm init --dry-run to generate the install, then retype the output each time
explain: kubeadm init --config takes a ClusterConfiguration/InitConfiguration file, which is the supported repeatable path — it lives in git and eliminates flag typos. Flags-only doesn't scale, post-hoc manifest edits can't cleanly set cert SANs or CIDRs, and --dry-run validates without installing anything.

q: kubeadm init fails halfway — the API server never came up — and you find and fix the root cause (a full disk). What is the fastest correct path forward?
options: Run kubeadm reset and start completely over — a failed init can never be resumed
Reboot the node — kubeadm detects the partial install and resumes automatically
Run kubeadm join on the node to finish the initialization
Re-run just the failed step with kubeadm init phase <phase> (e.g. kubeadm init phase control-plane apiserver) — phases let you retry one unit of work
explain: kubeadm init is decomposed into phases (certs, etcd, control-plane, kubelet-start, etc.), and kubeadm init phase reruns exactly one — the fast recovery after fixing the underlying issue. Reset wipes everything (overkill), nothing auto-resumes on reboot, and join is for adding nodes to a working cluster, not completing init.

q: Compliance requires the restricted PodSecurityStandard enforced on namespaces. You set the enforce labels, but privileged pods are still admitted. What is missing?
options: The PodSecurity admission plugin must be enabled on the API server via --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml — the labels are policy bindings, the plugin is the enforcement engine
Every namespace including kube-system must carry the label — admission only works cluster-wide
Enable it with --disable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity on the controller-manager
Restart the kube-scheduler — it enforces PodSecurity
explain: Namespace labels declare the desired standard, but nothing enforces them until the PodSecurity admission plugin is enabled on the API server (edit the static pod manifest; the kubelet recreates the pod). Labels alone are inert, the flag is enable not disable, and it belongs on the API server — not the scheduler or controller-manager.

q: You have ~/.kube/config (prod) and a team-provided ~/team-staging.conf. You need both clusters' contexts usable in one kubectl. How?
options: Copy team-staging.conf over ~/.kube/config — kubectl only reads a single file
Run kubectl config use-context — it merges files automatically
Set KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/team-staging.conf and run kubectl config view --merge --flatten to produce one merged kubeconfig
Drop both files in the same directory — kubectl merges co-located files on its own
explain: KUBECONFIG accepts a colon-separated list of files, and kubectl config view --merge --flatten combines them into a single kubeconfig. Overwriting destroys prod access, use-context only switches within the already-loaded config, and directory co-location merges nothing.

q: A CI job needs kubectl access for exactly its 2-hour run. The old approach — a long-lived ServiceAccount token Secret in the repo — leaked last quarter. What is the modern replacement?
options: kubectl create secret generic ci-token — Secrets are the only token source
kubectl create token ci-deployer --duration=2h — a bound, time-limited token that expires automatically when the pipeline ends
Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf into the CI runner — simplest and it always works
Tokens cannot expire, so set a calendar reminder to delete the binding afterward
explain: kubectl create token mints TokenRequest bound tokens with a TTL — least privilege by time, no cleanup to forget. Legacy SA Secrets are long-lived, admin.conf is cluster-admin (never belongs in CI), and bound tokens absolutely do expire.

q: You created ClusterRole db-reader (read-only on the database CRDs) and want everyone with the built-in view role to get it automatically, now and for future bindings. How?
options: Label db-reader rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: "true" — the view ClusterRole's aggregationRule automatically includes every ClusterRole carrying that label
Edit the system view ClusterRole and paste the rules in — system roles are meant to be hand-edited
Create a ClusterRoleBinding from db-reader to each user — aggregation does not exist
Labels on ClusterRoles are cosmetic and change nothing
explain: ClusterRole aggregation (aggregationRule + aggregate-to-* labels) is the designed extension point for the default roles. Hand-editing system roles is discouraged (upgrades can overwrite them), per-user bindings don't scale to future users, and these labels are functional, not cosmetic.

q: A 3-member stacked-etcd cluster loses two control-plane nodes to a rack power failure. The surviving member is healthy. What happens to the API?
options: Writes continue — one healthy member is enough to serve
The survivor elects itself leader and serves reads and writes alone
Reads keep working and writes queue until the members return
The API stops serving — etcd needs a majority (2 of 3) for quorum, and a single remaining member cannot commit anything
explain: Quorum is a majority: 2 of 3. With one member left there is no quorum, so no writes commit and the API is effectively down — etcd does not degrade to single-member mode. Recovery means restoring power/members or restoring from snapshot; restarting the survivor changes nothing.

q: kubectl is sluggish and you suspect etcd, but all the static pods show Running. How do you check etcd member health directly?
options: kubectl get pods -n kube-system — Running means the consensus is healthy
Restart the etcd pods and see whether it gets faster
Run etcdctl endpoint health --cluster (with the etcd PKI certs) to probe every member, plus etcdctl member list to inspect the member table
Check kubelet logs — they report etcd latency
explain: etcdctl endpoint health hits each member's health endpoint and member list shows the cluster's view — pod Running only means the process is up, not that consensus is healthy. Restarting is disruptive guessing, and the kubelet does not monitor etcd.

q: You are planning a 1.31 to 1.32 kubeadm upgrade and the cluster holds years of old manifests. What must you audit BEFORE upgrading?
options: Scan every manifest for apiVersions removed in the target version (e.g. extensions/v1beta1, PodSecurityPolicy) and migrate them — the new API server will reject removed versions outright
Nothing — kubeadm auto-converts all deprecated apiVersions during the upgrade
Skip it — apiVersions are cosmetic and every version is served forever
Run kubeadm upgrade apply --force to bypass API checks
explain: Removed APIs are hard failures after upgrade: objects stored under a removed version become unreadable. Audit with kubectl api-resources and grep, then migrate manifests first. kubeadm never rewrites your manifests, versions are retired on a schedule, and --force cannot conjure a removed API.

q: On a node you must list running containers and pull an image by hand. Docker is not installed — the runtime is containerd. What do you use?
options: Install Docker — Kubernetes requires it for node debugging
crictl ps, crictl images, crictl pull — the CRI-compatible CLI that works against any containerd or CRI-O node
kubectl docker ps — kubectl proxies runtime commands to nodes
crictl was removed — only journalctl works now
explain: crictl is the CRI debugging tool (ps, images, logs, exec, rmi) and ships for exactly this. Docker is unnecessary and often absent, kubectl has no docker subcommand, and crictl is current — not removed.

q: An ex-contractor's bootstrap token may still be valid. How do you audit and revoke join tokens?
options: Tokens cannot be listed — they are write-only by design
Delete /etc/kubernetes/pki — that invalidates every token at once
Tokens self-destruct on first use, so there is nothing to audit
kubeadm token list shows active tokens and their TTLs; kubeadm token delete <token> revokes one immediately
explain: Bootstrap tokens are Secrets in kube-system: listable, with visible TTLs, and deletable. They are not write-only, they do not self-destruct on use (only TTL expiry removes them), and deleting the PKI would destroy the cluster to solve a token problem.

q: A new worker has /etc/kubernetes/bootstrap-kubelet.conf but no kubelet.conf yet. What is bootstrap-kubelet.conf for?
options: It is the bootstrap credential (a short-lived token) the kubelet uses to authenticate its first certificate request — after the CSR is approved the kubelet uses kubelet.conf
It is the kubelet's permanent configuration — kubelet.conf is only a backup
It holds the cluster CA bundle for pods to mount
It is safe to delete before the node joins — the kubelet regenerates it
explain: TLS bootstrap in one line: bootstrap-kubelet.conf authenticates the initial CSR, the signed client cert lands in kubelet.conf, and the bootstrap file becomes irrelevant. It is the temporary credential, not the permanent config, and deleting it pre-join breaks bootstrap.

q: Before debugging a 403, you want to check what a ServiceAccount is allowed to do — without running its workload. Which command does this?
options: kubectl auth can-i only evaluates your own permissions — it cannot check a ServiceAccount
You must launch a test pod as that ServiceAccount and attempt the action
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n team --as=system:serviceaccount:team:deployer — impersonation evaluates RBAC for that identity
Only the audit log can answer this, after the denied request happens
explain: --as impersonates any user or ServiceAccount for an auth check, making can-i the fastest RBAC debugger. It is not self-only, a test pod is slow ceremony, and the audit log is reactive — can-i is proactive.

q: Your provisioning system cannot inject a bootstrap token into new nodes, but it can place files on disk. How can kubeadm join authenticate without a token?
options: It cannot — a bootstrap token is mandatory for every join
kubeadm join --discovery-file=cluster-info.yaml — file-based discovery carries the CA and API endpoint for TLS verification instead of a token
Pass --token="" — empty tokens are accepted when a file is present
The discovery file removes the need for CA verification
explain: --discovery-file supplies the cluster-info content (CA certificates plus API endpoints) so the node can verify TLS without a token. Tokens are not mandatory, empty tokens are rejected, and CA verification still happens — via the file.

q: Air-gapped nodes must pull images from an internal mirror (mirror.corp:5000) instead of registry.k8s.io. Where is this configured for containerd?
options: imagePullSecrets on every pod — the only per-image mechanism available
/etc/docker/daemon.json — containerd reads Docker's daemon config
A kubelet --registry-mirror flag in the kubelet config file
In /etc/containerd/config.toml under the registry.mirrors table, mapping the upstream host to the mirror endpoint — then restart containerd
explain: containerd's CRI plugin registry.mirrors table is the routing mechanism: upstream host → mirror endpoint. imagePullSecrets carry credentials, not routing; there is no Docker daemon to configure; and no --registry-mirror kubelet flag exists.

q: Every pod in namespace payments needs the same imagePullSecret for the private registry. Setting it pod-by-pod is toil. What is the DRY approach?
options: Attach the secret to the namespace's ServiceAccount via imagePullSecrets — every pod using that ServiceAccount inherits it automatically
imagePullSecrets can only be set per-pod — a templating tool must inject it
ServiceAccounts cannot reference secrets
Make the registry public instead of managing secrets
explain: ServiceAccounts carry imagePullSecrets to all their pods — set it once on the SA (commonly default, better a dedicated one). Per-pod is not required, SAs absolutely reference secrets, and exposing the registry trades a toil problem for a security incident.

q: You want to roll out the restricted PodSecurityStandard but fear breaking 200 existing workloads. How do you measure the blast radius BEFORE enforcing?
options: Set enforce: restricted everywhere at once — breakage is the only reliable detector
PodSecurity cannot report violations without enforcing them

Set pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted and pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted first — violations surface as warnings and audit events without blocking anything, then graduate to enforce
Warn and audit modes do not exist — only enforce is a real label value
explain: warn and audit are the staged-rollout modes: full visibility into what WOULD be denied, zero breakage. Enforce-first is reckless at scale, and the modes exist precisely so you never have to guess the blast radius.

q: Your kubeconfig accumulated contexts named cluster-east, cluster-east-2, and arn:aws:eks:…:cluster/prod. How do you tidy them?
options: Hand-edit the kubeconfig binary — it is not human-readable
kubectl config rename-context <old> <new> and kubectl config delete-context <name> — contexts are plain kubeconfig entries and both commands manage them
Contexts cannot be renamed — you must delete the cluster entry and re-add it
kubectl config use-context --delete — the combined rename/delete command
explain: kubeconfig is YAML and contexts are just entries: rename-context and delete-context are the built-in hygiene tools. Nothing is binary, renames are safe, and no combined flag exists.

q: A hardening review flags that the API server accepts unauthenticated requests. Which API server setting actually disables anonymous access?
options: Nothing — RBAC already blocks anonymous users, so no flag is needed
--authorization-mode=RBAC — authorization covers authentication too
Anonymous access cannot be disabled — the API needs it for health checks
--anonymous-auth=false on the kube-apiserver manifest — anonymous requests are rejected at authentication, before RBAC ever evaluates them
explain: Authentication (who are you) runs before authorization (RBAC: what may you do) — RBAC cannot evaluate a request that never authenticates. --anonymous-auth=false rejects anonymous requests outright. Authorization modes don't authenticate anyone, and health checks use authenticated or local paths.

q: Maintenance cannot wait, but the eviction API is failing (API server trouble) so kubectl drain cannot evict normally. Which drain flag falls back to plain deletes?
options: kubectl drain node-1 --disable-eviction — deletes pods directly instead of using the eviction API. It also bypasses PDB checks, so it is an escape hatch, not a routine flag
kubectl drain --force — force makes the eviction API work harder
--disable-eviction only affects DaemonSet pods
kubectl cordon — cordoning is equivalent to draining
explain: --disable-eviction swaps eviction calls for deletes — the designed fallback when the eviction API is unavailable. The cost is real: PDBs are bypassed too, so it is for emergencies, not routine drains. --force doesn't change which API is used, the flag isn't DaemonSet-scoped, and cordon never moves running pods.

q: You are about to apply a 400-line Deployment change and want to see exactly what will change against the live object before committing. Which command?
options: kubectl apply --preview — renders the diff before applying
git diff deploy.yaml — compares your file against the live cluster
kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml — computes the server-side diff between your file and the live object
kubectl apply --dry-run=client — prints the full diff against the cluster
explain: kubectl diff is the purpose-built preview: it diffs local manifests against live state (client or server side). --preview doesn't exist, git diff only compares files, and --dry-run=client renders locally without comparing to anything live.

q: A rollout has been stuck 45 minutes — new pods keep crash-looping and kubectl rollout status hangs forever. You want the Deployment to officially report failure instead of hanging. Which field?
options: progressDeadlineSeconds: 600 — if the rollout makes no progress within 10 minutes it gets the ProgressDeadlineExceeded condition
activeDeadlineSeconds — caps how long a rollout may take
revisionHistoryLimit — old revisions trigger the failure report
progressDeadlineSeconds only applies to StatefulSets
explain: progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s) is the stuck-rollout detector: no observed progress within the window marks the Deployment failed. activeDeadlineSeconds is for pods and Jobs, revisionHistoryLimit is retention, and the field absolutely applies to Deployments.

q: Your app warms its cache for 90 seconds; the readiness probe passes early but the pod still serves 500s. You want the Deployment to wait before counting the pod as available during rollouts. Which field?
options: initialDelaySeconds on the readiness probe — identical behavior
A startupProbe — it delays the pod being marked available
terminationGracePeriodSeconds — gives the pod more warm-up time
minReadySeconds: 120 — the pod must remain ready for 2 minutes before the Deployment considers it available
explain: minReadySeconds is the availability gate: ready isn't enough, it must STAY ready for the duration. initialDelaySeconds only delays when probing starts, a startupProbe gates liveness/readiness startup (not availability timing), and terminationGracePeriodSeconds is about shutdown, not warm-up.

q: One pod needs corporate DNS first (nameserver 10.0.0.53) plus an extra search domain — without changing CoreDNS for the whole cluster. How?
options: Edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap — DNS customization is cluster-wide only
Set dnsPolicy and dnsConfig on the pod — dnsConfig adds nameservers, searches, and options per-pod, and dnsPolicy: None lets you supply the entire resolv.conf
Use hostAliases — that is the per-pod DNS mechanism
dnsConfig can only be set on the kube-dns Service
explain: dnsConfig is the per-pod DNS override (nameservers/searches/options); dnsPolicy: None means 'use exactly my dnsConfig'. CoreDNS is global, hostAliases only adds static host entries (not nameservers), and dnsConfig is a pod-spec field.

q: You try to add an ephemeral debug container to a running pod by editing the pod spec and running kubectl apply. The API rejects it. Why, and what is the correct command?
options: Ephemeral containers cannot be added to running pods at all
You must delete and recreate the pod with the debug container in its spec
ephemeralContainers can only be added through the ephemeralcontainers subresource — use kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox, never a spec edit
kubectl apply works — you just need --force
explain: The API forbids editing ephemeralContainers via the normal pod update path; the only door is the /ephemeralcontainers subresource, which kubectl debug uses. No recreate is needed, they absolutely can join running pods, and --force doesn't bypass subresource rules.

q: A network-tool container needs the NET_ADMIN capability and nothing else. Cluster policy forbids privileged pods. How do you grant it?
options: securityContext.capabilities.add: ["NET_ADMIN"] (with drop: ["ALL"] first for least privilege) plus allowPrivilegeEscalation: false — fine-grained Linux capabilities without full privilege
privileged: true is required for any capability to take effect
Capabilities are set per-pod, not per-container
Add NET_ADMIN to the node's kernel — containers inherit host capabilities
explain: Linux capabilities are per-container and additive: you can grant NET_ADMIN alone while dropping everything else, no privileged needed. They are container-scoped (not pod-scoped), and nodes don't grant container capabilities.

q: Security wants a seccomp filter on app containers with the least operational risk. Which setting, and where?
options: Seccomp can only be configured per-node — per-workload filtering is impossible
securityContext.seccompProfile.type: Localhost with no profile file — safely disables seccomp
type: RuntimeDefault requires you to distribute a custom profile file to every node
securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault on the pod or container — applies the container runtime's default seccomp profile, no files to manage
explain: RuntimeDefault uses the runtime's built-in default profile — filtering with zero file management. Seccomp is per-pod/container, Localhost requires an actual profile file on the node, and RuntimeDefault needs no custom files.

q: A pod uses emptyDir for 50Gi of scratch space but the node is nearly full. You want the pod evicted before it can fill the disk. Which setting?
options: emptyDir has no size controls — it grows until the disk is full
emptyDir.sizeLimit: 20Gi — the kubelet evicts the pod if its emptyDir usage exceeds the limit
sizeLimit acts as a quota that blocks writes at the limit
sizeLimit only works with medium: Memory
explain: sizeLimit is an eviction threshold: exceed it and the pod is evicted. It is not a write-blocking quota, and it applies to disk-backed emptyDir too — not just memory medium.

q: Traffic drops to zero at night. You set the HPA's minReplicas: 0 hoping pods scale to zero, but they never go below 1. Why?
options: The HPA is broken — reinstall metrics-server
Set maxReplicas: 0 instead — that is the scale-to-zero knob
The HPA never scales below minReplicas, and 0 is not a usable floor — scale-to-zero is not an HPA feature (that is KEDA's job)
Scale-to-zero works — you just need to wait 24 hours
explain: The HPA's floor is minReplicas and it does not do scale-to-zero; that workload belongs to KEDA or similar event-driven scalers. metrics-server health is unrelated, maxReplicas: 0 is nonsense, and no waiting period changes the floor.

q: The 2 AM backup CronJob must be paused for a week during a migration, but you want to keep its schedule definition and history. How?
options: Set spec.suspend: true — the schedule stops firing; flip it back to false to resume with history intact
Delete the CronJob and recreate it next week
Set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — that pauses the schedule
Scale the CronJob to 0 — CronJobs support scaling like Deployments
explain: suspend is the pause switch: no new Jobs fire, everything else is preserved. Delete/recreate loses history, Forbid only prevents overlapping runs, and CronJobs don't scale.

q: 1,000 queue items must each be processed exactly once, 50 at a time, with each pod knowing which item index is its own. Which Job configuration?
options: completions: 50, parallelism: 1000 — completions counts the parallel pods
Use a StatefulSet — Jobs cannot index work items
Annotate each pod manually with its index
completionMode: Indexed, completions: 1000, parallelism: 50 — each pod gets its index via $JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX (0–999)
explain: Indexed completion mode assigns each pod a stable index exposed through the JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX env var and annotation. completions counts total successful pods (not parallelism), no manual annotation is needed, and indexed Jobs are the work-queue tool — not StatefulSets.

q: A Job's worker exits 42 when its queue shard is empty — expected, not a failure. But the Job keeps retrying it toward backoffLimit. How do you teach the Job that exit 42 means success?
options: Raise backoffLimit — more retries will eventually succeed
Add a podFailurePolicy rule: onExitCodes {values: [42], operator: In} with action: Ignore — that pod failure is excluded from backoffLimit accounting
Set restartPolicy: Never — that stops all retries
Set activeDeadlineSeconds — it caps the retries
explain: podFailurePolicy classifies pod failures: Ignore drops expected exit codes from retry accounting while real failures still count. backoffLimit counts all failures blindly, restartPolicy: Never still counts attempts toward the limit, and activeDeadlineSeconds is a wall-clock cap, not a classifier.

q: You add a readinessProbe to a regular initContainer so the next init step waits for a port. kubectl apply is rejected. Why?
options: Probes are silently dropped on init containers — the apply should have succeeded
Only livenessProbe is forbidden; readinessProbe is allowed on init containers
Regular init containers do not support lifecycle or any probes (liveness, readiness, startup) — validation rejects them, because an init container's readiness IS its successful completion
Probes on init containers require restartPolicy: Always on the pod
explain: Per the Kubernetes docs, non-sidecar init containers prohibit lifecycle and all three probe types — enforced at validation. An init container is 'ready' exactly when it exits 0, so probes are meaningless there. Nothing is silently dropped, and restartPolicy doesn't unlock probes.

q: A batch analytics pod has a high PriorityClass, but it must NEVER preempt production pods — it should simply wait for free capacity. How?
options: Set preemptionPolicy: Never on the pod — it keeps its priority for scheduling order but never evicts another pod; it stays Pending until capacity frees up
PriorityClasses always preempt — you must remove the PriorityClass
Set preemptionPolicy on the PriorityClass object
Set priorityClassName to empty — that selectively disables preemption
explain: preemptionPolicy: Never (a pod-spec field) keeps priority-based ordering while disabling eviction. It lives on the pod, not the PriorityClass, and removing the class would also lose the ordering benefit.

q: A 5-replica API must always keep at least 3 pods serving during voluntary disruptions. Which PDB field expresses 'at least N healthy' most directly?
options: maxUnavailable: 2 and minAvailable: 3 are completely different — only one exists
maxUnavailable: 2 — minAvailable is not a real field
minAvailable: 3 counts desired replicas, so it guarantees 3 of 5 desired at all times
minAvailable: 3 — it counts currently-available pods; maxUnavailable: 2 is the arithmetic equivalent, but minAvailable states the requirement directly
explain: Both fields are real and both work here (minAvailable: 3 ≡ maxUnavailable: 2 for 5 replicas), but minAvailable counts available pods and reads as the requirement itself. minAvailable counts available, not desired, and it is absolutely a real field.

q: An HPA manages the web Deployment at 70% CPU. During an incident you run kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=8. Ten minutes later it is back to 4. What happened?
options: The scale command failed silently — check for typos
The HPA reconciled it back — the autoscaler continuously drives replicas toward the metric target and overwrites manual scales; to hold 8, adjust the HPA (or remove it) instead
Manual scaling permanently disables the HPA
kubectl scale automatically raised the HPA's minReplicas to 8
explain: The HPA is a control loop: any out-of-band replica change gets reverted on the next sync. Manual scaling neither disables nor updates the HPA — if you need a fixed count during an incident, the HPA itself must be changed.

q: The ML team wants GPU nodes reserved for their jobs AND wants their jobs to actually land on those nodes. Which combination achieves both?
options: Taint the GPU nodes — taints both repel other teams and attract ML pods
nodeAffinity on the ML pods — affinity also repels other teams' pods

Taint the GPU nodes (repels everyone lacking the toleration) PLUS a matching toleration and nodeAffinity on ML pods (attracts them there) — taints only repel, affinity only attracts, so dedicated pools need both directions
nodeSelector on the ML pods — other pods then cannot schedule to GPU nodes
explain: Taints never attract and affinity never repels: the taint keeps other teams off, the toleration lets ML pods tolerate it, and nodeAffinity steers ML pods onto the GPUs. Taint alone strands ML pods; nodeSelector alone doesn't repel anyone.

q: A compliance workload must run under the Kata Containers sandboxed runtime installed on the nodes, while everything else uses runc. How do you select the runtime per-pod?
options: Create a RuntimeClass named kata and set runtimeClassName: kata on the pod — the kubelet runs that pod with the kata runtime
Runtimes are per-node only — you need dedicated kata nodes
Set privileged: true — that enables the sandboxed runtime
Set runtimeClassName on the Deployment's strategy block
explain: RuntimeClass + the pod's runtimeClassName field is the per-pod runtime selector — no dedicated nodes required. privileged is unrelated to runtime selection, and runtimeClassName is a pod-spec field, not a strategy field.

q: You inject two ConfigMaps via envFrom and both define LOG_LEVEL — the values collide. How do you namespace the injected variables without renaming keys?
options: Rename the keys — envFrom has no namespacing feature
Collisions resolve automatically by ConfigMap creation order
Switch to valueFrom — envFrom accepts no options
Use envFrom with prefix: APP_ on the configMapRef — every injected variable gets the prefix (APP_LOG_LEVEL), eliminating the collision
explain: envFrom supports a per-source prefix that namespaces every injected variable. Renaming works but prefix is the built-in tool; collisions do not auto-resolve (last write wins, silently); valueFrom is the verbose per-variable alternative.

q: Every pod gets a dozen {SVC}_SERVICE_HOST environment variables nobody uses, and a review flags the clutter. How do you stop injecting them?
options: You cannot — service environment injection is mandatory
Set enableServiceLinks: false on the pod spec — disables the automatic service host/port env vars; DNS-based discovery keeps working
Delete the Services — no Services, no env vars
Set dnsPolicy: None — that controls env injection
explain: enableServiceLinks toggles the legacy Docker-links-style env injection; DNS discovery is unaffected. It is optional, deleting Services would break discovery, and dnsPolicy governs resolv.conf — not env vars.

q: Every cloud LoadBalancer Service also allocates a NodePort from the cluster range, and the platform team wants those ports freed. What do you set on the Service?
options: Change type to ClusterIP — then you don't need the load balancer at all
allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false — skips NodePort allocation for the Service (note: some health-check flows rely on those ports, so verify first)
NodePorts are mandatory for LoadBalancer Services — they cannot be freed
Set nodePort: 0 — zero disables the allocation
explain: allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts exists precisely to skip nodePort allocation on LB Services. Changing type drops the load balancer itself, the ports are not mandatory, and nodePort: 0 is not valid configuration.

q: Two load-balancer implementations are installed (the cloud provider's and MetalLB). New Services keep picking the wrong one. How do you choose per-Service?
options: You cannot — a cluster supports exactly one LB implementation
Annotations are the only selection mechanism
Change the Service type — the type selects the implementation
Set spec.loadBalancerClass to the implementation's class name — Services with no class use the default (usually the cloud provider)
explain: loadBalancerClass selects among installed LB implementations per Service. Multiple implementations coexist fine, type doesn't select between them, and the field (not annotations) is the current mechanism.

q: ClientIP session affinity works, but the default 3-hour stickiness outlives your 20-minute deploys — clients stay pinned to dead backends. How do you shorten the pin?
options: sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds: 1200 — caps how long a client IP stays pinned to one backend (default 10800s)
The timeout is fixed at 3 hours and cannot be changed
Toggle sessionAffinity off and on — that resets the timer for everyone
The timeout is in milliseconds — set it to 1200000
explain: timeoutSeconds (default 10800) is tunable per Service. It is not fixed, it is measured in seconds, and toggling the feature doesn't tune it.

q: Cross-zone traffic is expensive. You want kube-proxy to prefer endpoints in the client's own zone when healthy, but still fail over cross-zone if local endpoints die. What provides exactly this?
options: internalTrafficPolicy: Local — identical behavior
Set routing hints manually as a field on the Service
Topology-aware routing hints: the endpoint controller adds per-zone hints to EndpointSlices, and kube-proxy prefers same-zone endpoints while keeping cross-zone endpoints as fallback
Hand-edit the EndpointSlices to add hints
explain: Hints give preference WITH fallback — unlike internalTrafficPolicy: Local, which drops traffic when no node-local endpoint exists. Hints are controller-managed (not a Service field, not hand-edited).

q: Your Ingress must serve the API at /api/*, but the backend expects paths WITHOUT the /api prefix. How do you strip it with ingress-nginx?
options: pathType: Prefix strips the matched prefix automatically
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2 combined with path /api(/|$)(.*) — the capture group rewrites the request path without the prefix
Create a second Ingress for the stripped paths
Put the annotation on the backend Service
explain: rewrite-target with capture groups rewrites the path before proxying. pathType only controls matching, never rewriting; a second Ingress can't strip prefixes; the annotation belongs on the Ingress.

q: With Gateway API you need a 90/10 canary split between v1 and v2 backends. Where do the traffic weights go?
options: On the Gateway — weights are a listener-level setting
Gateway API cannot split traffic — fall back to Ingress canary annotations
Create two Gateways — traffic splits across them
In the HTTPRoute's backendRefs: one backendRef per version with weight: 90 and weight: 10 — the route distributes requests proportionally
explain: Weights live on each backendRef inside the HTTPRoute rule — route-level, natively supported. Gateways don't carry weights, and two Gateways don't split anything.

q: One Gateway has listeners for web and admin. Your HTTPRoute must attach ONLY to the admin listener. How?
options: Set parentRefs with sectionName: admin on the HTTPRoute — binds the route to that specific listener (add namespace for cross-namespace attach)
Routes attach to every listener automatically — selective attach is impossible
