parentRefs goes on the Gateway, not on the route
The hostname field alone selects the listener
explain: parentRefs (+sectionName) is the attachment mechanism: the route names its parent Gateway and the specific listener section. Routes don't auto-attach everywhere, the ref lives on the route, and hostname matches within already-attached listeners.

q: A NetworkPolicy must allow ingress from 10.0.0.0/8 EXCEPT the quarantine subnet 10.0.5.0/24. How do you express the exception?
options: Two from entries — one allow, one deny; policies support deny rules
except takes a podSelector naming the quarantine pods
from: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 10.0.0.0/8, except: [10.0.5.0/24]}}] — except carves subnets out of the allowed CIDR
except widens the CIDR — it additionally allows 10.0.5.0/24
explain: except subtracts CIDRs from the allowed block. NetworkPolicy is allow-list only (no deny rules), except is CIDR-only (no selectors), and it narrows the allowance — never widens it.

q: You need the mirror of the classic default-deny: selected pods must have NO egress at all — not even DNS. Which policy does this?
options: An egress rule with action: deny — explicit deny rules
podSelector: {} with policyTypes: [Egress] and zero egress rules — selects all pods, isolates egress, allows nothing
Omit policyTypes — selecting a pod isolates its egress automatically
Egress cannot be fully denied — DNS is always exempted
explain: The default-deny pattern works for egress too, but policyTypes MUST include Egress — omitting it isolates only ingress. There is no deny action in NetworkPolicy, and even DNS is blocked here, which is precisely the intent.

q: NodePorts open on every node interface, including a public one. You want NodePorts bound only to internal 10.0.0.0/8 addresses. Where is this controlled?
options: On each Service — nodePortAddresses is a Service field
Nowhere — NodePorts always bind all interfaces
With a NetworkPolicy — it controls port binding
The kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses flag (a CIDR list) — restricts which node addresses NodePorts bind to
explain: --nodeport-addresses is a kube-proxy startup flag filtering NodePort bind addresses. It is not a Service field, binding is restrictable, and NetworkPolicy filters traffic — it doesn't control socket binding.

q: You need method-level gRPC routing with Gateway API: package.Service/GetUser goes to v2, everything else to v1. Which resource expresses this?
options: GRPCRoute — matches on gRPC service/method (plus headers) with weighted backendRefs, purpose-built for gRPC
HTTPRoute — it handles gRPC with identical matches
TCPRoute — method matching works at L4
An Ingress with gRPC annotations — Gateway API has no gRPC resource
explain: GRPCRoute is the purpose-built resource: service/method matches plus header matches and backend weights. HTTPRoute is HTTP-semantics, TCPRoute can't see methods, and Gateway API does include GRPCRoute.

q: The Ingress serves HTTPS, but http:// requests are served as plaintext instead of redirecting to https://. How do you force the redirect with ingress-nginx?
options: It is automatic as soon as the tls block exists
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true" on the Ingress — the controller redirects HTTP to HTTPS
Create a second Ingress without TLS — it redirects by default
Set the annotation on the backend Service
explain: ssl-redirect controls the HTTP→HTTPS redirect explicitly (global defaults can disable it). The tls block alone doesn't guarantee it, a second Ingress doesn't redirect, and the annotation belongs on the Ingress.

q: A game server needs UDP ports 30000-30100 reachable from players, locked down by a NetworkPolicy. Writing 101 port entries is absurd. How do you express the range?
options: NetworkPolicy ports don't support ranges — every port needs its own entry
Use port: "30000-30100" — the port field accepts range strings
ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 30000, endPort: 30100}] — endPort extends the entry into an inclusive range
Port ranges only work in ingress rules, never in egress
explain: endPort turns one port entry into an inclusive range (port must be numeric, not a named port). The port field takes a single port — not a range string — and endPort works in both ingress and egress rules.

q: With Gateway API you must route non-HTTP TLS traffic by SNI hostname to different backends WITHOUT terminating TLS at the edge. Which route type?
options: HTTPRoute with a TLS listener — it terminates and re-routes
TCPRoute — it matches SNI hostnames
An Ingress with ssl-passthrough — that is the Gateway API mechanism
TLSRoute — routes TLS streams by SNI hostname without decrypting
explain: TLSRoute is the SNI-based, no-termination route type. HTTPRoute is HTTP-only, TCPRoute has no hostname matching, and ssl-passthrough is the ingress-nginx equivalent — not a Gateway API resource.

q: On-prem with no LB provider, the network team routed 203.0.113.50 to the cluster and you need a Service reachable on exactly that IP. How?
options: Set spec.externalIPs: [203.0.113.50] — kube-proxy serves the Service on that IP on every node; you handle external routing, Kubernetes handles the serving
externalIPs is read-only — only the cloud provider may set it
Use type ClusterIP — external IPs are not a Service concept
Use type LoadBalancer — it will allocate 203.0.113.50
explain: externalIPs is user-settable: kube-proxy binds the Service IP on every node, and your external routing delivers traffic there. It is not read-only, it is a first-class Service field, and a LoadBalancer won't conjure a specific IP without a provider.

q: With Gateway API, every request to the api backend must gain an X-Tenant header, and the internal X-Debug header must be stripped before reaching the backend. Where does this transformation belong?
options: In the application code — Gateway API cannot modify headers
An HTTPRoute rule filter of type RequestHeaderModifier (add/set/remove) — the route transforms headers before forwarding to the backend
On the Gateway listener — listeners rewrite request headers
HTTPRoutes don't support filters — use an Ingress annotation instead
explain: HTTPRoute filters include RequestHeaderModifier for add/set/remove of headers — the edge is the right place for this, not app code. Listeners don't transform headers, and filters are a core HTTPRoute feature.

q: Behind the Ingress, your app's audit log shows the ingress controller's IP as the client on every request. How does the app learn the real client IP?
options: It cannot — SNAT at the edge hides the client permanently
Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on the Ingress — that preserves the source IP
Read the X-Forwarded-For header — the controller appends the real client IP there; the app must be configured to trust and use it
Controllers never set X-Forwarded-For — check X-Real-IP instead
explain: L7 proxies record the client in X-Forwarded-For; the app (or its framework) must be configured to consume it. It is not impossible, externalTrafficPolicy applies to Service-type traffic — not Ingress, and ingress-nginx sets X-Forwarded-For by default.

q: An Ingress backend points at service port 8080, but the Service defines port: 80 with targetPort: 8080. Requests fail. What is wrong?
options: The Ingress backend's service.port.number must reference the Service's port (80), not the container's targetPort — the Ingress talks to the Service, which forwards to targetPort itself
It must reference targetPort: 8080 — the Ingress bypasses the Service port
Ingress backends require port names, not numbers
The Service's port and targetPort must be equal for Ingress to work
explain: The Ingress addresses the Service (port 80); the Service maps to the container (targetPort 8080). Pointing the backend at 8080 addresses nothing the Service listens on. Names are allowed but numbers are fine, and port/targetPort equality is never required.

q: A LoadBalancer Service is internet-facing but must only accept traffic from the office (198.51.100.0/24) and the VPN (203.0.113.0/24). Where do you enforce this?
options: A NetworkPolicy — it filters load-balancer source traffic
loadBalancerSourceRanges is cloud-only metadata with no enforcement
On the NodePort — source ranges only apply to NodePort Services
spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges: [198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24] — the load balancer (or kube-proxy) drops packets from other sources
explain: loadBalancerSourceRanges is the enforcement point for LB ingress sources. NetworkPolicy governs in-cluster pod traffic, the field is effective (not metadata), and it is LB-scoped.

q: You switch a Service to headless (clusterIP: None) for a caching layer, and traffic is suddenly uneven — one client hammers a single pod. What changed?
options: Headless Services still load-balance via kube-proxy — the imbalance is a bug to report
With no ClusterIP there is nothing to balance: DNS returns every pod IP and the CLIENT picks (often naive round-robin or first address), so spread quality depends on the client
Headless Services guarantee DNS round-robin order
Set sessionAffinity: None — that restores even spread
explain: Headless means DNS-based discovery with no kube-proxy load balancing — the client library's choice decides the spread, and naive clients pin. There is no guaranteed round-robin, and sessionAffinity is a ClusterIP feature that doesn't exist here.

q: A local-storage StorageClass provisions a volume on node-a, but the pod schedules to node-b and stays Pending with a volume node-affinity conflict. The class uses volumeBindingMode: Immediate. What is the fix?
options: Delete the pod — the scheduler will retry it on node-a
Set volumeBindingMode on the PVC — binding mode is a per-claim field
Set volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer on the StorageClass — binding and provisioning wait until a pod exists, so the volume is created honoring the pod's scheduled node
Immediate is mandatory for local storage
explain: WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding/provisioning until scheduling, so topology (the pod's node) is known first. Immediate provisions first and schedules later — the classic conflict for local or zonal volumes. Binding mode is a StorageClass field, not a PVC field, and deleting the pod doesn't fix the ordering.

q: GPU jobs need EBS volumes, but only us-east-1a and us-east-1b have the required instance types. How do you keep dynamic provisioning out of us-east-1c?
options: Set allowedTopologies with matchLabelExpressions on topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone [us-east-1a, us-east-1b] in the StorageClass — the provisioner only creates volumes in those zones
Add nodeAffinity to every pod — that steers volume provisioning too
Put allowedTopologies on the PVC
Topology cannot restrict provisioning — only pod scheduling
explain: allowedTopologies is the StorageClass-level provisioning constraint. Pod nodeAffinity steers pods, not where the provisioner creates the disk, and the field lives on the StorageClass — not the PVC.

q: A PVC with reclaimPolicy: Retain is deleted. The PV now shows Released with data intact. The team wants to reuse the PV for a new PVC. What must happen first?
options: Create any matching PVC — Released PVs bind automatically
Delete the PV — Retain means the data was already copied elsewhere
Released PVs can never be reused — provision a new one
Manually clear the PV's spec.claimRef (kubectl edit pv) to return it to Available — only then can a new PVC bind
explain: Retain leaves the PV Released with a stale claimRef pointing at the dead PVC; an admin must clear it before the PV becomes Available again. No auto-rebind happens, deleting the PV drops your handle on the data, and reuse is manual but fully supported.

q: kubectl delete pvc data-db-0 hangs — the PVC is still mounted by a running pod. What protects it, and what is the correct move?
options: Nothing protects it — use --force to delete it anyway
The kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer blocks deletion while a pod uses the PVC — delete the pod first (or let it finish), then the PVC deletes cleanly
Finalizers only exist on PVs, never on PVCs
The PVC is corrupt — delete the PV instead
explain: pvc-protection is the guard: the PVC can't vanish under a running pod. --force risks data loss, finalizers exist on both PVs and PVCs, and deleting the PV doesn't resolve the in-use PVC.

q: A pod mounts a 2TB volume holding 3 million files. Every mount takes 20 minutes because fsGroup recursively chowns everything — and the ownership is already correct. How do you skip the chown?
options: Set fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch — the kubelet only performs the recursive chown when the volume root's ownership is wrong
Remove fsGroup — it is the only way to skip the chown
OnRootMismatch disables fsGroup entirely
The recursive chown is mandatory and cannot be skipped
explain: OnRootMismatch (vs Always) skips the recursive chown when the root already matches — the fix for slow mounts on huge file trees. fsGroup still applies to new files, it is not disabled, and the chown is very much skippable.

q: A secrets-store CSI driver must inject secrets directly into pods with no PVCs involved. Which volume type does this?
options: A normal persistentVolumeClaim — CSI always requires one
hostPath — CSI drivers mount through hostPath
An ephemeral inline CSI volume: volumes: [{csi: {driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io, volumeAttributes: {...}}}] — no PVC, lifecycle tied to the pod
A ConfigMap volume — CSI drivers are just ConfigMaps
explain: CSI inline ephemeral volumes skip PVCs entirely: the driver mounts directly with a pod-scoped lifecycle. Not every CSI use needs a PVC, hostPath is unrelated, and ConfigMap is a different volume type.

q: A 3-replica Deployment serves user uploads from one shared writable directory. Which access mode must the PVC request?
options: ReadWriteOnce — it works across nodes for Deployments
One RWO PVC per replica — that shares the directory
Access modes are advisory — any mode will work
ReadWriteMany — concurrent writers on multiple nodes; RWO would pin the volume to a single node
explain: Shared writable storage across nodes is ReadWriteMany by definition. RWO attaches to one node (replicas elsewhere can't write), per-replica PVCs don't share anything, and access modes are enforced binding predicates — not hints.

q: You edit a PVC from 20Gi to 40Gi and the API rejects the change outright. The StorageClass has no allowVolumeExpansion field. Why?
options: The edit was accepted — expansion just takes an hour to appear
Volume expansion must be explicitly enabled: without allowVolumeExpansion: true the API server rejects the resize
The kubelet resizes it anyway — the rejection is only a warning
You must delete and recreate the PVC — expansion is never possible
explain: allowVolumeExpansion gates the feature; absent or false, the API rejects the edit. It is not a delay, the kubelet cannot override the API, and no recreate is needed once the class allows expansion.

q: A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating: Multi-Attach error for volume pvc-xyz, already attached to node-1 — but the pod is scheduled to node-2. The old pod on node-1 was deleted 10 minutes ago. What is going on?
options: The volume is still attached to node-1 (detach never completed or the old pod object lingers) — RWO volumes attach to one node at a time; check VolumeAttachment objects and make sure the old pod is fully gone so detach can finish
RWO allows attachment to multiple nodes — this is a scheduler bug
Delete the PV — that force-detaches the volume
Multi-Attach errors always resolve by waiting — never investigate
explain: RWO means one node at a time: a stale attachment (or lingering pod object) blocks the new attach. VolumeAttachments show the true state. It is not a scheduler bug, deleting the PV is destructive, and 'just wait' misses stuck detaches that need the old pod finalized.

q: You suspect attach/detach problems between nodes and volumes. Which API objects record the actual attach state?
options: Only the cloud console shows attach state — Kubernetes cannot
kubectl describe node — it lists every attached volume with full status
VolumeAttachment objects (kubectl get volumeattachments) — the attach/detach controller's record of which volume is attached to which node
Attach state is invisible to kubectl
explain: VolumeAttachment is the API's attach record: attacher, node, and attached flag. Node describe shows mounted volumes, not the attach record, and the state is fully visible via kubectl.

q: You restore a VolumeSnapshot to a new PVC but request 100Gi while the snapshot is only 50Gi. Is this allowed?
options: Restores must match the snapshot size exactly — resize afterward only
Snapshots cannot be a dataSource — only PVCs can
The restored volume will be 50Gi regardless of what you request
Yes — set dataSource to the VolumeSnapshot with resources.requests.storage: 100Gi; the driver provisions a larger volume from the snapshot (normal expansion rules apply)
explain: Restore-and-resize in one step is supported where the driver allows expansion: the snapshot is the data source, the request is the target size. Snapshots are valid dataSources and the size is not pinned to the source.

q: You statically provisioned a PV with no StorageClass, but the cluster's default StorageClass keeps grabbing your PVC for dynamic provisioning. How do you force static binding to your PV?
options: Omit storageClassName — omitting it opts out of the default class
Set storageClassName: "" (empty string) on the PVC — it opts out of the default class and binds only to a classless PV
An empty storageClassName is invalid
Delete the default StorageClass
explain: Empty string is the explicit 'no class': omitting the field triggers the default class, but "" binds only to PVs with no class. It is valid and documented — no need to delete the default.

q: A database wants a raw block device. The PVC sets volumeMode: Block but stays Pending; the only free PVs use volumeMode: Filesystem. Why no bind?
options: volumeMode must match between PV and PVC — Block PVCs only bind Block PVs
The driver converts Filesystem PVs to Block automatically at bind time
volumeMode is set on the StorageClass, not on PVs and PVCs
volumeMode is informational and ignored during binding
explain: volumeMode is a binding predicate: Block↔Block, Filesystem↔Filesystem. No conversion happens, it is a PV/PVC field (not StorageClass), and mismatches leave the PVC Pending.

q: You try to clone PVC db-data into namespace reporting via a dataSource reference. It fails. What is the rule for PVC cloning?
options: Cloning requires a VolumeSnapshot as dataSource — PVC-to-PVC clones don't exist
Cross-namespace clones work fine with the right RBAC
A PVC clone's dataSource must live in the SAME namespace — clones cannot cross namespaces (snapshots are the cross-namespace path)
dataSource clones work across clusters
explain: dataSource references are namespace-local by design: source and clone must share a namespace. Cross-namespace copies go through snapshots (with their own constraints), and clones are strictly in-cluster.

q: A PVC requests ReadWriteMany but the only available PV offers ReadWriteOnce. What happens?
options: It binds — access modes are advisory
The scheduler overrides the mismatch at pod startup
The PV is transparently upgraded to RWX
The PVC stays Pending — accessModes must intersect for a bind
explain: accessModes are binding predicates, not hints: the requested modes must be a subset of what the PV offers. Nothing upgrades or overrides them — the PVC waits for a compatible PV.

q: A PVC requests 50Gi. The only free PV has 20Gi. What happens?
options: It binds and the PVC is capped at 20Gi
The PVC stays Pending — PV capacity must be greater than or equal to the PVC request
The PV expands to 50Gi automatically
Partial binding: 20Gi now, the remaining 30Gi later
explain: Capacity is a binding predicate with no partial binds and no auto-expansion of static PVs. The PVC waits until a ≥50Gi PV appears.

q: A statically provisioned PV (an existing cloud disk) has reclaimPolicy: Delete. You delete its PVC. What happens to the PV object and the underlying disk?
options: The PV object is deleted; the underlying disk is NOT automatically wiped — the admin must clean up the storage asset (Delete only removes the Kubernetes object for static PVs)
The disk is wiped and the PV stays Bound
The data migrates to another PV automatically
The PV becomes Available for the next PVC
explain: For static PVs, Delete reclaim removes the API object only — the external disk and its data remain until an admin deletes them. Nothing is wiped, nothing migrates, and the PV does not recycle to Available.

q: An app needs a config file rendered at startup (template + pod IP) before the main container runs, shared via a volume. Which pattern does this?
options: The app container renders it — initContainers cannot share volumes
Use hostPath — emptyDir cannot be shared between containers
An initContainer renders the config into a shared emptyDir; the app container mounts the same emptyDir and reads it — init ordering guarantees the file exists first
Impossible — ConfigMaps cannot be templated
explain: The classic init-populates-shared-volume pattern: volumes are pod-scoped so both containers mount the same emptyDir, and init completion ordering guarantees the file is ready. emptyDir is shareable, and templating at startup is exactly what init containers are for.

q: A legacy agent reads the pod's labels from files (it expects /etc/podinfo/labels), not env vars. How do you expose labels as files?
options: The Downward API only supports environment variables
Mount the API server's label store via hostPath
Grant the agent RBAC to query the API — files are impossible
Use a downwardAPI volume with items mapping fieldRef metadata.labels to a file path — the kubelet projects labels and annotations as files
explain: The Downward API has two forms: env vars AND volumes. A downwardAPI volume projects fields like metadata.labels into files. No hostPath hacks or API queries are needed.

q: Every new PVC stays Pending with zero provisioner-related events. The StorageClass sets provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.comm (note the typo). What is wrong?
options: Kubernetes fuzzy-matches provisioner names — the typo is harmless
No installed CSI driver claims that provisioner name, so nothing ever attempts provisioning — the name must exactly match the driver's registered name; the total absence of events is the tell
kubectl describe pvc would show the error immediately — events always appear
The default provisioner takes over when the name is unrecognized
explain: Provisioner matching is exact: a typo'd name matches no driver, so no provisioner ever sees the PVC — hence zero events. There is no fuzzy matching, no fallback provisioner, and the silence itself is the diagnostic.

q: A pod is misbehaving and you have thirty seconds before the war-room call. What is the single highest-signal first command?
options: kubectl logs — always start with the logs
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -n <ns> — the cluster's own timeline of scheduling, image pulls, probes, mounts, and evictions
kubectl describe node — start node-level, always
Delete the pod and watch what the replacement does
explain: Events show the system's decisions (FailedScheduling, FailedMount, Unhealthy, Evicted) in order — the fastest orientation. Logs come second (and may not exist yet), node describe is for node-level faults, and deleting destroys the evidence you're diagnosing.

q: A node reports plenty of free CPU and RAM, but kubectl describe node shows DiskPressure: True and pods are being evicted. What is happening?
options: Add more RAM — pressure means memory pressure
Cordon the node — that clears the pressure condition
DiskPressure is informational only — the evictions must come from elsewhere
The kubelet evicts pods when disk thresholds are crossed — reclaim disk (old images, container logs, unused volumes); cordoning doesn't free a single byte
explain: DiskPressure is an actionable kubelet condition: full image filesystem or root filesystem triggers pod eviction. It is about disk, not RAM; cordon only stops new scheduling; and the condition directly drives evictions.

q: kubectl suddenly fails with 'Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp ...: connect: connection refused'. The network path is fine. Where do you look first?
options: The API server itself — on a kubeadm control-plane node check the kube-apiserver static pod (crictl ps, crictl logs): connection refused means nothing is listening
Restart kubelet on the workers — that restores API access
Check etcd first — etcd is what kubectl talks to
It is always DNS — check CoreDNS
explain: Connection refused means no listener: the API server is down or unreachable. Worker kubelets don't serve kubectl, etcd is not kubectl's endpoint, and DNS failure produces a different error (no such host).

q: After a CA renewal and control-plane rebuild, kubectl fails with 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority'. The fresh admin.conf works on the control-plane node. What is wrong with your laptop's kubeconfig?
options: Your laptop's clock is wrong
The bootstrap token expired

Your kubeconfig still carries the OLD cluster CA (certificate-authority-data) — the CA changed, so the server certificate no longer chains to your trust anchor; refresh the CA data or take the new kubeconfig
The API server certificate expired — renew it
explain: Unknown authority after a rebuild is a trust-anchor mismatch, not an expiry: your cached CA no longer signs the serving cert. Clock skew gives 'not yet valid', tokens are for node join, and the server cert is fine — your copy of the CA is stale.

q: A pod stays Pending: '0/5 nodes are available: 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity'. The nodes exist and are Ready. What is the most likely cause?
options: The scheduler is broken — restart the kube-scheduler pod
The pod's nodeAffinity/nodeSelector terms don't match any node's labels — compare node labels against the pod's matchExpressions and fix whichever side is wrong
It is a taint problem — taints surface as affinity errors
Add more nodes — five are not enough
explain: The event names the failing predicate: label terms vs node labels disagree. The scheduler is working as designed, taints produce 'untolerated taint' messages (not affinity ones), and node count is irrelevant when terms match nothing.

q: Pods fail with ImagePullBackOff: 'toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit' from Docker Hub. The image name is correct. What is the fix?
options: Fix the image name typo — toomanyrequests means the repository wasn't found
Raise backoffLimit — more retries will eventually get through
Free disk on the node — pulls fail when the disk is full
Authenticate the pulls (an imagePullSecret with Docker Hub credentials raises the rate limit) or mirror the image to a private registry
explain: toomanyrequests is Docker Hub rate limiting on anonymous pulls — not a typo, not disk, and retries don't help. Authenticated pulls get a far higher quota; a private mirror removes the dependency entirely.

q: After a GitOps sync, every NEW pod gets a broken logging sidecar injected and CrashLoops. Pods created before the sync are fine. What is the likely culprit?
options: A mutating admission webhook (the logging injector) is injecting a bad sidecar template — check MutatingWebhookConfigurations, its failurePolicy, and fix the template or scope it with a namespaceSelector/objectSelector
Mutating webhooks cannot modify pods — suspect the scheduler instead
Delete all the new pods — fresh pods won't get the injection
Restart the API server — webhook configs are cached there
explain: 'Only new pods are broken' is the signature of admission-time mutation: the webhook injects at creation. Webhooks absolutely modify pods, deleting pods just recreates them broken, and the fix is the webhook's configuration — not an API server restart.

q: An HPA exists but never scales, and kubectl describe hpa says it cannot find its target. The Deployment itself is healthy. What is a common cause?
options: metrics-server is down — that shows <unknown> metrics, not a missing target
minReplicas is set too high
A typo in scaleTargetRef (wrong name, kind, or apiVersion) — the HPA points at a nonexistent target; correct the reference
The HPA needs RBAC permission to list pods
explain: 'Cannot find target' means the reference is wrong — name, kind, or apiVersion typo in scaleTargetRef. Metrics outages show <unknown>, minReplicas doesn't cause not-found, and HPAs don't need pod-list RBAC for this.

q: You apply a strict NetworkPolicy but traffic still flows freely. The CNI supports NetworkPolicy and the YAML applies cleanly. What should you check first?
options: Nothing — an applied policy is always enforced, so the CNI must be broken
Whether the policy's podSelector actually matches any pods — a selector matching nothing makes the policy a silent no-op
policyTypes is mandatory — without it nothing is enforced
A default-deny policy must exist first or no policy takes effect
explain: A policy that selects zero pods isolates zero pods — the most common silent failure, and it applies cleanly with no errors. policyTypes has defaults (ingress is implied by ingress rules), and no default-deny prerequisite exists.

q: kubectl drain fails with 'cannot delete Pods with local storage (use --delete-emptydir-data to override)'. The pods use emptyDir scratch space. What is the right call?
options: kubectl drain --force — force overrides the local-storage check
Just cordon — draining isn't necessary
Pods with emptyDir can never be drained — delete the node object instead
drain --delete-emptydir-data — explicitly acknowledges the scratch data will be lost and evicts the pods
explain: --delete-emptydir-data is the designed override for the local-storage guard. --force does not bypass this check, cordon never moves running pods, and emptyDir pods drain fine once you accept the data loss.

q: A node goes NotReady. The kubelet is running, but no containers start and crictl fails to connect. What is the likely fault?
options: The container runtime (containerd) is down — check systemctl status containerd and its socket; the kubelet cannot run containers without the CRI endpoint
The kubelet client certificate expired — that stops the kubelet itself, not the runtime
Reboot the node — always the first step
The API server is down — that is what makes nodes NotReady
explain: Kubelet running + crictl failing = dead runtime: the CRI endpoint is gone. Cert expiry stops the kubelet (which is running here), reboot is a last resort, and an API outage doesn't produce this shape — the kubelet would still run containers.

q: TLS between cluster components fails with 'x509: certificate is not yet valid' — but the certificates were just renewed and are definitely current. What causes this?
options: The wrong CA — that produces 'unknown authority', not this
The components need a restart to load the new certs — that produces expiry errors, not 'not yet valid'
Clock skew between nodes — a node whose clock runs behind sees valid certificates as not-yet-valid; fix NTP/chrony
The bootstrap token expired
explain: 'Not yet valid' with valid certificates means the verifier's clock is behind the cert's notBefore — classic NTP drift. CA mismatch is a different error, restarts don't produce this message, and tokens are unrelated to x509 validity windows.

q: A NodePort Service works from inside the cluster, but external clients cannot reach <nodeIP>:31080. Pod-to-pod and ClusterIP traffic are fine. What is the most likely external blocker?
options: kube-proxy is down — but then internal traffic would break too
A cloud firewall / security group blocking the NodePort range (30000-32767) on the nodes
The Service selector is wrong — but then internal access would fail
NodePort requires a LoadBalancer Service to work externally
explain: Internal works ⇒ the Service, endpoints, and kube-proxy are fine — the break is at the edge: security groups commonly block the NodePort range. A bad selector would break internal too, and NodePort is standalone (no LB required).

q: metrics-server is in CrashLoopBackOff: 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority' when scraping kubelets. What is the standard fix?
options: Reinstall metrics-server — the image must be corrupt
Install Prometheus — metrics-server requires it
Grant metrics-server cluster-admin — this is an RBAC problem

The kubelet serving certificates are self-signed, not issued by the cluster CA — serve proper certificates to kubelets, or set --kubelet-insecure-tls on metrics-server (testing only) to skip verification
explain: Kubelet serving certs are self-signed by default, so metrics-server's TLS verification fails — the textbook fix is --kubelet-insecure-tls (lab) or real kubelet certs (production). It is not an image, Prometheus, or RBAC problem.

q: It is upgrade night (1.32 to 1.33). Before running kubeadm upgrade apply, what single step gives you a rollback path?
options: Take an etcd snapshot (etcdctl snapshot save) — if the upgrade goes bad, you can restore cluster state from it
Skip backups — kubeadm upgrades never fail
Back up after the upgrade — that is when the new state matters
Back up only the YAML manifests — etcd can be rebuilt from manifests
explain: A pre-upgrade etcd snapshot is the rollback point: state (not just manifests) is what an upgrade risks. Post-upgrade backups don't roll anything back, manifests don't contain runtime state, and 'never fails' is not a strategy.

q: An Ingress returns 503. The pods are healthy, endpoints exist, and the Service answers via port-forward. What is a likely Ingress-specific cause?
options: The pods are down — but they are healthy
CoreDNS failure — that produces DNS errors, not HTTP 503
The Ingress backend's service port doesn't match the Service's port (e.g. it points at the container targetPort) — the controller cannot route to the Service
TLS misconfiguration — that produces TLS errors, not 503
explain: 503 with healthy backends means the controller→Service hop is broken — the classic is a backend port referencing targetPort instead of the Service's port. The scenario rules out dead pods, DNS, and TLS by their different symptoms.

q: A namespace is stuck in Terminating. Every resource in it is deleted, yet it never disappears. As a LAST resort — after verifying nothing remains — what unblocks it?
options: kubectl delete namespace --force — force works on namespaces
Remove the kubernetes finalizer from the namespace object (fetch the JSON, strip finalizers, push via the API) — only after confirming no resources remain
Wait — namespaces always resolve within 24 hours
Delete etcd — the namespace object lives there
explain: A lingering finalizer is the usual cause, and manual removal is the documented last resort once the namespace is truly empty. --force doesn't apply to namespaces, waiting isn't guaranteed, and deleting etcd is never the answer.

q: After a containerd upgrade, pods fail pulling from the private registry with auth errors. It worked yesterday; nothing changed in Kubernetes. What is the likely cause?
options: The registry went down overnight — possible, but check the local config first
The imagePullSecrets expired — Secrets don't expire
The kubelet must be upgraded in lockstep — version skew doesn't cause auth errors
The containerd upgrade reset /etc/containerd/config.toml, wiping the registry mirror/auth configuration — re-apply it and restart containerd
explain: Package upgrades can replace config.toml with defaults, silently dropping mirrors and auth config — 'worked yesterday, broken today, nothing changed in Kubernetes' is the tell. Secrets don't expire and kubelet skew produces different errors.

q: Pod creation is rejected: 'failed to admit: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy ... : evaluation failed'. RBAC permits the creation. What is rejecting the pods?
options: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy — CEL-based admission control evaluating the pod against its expressions; inspect the policy and its binding, or make the pod comply
RBAC — already ruled out by the premise
A ResourceQuota — that produces quota-exceeded errors, not admission evaluations
The scheduler — it places pods, it doesn't admit them
explain: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is admission-time CEL validation, independent of RBAC: the error names it directly. Quota and scheduler failures have distinct messages, and RBAC was already excluded.

q: A node's disk keeps hitting pressure even though app logs are rotated. crictl images shows 40GB of old, unused images. How do you reclaim the space?
options: Attach a bigger disk — the only fix
Delete pods — images are only kept for running pods
Run crictl rmi to prune unused images (the kubelet's image GC also reclaims at its thresholds) — unused images are the reclaimable bulk
Restart containerd — restarts trigger garbage collection
explain: Unused images persist independently of running pods and are reclaimed by image GC or manual crictl rmi. A bigger disk postpones it, deleting pods doesn't remove their images, and restarts don't garbage-collect.

q: Your kubeadm init failed halfway: the etcd phase errored because port 2380 was already in use by a leftover process. You killed the process and want to retry without tearing everything down. What is the cleanest way to resume?
options: Run kubeadm reset and start the full kubeadm init over from scratch
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml by hand and hope the other phases complete
Run kubeadm join on the same node to re-register it
Fix the port conflict, then run kubeadm init phase etcd local to re-execute just the failed phase
explain: kubeadm init is decomposed into phases (preflight, certs, etcd, control-plane, kubelet-start, etc.), and kubeadm init phase <phase> re-runs a single one, so you can resume exactly where it failed. A full reset plus re-init also works but discards the phases that already succeeded and costs time. Hand-editing the static manifest skips kubeadm's cert and config generation, and kubeadm join is for adding nodes to an existing cluster, not for finishing an init.

q: Corporate policy requires the cluster DNS suffix to be apps.corp.internal instead of cluster.local. You are building the cluster fresh with kubeadm. How do you set this?
options: Pass --dns-domain apps.corp.internal to kubeadm init
Build normally, then edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap — that alone renames the whole cluster domain
Write a kubeadm ClusterConfiguration file with networking: {dnsDomain: apps.corp.internal} and run kubeadm init --config
Rename the domain after init with kubeadm upgrade apply --dns-domain
explain: The DNS domain is a ClusterConfiguration field (networking.dnsDomain), consumed by kubeadm at init to configure CoreDNS, the API server, and kubelets consistently — a config file plus --config is the supported path. There is no --dns-domain flag on kubeadm init, editing only the CoreDNS ConfigMap leaves kubelet and service DNS out of sync, and you cannot rename the DNS domain on a live cluster.

q: Your edge nodes are small and you want the kubelet on each new worker to allow at most 30 pods. Where do you declare this so every future kubeadm join picks it up?
options: In the kubeadm config file under nodeRegistration.kubeletExtraArgs with max-pods: '30', applied at join time
As a --max-pods flag on kubeadm init, which propagates to all nodes automatically
By SSHing to each node after joining and editing /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml by hand
By tainting each node so the scheduler stops at 30 pods
explain: nodeRegistration.kubeletExtraArgs in the kubeadm configuration passes extra flags (like max-pods) to the kubelet when the node registers, so it applies uniformly to every joined node. kubeadm init has no --max-pods flag, hand-editing each node drifts and is wiped by upgrades, and taints control scheduling eligibility, not pod count.

q: You built a 3-control-plane kubeadm cluster but skipped --control-plane-endpoint at init. Everything works today. What is the latent risk, and how does it show up?
options: Joining workers fails immediately because the token cannot be validated without an endpoint
kubectl keeps working only while the first control-plane node is alive, because admin.conf points at its IP instead of a load balancer
etcd loses quorum because members cannot discover each other
The scheduler stops placing pods after 24 hours when the bootstrap token expires
explain: Without --control-plane-endpoint, kubeadm writes the first control-plane node's advertise address into kubeconfig files, so all clients depend on that single node — lose it and kubectl dies even though the cluster is otherwise healthy. Worker joins still work, etcd forms its own peer list independently, and token expiry does not affect the scheduler or existing kubeconfigs.

q: You create a bootstrap token with kubeadm token create --usages signing --print-join-command and the join fails with Unauthorized. The token shows up in kubeadm token list. What is wrong?
options: The token only has the signing usage, but kubeadm join authenticates the node, which requires the authentication usage
Bootstrap tokens cannot be used for join at all; you must use a certificate key instead
The token expired between creation and the join attempt
Join requires the token to be created on the joining node, not on the control plane
explain: Token usages gate what the token may do: signing lets it sign cluster info, authentication lets a node bootstrap its TLS identity — join needs authentication, so a signing-only token is rejected. Tokens are created on the control plane and consumed on joining nodes by design, and a freshly listed token has not expired; the certificate key is only needed for additional control-plane nodes.

q: You want to enable a beta feature gate cluster-wide. You add --feature-gates=MyFeature=true to the kubelet on one node and the feature behaves erratically. What is the rule for feature gates?
options: Feature gates only need to be set on the kubelet; the control plane reads them from the node
Set the gate on the API server only — it propagates the setting to every component
Beta features cannot be enabled on kubeadm clusters at all
The same --feature-gates value must be set consistently on the API server, controller-manager, scheduler, and every kubelet
explain: Feature gates are per-component flags, not cluster state: the API server, controller-manager, scheduler, and kubelets each parse their own copy, so a gate enabled on only one component produces split-brain behavior. Setting it in one place never propagates, and kubeadm clusters support feature gates fine — they just require uniform configuration.

q: Leadership wants the restricted PodSecurityStandard enforced on all namespaces next quarter, but you must first find out which of the 200 existing workloads would break. How do you preview violations without blocking anything?
options: Set the enforce label to restricted now and roll back the workloads that fail
Label namespaces with pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted and pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted, then review the audit log and warnings
Run kubectl apply --dry-run=server on every manifest and grep for securityContext
PodSecurity cannot preview; you must test in a staging cluster
explain: The audit and warn modes evaluate pods against the standard and record violations (audit events plus kubectl warnings) without rejecting anything, which is exactly the preview mechanism. Enforcing immediately causes an outage, --dry-run only validates the manifests you feed it rather than the live fleet, and a staging cluster would not reflect production's actual workloads.

q: The batch team wants bin-packing schedulers for nightly jobs while web workloads keep the default spread behavior. How do you run two scheduling policies in one cluster?
options: Deploy a second kube-scheduler binary with its own flags on another node
Encode the policy in node affinity rules on each workload
Write a KubeSchedulerConfiguration with two profiles and point batch pods at the second profile via schedulerName
Use taints and tolerations to separate the two workload classes
explain: One scheduler process can serve multiple profiles defined in a KubeSchedulerConfiguration; pods select a profile with schedulerName, giving different plugin sets per workload class. A second scheduler binary is the legacy multi-scheduler pattern and doubles operational load, affinity and taints steer placement rather than defining scheduling policy.

q: You switched kube-proxy to IPVS mode by editing the kube-proxy ConfigMap in kube-system and deleting the kube-proxy pods. How do you confirm on a node that the switch actually took effect?
options: kubectl get svc shows the Services with a new IPVS-READY annotation
iptables -S still lists the full set of KUBE-SVC chains, which proves IPVS is active
curl the ClusterIP from a pod; only IPVS answers
Check the kube-proxy logs for 'Using ipvs Proxier' and run ipvsadm -ln on the node to see the virtual servers
explain: The kube-proxy log line naming the proxier plus ipvsadm showing programmed virtual servers is the direct proof the dataplane switched. No annotation is added to Services, a full KUBE-SVC iptables chain set indicates iptables mode is still in use, and a working curl cannot distinguish the two dataplanes.

q: Your cluster grew to 200 nodes and the two CoreDNS replicas are saturated, causing DNS timeouts. Manually scaling the Deployment works, but you want replica count to track cluster size automatically. Which component does this?
options: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CoreDNS CPU, which is the recommended DNS autoscaler
The cluster-proportional-autoscaler (dns-horizontal-autoscaler), which scales CoreDNS replicas from node and core counts
The kube-dns-autoscaler sidecar, which only works with kube-dns, not CoreDNS
A CronJob that runs kubectl scale on the CoreDNS Deployment hourly
explain: The cluster-proportional-autoscaler watches the number of nodes/cores and adjusts CoreDNS replicas linearly — the purpose-built solution for DNS scaling. HPA on CPU reacts to load spikes rather than cluster size and is not the recommended pattern here, the kube-dns autoscaler targets the legacy kube-dns, and a CronJob is a fragile hand-rolled substitute.

q: Upgrade night: you must upgrade the kubelet on a control-plane node. A teammate says never drain a control-plane node because it will kill the API server. What actually happens when you kubectl drain it?
options: Drain deletes the static pod manifests, so the API server, scheduler, and etcd are destroyed
Drain is refused on control-plane nodes by an admission webhook
Drain cordons the node and evicts regular workloads; the static pods (API server, etcd, scheduler) are mirror pods managed by the kubelet from manifests, not by the scheduler, so they are untouched
Drain works but you must uncordon within 60 seconds or etcd loses quorum
explain: Static pods are created by the kubelet directly from /etc/kubernetes/manifests and are invisible to the scheduler, so drain — which works through the eviction API on scheduled pods — cannot remove them; only your regular workloads move. There is no webhook refusing the drain and no 60-second quorum timer; draining control-plane nodes during upgrades is normal practice.

q: On your single-node kubeadm lab cluster, a test Deployment's pods stay Pending: the node has the control-plane NoSchedule taint. You accept the risk for a lab. Which command lets workloads schedule there?
options: kubectl delete node lab-1 and rejoin it as a worker
kubectl taint nodes lab-1 node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule-
kubectl label nodes lab-1 workload=allowed
Edit the scheduler manifest to ignore taints
explain: The trailing dash in the taint command removes that exact taint key/effect from the node, lifting the scheduling barrier. Deleting and rejoining the node is destructive overkill, a label does nothing unless the scheduler is told to consider it, and the scheduler has no ignore-taints mode.

q: Your existing nodes run containerd, but the new node pool was built with CRI-O. kubeadm join on a new node fails because it probes the containerd socket. How do you join the CRI-O node?
options: Run kubeadm join with --cri-socket /var/run/crio/crio.sock so kubeadm configures the kubelet for CRI-O
Uninstall CRI-O and install containerd; kubeadm requires a uniform runtime
Pass --runtime=crio to kubeadm join
Edit /etc/containerd/config.toml to point at the CRI-O socket
explain: --cri-socket tells kubeadm which CRI endpoint the kubelet should use, and mixed runtimes across nodes are fully supported. kubeadm does not require cluster-wide runtime uniformity, there is no --runtime join flag, and containerd cannot front CRI-O's socket.

q: etcd's database file keeps growing even though compaction is running, and you are approaching the backend quota. Compaction only marks revisions free. Which operation actually reclaims the disk space?
options: Deleting old keys manually with etcdctl del --prefix
Restarting the etcd static pod, which compacts on boot
Adding more etcd members to spread the data
Running etcdctl defrag (during a maintenance window), which rewrites the backend file and releases freed pages
explain: Compaction discards old revisions logically but the backend file keeps the pages until defrag rewrites the database and returns the space to the OS — that is why defrag is the documented follow-up to quota pressure. Deleting keys creates more revisions rather than freeing space, restarts do not defragment, and new members each replicate the full dataset.

q: You enabled kubelet serving-certificate rotation with --server-tls-bootstrap. A CSR of signerName kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving sits in Pending forever, while client CSRs get approved automatically. What is different about serving CSRs?
options: Serving CSRs are invalid; the kubelet should reuse its client certificate for serving
The CSR must be deleted so the kubelet falls back to a self-signed serving cert
Restarting the kubelet auto-approves serving CSRs on the second attempt
Automatic approval only covers client CSRs — kubelet-serving CSRs always need explicit kubectl certificate approve (after verifying the node identity)
explain: The built-in CSR approver only auto-approves node client certificates; serving-certificate CSRs are deliberately left for manual approval so an admin verifies the requestor. Deleting the CSR just recreates the wait, restarts do not approve anything, and reusing the client cert for serving is not how TLS bootstrap works.

q: You created a ClusterRole named monitoring-read and want every subject who already has the built-in view ClusterRole to gain it automatically, without editing the built-in role. Which mechanism does this?
options: Editing the view ClusterRole to add the monitoring rules; built-in roles are meant to be customized
Creating the monitoring-read ClusterRole with an aggregationRule and the label rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: 'true', so the API server merges its rules into view
Binding monitoring-read with a second ClusterRoleBinding to every view holder
Copying the view ClusterRole's subjects into a new RoleBinding
explain: Aggregated ClusterRoles use an aggregationRule plus the aggregate-to-* labels; the API server unions matching rules into view (and edit/admin), so all view holders inherit the new permissions with zero binding changes. Editing built-in roles is discouraged and gets clobbered by upgrades, extra bindings per subject do not scale, and RoleBindings cannot reference ClusterRole subjects.

q: After a hardening pass set automountServiceAccountToken: false on a pod, its app suddenly cannot list ConfigMaps via the API, though RBAC is unchanged. What broke?
options: With automount disabled, the pod gets no ServiceAccount token volume, so the in-cluster client has no credentials at all
The API server now rejects the pod's requests because the ServiceAccount was deleted
A NetworkPolicy was implicitly created by the hardening
The pod's DNS no longer resolves kubernetes.default
explain: automountServiceAccountToken: false stops the kubelet from mounting the projected token volume, so the app's client library finds no credentials and every API call fails — RBAC never gets evaluated. The ServiceAccount still exists, no policy is created implicitly, and DNS is unrelated to authentication.

q: You are installing a cluster in an air-gapped datacenter. All control-plane images must come from mirror.corp:5000 instead of registry.k8s.io. Which kubeadm init option rewrites every default image reference?
options: Pre-pulling the images and retagging them locally on each node before init
--pod-network-cidr, which also redirects image pulls
Editing each static manifest after init to fix the image fields
kubeadm init --image-repository mirror.corp:5000, which prefixes all control-plane images
explain: --image-repository replaces the default registry prefix for every image kubeadm manages (API server, etcd, CoreDNS, pause), which is the supported air-gap path. Retagging by hand on every node is error-prone and missed by upgrades, the pod CIDR is unrelated to registries, and post-hoc manifest edits leave CoreDNS and other components pointing at the unreachable default.

q: You ran kubeadm certs renew all and it reported success, but openssl still shows the API server serving the OLD certificate. What step is missing?
options: Running kubeadm certs renew a second time; the first run only stages the certs
Rebooting the control-plane node to reload the kernel keyring
Restarting the control-plane static pods (or the kubelet), because the running API server loaded its certificates at startup
Copying the renewed certs into /etc/kubernetes/pki by hand
explain: Static pods read their certificate files once at startup, so renewed files on disk have no effect until the API server, etcd, and other components restart and reload them. Renew does write the files in place (no second run or manual copy needed), and no reboot is required — a pod restart suffices.

q: You join a second control-plane node that has two NICs (10.0.0.6 management, 192.168.99.6 storage). The join succeeds, but the new API server is unreachable: its certificate and advertise address used the storage IP. Which join flag would have prevented this?
options: --control-plane-endpoint, which sets the load-balancer address for clients
--node-name, which pins the node object to the right interface
--apiserver-advertise-address 10.0.0.6 on the kubeadm join --control-plane command, so the new API server advertises the management IP with matching SANs
--cri-socket, which selects the network interface for the runtime
explain: --apiserver-advertise-address on the join command controls which IP the additional control-plane node's API server advertises and bakes into its certificates. --control-plane-endpoint is set at init for client kubeconfigs, --node-name only names the Node object, and --cri-socket selects the container runtime socket, not networking.

q: A payment API runs 2 replicas and must NEVER drop below 2 available pods during a rollout. Which rolling-update strategy guarantees zero downtime here?
options: The defaults (maxUnavailable 25%, maxSurge 25%), which are safe for any replica count
strategy: {type: Recreate}, which is the fastest way to swap images
maxUnavailable: 0 (with maxSurge: 1), so the old pods stay until replacements are ready
maxSurge: 0, which prevents any extra pods from starting
explain: With 2 replicas, the 25% default allows maxUnavailable to round to 1, so one pod can be down mid-rollout; maxUnavailable: 0 forbids that while maxSurge: 1 lets the replacement start first. Recreate kills everything before starting replacements (guaranteed downtime), and maxSurge: 0 alone still permits one unavailable pod.

q: A bad environment variable shipped three revisions ago. kubectl rollout history shows the revisions but the CHANGE-CAUSE column is empty, because --record was removed long ago. How do you restore change tracking going forward?
options: Annotate each Deployment change with kubectl annotate deployment/web kubernetes.io/change-cause='...', which populates the history column
Reinstall kubectl with the --record flag compiled back in
Switch to Recreate strategy, which logs causes automatically
Change-cause is stored in etcd; run etcdctl get to read it
explain: The history column reads the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation, so setting it (manually or in CI) on every change restores the audit trail that --record used to provide. --record was removed from kubectl and cannot be compiled back in any supported way, the strategy does not affect annotations, and change-cause is not an etcd implementation detail you query directly.

q: A legacy Java app needs up to 3 minutes to start, and the liveness probe keeps killing it at 60 seconds. Raising initialDelaySeconds to 4 minutes would work but leaves the container unmonitored during startup. Which probe is designed for this?
options: A readiness probe with a long initialDelaySeconds, which also gates liveness
Removing the liveness probe entirely for slow-starting apps
A startupProbe with a generous failureThreshold; while it runs, liveness and readiness are disabled, then they take over
An exec probe that sleeps 180 seconds before checking
explain: startupProbe exists precisely for slow starters: it runs first with its own generous budget, and liveness/readiness only begin after it succeeds, so you keep full protection without the kill loop. A long initialDelaySeconds on readiness does not gate liveness, deleting the probe loses crash detection forever, and sleeping inside the probe just delays the same failure.

q: A pod with a database-migration init container sits in Init:0/1 forever; the app container never starts. kubectl logs shows the migration exited with code 1. What is the pod waiting for, and what fixes it?
options: The kubelet is waiting for the node's disk to free up; cordon the node
Init containers run sequentially and every one must exit 0 before app containers start — fix the migration (or the init logic) so it succeeds
The pod needs a liveness probe on the init container to restart it
Init containers require a restartPolicy of Always to retry
explain: Init containers are a hard gate: they execute in order and the pod cannot proceed until each exits successfully, so a failing migration blocks startup by design and the fix is in the migration itself. Disk pressure, liveness probes on init containers (not supported), and restartPolicy (init containers always retry with backoff on failure) are all red herrings.

q: A node hits memory pressure. Three pods: db (Guaranteed), web (Burstable, using double its request), batch (BestEffort). In what order does the kubelet evict them?
options: db first, because Guaranteed pods hold the most memory
All three simultaneously; eviction order is random
batch first, then web if pressure remains, then db last — BestEffort goes before Burstable exceeding its requests, and Guaranteed is evicted last
web first, because it is the only one exceeding its request
explain: The kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods (prioritizing those furthest over their requests), and Guaranteed pods last — QoS class dominates the ordering. Guaranteed is the most protected, not the first victim; eviction is deterministic by QoS and usage-vs-request, never random; and web is only second in line, not first.

q: Applying a pod fails with: pods is forbidden: maximum cpu usage per Container is 2, requested 4. The node has 32 free cores. What is rejecting the pod?
options: A LimitRange in the namespace capping each container at 2 CPUs — lower the request or raise the LimitRange
The ResourceQuota, which ran out of CPU
The node's allocatable CPU, which is smaller than its capacity
A taint on the node reserving CPUs for system daemons
explain: That exact 'maximum cpu usage per Container' message comes from a LimitRange's max constraint, an admission-time per-container ceiling independent of node capacity. A quota rejection names the quota and its usage, node allocatable would surface as Insufficient cpu at scheduling time, and taints produce toleration errors rather than usage ceilings.

q: A critical pod uses a high-value PriorityClass but sets preemptionPolicy: Never. The cluster is full and the pod stays Pending instead of evicting lower-priority pods. Why?
options: The priority value is still too low; only values above 1 billion preempt
A PodDisruptionBudget is blocking the preemption
The scheduler is down, so no preemption decisions are being made
preemptionPolicy: Never means this pod will never preempt others — it waits for free capacity instead
explain: preemptionPolicy: Never explicitly opts the pod out of preempting lower-priority victims, so it stays Pending until capacity frees up; remove the policy (default is PreemptLowerPriority) if it should evict. Priority value is irrelevant once preemption is disabled, PDBs constrain voluntary evictions rather than preemption, and a down scheduler would leave the Pending reason empty rather than scheduling-gated.

q: You set a PDB with minAvailable: 2 and selector app: web, but during a node drain all web pods were evicted at once and the site went down. kubectl get pdb shows 0 allowed disruptions. What went wrong?
options: minAvailable: 2 requires maxUnavailable instead; the two fields cannot be mixed
The PDB's selector does not match the Deployment's pod labels (app: web-v2), so the PDB protects zero pods
PDBs only apply to StatefulSets, not Deployments
The drain used --force, which bypasses all PDBs
explain: A PDB only guards pods its selector matches; with a label mismatch it selects nothing, so the eviction API sees no budget and drain proceeds. minAvailable is valid on its own, PDBs cover any pods including Deployments, and --force does not exist for drain — the failure here is purely the selector gap, visible as disruptions-allowed 0 with healthy pods.

q: You add topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule to a 2-zone Deployment. With 3 replicas running (2 in zone-a, 1 in zone-b), scaling to 4 leaves the new pod Pending. Why?
options: The cluster autoscaler is disabled, so the 4th pod has no node
Anti-affinity rules from another workload are interfering
Placing the 4th pod would make the skew 2 (3 vs 1), exceeding maxSkew: 1, so DoNotSchedule blocks it until zone balance allows
topologySpreadConstraints only works with 3 or more zones
explain: maxSkew: 1 permits at most a one-pod difference between zones; a 4th pod would land in zone-a making it 3-vs-1 (skew 2), so DoNotSchedule correctly holds it Pending. The autoscaler is irrelevant to the scheduling decision, no anti-affinity is involved, and the constraint works with any number of topology domains.

q: You set a preferredDuringScheduling nodeAffinity for disktype=ssd, but during a busy hour several pods landed on hdd nodes. The YAML is valid. Is this a bug?
options: No — preferred affinity is a soft hint; the scheduler honors it only when it does not conflict with hard constraints and available capacity
Yes — preferred affinity is a hard requirement and the scheduler is malfunctioning
Yes — the node labels must be wrong, since affinity never fails silently
No — but only because the SSD nodes were tainted
explain: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is explicitly best-effort: the scheduler weights it but will place pods on non-matching nodes when SSD capacity is exhausted or other constraints win. It is not a guarantee (that is what required affinity is for), labels can be perfectly correct while the preference is simply outweighed, and taints are not required for this behavior.

q: You taint a node maintenance=true:PreferNoSchedule during a rolling hardware check, but new pods still land on it. The taint is spelled correctly. Why did they schedule there?
options: The taint key must be prefixed with the node name to take effect
All pods automatically tolerate PreferNoSchedule taints
kubectl taint silently failed; only NoSchedule taints are real
PreferNoSchedule is a soft hint — the scheduler avoids the node when possible but still places pods there if it is the only feasible fit
explain: PreferNoSchedule is advisory by design: the scheduler tries to avoid the node but will schedule there rather than leave a pod Pending, unlike the hard NoSchedule barrier. No prefixing is needed, pods do not auto-tolerate it (it simply does not repel hard), and the taint applied fine — the softness is the documented semantic.

q: Your logging DaemonSet uses updateStrategy: OnDelete. You applied a new image an hour ago but every pod still runs the old one. What must you do?
options: Wait — OnDelete propagates the update after a one-hour grace period
Delete the DaemonSet pods (e.g. kubectl delete pod -l app=logger); OnDelete only replaces pods when they are deleted
Run kubectl rollout restart daemonset/logger, which is blocked by OnDelete
Drain every node to force pod recreation
explain: OnDelete means the controller updates the DaemonSet template but never replaces running pods on its own — you delete pods (or the nodes recycle) and the replacements come up on the new template. There is no grace-period delay, rollout restart actually does work around OnDelete by deleting pods, and draining nodes is a far heavier hammer than deleting the pods.

q: A StatefulSet of 30 stateless worker pods scales from 0 to 30 painfully slowly: each pod waits for the previous one to become Ready. The app needs no ordering at all. Which field removes the sequential startup?
options: podManagementPolicy: Parallel, which lets the controller create (and delete) pods concurrently instead of strict ordinal order
partition: 30, which disables the ordinal index
replicas: 30 with updateStrategy RollingUpdate, which parallelizes creation
podAffinity, which groups the pods onto fewer nodes
explain: podManagementPolicy: Parallel drops the OrderedReady guarantee so all pods launch at once — the right choice when ordinals carry no meaning. partition only gates which ordinals update during rollouts, the update strategy does not parallelize scale-up, and affinity affects placement rather than creation ordering.

q: You must pre-provision PVs for a StatefulSet named db with a volumeClaimTemplate named data. What will the PVCs be called so your PVs (or selectors) can target them?
options: data-db-0, data-db-1, ... — <claim-template-name>-<statefulset-name>-<ordinal>
db-data-0, db-data-1, ... — <statefulset-name>-<claim-template-name>-<ordinal>
Random names assigned by the provisioner; StatefulSet PVCs cannot be predicted
pvc-<uid> like any dynamically provisioned claim
explain: The StatefulSet controller names each claim <volumeClaimTemplate metadata.name>-<statefulset name>-<ordinal>, so data-db-0 is deterministic and pre-provisioned PVs or selectors can rely on it. The reversed order is wrong, the names are never random, and pvc-<uid> style names belong to other provisioning flows.

q: A Job's worker occasionally hangs on a network call forever: completions never arrive and the Job sits active for days. backoffLimit does not help because the pod never fails. Which field caps the total runtime?
options: ttlSecondsAfterFinished, which deletes the Job after it completes
parallelism: 1, which prevents concurrent hangs
restartPolicy: Never, which stops the retries
activeDeadlineSeconds, which terminates the whole Job once its total active time exceeds the limit
explain: activeDeadlineSeconds is the wall-clock cap on a Job's active lifetime — exceeding it terminates running pods and marks the Job failed, which is exactly the hung-worker guard. ttlSecondsAfterFinished only cleans up after completion, parallelism does not bound time, and restartPolicy governs pod retries rather than total duration (and backoffLimit only counts failures, not hangs).

q: Nightly Jobs accumulate by the hundreds; you want each finished Job (and its pods) garbage-collected automatically one hour after completion. Which field does this?
options: successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 0 on the CronJob, which deletes finished Jobs
ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 on the Job, which deletes it one hour after it finishes
backoffLimit: 0, which prevents Job accumulation
A CronJob with suspend: true, which stops new Jobs from piling up
explain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished triggers automatic deletion of the finished Job after the given delay — the built-in TTL controller for Job cleanup. History limits only apply to CronJob-managed Jobs and cap counts rather than time, backoffLimit controls retries, and suspending the CronJob stops future runs without cleaning past ones.

q: The 2 AM backup CronJob is healthy, but you need a backup RIGHT NOW before a risky migration — without touching the schedule. What is the fastest correct way?
options: Edit the CronJob schedule to '* * * * *', wait for a run, then change it back
Copy the CronJob YAML into a Job manifest by hand and apply it
Run kubectl create job backup-now --from=cronjob/backup, which stamps a one-off Job from the CronJob template
Set suspend: false on the CronJob, which triggers an immediate run
explain: --from=cronjob/<name> instantiates a single Job from the live CronJob template — the intended manual-trigger path that leaves the schedule untouched. Editing the schedule risks a forgotten revert and extra runs, hand-copying YAML drifts from the template, and suspend: false merely allows scheduled runs rather than triggering one.

q: Every deployment causes a 2-minute CPU spike that makes the HPA double the replicas, then it scales back down — churn on every release. You want the HPA to tolerate brief spikes before scaling UP. Which setting does this?
options: Lowering targetCPUUtilizationPercentage so the spike stays under target
Setting minReplicas equal to the spike peak, which wastes capacity permanently
behavior.scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 180, which makes scale-up consider the lowest recommendation over a 3-minute window
Deleting the HPA during deployments with a CI hook
explain: The scale-up stabilization window dampens reactions to transient spikes by holding the recommendation at its recent minimum for the window — the designed anti-flap control for scale-up. Lowering the target moves the threshold rather than adding damping, pinning minReplicas wastes capacity around the clock, and CI hooks are fragile operational toil.

q: You installed the Vertical Pod Autoscaler in auto mode on a Deployment that also has an HPA targeting CPU. The pods now thrash: VPA restarts them with new requests while HPA scales on the moving target. What is the guidance here?
options: Delete the HPA; VPA replaces it
Raise the VPA update frequency so it settles faster
Run both in full auto mode; the thrash resolves once recommendations converge
Do not run VPA and HPA on the same metric — use VPA for memory and HPA for CPU, or run VPA in recommendation-only (off) mode
explain: VPA (which mutates requests) and HPA (which scales on utilization against those requests) form a feedback loop when both drive CPU — the documented fix is to split metrics or run VPA in off mode for recommendations only. Deleting the HPA loses horizontal scaling, tuning VPA frequency does not break the loop, and the thrash does not self-resolve because each controller keeps moving the other's input.

q: A production pod is crash-looping and you must test a hypothesis with a modified image, but you cannot disturb the live pod. Which kubectl debug invocation gives you an isolated copy to experiment on?
options: kubectl debug pod/web-0 --image=debug:v2, which replaces the live pod's image in place
kubectl debug pod/web-0 --copy-to=web-debug --set-image=app=debug:v2, which creates a separate copy of the pod with the new image
kubectl edit pod web-0 and change the image field directly
kubectl exec into the pod and hot-swap the binary
explain: --copy-to clones the pod into a new object (optionally overriding the image with --set-image), leaving the original untouched for safe experimentation. Plain kubectl debug without --copy-to attaches an ephemeral container to the live pod, most pod spec fields (including image) are immutable on a running pod, and hot-swapping binaries inside a container is neither reproducible nor safe.

q: A clustered database discovers peers via DNS on a headless Service, but new members can never join: they only appear in DNS after passing their readiness probe, and they need DNS to become ready. How do you break the deadlock?
options: Set publishNotReadyAddresses: true on the headless Service so DNS includes pods before they are ready
Delete the readiness probes; clustered apps should not use them
Switch the Service to ClusterIP so kube-proxy handles discovery
Add the pod IPs to the CoreDNS ConfigMap by hand
explain: publishNotReadyAddresses: true makes the headless Service publish DNS records for all backing pods regardless of readiness — the designed escape hatch for bootstrap deadlocks where readiness depends on discovery. Removing probes loses health gating everywhere, a ClusterIP Service never publishes per-pod records, and hand-editing CoreDNS is static and unmaintainable.

q: You created a headless Service with clusterIP: None but no selector, intending to point it at an external appliance. Pods querying the name get NXDOMAIN. What is missing?
options: Headless Services require a selector; without one the Service is invalid
An ExternalName Service must be used instead — headless cannot point outside
A second Service of type ClusterIP to back the headless one
An EndpointSlice (or Endpoints) object with the same name, manually listing the appliance addresses — selector-less Services need hand-managed endpoints
explain: Without a selector the endpoints controller has nothing to watch, so you must create the EndpointSlice/Endpoints yourself with the Service's name; then DNS resolves. Selector-less Services are valid and commonly used for external targets, ExternalName is a different mechanism (CNAME), and no ClusterIP backer is needed.

q: You set spec.trafficDistribution: PreferClose on a Service, but traffic still flows cross-zone freely. The cluster is on-prem and nodes have no zone labels. Why is the setting having no effect?
options: PreferClose needs topology.kubernetes.io/zone labels on nodes to know what 'close' means — without them every endpoint looks equidistant
trafficDistribution only works on LoadBalancer Services
kube-proxy must be restarted on every node before the field is read
PreferClose is a hint for the cloud load balancer, not for kube-proxy
explain: PreferClose ranks endpoints by the node's zone (then node) labels; with no zone labels the scheduler of traffic has no topology to prefer, so it behaves like Cluster. The field applies to ClusterIP Services via kube-proxy, it is read on Service updates without restarts, and it is a kube-proxy/endpointslice feature, not a cloud-LB one.

q: You need the real client IP preserved for pod-to-pod calls through a Service, so you set internalTrafficPolicy: Local. Traffic from nodes WITHOUT a local endpoint now fails entirely. Is this expected?
options: No — internalTrafficPolicy: Local is a no-op for in-cluster traffic
Yes — with Local, traffic is only routed to endpoints on the same node; nodes without local endpoints drop it instead of forwarding, by design
No — the policy only applies to NodePort Services
Yes — but only until kube-proxy resyncs, after which it load-balances normally
explain: internalTrafficPolicy: Local restricts routing to node-local endpoints and drops traffic otherwise — the documented trade-off for preserving source IP without extra hops. It is not a no-op, it applies to ClusterIP Services (not just NodePort), and no resync changes the semantics; if every node must reach the Service, keep the default Cluster policy.

q: Your Ingress routes /api to the API and / to the web app for shop.example.com. Requests to /old-docs (matched by no rule) get the controller's generic 404. You want those to land on the web app instead. Where do you configure this?
options: In the Ingress spec.defaultBackend, which serves requests matching no rule
By adding a rule with path: /*, which Prefix already covers
With the rewrite-target annotation, which only rewrites matched paths
By creating a second Ingress with host: '*'
explain: spec.defaultBackend is the fallback backend for requests that match no rule — the per-Ingress catch-all. A /* Prefix rule is redundant with / and can behave unexpectedly across controllers, rewrite-target only transforms already-matched paths, and a wildcard-host Ingress still needs its own rules rather than acting as a fallback.

q: After upgrading ingress-nginx, Ingresses using the kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx annotation are ignored, while ones with spec.ingressClassName work. What changed?
options: The annotation value must now be prefixed with the controller version
Ingress resources no longer support annotations at all
The controller now requires TLS on every Ingress using the old annotation
spec.ingressClassName is the supported field; the legacy annotation is deprecated and newer controllers no longer honor it
explain: The class moved from the informal kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation into the formal spec.ingressClassName field, and current controllers only watch the field — annotated Ingresses become invisible to them. No version prefix exists, annotations work fine generally, and TLS is unrelated to class matching.

q: With Gateway API, you must route requests with the query string ?version=v2 to the v2 Service while all other traffic goes to v1, on the same path. Which HTTPRoute match expresses this?
options: Two separate Gateways, one per version
A header match on X-Version: v2
A rule with matches: [{queryParams: [{name: version, value: v2}]}] pointing at v2, plus a default rule to v1
A path match on /?version=v2
explain: HTTPRoute matches support queryParams explicitly, so one rule matching version=v2 routes to v2 and a lower-precedence default rule catches the rest. Separate Gateways are unnecessary, a query string is not a header, and paths never include the query string in Gateway API matching.

q: You want to shadow production traffic to the v2 backend for testing — v2 sees real requests, but clients only ever get v1's response. Which Gateway API filter does this?
options: A 50/50 weight split between v1 and v2
The RequestMirror filter on the HTTPRoute rule, which copies requests to v2 while the response comes from v1
Two HTTPRoutes with overlapping hostnames
A header modifier adding X-Shadow: true
explain: RequestMirror is the traffic-shadowing filter: the primary backend serves the client while a copy of each request goes to the mirror backend. Weight splits change what clients receive, overlapping routes do not duplicate requests, and a header modifier only mutates headers rather than copying traffic.

q: A hostNetwork monitoring pod keeps reaching endpoints that a NetworkPolicy should deny. The policy's podSelector matches it and the CNI supports policies. Why is it unaffected?
options: NetworkPolicy is not enforced on hostNetwork pods — they share the host's network namespace, bypassing pod-level policy
The policy needs policyTypes: [Egress] explicitly even with egress rules
hostNetwork pods must be in the host's namespace to match selectors
The CNI applies policies only to the first pod on each node
