explain: NetworkPolicies attach to pod network namespaces; a hostNetwork pod uses the node's namespace directly, so pod-level ingress/egress rules cannot intercept its traffic — a documented limitation. policyTypes defaults are derived from the rules present, namespace placement does not change the bypass, and the CNI enforces per-pod regardless of ordering.

q: With a default-deny egress policy in place, pods cannot resolve DNS. You want to allow DNS and nothing else. Which egress rule is correct and minimal?
options: Allow UDP to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 53; DNS only needs UDP
Allow TCP port 53 to the CoreDNS ClusterIP; the IP never changes
Allow all traffic to the kube-system namespace; CoreDNS lives there
An egress rule to namespaceSelector {name: kube-system} plus podSelector {k8s-app: kube-dns} on ports 53 UDP and TCP
explain: The precise rule targets the CoreDNS pods by namespace and label on port 53 for both UDP and TCP (large responses fall back to TCP) — minimal and robust. 0.0.0.0/0 on 53 opens DNS to the world, hardcoding the ClusterIP breaks if the Service is recreated, and allowing all of kube-system is far broader than DNS.

q: A pod with hostNetwork: true resolves in-cluster names like api.default via the node's DNS instead of CoreDNS, breaking service discovery. Which dnsPolicy fixes it?
options: dnsPolicy: Default, which is already the behavior you are seeing
dnsPolicy: None with a custom dnsConfig pointing at CoreDNS
dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet, which gives host-networked pods cluster DNS like normal pods
Removing hostNetwork; DNS cannot work with it enabled
explain: Kubelet defaults hostNetwork pods to dnsPolicy: Default (node DNS); ClusterFirstWithHostNet explicitly gives them the cluster DNS configuration instead. Default is the broken behavior described, None requires fully manual DNS config, and hostNetwork plus cluster DNS is a supported, common combination.

q: External lookups from pods take ~5 seconds (in-cluster names are instant). You know ndots: 5 makes the resolver try every search domain first. Without changing cluster DNS config, how can the app avoid the delay for a known external name?
options: Add more search domains so the name matches earlier
Query the fully-qualified name with a trailing dot (db.example.com.), which skips the search-domain expansion
Increase the CoreDNS cache TTL
Set ndots: 1 in the pod's dnsConfig
explain: A trailing dot marks the name as already fully qualified, so the resolver skips the ndots search-list expansion that causes the multi-second stall. More search domains add attempts rather than removing them, cache TTL does not affect the expansion attempts, and lowering ndots changes resolution semantics for short names cluster-wide.

q: You need five minutes of access to the web Deployment's port 8080 from your laptop. There is no Service yet and you do not want to create one. What works?
options: kubectl port-forward deployment/web 8080:80 — port-forward supports Deployments and picks a backing pod
Port-forward only works on pods and Services; you must create a Service first
kubectl exec into a pod and curl localhost; that exposes it to your laptop
Port-forward requires a NodePort Service to already exist
explain: kubectl port-forward accepts Deployments (and ReplicaSets, DaemonSets, StatefulSets), selecting a ready pod behind them — no Service needed. The claim that only pods and Services work is outdated, exec-plus-curl keeps traffic inside the cluster, and NodePort is unrelated to port-forward.

q: Security mandates that NodePorts be allocated from 31000-32000 instead of the default range. Where is the Service NodePort range actually defined?
options: In the kube-proxy ConfigMap; restart kube-proxy after editing
As an annotation on each Service
It is compiled into kubectl and cannot be changed
In the kube-apiserver flag --service-node-port-range; changing it requires restarting the API server
explain: --service-node-port-range is an API server flag because the API server allocates NodePorts at Service creation; kube-proxy merely implements them. The kube-proxy ConfigMap has no such field, no per-Service annotation overrides the range, and it is a runtime flag, not compiled into kubectl.

q: From your laptop (with VPN access to the nodes) you curl a Service's ClusterIP and it hangs. From a pod, the same ClusterIP answers instantly. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A NetworkPolicy is blocking your laptop's IP
kube-proxy is down on the node you reached
ClusterIPs are virtual IPs programmed only on cluster nodes; they are not routable from outside the cluster, even with node network access
The Service's endpoints are empty
explain: ClusterIPs exist only as iptables/IPVS rules on nodes for in-cluster traffic; off-cluster clients cannot route to them by design, so the pod works and the laptop hangs. A NetworkPolicy would not distinguish based on source network here, kube-proxy being down would break the pod too, and empty endpoints would fail from the pod as well.

q: On a dual-stack cluster, some pods get IPv4 first and others IPv6 first in their status.podIPs list, and an old app that binds only the first address behaves inconsistently. What determines which family is primary?
options: The order is random per pod; dual-stack has no primary family
The order of ipFamilies on the pod or Service — the first entry is the primary, single-stack clients use it
The CNI plugin decides per node based on available addresses
The kernel's address selection on each node
explain: ipFamilies is an ordered list and the first family is the primary (used for the single ClusterIP and by single-stack consumers); inconsistent ordering means the field differs or was defaulted differently. It is not random, the CNI assigns from the configured families rather than choosing primary, and kernel address selection does not reorder podIPs.

q: One Gateway has a listener with hostname: '*.example.com'. Two HTTPRoutes attach: one with hostnames: ['shop.example.com'], another with hostnames: ['other.io']. Which route actually binds?
options: The shop.example.com route — a route's hostnames must intersect the listener's hostname to attach
The other.io route — routes override the listener hostname
Both — listeners accept any route hostname
Neither — wildcard listeners cannot be shared
explain: Attachment requires the route's hostnames to intersect the listener's hostname; shop.example.com falls inside *.example.com while other.io does not, so only the first binds. Routes cannot override the listener, listeners do not accept arbitrary hostnames, and wildcard listeners are shareable within their scope.

q: Your Gateway terminates TLS at the edge, but the backend pods themselves require HTTPS with certificates from a private CA. The HTTPRoute points at the Service and the Gateway gets 502s on the TLS handshake to the backend. Which Gateway API object configures the Gateway-to-backend TLS?
options: A second Gateway with a TLS listener for the backend
An HTTPRouteFilter RequestMirror to retry over HTTPS
The backendProtocol: HTTPS annotation on the Service, which Gateway API controllers honor
A BackendTLSPolicy targeting the Service, specifying the CA certificates and hostname for validating the backend's TLS
explain: BackendTLSPolicy is the Gateway API policy for TLS origination toward backends: it tells the Gateway which CA to trust and which hostname to verify when dialing the Service over HTTPS. A second Gateway does not change backend dialing, RequestMirror copies rather than secures traffic, and backendProtocol is an ingress-nginx annotation, not a Gateway API concept.

q: A Service sets spec.loadBalancerClass: metallb but its EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending> forever. MetalLB was never actually deployed to this cluster. What is wrong?
options: The loadBalancerClass names a controller that is not installed, so nothing reconciles the Service — install MetalLB or remove the class field
The cloud provider quota for load balancers is exhausted
A firewall is blocking the MetalLB speaker ports
The Service must be type NodePort for a class to apply
explain: loadBalancerClass hands the Service to exactly one controller; if no installed controller claims that class value, the Service waits forever with no events from any reconciler. Cloud quotas produce provider errors rather than silence, speaker connectivity matters only once MetalLB is running, and the class field applies to LoadBalancer Services, not NodePort.

q: Under heavy load with many short-lived connections, nodes log 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' and new connections fail intermittently. Pods and Services are otherwise healthy. What is the fix?
options: Add more worker nodes to spread the connections
Raise nf_conntrack_max (and/or lower conntrack timeouts) on the nodes — the connection-tracking table is exhausted
Switch kube-proxy from iptables to IPVS, which does not use conntrack
Increase the Service's sessionAffinity timeout
explain: The kernel's conntrack table has a fixed size; when short-lived connections churn faster than entries expire, the table fills and the kernel drops new connections — raising the max or shortening timeouts is the direct fix. More nodes do not raise any single node's table, IPVS still uses conntrack, and session affinity is unrelated to connection tracking.

q: A developer deletes a test PVC and is shocked that the 500 GB cloud disk is gone too — they assumed delete only removed the claim. The StorageClass was created with no explicit reclaimPolicy. What happened, and how do you change the default?
options: The CSI driver deleted it erroneously; file a bug with the driver vendor
The PV had an ownerReference to the PVC, which always cascades
Kubernetes never deletes cloud disks; the cloud provider reclaimed it for billing
StorageClasses default to reclaimPolicy: Delete, so PVC deletion deletes the volume — set reclaimPolicy: Retain on the StorageClass to keep disks
explain: When a StorageClass omits reclaimPolicy it defaults to Delete, meaning the provisioned volume is destroyed with the PVC — the number-one surprise for newcomers. The driver behaved correctly, there is no ownerReference cascade on PVs, and Kubernetes absolutely can delete cloud disks; Retain on the class flips the default for future claims.

q: You mount a single file app.conf from a ConfigMap using subPath. After editing the ConfigMap, pods mounting the whole ConfigMap directory pick up the change, but the subPath-mounted file stays stale forever. Why?
options: The kubelet caches subPath mounts for 24 hours; wait and it updates
subPath mounts are bind-mounts of a specific file version and never receive ConfigMap updates — mount the directory or use a projected volume instead
The ConfigMap edit did not actually save; subPath validates the API write
subPath requires readOnly: false to receive updates
explain: A subPath mount bind-mounts the file as it existed at mount time; the kubelet's periodic ConfigMap refresh only updates full directory mounts, so subPath files are frozen until the pod restarts. There is no 24-hour cache, the API write succeeded (other mounts prove it), and readOnly is unrelated to update propagation.

q: Each replica needs real provisioned scratch space with capacity tracking and proper scheduling (unlike emptyDir), but the volume must die with the pod — no lingering PVCs. Which volume type fits?
options: A manually pre-provisioned PVC per replica, deleted by a CronJob
hostPath, which is automatically cleaned when the pod dies
An ephemeral volume with volumeClaimTemplate inline in the pod spec — PVC-like lifecycle bound to the pod
A projected volume, which provisions storage dynamically
explain: Generic ephemeral volumes embed a volumeClaimTemplate directly in the pod spec: the PVC is created for the pod, participates in scheduling and capacity tracking, and is garbage-collected with the pod. Manual PVCs linger, hostPath is node-local and never cleaned, and projected volumes only compose ConfigMaps/Secrets/downward API — they provision no storage.

q: A monitoring agent reads an optional config file at /etc/agent/agent.conf from the host. On nodes where the file does not exist, the pod fails to start. Which hostPath type tolerates the missing file by creating an empty one?
options: type: Directory, which creates the path as a directory
type: Socket, which creates a socket file
type: FileOrCreate, which creates an empty file if it does not exist, then mounts it
type: CharDevice, which works for any file type
explain: FileOrCreate creates an empty file at the path when absent, so the mount succeeds on nodes without the config; plain File (like Directory) requires existence. Directory would create a directory rather than a file, and Socket/CharDevice types do not match a regular config file.

q: You try to change an existing PVC from accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] to [ReadWriteOncePod] with kubectl apply, and the API rejects it as a forbidden update. What is the rule, and what is the path forward?
options: accessModes is immutable on a bound PVC — recreate the PVC (with a Retain-backed PV your data survives and can be rebound)
Only the StorageClass may change access modes; edit the class instead
Restart the pods; the access mode updates on remount
Delete the PV; the PVC then becomes editable
explain: A PVC's accessModes cannot be changed after creation — the API forbids it — so you recreate the claim; with reclaimPolicy: Retain the PV and its data persist for rebinding. The StorageClass does not dictate a claim's modes, remounts do not mutate the API object, and deleting the PV destroys the very data you want to keep.

q: Your analytics workload's PersistentVolume holds millions of small files with the correct GID already. Pod startup blocks for half an hour while Kubernetes walks the filesystem fixing ownership, even though nothing needs changing. Which pod-level field skips the recursive chown when ownership already matches?
options: runAsGroup, which sets the group without walking the volume
securityContext.fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch, which only recurses when the root directory's ownership differs
supplementalGroups, which bypasses fsGroup entirely
fsGroup: 0, which disables ownership management
explain: fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch makes the kubelet check only the volume root and skip the recursive chown when it already matches — the designed fix for slow mounts on file-dense volumes. runAsGroup sets process groups but does not gate the volume walk, supplementalGroups are additive rather than a bypass, and fsGroup: 0 still triggers the recursive change (to root).

q: An app wants to size its thread pool from its own CPU limit without hardcoding values. How can the pod expose its limit to the container?
options: Mount /sys/fs/cgroup and parse the files at startup
Hardcode the limit in an environment variable in the Deployment
A downwardAPI volume (or env) with resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.cpu}, which projects the container's own limit
Query the metrics-server from inside the container
explain: The downward API's resourceFieldRef exposes the container's requests/limits as files or env vars, so the app reads its actual configured limit with no hardcoding. Parsing cgroup files couples the app to cgroup v1/v2 layouts, hardcoded env vars drift from the real spec, and metrics-server reports usage rather than configured limits.

q: A backup agent pod mounts the host's /mnt/data and needs mounts it creates inside the container to become visible on the host (so the host backup job sees them). The default propagation does not do this. Which setting does?
options: mountPropagation: Bidirectional on the volumeMount (the pod needs appropriate privilege), so mounts propagate both ways
mountPropagation: HostToContainer, which is the default and already bidirectional
A second hostPath volume mounted at the same path
privileged: true alone, which implies bidirectional propagation
explain: Bidirectional propagation shares mount/unmount events both from host to container and container to host — the only mode that publishes container-created mounts to the host (it requires privileged). HostToContainer is one-way (host to container), a duplicate volume changes nothing about propagation, and privileged alone does not alter the default propagation mode.

q: With volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer, how does the scheduler avoid placing a pod on a node whose backend has no free capacity for the PVC?
options: It cannot — WaitForFirstConsumer disables capacity-aware scheduling
The provisioner reserves capacity when the PVC is created
The storage admin must label nodes with available capacity by hand
Through CSIStorageCapacity objects published by the CSI driver, which the scheduler reads during delayed binding
explain: CSI drivers publish CSIStorageCapacity objects per topology segment, and the scheduler consults them when binding is delayed to the scheduling step — that is the capacity-aware half of WaitForFirstConsumer. Binding is not capacity-blind, no reservation happens at PVC creation, and manual labeling is unnecessary when the driver reports capacity itself.

q: Two pods with different SELinux contexts must share a volume, but SELinux denials block access. The cluster runs SELinux-enforcing nodes. Where do you set the SELinux labels for the pod's volumes?
options: In the container image's Dockerfile with chcon
podSecurityContext.seLinuxOptions, which sets the SELinux user, role, type, and level for the pod's volumes and processes
fsGroup, which also sets SELinux contexts
On the StorageClass as a parameter; SELinux is a storage concern
explain: seLinuxOptions in the pod's securityContext assigns the SELinux context (user/role/type/level) under which the pod's processes run and its volumes are labeled. Image builds cannot know the cluster's policy, fsGroup manages POSIX ownership rather than SELinux labels, and StorageClasses carry provisioner parameters, not pod security settings.

q: An NFS-backed app needs its volumes mounted with the noatime option for performance. The pods just declare PVCs. Where do you set the mount option so every dynamically provisioned volume gets it?
options: In each pod's volumeMounts as mountOptions: [noatime]
In the StorageClass as mountOptions: ['noatime'], applied at mount time for every volume it provisions
In the NFS server's /etc/exports; clients cannot set mount options
As an annotation on the PVC; the kubelet reads it
explain: StorageClass mountOptions are passed to the mount call for every volume the class provisions — the central place for options like noatime. Pod volumeMounts have no mountOptions field, the server's exports control server-side behavior rather than client mount flags, and PVC annotations are not interpreted by the kubelet for mounting.

q: The platform team must cap each team's total persistent storage at 100 Gi across all their PVCs. Which ResourceQuota entry enforces an aggregate storage ceiling?
options: requests.storage: 100Gi in the ResourceQuota, which sums storage requests across all PVCs in the namespace
count/persistentvolumeclaims: 5, which limits the number of claims
A LimitRange with max storage per PVC
Setting the StorageClass capacity to 100Gi
explain: ResourceQuota supports requests.storage, which totals the storage requested by every PVC in the namespace and rejects new claims past the cap — the aggregate control asked for. count/ limits object numbers rather than bytes, LimitRange caps individual PVCs rather than the sum, and StorageClasses have no capacity field.

q: You want PVCs that omit storageClassName to be provisioned by your fast-ssd class automatically. How do you mark it as the cluster default?
options: Name it default; Kubernetes treats a class named default specially
Set provisioner to the default driver; the driver implies default status
List it first in kubectl get storageclass output
Annotate it with storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: 'true'
explain: The is-default-class annotation is the official marker the PVC controller looks for when storageClassName is empty — name and ordering are irrelevant. The provisioner identifies the backend driver rather than default status, and kubectl's display order has no semantic meaning.

q: You expanded a PVC from 20Gi to 40Gi; the API accepted it and the cloud volume grew, but df inside the pod still shows 20Gi an hour later. The driver only supports offline expansion. What completes the resize?
options: Wait — filesystem resize always happens automatically within 24 hours
Restart (recreate) the pod so the volume is remounted and the filesystem expanded
Delete and recreate the PVC with 40Gi; expansion never applies to attached volumes
Run resize2fs inside the container manually
explain: With offline expansion the block device grows but the filesystem resize happens at mount time, so the pod must be recreated for the kubelet to remount and expand the filesystem. There is no 24-hour automatic pass, recreating the PVC would destroy the data, and hand-running resize tools inside the container fights the kubelet's own resize flow.

q: A team's custom CSI driver is installed (node plugin healthy, volumes can be attached by hand), but PVCs using its StorageClass stay Pending with no provisioner events. The provisioner string matches the driver name exactly. What component is likely missing?
options: The CSI attacher sidecar, which only handles existing volumes
A second copy of the driver on the control-plane nodes
Node labels matching the driver's topology keys
The external-provisioner sidecar (controller deployment) — without it nothing watches the StorageClass to create volumes
explain: Dynamic provisioning needs the external-provisioner sidecar watching StorageClasses and calling the driver's CreateVolume; a driver chart that ships only the node plugin can attach volumes but never provisions them, yielding zero provisioner events despite a correct provisioner string. The attacher handles attach/detach rather than provisioning, control-plane copies are unnecessary, and topology labels only constrain placement.

q: You set sizeLimit: 1Gi on an emptyDir volume expecting writes past 1Gi to fail. Instead, when the app exceeds it, the pod gets evicted. Is this the expected behavior?
options: Yes — sizeLimit is enforced through eviction: exceeding it marks the pod for eviction rather than returning ENOSPC to the writer
No — exceeding sizeLimit should return 'disk quota exceeded' to the application
No — sizeLimit is only advisory and is never enforced
Yes — but only for emptyDir with medium: Memory
explain: The kubelet enforces emptyDir sizeLimit via eviction: usage over the limit triggers pod eviction, it does not impose a filesystem quota that fails writes. Expecting ENOSPC is the common misconception; the limit is real and enforced, and it applies to both disk and memory-medium emptyDirs.

q: A pod fails with CreateContainerConfigError. The ConfigMap exists, but the volume defines items: [{key: db_host, path: db.host}] while the ConfigMap's actual key is db-host. What is the rule?
options: Items keys are case-insensitive, so this should have worked; the error is elsewhere
Every key named in items must exist in the ConfigMap — a typo'd key fails pod creation; fix the key or mark the item optional
The kubelet creates missing keys as empty files automatically
items only renames keys; nonexistent keys are silently skipped
explain: The items list is a strict projection: each named key must exist in the ConfigMap, otherwise volume setup fails and the container never creates — the classic CreateContainerConfigError. Keys are case-sensitive, the kubelet creates nothing on its own, and nothing is silently skipped.

q: Your backup strategy keeps VolumeSnapshots, but after a namespace cleanup you discover the backend snapshot data in the storage system was deleted along with the VolumeSnapshot objects. Which setting caused the backend data to follow the API object into deletion?
options: reclaimPolicy: Delete on the StorageClass, which cascades to snapshots
The snapshots were never readyToUse, so the backend reclaimed them
deletionPolicy: Delete on the VolumeSnapshotClass — the snapshot controller deletes the backend snapshot content when the API object is removed; Retain keeps it
The CSI driver was uninstalled, which garbage-collects all snapshots
explain: VolumeSnapshotClass deletionPolicy governs the backend lifecycle: Delete removes the storage-system snapshot when the VolumeSnapshot object is deleted, while Retain leaves the backend content in place — the setting that silently ate the backups. The StorageClass reclaim policy covers volumes rather than snapshots, readiness does not trigger reclamation, and uninstalling the driver does not delete backend snapshots by itself.

q: A pod using a local PV is deleted. A replacement pod schedules to the same node, binds the same local PV, and sees the previous pod's stale data. Is this expected, and what is the implication?
options: No — deleting a pod wipes its local PV; the data must be coming from a different volume
Yes — local PVs are tied to the node, not the pod lifecycle, so stale data persists; do not rely on local volumes for fresh state without explicit cleanup
Yes — but only if the PV's reclaimPolicy is Retain; Delete would have wiped it
No — the scheduler never places a pod on a node with a dirty local PV
explain: Local persistent volumes live and die with the node/disk, not the pod: pod deletion leaves the data in place, and a rescheduled pod reattaching the same PV inherits whatever was there. ReclaimPolicy governs PVC deletion rather than pod deletion, and the scheduler happily reuses the node — stale local data is a well-known operational gotcha.

q: A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating with FailedMount: 'mount failed: connection timed out' for an NFS volume. The PVC is Bound and the StorageClass is fine. Where is the most likely fault?
options: The NFS server is unreachable (down, firewalled, or exports misconfigured) — the kubelet cannot complete the mount
The PVC's access mode is wrong; NFS requires ReadWriteMany
The kubelet needs a restart to pick up the NFS client
The PV's capacity is smaller than the PVC's request
explain: A Bound PVC with a mount timeout points below Kubernetes at the NFS server itself: unreachable host, blocked port 2049, or a missing export entry. Access mode does not cause timeouts, kubelet restarts do not fix server reachability, and capacity mismatches prevent binding rather than failing mounts.

q: A deploy pipeline's ServiceAccount gets Forbidden creating Deployments in staging. You want to test exactly what that ServiceAccount may do without running its workload. Which command answers 'can it?' directly?
options: kubectl describe role -n staging and eyeball the rules
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:staging:deployer -n staging, which evaluates the request as that identity
kubectl get clusterroles and guess which one is bound
Reading the API server audit log for past denials
explain: kubectl auth can-i with --as impersonates the ServiceAccount and returns the authoritative yes/no from the authorizer, accounting for all Roles and bindings. Describing roles is manual and error-prone across aggregated roles, listing clusterroles shows nothing about bindings, and the audit log only records requests that were actually attempted.

q: New Deployments are created but no ReplicaSets ever appear. The API server is healthy and kubectl works. On the control-plane node, the kube-controller-manager static pod is CrashLoopBackOff. What is the relationship, and where do you look?
options: The controller-manager creates ReplicaSets from Deployments; a crash-looping one explains the symptom — check its logs via crictl on the control-plane node
The scheduler creates ReplicaSets; the controller-manager is unrelated
etcd creates ReplicaSets; restart the etcd pod
Deployments create their own ReplicaSets; the controller-manager only handles nodes
explain: The deployment controller inside kube-controller-manager is what spawns ReplicaSets, so its crash loop (often a bad flag) freezes all Deployment rollouts while the API stays up. The scheduler only places pods, etcd stores rather than creates objects, and Deployments never self-replicate — the controller-manager's container logs hold the actual error.

q: All new pods stay Pending with no scheduling events at all, and existing workloads run fine. The kube-scheduler static pod is CrashLoopBackOff after someone edited its config to enable a custom plugin. What is the diagnosis path?
options: Restart the kubelets; they cache the scheduler's address
Cordon all nodes; the scheduler needs empty nodes to start
Delete the Pending pods; they are blocking the scheduler
Read the scheduler's container logs (crictl logs) to find the config error — e.g. an unknown plugin name — fix the KubeSchedulerConfiguration, and let the kubelet restart the static pod
explain: A crash-looping scheduler schedules nothing, which matches Pending-with-no-events exactly; its logs name the bad plugin or malformed config, and static pods restart automatically once the manifest/config is fixed. Kubelets do not cache scheduler addresses, cordoning changes nothing about the scheduler process, and deleting pods cannot revive a dead scheduler.

q: A node goes NotReady. The kubelet is running, containerd appears healthy, but kubelet logs repeat 'PLEG is not healthy'. Restarting the kubelet did not help. What is PLEG telling you, and what is the next step?
options: The API server is unreachable; check the control-plane network
The node's disk is full; free space under /var/lib/kubelet
The pod lifecycle event generator cannot get container states from the runtime — the runtime is wedged; restart containerd (or the node) to unstick it
A NetworkPolicy is blocking the kubelet's health checks
explain: PLEG (pod lifecycle event generator) relays container state from the CRI to the kubelet; 'not healthy' means the runtime stopped responding to status queries even though its process is alive — a wedged containerd that a kubelet restart cannot fix. API reachability produces different errors, disk pressure has its own explicit condition, and NetworkPolicies do not apply to the kubelet's local runtime socket.

q: On a dual-homed node, the kubelet registered with the storage-network IP, and pods scheduled there cannot reach the API server or each other on the pod network. Which kubelet setting controls the address the node advertises?
options: --hostname-override, which sets the node's DNS name
--node-ip, which sets the node's primary address used for communication
--pod-cidr, which assigns the pod address range
--cluster-dns, which sets the DNS server IP
explain: --node-ip pins the address the kubelet reports as the node's IP; when auto-detection picks the wrong NIC, components dial an unreachable address. --hostname-override only renames the node object, --pod-cidr governs pod IP allocation rather than node addressing, and --cluster-dns points pods at CoreDNS rather than fixing node identity.

q: In an air-gapped cluster a pod fails with ErrImagePull even though the image was loaded onto most nodes with crictl pull. The pod spec sets imagePullPolicy: Never. What is the contradiction?
options: Never means the kubelet never uses a local image and always contacts the registry — which is unreachable
The image tag was mistyped; Never ignores tag errors
The image exists on most nodes but not on the node the pod scheduled to — Never forbids pulling, so the pod can only run where the image is already present
imagePullSecrets are required even with Never
explain: imagePullPolicy: Never strictly forbids any pull, so scheduling onto a node lacking the preloaded image fails deterministically — the image must be present on every candidate node (or constrain scheduling). Never does not mean 'always pull' (that is Always), tag typos produce a different failure mode, and pull secrets are irrelevant when no pull is attempted.

q: A pod never becomes ready: the readiness exec probe keeps failing, yet exec'ing into the container and running the same command by hand succeeds. The probe is configured as exec: {command: ['/bin/check.sh']}. What is the likely cause?
options: The Service selector is wrong, so the probe has no endpoints to check
A NetworkPolicy is blocking the probe traffic
kube-proxy is not running, so probes cannot reach the pod
The probe runs the command directly without a shell — /bin/check.sh may rely on PATH entries, env vars, or shell features absent in the probe's minimal environment
explain: Exec probes run the binary directly, not through a shell, so scripts depending on shell builtins, PATH lookups, or login env fail under the probe while working in your interactive shell — the classic probe-vs-shell discrepancy. Service selectors affect traffic rather than probes, NetworkPolicies do not filter kubelet-local probe execution, and kube-proxy plays no role in probes.

q: A Java pod is OOMKilled (exit 137) at what looks like a modest heap size. The container has memory limit 1Gi but the JVM was started with -Xmx2g. What is the mismatch?
options: The node is out of memory; the pod needs a bigger node
CPU throttling is killing the container; raise the CPU limit
The JVM heap (2g) exceeds the container's cgroup memory limit (1Gi) — the kernel OOM-kills the container when the JVM plus overhead passes 1Gi; set -Xmx below the limit or raise the limit
Exit 137 means the liveness probe failed; fix the probe
explain: The container's memory limit is enforced by the kernel cgroup, not by the JVM: a 2g heap inside a 1Gi container guarantees the OOM killer fires once usage crosses the limit. The node may have free memory — the kill is per-cgroup, CPU limits cause throttling rather than kills, and 137 is SIGKILL (OOM), not a probe failure.

q: In the middle of an incident you need a cluster-wide timeline — what happened, in order — rather than per-object details. Which single command gives you a chronologically sorted event stream?
options: kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl describe on each suspicious pod
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=100
kubectl top pods -A, which shows the event history
explain: kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp streams every namespaced event in true chronological order — the fastest way to reconstruct an incident timeline. Describe is per-object and unsorted across objects, logs show application output rather than cluster events, and top shows metrics with no event data.

q: Tiny utility pods keep going Pending with Insufficient memory on nodes that have gigabytes free. The namespace has a LimitRange, and kubectl describe limitrange shows default memory request 2Gi. What is happening?
options: The LimitRange's default request injects a 2Gi memory request into every pod that omits one, so each tiny pod reserves 2Gi and the scheduler sees no room
The nodes are actually out of memory; the metrics are stale
A ResourceQuota is blocking the pods with a misleading message
The scheduler is down and reporting phantom capacity
explain: LimitRange defaults mutate pods at admission: a pod without resource fields silently gains the 2Gi default request, and the scheduler bins-packs against requests — so 'tiny' pods each consume 2Gi of schedulable memory. Node metrics are fine (requests, not usage, gate scheduling), quota rejections name the quota explicitly, and a down scheduler would not emit Insufficient memory events.

q: Fresh cloud nodes join the cluster but stay NotReady with the taint node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized:NoSchedule, which nothing ever removes. The kubelet is healthy. What does this taint indicate?
options: The CNI is not installed; install the CNI DaemonSet
The bootstrap token expired before the node finished joining
The nodes were joined with the wrong --node-ip
The cloud-controller-manager is not running (or cannot reach the cloud API), so node initialization — addresses, instance IDs, route setup — never completes
explain: That taint is placed by kubelet on cloud providers and is only removed by the cloud-controller-manager after it initializes the node object; its persistence means the CCM is down or misconfigured, not that the kubelet or CNI failed. A missing CNI shows a different taint/condition, token expiry blocks joining entirely, and --node-ip affects addressing rather than initialization.

q: You run kubectl logs deploy/web and get: 'error: a container name must be specified for pod web-xxx, choose one of: [app metrics-proxy]'. What does this tell you, and what is the fix?
options: The pod is crash-looping; check the previous container's logs
The Deployment has no pods; wait for rollout
The pod runs multiple containers, so disambiguate with kubectl logs deploy/web -c app
Logs are disabled on this cluster; enable the logging agent
explain: kubectl logs requires -c when a pod has more than one container because it cannot guess which stream you want — the error even lists the candidates. It says nothing about crash loops (that would be --previous territory), the pods clearly exist, and cluster logging agents are unrelated to kubectl's container selection.

q: After the control-plane VIP moved to a new IP, kubectl fails with 'Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp <old-ip>:6443: connect: connection refused'. Cluster and certs are fine. What is the minimal fix on your workstation?
options: Renew all cluster certificates; the SANs changed with the IP
Update the server field in your kubeconfig (kubectl config set-cluster <name> --server=https://<new-ip>:6443) to point at the new address
Reinstall kubectl; it caches the old endpoint in its binary
Delete ~/.kube/config and re-run kubeadm init
explain: The kubeconfig still dials the old VIP — 'connection refused' at the stale address is a client-side endpoint problem, fixed by updating the cluster server URL. Certificates are fine (the TLS handshake never got that far), kubectl holds no endpoint cache, and re-running kubeadm init would destroy the cluster to fix a local config file.

q: A production Deployment vanished overnight. Nobody admits to deleting it, and the event history has aged out. Audit logging was enabled on the API server. How do you identify who deleted it?
options: Search the Kubernetes audit log for delete requests on deployments with the Deployment's name — audit records the user, source IP, and timestamp
Restore the etcd snapshot; it records the deleter's identity
Check kube-controller-manager logs; it logs all deletions with usernames
The information is unrecoverable; audit logs only record failed requests
explain: The audit log records every API request including the requesting user, verb, resource, and result — filtering for delete on that Deployment name identifies the actor. etcd stores object state, not actor identity; the controller-manager does not log user actions; and audit logs record successful requests too (policy-dependent), not just failures.

q: You restored an etcd snapshot into a freshly rebuilt cluster. Workloads reappear, but every pod gets 401 Unauthorized from the API server. What broke in the restore?
options: RBAC roles were not included in the snapshot; recreate them
The snapshot is corrupt; only a fresh backup will work
A NetworkPolicy is blocking the pods' API traffic
The ServiceAccount token signing keys differ: the new cluster generated fresh service-account keys, so tokens minted against the old key no longer validate
explain: ServiceAccount tokens are JWTs signed by the cluster's service-account private key, which lives outside etcd (a flag/file on the API server); a rebuilt cluster mints a new key, invalidating every restored token — the fix is restoring the original key material or reissuing tokens. RBAC objects live in etcd and were restored, corruption would break reads rather than auth specifically, and NetworkPolicies produce timeouts rather than 401s.

q: After a security team tightened a mutating webhook, pod creations intermittently fail with 'context deadline exceeded' calling the webhook. The webhook itself is healthy but slow (4s responses). Which setting accommodates it?
options: Increase the API server's --request-timeout; webhooks inherit it
Add more API server replicas; the webhook calls are load-balanced
Raise the webhook configuration's timeoutSeconds (up to 30s) so the API server waits longer for the slow webhook
Set failurePolicy: Ignore; timeouts are then skipped silently
explain: Each webhook has its own timeoutSeconds (default 10s, max 30s) bounding how long the API server waits; a slow-but-healthy webhook needs a higher value. --request-timeout governs overall request handling rather than webhook dials, API replicas do not parallelize a single webhook call, and Ignore would mask failures rather than accommodating legitimate slowness.

q: Right after scaling a Deployment down, scaling it back up fails with 'exceeded quota: requested: pods=1' even though running pods are well under the limit. kubectl get pods still shows the old pods in Terminating. What is happening?
options: Terminating pods still count against the ResourceQuota until they are fully gone — wait for termination (or force-delete stuck ones), then scale up
The quota is corrupt; delete and recreate the ResourceQuota object
The Deployment's revision history counts against the pod quota
Quotas are evaluated per-node; the new pods target a node at capacity
explain: Quota accounting includes pods in Terminating state until the API object is removed, so a recent scale-down still holds quota — the classic 'phantom usage' right after churn. The quota object is fine, revision history is not quota-counted as pods, and quotas are namespace-scoped rather than per-node.

q: You raised kubelet --max-pods to 250, but pods beyond roughly 110 per node fail with IP allocation errors ('failed to assign an IP address'). The nodes are otherwise healthy. What caps the usable pod IPs?
options: The CNI config's hardcoded 110-pod limit, which overrides the kubelet flag
etcd's per-node object limit, which rejects the extra pod IPs
The scheduler's max-pods cache, which needs a restart to refresh
The per-node pod CIDR (default /24 from --node-cidr-mask-size) — only ~250 addresses exist and system reservations eat into them, so widen the mask to enlarge each node's block
explain: Each node gets a fixed-size pod CIDR (default /24, ~256 IPs); raising --max-pods without enlarging the CIDR just moves the bottleneck to IPAM, which fails once the block is exhausted. The CNI does not hardcode 110, etcd has no per-node IP limit, and the scheduler reads max-pods live — the address space is the real ceiling.

q: A one-off data-migration container runs to completion (exit 0) in 40 seconds, then Kubernetes restarts it — it migrates again, exits, restarts, forever. The pod spec uses the default restartPolicy. What is the fix?
options: Add a liveness probe so the kubelet knows the work is done
Set activeDeadlineSeconds to stop the loop after one run
Increase backoffLimit so it eventually gives up
Set restartPolicy: OnFailure (or Never) — the default Always restarts even successful containers; run-to-completion work should not use Always
explain: restartPolicy: Always (the default) restarts containers regardless of exit code, so a successful run just loops; OnFailure restarts only on nonzero exits and Never leaves the completed container alone. A liveness probe cannot signal completion, activeDeadlineSeconds kills the Job/pod rather than marking success, and backoffLimit is a Job field that counts failures, not successful exits.

q: Exam task: a broken cluster has three faults at once — the scheduler is CrashLoopBackOff (bad config), CoreDNS is down, and a NetworkPolicy blocks DNS. You have limited time. Which repair order is correct, and why?
options: NetworkPolicy first, then CoreDNS, then scheduler — network issues always come first
All three at once with parallel kubectl applies; order does not matter
Scheduler first, then CoreDNS, then the NetworkPolicy — nothing can be (re)scheduled until the scheduler runs, DNS must exist before policy exceptions for it matter, and the policy edit is last
CoreDNS first, then scheduler, then NetworkPolicy — DNS is the foundation of everything
explain: Dependencies dictate the order: without a working scheduler no new or replacement pods (including fixed CoreDNS pods) can be placed, so the scheduler comes first; CoreDNS must actually be running before its NetworkPolicy exception has anything to protect; the policy edit is therefore last. Fixing DNS first is futile if its pods cannot schedule, and parallel fixes risk masking which change resolved what.

q: You are decommissioning control-plane node cp-3 from a 3-member stacked-etcd cluster. You drain it, run kubectl delete node cp-3, then run kubeadm reset on cp-3. A teammate then runs etcdctl member remove for cp-3's member ID and gets an error that the member does not exist. What happened?
options: kubectl delete node already removed the etcd member, so the manual removal was redundant
kubeadm reset never touches etcd; the member must have been removed by the drain
The etcd member removes itself automatically once its static pod stops
kubeadm reset runs a remove-etcd-member phase on control-plane nodes, which already removed cp-3's etcd member
explain: kubeadm reset executes phases including remove-etcd-member on control-plane nodes, so the stacked etcd member was already cleanly removed and the teammate's command found nothing to remove. kubectl delete node only removes the Node API object, drain only evicts pods, and etcd members never self-remove — skipping kubeadm reset is what leaves a dead member behind.

q: You are installing Cilium to replace kube-proxy entirely (eBPF datapath, kube-proxy replacement mode). If kubeadm installs its default kube-proxy DaemonSet, the two will fight over Services. How do you prevent kubeadm from installing kube-proxy in the first place?
options: kubeadm init --without-kube-proxy
Delete the kube-proxy DaemonSet after init and scale it to 0 replicas
kubeadm init --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
Install Cilium first; kubeadm detects it and skips kube-proxy automatically
explain: The addon/kube-proxy phase can be skipped at init time with --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy, the documented path for CNI kube-proxy replacement. There is no --without-kube-proxy flag, kubeadm does not auto-detect Cilium, and deleting the DaemonSet post-install works but leaves a window where both program rules — skipping the phase is cleaner.

q: You added k8s.corp.example.com to certSANs in the kubeadm-config ConfigMap, then ran kubeadm certs renew apiserver and restarted the API server. openssl still shows the old certificate without the new SAN. Why did renew not work?
options: The kubelet caches serving certificates for 24 hours; wait and re-check
kubeadm certs renew reissues certificates with their existing SANs — it does not pick up certSANs changes. You must regenerate with kubeadm init phase certs apiserver so the new SANs are baked in
certSANs only applies at kubeadm init time and can never be changed afterward
You must run kubeadm certs renew all, not just apiserver
explain: renew extends expiry while keeping the same subject and SANs; changing SANs requires regenerating the certificate through the certs phase, which reads the updated ClusterConfiguration. There is no 24-hour serving-cert cache, certSANs edits are honored by the phase rerun, and renew all preserves SANs exactly the same way.

q: kubeadm join fails with a CA certificate hash mismatch. A teammate suggests re-running join with --discovery-token-unsafe-skip-ca-verification to get the node in quickly. Why is this dangerous, and what is the correct fix?
options: It skips pinning the cluster CA, so a man-in-the-middle could feed the node a rogue API server and steal the bootstrap token — instead fetch the correct hash with openssl from a control-plane node and pass --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
The flag does not exist; the only fix is to reinstall the node
The flag permanently disables TLS on the kubelet
It is safe on private networks — the correct fix is the same flag plus --force
explain: The CA hash is what lets the joining node verify it is talking to the real cluster; skipping it invites MITM token theft. The flag exists but is explicitly unsafe, it does not disable kubelet TLS permanently, and the right fix is supplying the genuine CA hash (e.g. via openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -noout -pubkey).

q: You are building an air-gapped cluster. Before disconnecting the build network, you want to list every image kubeadm needs and pre-pull them into containerd. Which commands do this?
options: kubeadm init --dry-run --upload-certs
crictl images list, then ctr pull for each image by hand
kubeadm config images list and kubeadm config images pull
kubectl get images --all-namespaces
explain: kubeadm config images list prints the exact control-plane images for the target version and kubeadm config images pull fetches them. There is no kubectl get images, crictl/ctr operate on the local runtime without knowing kubeadm's pinned versions, and --dry-run does not pull anything.

q: kubeadm init on a small edge VM fails preflight with [ERROR NumCPU]: the system has 1 CPU (minimum 2), and [ERROR Mem]: 1.5G is below 1700M. The workload is tiny and you accept the risk. How do you proceed?
options: kubeadm init --ignore-preflight-errors=NumCPU,Mem
kubeadm init --force
kubeadm init --skip-preflight-checks
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests to lower the minimums
explain: --ignore-preflight-errors takes a list of checks to downgrade to warnings, the supported escape hatch for constrained nodes. kubeadm init has no --force flag, --skip-preflight-checks was removed in favor of --ignore-preflight-errors, and no manifest controls preflight minimums.

q: Your CI pipeline deploys metrics-server with Helm on every run. helm install fails on the second run because the release already exists, and helm upgrade fails on a fresh cluster where it does not. Which single command is idempotent for both cases?
options: helm install --replace metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system
helm upgrade --install metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system --create-namespace
helm upgrade --force metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system
helm template metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server | kubectl apply -f -
explain: helm upgrade --install installs when the release is absent and upgrades when present, making pipelines idempotent; --create-namespace handles fresh clusters. helm install has no --replace flag, --force on upgrade does not create a missing release, and template|apply abandons Helm release tracking entirely.

q: You deploy with helm upgrade -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml --set image.tag=v2.1. base.yaml sets image.tag=v1.9 and prod.yaml sets image.tag=v2.0. Which tag is deployed, and what is the precedence rule?
options: v1.9 — the first -f file wins
v2.0 — values files always beat --set
It merges into something unpredictable; Helm refuses conflicting tags
v2.1 — --set beats all -f files, and among -f files the rightmost wins
explain: Precedence is: --set values override everything, and among multiple -f files the last one wins, so v2.1 is deployed. Values files never beat --set, the first file does not win, and Helm does not refuse or unpredictably merge scalar conflicts.

q: Your Kustomize base uses configMapGenerator for app-config. After editing a value and re-applying, the Deployment's pods do not pick up the change even though the ConfigMap object updated. What happened, and which generator option changes this behavior?
options: configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the ConfigMap name, so the Deployment still references the old hashed name — wire the Deployment through the same kustomization so Kustomize rewrites the reference (which also triggers a rollout), or set generatorOptions: disableNameSuffixHash: true
ConfigMaps are immutable; you must delete and recreate them
Kustomize caches generators — run kustomize build --no-cache
Generators never trigger rollouts; you must always rollout restart manually
explain: By default the generator suffixes the name with a hash, so a plain Deployment manifest pointing at app-config keeps pointing at the old object; wiring the Deployment through the same kustomization lets Kustomize update the reference (which also triggers a rollout), or disableNameSuffixHash keeps a stable name. ConfigMaps are not immutable by default and there is no --no-cache flag for this.

q: On dual-homed workers you must pass --node-ip=10.0.0.6 to the kubelet so it registers on the management network. The kubelet is started by systemd from the kubeadm-installed unit, and /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml is managed. Where do you persist this flag?
options: Append it to /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml under extraArgs
In the kubelet's environment file (/etc/default/kubelet or /etc/sysconfig/kubelet) via KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--node-ip=10.0.0.6, then reload systemd and restart the kubelet
Pass --node-ip to kubeadm join
Add it to the kube-proxy ConfigMap
explain: kubeadm's kubelet unit sources the environment file, so KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS is the supported extension point that survives upgrades. config.yaml has no extraArgs field for CLI flags, kubeadm join has no --node-ip flag, and the kube-proxy ConfigMap configures the proxy, not the kubelet.

q: A contractor needs a client certificate for kubectl (not a ServiceAccount, not the admin kubeconfig). Which is the correct Kubernetes-native flow?
options: Run kubeadm token create --print-join-command and give them the join command
Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf — it is the only supported client credential

Generate a private key and CSR, create a CertificateSigningRequest object with signerName kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client, approve it with kubectl certificate approve, then extract the issued certificate into their kubeconfig
Create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls in kube-system; the API server auto-approves it
explain: The CSR API with the kube-apiserver-client signer is the native way to mint client certs: submit, approve, distribute. Bootstrap tokens authenticate nodes not humans, admin.conf is full cluster-admin (violating least privilege), and TLS Secrets do not feed the CSR signer.

q: You create a ServiceAccount ci-deployer and expect the cluster to auto-create a token Secret for it, as old tutorials describe. No Secret appears. Why, and what is the current approach?
options: ServiceAccounts no longer support tokens at all; use client certificates instead
The Secret is created after 24 hours; just wait

Kubernetes v1.24+ stopped auto-creating long-lived token Secrets for ServiceAccounts — create short-lived tokens with kubectl create token, or let pods receive tokens via the automatic projected serviceAccountToken volume
You must create the Secret manually with type: Opaque
explain: The v1.24 change removed auto-generated legacy tokens (they never expired and were a leak risk); bound tokens via the TokenRequest API — kubectl create token or projected volumes — are the replacement. Tokens are fully supported, there is no 24-hour delay, and Opaque secrets are not API credentials.

q: An attacker steals a kubelet client certificate from worker-2. They try to delete pods on worker-5 and read Secrets cluster-wide, but both are denied despite the certificate being valid. Which mechanisms contained the blast radius?
options: RBAC ClusterRoles bound to the kubelet's ServiceAccount
The PodSecurity admission plugin
NetworkPolicies on the worker nodes

The Node authorizer, which scopes each kubelet's credentials to its own Node object, its own pods, and node-scoped resources — plus the NodeRestriction admission plugin limiting which Node/Pod objects it can modify
explain: Kubelets authenticate with client certs in the system:nodes group and are authorized by the Node authorizer (not RBAC bindings), which restricts them to their own node and pods; NodeRestriction further limits mutations. There is no ServiceAccount/RBAC binding for kubelets, PodSecurity governs pod specs not API access, and NetworkPolicies do not authorize API calls.

q: A developer needs get/list on exactly one ConfigMap, app-config, in namespace dev — not every ConfigMap. How do you express this in a Role?
options: resources: [configmaps/app-config], verbs: [get, list]
resources: [configmaps], resourceNames: [app-config], verbs: [get, list]
Add a label selector to the Role's rules
Create one Role per ConfigMap key
explain: resourceNames restricts the rule to named instances — the standard least-privilege pattern. resources takes only resource types (no slashes), RBAC rules have no label selectors, and per-key Roles confuse objects with keys.

q: You try kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer and get 'Error from server (Forbidden): ... User "cori" cannot impersonate resource "serviceaccounts"'. What is missing?
options: Impersonation is admin-only; use sudo instead
Your own user needs the impersonate verb on the target kind (e.g. a ClusterRole with resources: [serviceaccounts], verbs: [impersonate]) — impersonation is itself RBAC-gated
Add --as-group=system:authenticated to the command
The ServiceAccount must grant you permission first
explain: --as does not bypass RBAC: the API server checks whether your identity may impersonate the target (verb impersonate on the resource kind). There is no sudo for the API, --as-group adds groups rather than granting rights, and the target cannot authorize your impersonation.

q: Audit log volume is crushing your log shipper. You need who-did-what-when for all writes, but full request/response bodies only for Secret access. How do you tune the audit policy?
options: Set level: None on everything except Secrets
Audit levels are cluster-wide; per-resource tuning is impossible
Set level: Request on everything and compress the log files
Use level: Metadata for the broad write rule (who, what, when without bodies) and a higher-precedence level: RequestResponse rule scoped to secrets — rules are evaluated in order, first match wins
explain: Audit policy rules are ordered and first-match-wins, with levels None < Metadata < Request < RequestResponse, so a narrow RequestResponse rule for secrets plus a broad Metadata rule gives full coverage without the volume. level: None would blind you, levels are per-rule not cluster-wide, and Request still omits response bodies while costing nearly as much.

q: You set pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted on every application namespace, but a teammate's new namespace (with no PSA labels at all) happily admits a privileged pod. Why, and where do cluster-wide defaults and kube-system-style exemptions actually live?
options: The labels take 24 hours to propagate; wait and re-test
PSA is broken on namespaces created after the API server started

Unlabeled namespaces default to the privileged standard (enforce nothing) — cluster-wide defaults and exemptions (usernames, runtimeClasses, namespaces like kube-system) live in a PodSecurityConfiguration file passed to kube-apiserver via --admission-control-config-file, not in namespace labels
Restricted is only a warning level; it never blocks
explain: Upstream PSA defaults are privileged for every mode, so labels are what opt namespaces into enforcement; the AdmissionConfiguration file sets cluster defaults and the exemption list. Labels apply immediately, restricted in enforce mode absolutely blocks, and there is no startup-time cutoff.

q: etcd raised a NOSPACE alarm at its quota. You compacted and defragmented, df shows free space, but all writes are still rejected with 'etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded'. What is missing?
options: Run etcdctl alarm disarm — the NOSPACE alarm latches and stays raised until explicitly disarmed, even after space is reclaimed
Restart the etcd static pod — alarms clear on restart
Restore from snapshot — defrag corrupts the backend
Delete the alarm key with etcdctl del
explain: etcd alarms are sticky by design: defrag reclaims space but the NOSPACE alarm must be cleared with etcdctl alarm disarm before writes resume. Restarting does not clear alarms, defrag does not corrupt data, and alarms are not plain keys you can delete.

q: You must rotate the data-encryption key used for Secrets at rest (aescbc provider). You generated a new key. What is the correct sequence?
options: Replace the old key in the EncryptionConfiguration and restart the API server — etcd re-encrypts everything automatically
Delete all Secrets and recreate them; rotation is not supported in place

Prepend the new key to the keys list (first key encrypts new writes), restart the API server(s), then rewrite every Secret (kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -) so stored ciphertext migrates to the new key — only then remove the old key
Run kubeadm certs renew all — it rotates encryption keys too
explain: Envelope encryption uses the first key for new writes while all listed keys can decrypt, so rotation is: add new key first, restart API servers, rewrite all Secrets to re-encrypt under the new key, then drop the old key. Simply replacing the key orphans old ciphertext, Secrets are never auto-rewritten, and kubeadm certs renew handles TLS certs not encryption keys.

q: Engineers should authenticate to the API server with their corporate identity tokens instead of client certificates. Which API server configuration enables this?
options: --oidc-issuer-url, --oidc-client-id (plus username/group claim flags) so the API server validates OIDC ID tokens
--client-ca-file pointed at the corporate CA
--token-auth-file with the engineers' passwords
OIDC is configured on the kubelet, not the API server
explain: The API server is the authentication front door: --oidc-issuer-url and --oidc-client-id (with --oidc-username-claim/--oidc-groups-claim) make it accept and validate OIDC ID tokens. --client-ca-file is for client-cert auth, --token-auth-file is the legacy static token file, and the kubelet does not authenticate users.

q: An image has ENTRYPOINT ['/app/server'] and CMD ['--port=8080']. You need the container to run /app/server --port=9090 --tls. Which fields do you set, and what is the classic mix-up?
options: command: ['--port=9090', '--tls'] — command appends to the entrypoint
args: ['/app/server', '--port=9090', '--tls'] — args replaces the entrypoint
args: ['--port=9090', '--tls'] — args overrides CMD (appended to the entrypoint); command would override ENTRYPOINT. The trap is setting command to the flags, which replaces /app/server itself
command and args are aliases; set either one
explain: In Kubernetes, command maps to Docker ENTRYPOINT and args maps to CMD: args replaces the default flags while keeping the entrypoint binary. Setting command to flag values would try to execute '--port=9090' as a binary, and args never replaces the entrypoint.

q: A pod sets env: [{name: APP_NAME, value: api}, {name: LOG_PATH, value: '/var/log/$(APP_NAME)'}] and the app sees /var/log/api. A teammate reorders the list so LOG_PATH comes first and now sees the literal string /var/log/$(APP_NAME). Why?
options: Expansion only works in args, not in env values
The syntax requires ${APP_NAME} with braces in env
$(VAR) expansion only resolves variables defined earlier in the env list — order matters; referencing a later variable leaves it unexpanded
Kubernetes never expands variables; the first result was a coincidence
explain: Variable expansion in env values (and command/args) resolves against previously defined variables, so order is significant. Expansion works in env, $(VAR) is the valid syntax (with $$ for escaping), and the behavior is deterministic, not coincidental.

q: You write a Secret manifest using stringData: {password: s3cret!} for readability, apply it, then kubectl get secret -o yaml shows only data: {password: czNjcmV0IQ==}. A teammate fears the plaintext was stored. What happened?
options: stringData is write-only convenience: the API server base64-encodes it into data at write time and never returns stringData on read — etcd holds only the base64 data field
The API server rejected stringData and stored nothing
stringData is stored as plaintext in etcd — this is a security bug
kubectl is hiding it; etcd still holds the plaintext
explain: stringData exists so manifests can carry plaintext that the API server encodes into data on write; it is never persisted or returned. The API accepts it (no rejection), and etcd stores the same base64 bytes as if you had supplied data directly — base64 is encoding, not encryption, which is why encryption-at-rest matters.

q: A hot-path ConfigMap is read by hundreds of pods and changes rarely. You set immutable: true on it. What does this buy you, and what is the catch?
options: The ConfigMap can never be deleted — it is permanent
It encrypts the ConfigMap automatically
It can no longer be updated in place (any change needs delete + recreate), but the kubelet can skip watching it, which significantly reduces API server load at scale
Immutable ConfigMaps bypass RBAC — anyone can read them
explain: immutable: true forbids updates, trading in-place edits for watch-free kubelet reads — a real scalability win for large clusters. The object can still be deleted, it does not encrypt anything, and RBAC still applies.

q: An app reads its memory limit from an env var set via valueFrom.resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.memory}. The manifest says 2Gi but the app sees '2147483648'. Why, and how do you get friendlier units?
options: The API server has a bug; file it upstream
Use fieldRef instead of resourceFieldRef
Memory limits cannot be exposed to containers
The downward API exposes quantities in base units (bytes for memory) — set divisor: 1Gi to render gibibytes ('2')
explain: resourceFieldRef formats the quantity using divisor (default 1), so memory renders in bytes; divisor: 1Gi (or 1Mi) rescales the output. This is documented behavior not a bug, fieldRef exposes pod fields not resources, and limits are fully exposable.

q: A pod has an init container requesting 4 CPU (a heavy migration) and an app container requesting 1 CPU. How much CPU does the scheduler reserve for this pod, and why?
options: 5 CPU — init and app requests are always summed
1 CPU — init containers are ignored for scheduling
4 CPU — the effective request is the maximum of (each init container's request) and (the sum of app containers' requests), since init containers run sequentially before the app starts
4 CPU, but only if the init container also sets a limit
explain: Init containers run one at a time before app containers, so scheduling takes the max across the init sequence versus the app sum — 4 CPU here. Summing would over-reserve, ignoring init containers would under-reserve and risk contention, and limits do not affect the request calculation.

q: A gRPC service (no HTTP endpoints) needs a liveness probe. httpGet fails, and exec with grpcurl works but forks a process every 10 seconds. What is the purpose-built probe?
options: tcpSocket — it performs a full gRPC health check
There is no gRPC probe; exec is the only option
The native grpc probe: livenessProbe: {grpc: {port: 50051}} — the kubelet speaks the gRPC health protocol directly
Use a readiness probe instead — liveness does not support gRPC
explain: Kubernetes has a native grpc probe type that performs a gRPC health check without shelling out. tcpSocket only verifies the port accepts connections, exec works but is heavier, and probe-type support does not differ between liveness and readiness.

q: You set livenessProbe: {successThreshold: 3, ...} hoping the kubelet will require 3 consecutive successes before trusting the container. kubectl apply is rejected. Why?
options: successThreshold is not a valid probe field at all
The value must be a string, not a number
Liveness probes do not support thresholds; use failureThreshold instead
For liveness and startup probes successThreshold must be 1 — the field is only meaningful (and >1 allowed) on readiness probes
explain: The API validates successThreshold: 1 for liveness/startup (a live container is trusted on first success); only readiness probes accept higher values to delay the ready signal. The field exists and is numeric, and failureThreshold governs the failure side.

q: After the main container starts, the app must register itself with an external service-discovery endpoint exactly once per container start. An initContainer runs too early (the app is not listening yet). Which hook fits?
options: lifecycle.postStart — it fires after the container is created, alongside container start
lifecycle.preStop — it runs before termination
A second initContainer with restartPolicy: Always
A readiness probe — it runs once at startup
explain: postStart executes right after container creation (concurrently with the entrypoint), which is the hook for start-time registration. preStop runs at termination, initContainers (even native sidecars) run before app containers start, and readiness probes gate traffic rather than run one-shot actions.

q: A pod shows STATUS SchedulingGated for 20 minutes. Describe shows no failed scheduling events, resources are plentiful, and the scheduler logs are quiet. What is going on, and who clears it?
options: The scheduler is deadlocked — restart kube-scheduler

An external controller placed schedulingGates on the pod (PodSchedulingReadiness) to hold it out of scheduling until some precondition is met — only removing the gates (by the controller, or by updating the pod spec) lets the scheduler consider it
The pod is unschedulable — add more nodes
Delete and recreate the pod; gates are a stuck finalizer
explain: SchedulingGated means spec.schedulingGates is non-empty: the scheduler deliberately ignores the pod until every gate is removed, typically by the controller that added them. No scheduler failure or capacity issue is involved, and recreating the pod recreates the gates if a mutating webhook re-adds them.

q: Pods must not receive traffic until an external cloud load balancer finishes attaching them — a condition the kubelet cannot observe. How do you gate readiness on it?
options: Add a second readiness probe that polls the cloud API
Set the pod's phase manually with kubectl patch

Define readinessGates: [{conditionType: example.com/lb-attached}] on the pod and have an external controller set that condition to True — the pod stays unready regardless of its probes until the condition is true
Use an initContainer that waits for the load balancer
explain: readinessGates add custom conditions to the readiness calculation: all gates plus passing probes are required before the pod is marked Ready. A probe could poll but readinessGates is the designed mechanism, pod phase is not user-settable, and initContainers complete before the app runs.

q: With hostname: web and subdomain: apps, a pod's hostname is 'web' and its FQDN resolves via DNS. A legacy app calls gethostname() and requires the FQDN 'web.apps.default.svc.cluster.local'. Which field delivers this?
options: hostname: web.apps.default.svc.cluster.local
dnsPolicy: None
hostNetwork: true
setHostnameAsFQDN: true — the kernel hostname becomes the full FQDN (requires hostname + subdomain)
explain: setHostnameAsFQDN: true sets the pod's hostname to its FQDN. Putting the FQDN in hostname is invalid, dnsPolicy: None only changes resolvers, and hostNetwork gives the node's hostname.

q: A team runs pods under a Kata Containers RuntimeClass. Pods get OOM-killed even though container memory limits look generous and the app stays well under them. What is the likely accounting gap?
options: Kata ignores memory limits entirely
The OOM killer is misconfigured on Kata nodes
Overhead only applies to CPU, not memory
Pod overhead — the VM/shim memory for the sandboxed runtime is charged to the pod via spec.overhead, and it was not accounted for in the limits
explain: RuntimeClass overhead (spec.overhead, set via the RuntimeClass) accounts for the sandbox VM's memory against the pod's cgroup; sizing limits without it starves the sandbox. Kata honors limits, the OOM killer is not misconfigured, and overhead covers both CPU and memory.

q: A high-connection proxy pod needs net.core.somaxconn=4096 in its network namespace, but the nodes keep the default 128. The pod is unprivileged. How do you set it, and what is the boundary?
options: privileged: true is required for any sysctl
Sysctls are node-only; tune every node instead
securityContext.sysctls: [{name: net.core.somaxconn, value: '4096'}] — net.* sysctls are namespaced and allowed per-pod; node-level sysctls are rejected by the API
Set it in the CNI plugin's configuration
explain: Kubernetes allows namespaced sysctls (net.*, kernel.shm* etc.) via pod securityContext without privilege; node-level sysctls are rejected at admission. Privileged is not required, per-pod sysctls are a supported feature, and the CNI config does not carry sysctls.

q: You edited a ConfigMap consumed as a volume. The files update in the pods, but the app only reads config at startup. You need every pod recreated on the current revision — without changing the Deployment spec. Which command?
options: kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
kubectl delete pods -l app=web
kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=0, then scale back up
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web — it stamps the pod template (kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation) to force a rolling recreation without a spec change
explain: rollout restart forces a rolling recreation honoring surge/unavailability guarantees. Undo would revert revisions, deleting pods works but bypasses the rollout machinery, and scale-to-zero causes full downtime.

q: A Deployment has 3 replicas, strategy: {maxUnavailable: 34%, maxSurge: 34%}. During a rollout, how many pods may be unavailable and how many extra may exist?
options: 1 unavailable (maxUnavailable rounds down: floor(1.02)=1), 2 extra (maxSurge rounds up: ceil(1.02)=2)
2 unavailable, 2 extra — percentages round up
1 unavailable, 1 extra — 34% of 3 is 1.02, truncated
0 unavailable — percentages below 50% mean zero
explain: Kubernetes rounds maxUnavailable DOWN and maxSurge UP when converting percentages to pod counts, so 34% of 3 gives 1 unavailable and 2 surge. Rounding both up, truncating both, or treating sub-50% as zero are all wrong.

q: A CI pipeline applies a Deployment and must block until it is fully available (or fail after 2 minutes). Which command expresses this without a sleep loop?
options: kubectl rollout status deployment/web --watch=false
kubectl wait --for=condition=available --timeout=120s deployment/web
kubectl wait --for=delete pod -l app=web
sleep 120 && kubectl get deployment web
explain: kubectl wait blocks on an arbitrary resource condition with a timeout and exits non-zero on timeout — ideal for pipelines. rollout status without watch returns immediately, waiting for delete is the wrong condition, and sleeping is both slow and blind.

q: You need to change a Deployment's image and add an annotation in one shot from a script. When is strategic merge patch (the kubectl patch default) the better choice over --type=json?
options: Strategic merge is deprecated — always use --type=json

Strategic merge understands Kubernetes list merge keys, so a partial containers patch updates the image in place — JSON patch (RFC 6902) needs exact positional paths like /spec/template/spec/containers/0/image and is brittle when ordering changes
--type=json can only change one field at a time
Strategic merge requires the object to already exist; JSON patch does not
explain: Strategic merge understands Kubernetes list merge keys, making partial updates safe; JSON patch is precise but positional and breaks if list order shifts. Strategic merge is not deprecated, JSON patch can carry many operations, and both require the object to exist.

q: Your StatefulSet was created with serviceName: db-svc, but the headless Service is actually named db-headless, so stable pod DNS is broken. kubectl apply with the corrected serviceName is rejected: field is immutable. The data on the PVCs must survive. What is the correct fix?
options: kubectl edit the StatefulSet — the editor bypasses immutability checks
kubectl patch --type=merge — patches are not subject to immutability validation
Rename the headless Service to db-svc — but production clients already resolve db-headless, so this breaks them

kubectl delete statefulset db --cascade=orphan, then re-apply with serviceName: db-headless — serviceName is create-only; orphaning keeps the pods (and their PVCs/data) running, then delete the orphaned pods so the new StatefulSet creates replacements that reattach the existing PVCs
explain: serviceName is immutable after creation, and edit/apply/patch all hit the same validation — only delete+recreate works. --cascade=orphan preserves the running pods and their PVCs during the swap. Renaming the Service would fix DNS but breaks every client already using db-headless.

q: Two controllers (your GitOps tool and an autoscaler) both manage the web Deployment's replicas field. Client-side kubectl apply keeps flip-flopping the value and printing warnings about managedFields. What is the robust fix?
options: Move the GitOps tool to kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=gitops (and --force-conflicts only after confirming ownership) — server-side apply tracks per-field ownership in managedFields so each manager owns its fields
Delete the managedFields from the object with kubectl patch
Have both controllers use kubectl apply with --overwrite
Server-side apply is only for CRDs, not Deployments
explain: Server-side apply moves the merge to the API server with per-field ownership, ending client-side last-write-wins fights. Stripping managedFields destroys ownership data, --overwrite does not exist for apply, and server-side apply works for all objects.

q: A teammate writes a NetworkPolicy port entry as {protocol: UDP, port: game-server, endPort: 30100} to cover a named port plus a range. kubectl apply is rejected. What is the rule?
options: endPort only works with TCP
endPort requires port to be a numeric port — it cannot be combined with a named (string) port, and endPort must be >= port
Named ports cannot be used in NetworkPolicies at all
endPort must be less than port
explain: The API validates that endPort is only set alongside a numeric port with endPort >= port; a named port plus endPort is rejected. endPort works for UDP/SCTP too, named ports are fine without endPort, and the range runs upward from port.

q: You apply a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {app: api}, an egress section allowing only DNS, and no policyTypes field. Afterwards the API pods cannot be reached by the frontend at all — even though the policy says nothing about ingress. What is the right diagnosis?
options: This should NOT be caused by this policy alone — with only egress rules present, policyTypes defaults to [Egress], so ingress stays unrestricted; look for another policy (e.g. a default-deny ingress) causing the frontend outage
The policy is malformed and blocks everything
DNS egress rules implicitly deny all ingress
policyTypes omitted means both Ingress and Egress are enforced
explain: policyTypes defaults are inferred from the rules present: egress-only rules imply Egress only, leaving ingress wide open.
