The symptom contradicts the policy, so a second policy is the real culprit. The policy is not malformed, DNS rules do not affect ingress, and omitted policyTypes does not mean 'both'.

q: External DNS lookups from pods take ~5s (the ndots search-domain walk); in-cluster names are instant. You cannot change every app's resolv.conf. Which cluster-level fix short-circuits the ndots walk for external names?
options: Set ndots: 1 in every pod's dnsConfig
Increase CoreDNS replicas to 50
Set dnsPolicy: Default on every pod

Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache — a DaemonSet that runs a DNS cache on each node's link-local 169.254.25.10, so the search-domain walk happens against the local cache instead of traversing the network to CoreDNS
explain: NodeLocal DNSCache keeps a per-node cache at a link-local IP injected into pod resolv.conf, absorbing the ndots retry storm locally. ndots: 1 would break short-name resolution, more CoreDNS replicas do not remove the per-query walk latency, and dnsPolicy: Default just inherits the node's resolver.

q: You add a dnsConfig with 4 nameservers and 8 search domains to a pod. kubectl apply is rejected. What are the limits?
options: At most 3 nameservers and 6 search domains — the API validates dnsConfig sizes
No limits exist — the rejection must come from CoreDNS
1 nameserver and 3 search domains max
dnsConfig is only allowed with dnsPolicy: None
explain: The API caps dnsConfig at 3 nameservers and 6 search domains. There are real limits (it is not a CoreDNS issue), the caps are not 1/3, and dnsConfig works with ClusterFirst and other policies.

q: You have tls.crt and tls.key for shop.example.com and need a Secret for an Ingress TLS block. Which command builds it correctly?
options: kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key — the Ingress tls: [{hosts: [shop.example.com], secretName: shop-tls}] references it; the Secret must be type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt/tls.key keys
kubectl create secret generic shop-tls --from-file=tls.crt --from-file=tls.key
Any Opaque secret works as long as the Ingress names it
TLS secrets must be created in kube-system
explain: kubectl create secret tls produces the kubernetes.io/tls type with the exact tls.crt/tls.key keys the ingress controller expects. A generic Opaque secret has the wrong type/keys, and TLS secrets live in the Ingress's own namespace.

q: With ingress-nginx you want path /api/v1/users/42 rewritten to /users/42 using a capture group: path: /api/v1/(.*), rewrite-target: /$1. It does not match. What is missing?
options: rewrite-target does not support capture groups
pathType must be Exact for regex
Capture groups only work in Gateway API
The nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-regex: 'true' annotation — without it the path is treated as a literal prefix, so the regex never engages
explain: ingress-nginx treats paths literally unless use-regex is enabled; with it, capture groups in path flow into rewrite-target's $1. rewrite-target supports captures, Exact would prevent prefix/regex matching, and this is ingress-nginx behavior not Gateway API.

q: A legacy app keeps session state in memory. ClientIP session affinity breaks because all clients arrive behind one corporate NAT IP. What is the ingress-native fix with ingress-nginx?
options: sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service — NAT does not matter
Increase the Service's sessionAffinity timeout
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: 'cookie' — the controller sets a sticky cookie so sessions pin to backends regardless of shared source IPs
Use ipvsadm to pin connections
explain: Cookie affinity moves stickiness from source IP to an ingress-set cookie, surviving NAT where ClientIP affinity collapses everyone onto one backend. Service-level ClientIP cannot distinguish NAT'd clients, and ipvsadm is node-level plumbing, not a fix.

q: File uploads larger than ~1MB through ingress-nginx fail with 413. The backend accepts 100MB uploads directly. What is the fix?
options: Increase the Ingress controller's memory limits
Set client_max_body_size in the backend app
Switch the Ingress pathType to Exact
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 100m — ingress-nginx defaults client_max_body_size to 1m, and the annotation raises it per-Ingress
explain: The 413 comes from nginx's default 1m client_max_body_size at the ingress layer, before traffic reaches the backend; the per-Ingress annotation overrides it. Controller memory and backend settings are not the limiting factor, and pathType is unrelated.

q: The staging Ingress must be reachable only from the CI runners behind NAT gateway 203.0.113.7 (a single /32), so engineers cannot stumble onto it. Where do you enforce this with ingress-nginx?
options: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range: 203.0.113.7/32 on the staging Ingress — nginx returns 403 for all other sources
A NetworkPolicy on the ingress-nginx namespace
loadBalancerSourceRanges on the backend ClusterIP Service
DNS split-horizon so the hostname only resolves for CI
explain: The whitelist-source-range annotation makes nginx itself reject other sources at the edge, before the backend. A NetworkPolicy acts on pod traffic at a different layer, loadBalancerSourceRanges only applies to LoadBalancer-type Services, and DNS tricks do not block direct access.

q: Every request to the /admin Ingress path must first be validated against the company's SSO sidecar at http://auth-service:8080/verify, which returns 200/401. How do you wire this with ingress-nginx?
options: A NetworkPolicy allowing only the auth service
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url: http://auth-service:8080/verify — nginx subrequests each call to the auth URL and only proxies upstream on 2xx
Basic auth annotations with the SSO password
It requires a service mesh
explain: The auth-url annotation implements external authentication via nginx auth_request: non-2xx from the verifier rejects the request. NetworkPolicies do not authenticate, basic auth is a different mechanism, and no mesh is needed.

q: Behind a cloud load balancer, your app's audit log shows the LB's IP as the client on every request, even with externalTrafficPolicy: Local. The LB is configured to send PROXY protocol headers. What must the ingress layer do?
options: Nothing — PROXY protocol is automatic
Enable use-proxy-protocol on the ingress controller (and the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/use-proxy-protocol annotation) so nginx parses the PROXY header and restores the real client IP
Set X-Forwarded-For manually on the load balancer
Switch the Service to ClusterIP
explain: PROXY protocol is opt-in on both ends: the LB sends it, but nginx must be told to parse it, otherwise it logs the TCP peer (the LB). It is not automatic, X-Forwarded-For is a separate HTTP-header mechanism, and Service type does not decode PROXY bytes.

q: You run kubectl port-forward deployment/api 8080:80 to debug. It works, but after a rollout the forward dies with 'error: lost connection to pod'. What happened?
options: port-forward tracks Deployments automatically; this is a kubelet bug

port-forward resolves its target once at startup (for a Deployment it picks one pod) — the rollout replaced that pod, breaking the tunnel. port-forward does not follow rolling targets; re-run it after the rollout
Deployments are not valid port-forward targets — only pods are
The Service's ClusterIP changed during the rollout
explain: kubectl port-forward binds to a single pod chosen when the command starts; it has no controller watching for replacements. Deployments are valid targets (one pod is selected), and ClusterIP is irrelevant to the tunnel.

q: Two Gateway API implementations are installed (the cloud provider's and Istio). You create a Gateway and it gets claimed by the wrong controller. How do you select the implementation?
options: Set gatewayClassName on the Gateway to reference the GatewayClass managed by the intended controller
Add an annotation to the HTTPRoute
Gateways are claimed round-robin; delete and recreate until the right one takes it
The first installed controller always wins
explain: GatewayClass is the selection mechanism: each implementation publishes a GatewayClass, and gatewayClassName binds a Gateway to one. HTTPRoute annotations do not select the implementation, there is no round-robin, and install order does not decide.

q: An HTTPRoute in namespace team-a must route to a Service in namespace team-b. You set the cross-namespace backendRef and the route's status shows ResolvedRefs: False. What is missing?
options: A ReferenceGrant in namespace team-b explicitly permitting HTTPRoutes from team-a to reference that Service — cross-namespace references require the target namespace's consent
Cross-namespace backendRefs are forbidden entirely
The HTTPRoute must be created in team-b
A ClusterRole allowing route-to-service
explain: Gateway API requires a ReferenceGrant in the target namespace authorizing the specific from/to reference; without it the ref is rejected. Cross-namespace routing is allowed with the grant, the route stays in team-a, and RBAC is not the mechanism.

q: Your Gateway's admin listener must only accept HTTPRoutes from the platform team's namespace, while the web listener accepts routes from any namespace. Where do you enforce this?
options: On the HTTPRoute's parentRefs — routes choose their own listeners unconditionally
With a NetworkPolicy on the Gateway's namespace
Listeners cannot restrict route namespaces; you need two Gateways
On the admin listener: allowedRoutes: {namespaces: {from: Selector, selector: {matchLabels: {team: platform}}}} — listeners control which routes may bind to them
explain: allowedRoutes on a listener gates binding by route kind and namespace (All/Selector/Same); parentRefs sectionName selects the listener from the route side but cannot grant permission the listener denies. NetworkPolicies govern pod traffic not route attachment, and a second Gateway is unnecessary.

q: With Gateway API you must redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS (same host and path) at the edge, before any backend is involved. Which HTTPRoute filter does this?
options: RequestRedirect with scheme: https — it returns a 301/302 to the client without proxying to a backend
RequestHeaderModifier — it can change the scheme
URLRewrite with scheme: https
ResponseHeaderModifier
explain: RequestRedirect issues the redirect response itself (configurable statusCode); no backend receives the request. Header modifiers mutate proxied requests, and URLRewrite rewrites the upstream request rather than redirecting the client.

q: The HTTPRoute matches path /api/v2 and the backend expects the prefix stripped (/users not /api/v2/users). Which filter rewrites the path before proxying?
options: RequestRedirect — it rewrites backend paths
RequestMirror — it copies the path
Path rewriting is not supported in Gateway API
URLRewrite with path: {type: ReplacePrefixMatch, replacePrefix: /} — the backend receives the rewritten path while the client-facing match stays /api/v2
explain: URLRewrite mutates the request forwarded upstream (ReplacePrefixMatch/ReplaceFullPath), which is exactly prefix-stripping. RequestRedirect responds to the client instead of proxying, RequestMirror duplicates traffic, and rewriting is a core filter.

q: A slow report endpoint needs up to 120s; the Gateway's default backend timeout kills it at 30s. Other routes must keep the 30s default. How do you scope the longer timeout?
options: Change the Gateway's global timeout — it applies per-route automatically
Set a timeout annotation on the backend Service
On that HTTPRoute rule, set timeouts: {backendRequest: 120s} — timeouts are per-rule, so only the report route gets the longer budget
Timeouts cannot differ per route
explain: HTTPRoute timeouts (request/backendRequest) are set per rule, scoping the 120s budget to the slow endpoint while the default stands elsewhere. There is no global-timeout override need, Service annotations do not carry Gateway timeouts, and per-route timeouts are the designed mechanism.

q: You set externalTrafficPolicy: Local on a NodePort Service. Traffic works, but you notice kube-proxy opened an extra high port on every node. What is it?
options: A bug — kube-proxy should not open extra ports
The healthCheckNodePort — with Local policy, kube-proxy serves /healthz on an allocated node port so external load balancers can probe which nodes actually have local endpoints
The NodePort duplicated by the Local policy
A metrics port that cannot be disabled
explain: externalTrafficPolicy: Local needs per-node health visibility, so the Service gets a healthCheckNodePort (auto-allocated, overridable via spec.healthCheckNodePort) for LB health checks. It is by design, not a duplicate NodePort, and it can be set explicitly.

q: Your HTTPRoute was accepted by kubectl but traffic 404s. Where do you look first to see whether the route actually bound to the Gateway and resolved its backends?
options: kubectl logs on the kube-apiserver
The Gateway's pod logs only
HTTPRoutes have no status; re-apply until it works
kubectl describe httproute <name> — the status.conditions (Accepted, ResolvedRefs, Programmed) and status.parents show per-Gateway attachment and backend resolution errors
explain: Gateway API is status-driven: describe shows Accepted/ResolvedRefs/Programmed conditions pinpointing binding vs backend problems. API server logs will not show route programming, controller logs are second-line, and HTTPRoutes absolutely carry status.

q: A Deployment mounts an RWO PVC. During rolling updates the new pod sits in ContainerCreating with a Multi-Attach error until the old pod is fully terminated, stalling every rollout. What is the structural fix?
options: Increase maxSurge so more new pods start

Set strategy: type: Recreate — with RWO storage only one pod can hold the volume, so rolling updates deadlock on attach; Recreate tears down the old pod (releasing the volume) before starting the new one
Delete the PVC between rollouts
RWO volumes support multi-attach during rollouts; this is a driver bug
explain: RWO means single-writer: RollingUpdate's old/new overlap means the new pod cannot attach until detach completes. Recreate serializes it. maxSurge worsens the contention, deleting the PVC destroys data, and the driver is behaving correctly.

q: A projected volume combines a ConfigMap, a Secret, and the downward API, and two sources define the same key app.conf. Which content wins?
options: The first source listed wins
The last source listed wins — later projected sources override earlier ones on key collisions
The pod fails to start with a duplicate key error
The keys are merged line by line
explain: Projected sources are merged in order with later sources overriding earlier ones for the same path. There is no error and no line-merging; ordering in the sources list is the control.

q: A PVC manifest omits storageClassName and the cluster has a default StorageClass, so it gets dynamically provisioned. For one special PVC you want to bind only to a hand-created PV and never trigger dynamic provisioning, even though a default class exists. What do you set?
options: Delete the default StorageClass
storageClassName: none
Add an annotation to the PVC
storageClassName: '' (empty string) — this explicitly disables dynamic provisioning for the PVC, so it can only bind to a matching pre-provisioned PV
explain: An empty-string storageClassName opts out of the defaulting logic entirely: no dynamic provisioning, static binding only. Omitting the field inherits the default class, 'none' is not a special value, and annotations do not control provisioning.

q: You pre-provisioned PV backup-pv for a specific PVC. Selectors could match other PVs later, and you want a hard pin. Which PVC field binds it to exactly that PV?
options: metadata.name: backup-pv on the PVC
A nodeSelector on the PVC
claimRef on the PVC
spec.volumeName: backup-pv — a direct, exclusive binding to the named PV
explain: spec.volumeName pins the claim to one PV by name, bypassing selector matching. Renaming the PVC does nothing, PVCs have no nodeSelector, and claimRef lives on the PV side.

q: You hand-created a PV with platinum SSDs for the database team's upcoming PVC db-data in namespace prod. Other PVCs with matching selectors keep grabbing it first. How do you reserve this PV for exactly that PVC?
options: Set spec.claimRef: {name: db-data, namespace: prod} on the PV — a pre-set claimRef reserves the PV so only that PVC can bind to it
Delete the other PVCs
claimRef can only be set by the controller, never by hand
Set storageClassName: '' on the other PVCs
explain: A PV with claimRef pre-populated reserves it for that specific claim; the controller completes the binding when the PVC appears. Deleting other PVCs is whack-a-mole, claimRef is user-settable for reservation, and empty storageClassName on others does not reserve this PV.

q: Deleting a PVC that is still mounted hangs thanks to the kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer. What is the analogous protection on the PV side that prevents deleting a PV still bound to a PVC?
options: Nothing — bound PVs can be deleted freely
The kubernetes.io/pv-protection finalizer — the API server refuses to remove a bound PV until it is unbound (Released), just as pvc-protection guards in-use PVCs
The StorageClass reclaimPolicy
A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
explain: PVs carry the pv-protection finalizer while bound, blocking deletion until unbound — the mirror of pvc-protection for in-use claims. Bound PVs are not freely deletable, reclaimPolicy governs post-release behavior not deletion, and no admission policy is involved.

q: Your team's custom CSI driver serves NFS-like shared storage: no per-node attach step exists (any node can mount directly). But every pod stays Pending waiting for attach. Which CSIDriver setting fixes the controller's assumption?
options: Set volumeBindingMode: Immediate
Delete the VolumeAttachment objects manually
Run the driver as a DaemonSet instead
CSIDriver attachRequired: false — tells the attach/detach controller to skip the ControllerPublish (attach) step for this driver, since there is nothing to attach
explain: attachRequired defaults true, making the controller wait for attach confirmation; drivers without an attach concept (NFS-style, secrets-store) must set it false. Binding mode does not skip attach, manually deleting VolumeAttachments fights the controller, and the DaemonSet form is unrelated.

q: The database team requires XFS, not the driver's default ext4, on dynamically provisioned volumes. The pods only declare PVCs. Where do you set the filesystem type?
options: In the pod's securityContext
In the StorageClass parameters: {fsType: xfs} — the external-provisioner passes it to the CSI CreateVolume call
As a mountOption on the PVC
Filesystems cannot be chosen for dynamic volumes
explain: Driver-specific settings like fsType live in StorageClass parameters. securityContext does not format disks, mountOptions affect the mount (not the mkfs), and dynamic provisioning fully supports fsType selection.

q: A pod with a 50Gi emptyDir scratch volume keeps getting evicted under disk pressure, though its container ephemeral-storage limit was never set. How does the emptyDir factor into eviction accounting?
options: emptyDir is free — it never counts against the pod

emptyDir usage counts toward the container's (and pod's) ephemeral-storage consumption — writes to emptyDir, container logs, and image layers all draw from the same ephemeral-storage budget the kubelet evicts against
Only hostPath counts toward ephemeral storage
emptyDir counts against memory, not disk
explain: Ephemeral storage accounting includes emptyDir volumes, writable layers, and logs; exceeding the available budget triggers eviction with the pod's usage charged accordingly. emptyDir is not free, hostPath is outside the accounting, and disk-backed emptyDir counts as ephemeral storage (only medium: Memory counts as RAM).

q: A log-heavy pod is evicted for exceeding ephemeral storage, but you want it to get a guaranteed slice and a hard cap instead of BestEffort treatment. Which resource controls this?
options: memory request/limit — ephemeral storage is part of memory
emptyDir sizeLimit alone
The ephemeral-storage resource: set resources.requests/limits {'ephemeral-storage': '2Gi'/'5Gi'} on the container — requests affect scheduling and limits trigger eviction when exceeded
A ResourceQuota on the namespace
explain: ephemeral-storage is a first-class schedulable resource with request/limit semantics; limits are enforced by eviction when exceeded. It is not part of memory accounting, sizeLimit only caps one volume (and evicts the pod when hit), and quotas cap aggregates not per-pod enforcement.

q: A Deployment uses env with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef: {name: app-config, key: LOG_LEVEL, optional: true}. The ConfigMap exists but someone renamed the key to LOGLEVEL. What happens at pod start?
options: The pod starts with LOG_LEVEL unset — optional: true tolerates both a missing ConfigMap AND a missing key (unlike the default, which blocks in CreateContainerConfigError)
The pod blocks — optional only covers a missing ConfigMap, not a missing key
The API server rejects optional on keyRef
The pod starts with the old value cached
explain: optional: true on configMapKeyRef/secretKeyRef (and on envFrom refs) tolerates absence at either level; without it the container blocks in CreateContainerConfigError. The API accepts it, and there is no value caching.

q: Pods fail ErrImagePull against the private registry. You have the registry credentials. Which single command creates the right Secret type, and how do pods consume it?
options: kubectl create secret generic regcred --from-literal=user=...
kubectl create secret tls regcred --cert=... --key=...
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=... — then reference it in pod spec imagePullSecrets (or attach it to the ServiceAccount)
Encode the credentials in the image name
explain: The docker-registry type builds the .dockerconfigjson payload registries expect; pods reference it via imagePullSecrets or the ServiceAccount. A generic secret has the wrong key/type, tls is for certificates, and credentials never go in image names.

q: The platform team must cap each team at 100Gi of requested storage AND at most 20 PVCs, across all StorageClasses. Which ResourceQuota entries enforce both?
options: requests.storage: 100Gi plus persistentvolumeclaims: '20' — quotas support both resource aggregates and object counts
limits.storage: 100Gi — quotas use the limits prefix
Only requests.storage is supported; object counts cannot be quota'd
A LimitRange with max storage
explain: ResourceQuota covers requests.storage aggregates and the persistentvolumeclaims object count in one object. There is no limits.storage quota key, counts are quota-able, and LimitRange constrains per-object sizes not totals.

q: You change the cluster's default StorageClass from standard to fast-ssd. Existing PVCs bound with standard keep working. A teammate expects them to migrate to fast-ssd automatically. Why don't they?
options: The change failed — defaults apply retroactively
The default class is only consulted at provision time; binding is permanent — existing PVCs keep their PVs, and only new PVCs that omit storageClassName get fast-ssd
You must restart the kube-controller-manager
PVCs always follow the current default dynamically
explain: StorageClass selection happens once at dynamic provisioning; the bound PV is forever. Changing the default annotation affects only future claims. No restart changes this, and PVCs never float between classes.

q: A DaemonSet pod must read the node's /etc/machine-id (a single file). On some nodes the file is missing and the pod fails. Beyond type: FileOrCreate, what is the sharper alternative, and what is the caveat?
options: type: Directory — it auto-creates the file
Use emptyDir instead
hostPath always creates missing paths

type: File — fails clearly if absent, which is better than silently creating an empty file that the agent misreads as a valid ID; and hostPath paths are node-local, so content differs per node and fresh nodes may lack the path
explain: FileOrCreate would fabricate an empty machine-id that downstream code misreads; File fails fast on absence, which is the honest signal — and hostPath remains node-local and fragile across fresh nodes. Directory does not create files, emptyDir is pod-local not host data, and only the *OrCreate variants create paths.

q: You run databases on local persistent volumes. Pods sometimes schedule to a node, then sit Pending because the only free local PV is on another node. Which StorageClass binding mode fixes the scheduling race, and why?
options: Immediate — it binds faster
Delete the nodeAffinity from the PVs
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer — binding is delayed until a pod exists, so the scheduler can consider the PV's nodeAffinity during placement and put the pod where the volume actually is
Use hostPath instead of local PVs
explain: WaitForFirstConsumer makes the scheduler volume-aware: it only binds after scheduling, choosing a node whose local PV can satisfy the claim. Immediate binds first and schedules second (the race), removing nodeAffinity breaks local-volume correctness, and hostPath is not persistent volume management.

q: Your storage admin hand-created a snapshot in the array and registered a VolumeSnapshotContent for it. How do you expose it to users as a VolumeSnapshot they can restore from?
options: Users cannot use admin-created snapshots
Create a VolumeSnapshot with source.pvc — it will discover the content
Copy the data into a new PVC manually
Create a VolumeSnapshot with source.volumeSnapshotContentName pointing at the pre-provisioned content — static snapshot provisioning, mirroring static PV provisioning
explain: VolumeSnapshots support static provisioning via source.volumeSnapshotContentName, binding the snapshot object to existing content — the exact analog of static PVs. source.pvc triggers dynamic snapshotting instead, and manual copying defeats the purpose.

q: Dynamically provisioned PVs keep disappearing with their cloud disks when test PVCs are deleted, destroying test data the team wanted to keep. The PVs show reclaimPolicy: Delete. Where is this inherited from?
options: The StorageClass's reclaimPolicy — dynamic PVs inherit it at provisioning time; set reclaimPolicy: Retain on the class (or per-PV) to keep disks after PVC deletion
It is hardcoded for dynamic provisioning
The PVC's annotations
The reclaimPolicy of the default StorageClass only
explain: The StorageClass defines the default reclaimPolicy stamped onto each dynamically provisioned PV; changing the class (or patching individual PVs) to Retain preserves the disks. It is not hardcoded, PVC annotations do not set it, and each class carries its own.

q: You update a Secret consumed via env vars. The pods keep the old values forever, while pods mounting the same Secret as a volume pick up the change within a minute. Why the asymmetry?
options: Secrets never update anywhere
The volume mount is stale too; both need restarts
env vars update on the next liveness probe
Environment variables are resolved once at container creation — the kubelet does not re-resolve them; only volume mounts (kubelet-synced, except subPath) refresh. The fix is to recreate/roll the pods
explain: Env injection is a start-time snapshot; the kubelet only refreshes projected/volume file contents (with the subPath exception). The standard fix is a rollout restart. Secrets do update via volumes, volumes are not stale here, and probes do not re-inject env.

q: Team A wants fast-ssd as their default, Team B wants standard as theirs. Can you set a different default StorageClass per namespace?
options: Yes — annotate each namespace with its default class

No — the default StorageClass is cluster-scoped (one storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class annotation across the cluster); per-team control comes from RBAC/quotas or explicit storageClassName, not per-namespace defaults
Yes — set storageClassName: default in each team's PVCs
Yes — create a StorageClass named default in each namespace (StorageClasses are namespaced)
explain: StorageClasses are cluster-scoped and at most one may carry the is-default-class annotation; there is no namespace-level defaulting. Namespaces cannot hold StorageClasses, and 'default' as a storageClassName has no special meaning.

q: kubectl calls fail. Case 1: 'error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)'. Case 2: 'Error from server (Forbidden): ... is forbidden'. What is the operational difference?
options: They are the same — both mean RBAC denied
401 Unauthorized = authentication failed (bad/missing/expired credentials — fix the kubeconfig/token); 403 Forbidden = authenticated but RBAC denied the action (fix Roles/Bindings)
401 means RBAC denied; 403 means the API server is down
Both require regenerating cluster certificates
explain: 401 is the authentication stage (who are you — credential problem), 403 is authorization (what may you do — RBAC problem). Conflating them sends you fixing Bindings for an expired token or vice versa; the API server being down gives connection errors, not these codes.

q: You want to browse the Kubernetes API (e.g. /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods) from your laptop's browser using your kubeconfig credentials, without exposing the API server. Which command?
options: kubectl proxy — it starts a local authenticated reverse proxy to the API server using your kubeconfig, so http://127.0.0.1:8001/api/... works with your credentials
kubectl port-forward on port 6443
ssh -L to the control-plane node
kubectl expose the kubernetes Service
explain: kubectl proxy authenticates to the API server as you and serves it on localhost, the intended way to curl/browse the API with your identity. port-forward targets pods/services not the API, SSH tunneling is heavier, and exposing the kubernetes Service changes cluster networking.

q: kubectl top nodes fails with 'metrics not available', and kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1 returns 503. The metrics-server Deployment looks healthy. Where do you check next?
options: Restart the kube-apiserver
The metrics API cannot fail independently

kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o yaml — the APIService object for the aggregated API may be failing its discovery check, which breaks the metrics API path even if the Deployment pods run
Delete the metrics-server namespace
explain: Aggregated APIs are registered via APIService objects; if its service reference or discovery check fails, the API path 503s regardless of pod health. The API server itself is fine, the metrics API absolutely can fail independently, and deleting the namespace destroys the working parts.

q: An exam task says to create a 'Widget' custom resource, but you are not sure of its exact resource name or whether it is namespaced. Which command answers both in one shot?
options: kubectl get widgets --all-namespaces and hope
kubectl api-versions | grep widget
kubectl api-resources | grep -i widget — it lists resource names, shortnames, API group, namespaced scope, and kind
Custom resources cannot be introspected
explain: kubectl api-resources is the discovery command: NAME, SHORTNAMES, APIVERSION, NAMESPACED, KIND. Guessing plural forms wastes time, api-versions lists groups not resources, and CRDs are fully introspectable.

q: A pod is stuck with reason ContainerCannotRun and message 'exec: "/app/start.sh": permission denied'. The image pulled fine and the command is spelled correctly. What is wrong?
options: The image is for the wrong architecture
The binary/script lacks the executable bit (or the shebang interpreter is missing) — the container runtime could not exec it; fix the image's file permissions
The liveness probe is misconfigured
The node is out of memory
explain: ContainerCannotRun means the runtime failed to start the process: classic causes are a non-executable entrypoint or bad shebang. Wrong architecture gives exec format errors at a different layer, probes and memory produce different statuses.

q: Two pods: pod-a shows Init:Error, pod-b shows Init:CrashLoopBackOff. Both have failing init containers. What is the distinction?
options: They are identical; Kubernetes picks one at random
Init:Error means the app container failed

Init:Error = the init container failed and is waiting before its first retry; Init:CrashLoopBackOff = it has failed repeatedly and is now in exponential backoff — both mean 'the init container has not succeeded yet', just different retry phases
Init:CrashLoopBackOff is worse — the node is failing
explain: Both statuses describe an init container that has not completed; Error is the initial failure state, CrashLoopBackOff is the repeated-failure backoff state. Neither involves the app container (it has not started) nor node health.

q: A pod stays Pending with event 'UnexpectedAdmissionError: ... TopologyAffinityError ...'. CPU and memory are free. What does this mean?
options: The API server rejected the pod
An admission webhook blocked it
The image is too large

The pod passed scheduling but a kubelet admission check rejected it — e.g. conflicting node affinity/anti-affinity or topology constraints the scheduler's predicates missed; inspect the affinity/topologySpreadConstraints for contradictions
explain: UnexpectedAdmissionError is the kubelet refusing an assigned pod at admission time (topology/affinity contradictions, resource conflicts), distinct from scheduler FailedScheduling. The API accepted it (it exists), webhooks run pre-persist, and image size gives different errors.

q: A node goes NotReady. Pods on it are NOT evicted for about 5 minutes, then all terminate at once. Nobody configured any tolerations. Why the 5-minute delay?
options: The kubelet waits 5 minutes before reporting NotReady

Every pod gets default tolerations for node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable with tolerationSeconds: 300 — the node lifecycle controller waits out the grace period before taint-eviction, in case the node recovers
Eviction is broken — it should be immediate
The 5 minutes is the image pull backoff
explain: The API server injects the 300s not-ready/unreachable tolerations into every pod without explicit tolerations; the node lifecycle controller only evicts after they expire. The kubelet reports quickly, eviction is working as designed, and image backoff is unrelated.

q: A fresh worker joins: kubelet running, node registered, but status shows Ready: False with condition NetworkReady: False / reason NetworkNotReady, and no pods can start. What is missing?
options: No CNI plugin is installed/configured on the node — the kubelet reports NetworkNotReady until a CNI config appears in /etc/cni/net.d and the plugin binary exists
The kubelet needs --network-plugin=cni
The node needs a reboot
CoreDNS is down
explain: NetworkReady reflects CNI readiness: without a CNI config + binary the runtime has no pod network. The --network-plugin flag is long removed (dockershim era), reboots do not install CNIs, and CoreDNS affects DNS not node readiness.

q: Cross-node pod traffic fails on one node only; the CNI DaemonSet pod on that node is CrashLoopBackOff. Where do you look on the node itself to verify the CNI's local state?
options: /var/log/kubernetes.log
kubectl get cni -A
/etc/cni/net.d/ for the plugin's config (conflist) and /opt/cni/bin/ for the plugin binaries — a missing config or binary explains a node-local CNI failure that the DaemonSet pod logs will confirm
The API server's etcd
explain: CNI state is node-local: configs in /etc/cni/net.d, binaries in /opt/cni/bin. There is no kubectl get cni, the API server does not hold CNI state, and the generic log path is not where CNI config lives.

q: In the middle of an incident you need the last 50 lines from every container of every web pod, in one command. Which does it?
options: kubectl logs deploy/web --tail=50
kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=50 (containers are included by default)
You must loop over pods and containers manually
kubectl logs -l app=web --all-containers=true --tail=50
explain: kubectl logs accepts a selector (-l) plus --all-containers to fan out across containers, with --tail bounding output. deploy/web without -c fails on multi-container pods, -l alone still requires a container choice for multi-container pods, and no manual loop is needed.

q: An exam task says: 'In context cluster-prod, delete the broken Deployment.' You are currently on cluster-staging and do not want to switch your shell's context back and forth. What is the safest one-off form?
options: kubectl config use-context cluster-prod && kubectl delete deploy broken — then hope you switch back
KUBECONFIG=/tmp/prod.conf kubectl delete deploy broken
Contexts are just display names; the command runs everywhere
kubectl --context cluster-prod -n prod delete deployment broken — the flag scopes exactly one command, eliminating the wrong-context risk that fails exam tasks
explain: --context pins a single invocation to the right cluster with no shell state to forget — the direct antidote to the classic wrong-context exam failure. use-context mutates state you must remember to revert, swapping KUBECONFIG files is heavier, and contexts absolutely scope the command.

q: A mutating webhook injects a broken sidecar into every new pod cluster-wide, including kube-system. You cannot fix the webhook image right now. How do you scope the blast radius without deleting the configuration?
options: Set namespaceSelector on the webhook configuration to match only the namespaces it should target (e.g. exclude kube-system) — webhooks support namespace and object selectors to limit their scope
Delete the webhook — there is no scoping mechanism
Add a NetworkPolicy blocking the webhook
Webhooks only run in the namespace where they are created
explain: Admission webhooks carry namespaceSelector/objectSelector to bound their blast radius — excluding kube-system is the standard guardrail. Deletion is not the only lever, NetworkPolicies do not gate API admission, and webhook scope is configuration-driven not namespace-bound.

q: A pod shows OOMKilled, but its memory limit looks generous and metrics show the container well under it. You suspect node-level memory pressure killed it. How do you confirm on the node?
options: kubectl describe pod — it shows node pressure
The container metrics are wrong; raise the limit

Check dmesg / journalctl -k on the node for the kernel OOM killer's victim lines — node-pressure OOMs are logged by the kernel with the killed process, distinct from cgroup-limit OOMs which name the container's cgroup
OOMKills only ever come from container limits
explain: The kernel logs every OOM kill with the victim and the triggering constraint; node-level pressure kills name the node's out-of-memory condition while limit kills reference the container cgroup. describe shows the outcome not the cause, metrics are not necessarily wrong, and limits are not the only OOM source.

q: An app is mysteriously slow but never crashes and never restarts. CPU metrics show it flatlining exactly at its limit. Memory is fine. What is happening, and how does it differ from an OOMKill?
options: It is being OOMKilled and restarted too fast to see
CPU throttling — the CFS quota caps the container at its cpu limit, so it runs slower instead of dying; unlike memory limits (which kill via OOM), CPU limits degrade performance silently
CPU limits kill the process like memory limits do
The node is out of CPU
explain: CPU is a compressible resource: hitting the limit throttles (CFS bandwidth control), producing the flatline-slowdown signature; memory is incompressible, so breaching it OOM-kills. No restarts occur with throttling, CPU limits never kill, and node exhaustion would show scheduling/pressure signals.

q: kubectl top pod web-0 shows 950m CPU for the pod, but you need to know whether the app container or the metrics-proxy sidecar is the hog. Which command breaks it down?
options: kubectl top pod web-0 --containers — per-container metrics from metrics-server
kubectl top pod web-0 --all
kubectl describe pod web-0
Per-container metrics are not available
explain: --containers splits pod metrics into per-container rows, identifying the hog. There is no --all flag for this, describe shows requests/limits not usage, and metrics-server does serve per-container data.

q: crictl ps hangs and crictl images fails to connect, yet pods on the node keep running. You need to list containers via the lower-level runtime CLI. What is the correct invocation, and why did the obvious one fail?
options: ctr containers list — the namespace flag is optional
crictl is the only supported tool; wait for it to recover
ctr -n k8s.io containers list — ctr defaults to the 'default' namespace while Kubernetes/containerd uses the 'k8s.io' namespace; bare ctr commands silently look in the wrong place
docker ps — containerd is Docker-compatible
explain: containerd namespaces isolate content; Kubernetes uses k8s.io, so ctr needs -n k8s.io explicitly. The flag is not optional for seeing K8s containers, crictl failing does not block ctr (same socket, different client), and docker is not installed with containerd.

q: A node reports DiskPressure with plenty of free bytes (df -h shows 60% free), yet pods get evicted. What hidden exhaustion should you check, and with what command?
options: Inodes — df -i: millions of small files (or image layers) can exhaust inodes while bytes remain, and the kubelet counts inode pressure as disk pressure
RAM — with free -m
DiskPressure never triggers without full bytes; the metrics are wrong
Network bandwidth — with iftop
explain: The kubelet watches both byte and inode pressure; df -i reveals inode exhaustion that df -h hides. RAM has its own pressure signal, the metrics are not wrong, and bandwidth is not disk pressure.

q: kubectl describe node shows PIDPressure: True and pods are being evicted, though CPU, memory, and disk all look healthy. What is exhausted?
options: It is a synonym for MemoryPressure
The pod count limit
Process IDs — the node's kernel PID allocation is exhausted (often by a fork bomb or leaked processes); the kubelet evicts pods to reclaim PIDs
PIDPressure is informational only and never evicts
explain: PIDPressure is the kubelet's fourth pressure signal, tracking kernel PID exhaustion; like other pressures it drives eviction. It is distinct from memory, distinct from the --max-pods count, and it absolutely triggers eviction.

q: You must delete a Job but keep the pods it created for post-mortem log inspection. A plain kubectl delete job also removes the pods. Which flag keeps them?
options: --force — it skips graceful deletion
kubectl delete job myjob --cascade=orphan — the dependents' ownerReferences are removed so the garbage collector leaves the pods behind
--grace-period=0 — it is faster
Orphaning is impossible; back up the logs first
explain: --cascade=orphan deletes only the owner and strips ownerReferences from dependents, so the GC spares the pods for inspection. --force/--grace-period affect termination speed not ownership, and orphaning is a standard deletion propagation policy (Orphan).

q: Three control-plane nodes are healthy, but you need to know which one is the ACTIVE kube-scheduler right now (the others are standby). Which command answers this directly?
options: etcdctl endpoint status — the etcd leader is always the scheduler leader
kubectl get lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system -o yaml and read the holderIdentity field
kubectl describe nodes and check the controller-manager annotation
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler — the Running pod is the leader
explain: The scheduler and controller-manager use leader election via Lease objects in kube-system; holderIdentity names the current leader. Listing scheduler pods shows all replicas (standbys included), and the etcd leader is a separate election that says nothing about scheduler leadership.

q: Before running kubeadm init on a production-bound VM, you want to validate your cluster.yaml config file and run the preflight checks without changing anything on the machine. Which command does this?
options: kubeadm init --config cluster.yaml --v=5
kubeadm init --config cluster.yaml --dry-run
kubeadm config validate --config cluster.yaml
kubeadm init --config cluster.yaml --skip-phases=all
explain: --dry-run runs validation and preflights without mutating the system, which is exactly the pre-init sanity check. There is no kubeadm config validate subcommand; --skip-phases=all still writes state, and --v=5 only raises log verbosity while performing the real init.

q: You want every new worker to register with the label workload=batch at join time. There is no --node-labels flag on kubeadm join. What is the supported way to do this?
options: Pass a JoinConfiguration file via kubeadm join --config join.yaml with nodeRegistration.kubeletExtraArgs: {"node-labels": "workload=batch"}
Rely on the NodeRestriction admission plugin to apply the label automatically
Add the label to /etc/kubernetes/bootstrap-kubelet.conf before joining
Run kubeadm join --node-labels workload=batch
explain: kubeadm join accepts a JoinConfiguration file, and nodeRegistration.kubeletExtraArgs forwards node-labels to the kubelet at registration. kubeadm join has no --node-labels flag, bootstrap-kubelet.conf only carries the bootstrap token, and NodeRestriction restricts (never adds) labels.

q: Your autoscaler joins nodes at unpredictable times, so you mint tokens with kubeadm token create --ttl 0 --print-join-command. What does --ttl 0 mean, and what is the operational catch?
options: The token is valid for zero seconds, so the join will fail immediately
--ttl 0 disables token authentication and joins nodes anonymously
The token never expires — convenient for automation, but you must audit and revoke it with kubeadm token delete if it leaks
--ttl 0 falls back to the default 24-hour TTL
explain: A zero TTL means no expiry, which suits automation but creates a long-lived credential that must be tracked and revoked. It does not mean instant expiry, it does not fall back to 24h, and token auth stays fully in force.

q: You combined two kubeconfigs with the KUBECONFIG environment variable, but one context references certificate-authority: ca.crt as a relative path that only resolves from its original directory. How do you produce a single portable kubeconfig?
options: Reorder the files in KUBECONFIG — later files override earlier path resolution
kubectl config view --flatten > merged.conf — it inlines all certificate data so relative paths disappear
kubectl config rename-context on each context until the paths resolve
kubectl config view --minify > merged.conf
explain: --flatten merges the configs and embeds certificate data inline, eliminating relative-path breakage. --minify only trims to the current context, renaming contexts changes nothing about paths, and KUBECONFIG order controls precedence (first file wins), not path resolution.

q: Your cluster uses external etcd on dedicated hosts. One member's data directory is corrupt and you have a good snapshot. What must happen BEFORE you run etcdctl snapshot restore on that host?
options: Stop the etcd process on that member — restore writes a brand-new data directory and cannot run against a live member
Nothing — snapshot restore is an online operation that compacts the running member
Delete the snapshot first so the member is forced to resync from peers
Run the restore from the Kubernetes API server so the cluster picks it up
explain: Restore is an offline operation: the member must be stopped, then you restore into a fresh --data-dir and restart pointing at it. Restoring into a running member corrupts state, the API server has no restore path, and deleting your only good snapshot destroys the recovery option.

q: You are adding a fourth member to a 3-member etcd cluster, but the new host is slow and you fear it will drag down quorum write latency while it catches up. What is the safe way to add it?
options: Add it as a normal voting member immediately — slow members never affect quorum latency
Learner members can serve reads but can never be promoted
Add two members at once so they catch up in parallel
Add it as a learner with etcdctl member add <name> --learner, let it replicate, then promote it to a full voting member
explain: Learners replicate the log without voting, so a slow new member cannot stall quorum commits; promotion happens after catch-up. A slow voting member absolutely can increase commit latency, adding two members at once risks quorum loss, and learners are designed to be promoted.

q: You wrote /etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml on the control-plane node and added --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml to the API server flags, but the API server CrashLoops with 'no such file or directory'. Why?
options: Static-pod flags do not cross the container boundary by themselves — the manifest needs a hostPath volume mounting the policy file into the API server pod
The audit policy must be stored inside etcd, not on the filesystem
Restarting the kubelet would have mounted the file automatically
You used the wrong flag — --audit-log-path is the one that takes the policy file
explain: The API server runs in a container; host paths are invisible unless mounted via a hostPath volume in the static pod manifest. etcd does not store the policy, --audit-log-path sets the log output destination (not the policy), and a kubelet restart cannot invent a missing volume mount.

q: While debugging, you disabled every API server admission plugin — and immediately noticed kubelets could suddenly update Node objects belonging to OTHER nodes. Which plugin had been preventing that?
options: NodeRestriction — it limits each kubelet's API access to its own Node object and the pods bound to it
PodSecurity — it governs pod admission, not kubelet API scope
NamespaceLifecycle — it only blocks operations in terminating namespaces
AlwaysAdmit — it permits everything and would not have restricted the kubelets
explain: NodeRestriction authorizes kubelets only for their own node/pods resources; without it a compromised kubelet credential is far more powerful. PodSecurity admits or rejects pods, NamespaceLifecycle is about namespace termination, and AlwaysAdmit is the opposite of a restriction.

q: After a containerd upgrade on air-gapped nodes, every new pod fails with an error pulling the sandbox (pause) image from registry.k8s.io. Pods' own imagePullSecrets do not help. Where is the fix?
options: Pass --pod-infra-container-image to the kubelet on the command line
Re-run kubeadm init with --image-repository pointing at the mirror
Set sandbox_image to the internal mirror in containerd's config.toml under the CRI plugin, then restart containerd
Add an imagePullSecret for registry.k8s.io to every pod spec
explain: The pause image is pulled by the CRI itself, outside any pod spec, so its source is the containerd CRI config (sandbox_image). --image-repository only affects images kubeadm pulls, pod imagePullSecrets never apply to the sandbox image, and the kubelet flag for it is long deprecated/removed.

q: crictl is unresponsive and you need the raw containerd view of running containers. You run ctr containers list and get nothing, even though pods are running. What is wrong?
options: containerd uses namespaces — Kubernetes containers live in the k8s.io namespace, so run ctr -n k8s.io containers list
crictl and ctr share state, so if crictl hangs, ctr can never work
ctr only works when Docker is installed alongside containerd
The correct namespace is default, which ctr already uses
explain: ctr defaults to the default namespace, which is empty on a Kubernetes node; the kubelet's containers are under k8s.io. ctr needs no Docker, the default namespace is the wrong one here, and ctr talks to containerd directly so it works even when the CRI plugin (crictl's path) is wedged.

q: On a node running CRI-O, kubeadm reset fails while trying to connect to the containerd socket. The node has both runtimes' sockets present. How do you reset it correctly?
options: kubeadm reset always auto-detects the right socket, so the failure must be something else
Uninstall CRI-O first, then reset will fall back to containerd
Run kubeadm reset --force, which skips all CRI interaction
kubeadm reset --cri-socket unix:///var/run/crio/crio.sock
explain: With multiple CRI sockets present, auto-detection can pick the wrong one; --cri-socket pins the reset to CRI-O's socket. Uninstalling the runtime to satisfy a reset is backwards, and --force does not bypass the CRI preflight/socket probing.

q: Your laptop runs kubectl v1.30 against a v1.33 API server. Most commands work but one subcommand behaves oddly. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The supported move is to downgrade the cluster to v1.30
kubectl must match the API server version exactly or nothing works
kubectl is only supported within one minor version (n-1/n/n+1) of the API server — v1.30 against v1.33 is out of skew, so upgrade kubectl
kubectl is version-independent and the oddity must be a cluster bug
explain: The documented client skew policy is ±1 minor version; two minors out is unsupported and produces exactly these subtle misbehaviors. Exact matching is not required, kubectl is not version-independent, and downgrading a cluster to match a client is never the answer.

q: You put a load balancer in front of the API servers and updated control-plane-endpoint in the kubeadm-config ConfigMap. New workers join through the LB fine, but your laptop's kubectl still talks to the old node IP. Why?
options: Restarting the kubelet on the control-plane nodes propagates the new endpoint
The endpoint is cached in etcd and takes 24 hours to refresh
You must run kubeadm upgrade apply --config to push the endpoint to clients
Editing kubeadm-config does not rewrite existing kubeconfigs — update the server field in ~/.kube/config (and cert SANs if you switched to a DNS name)
explain: kubeadm-config drives future kubeadm operations, not already-issued kubeconfigs; each client stores its own server address. kubeadm upgrade apply does not touch user kubeconfigs, kubelet restarts change nothing client-side, and there is no 24-hour etcd cache for this.

q: kubeadm token list shows the token abcdef.0123456789abcdef, and you must revoke exactly this token without touching the others. Which command does it?
options: Edit the bootstrap-token Secret and blank out its token-secret field
kubeadm token delete 0123456789abcdef — the secret half is the identifier
Tokens cannot be revoked individually; you must rotate the cluster CA
kubeadm token delete abcdef — the part before the dot is the token ID used for deletion
explain: Bootstrap tokens are id.secret; kubeadm addresses them by the public ID prefix. The secret half is not the identifier, individual revocation is fully supported (no CA rotation needed), and hand-editing the Secret is fragile compared to the dedicated delete command.

q: During the next upgrade you also need to roll out a new ClusterConfiguration (a changed dnsDomain). Which command both upgrades the control plane AND applies the new configuration to the static pod manifests?
options: Hand-edit each static pod manifest and let kubeadm upgrade apply merge them
kubectl edit configmap kubeadm-config -n kube-system — the manifests pick it up automatically
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34 --config new-cluster.yaml
kubeadm upgrade node — it upgrades the local node's config
explain: upgrade apply --config re-renders the control-plane manifests from the supplied ClusterConfiguration while upgrading. upgrade node only handles a single node's kubelet-side config, editing the ConfigMap never re-renders manifests, and hand edits get overwritten or cause drift from kubeadm's state.

q: Someone accidentally deleted the CoreDNS Deployment and its ConfigMap. The cluster is otherwise healthy and you do not want to re-run full kubeadm init. What is the supported recovery?
options: kubectl apply the CoreDNS manifest from the latest GitHub release
kubeadm upgrade apply — it reinstalls all missing addons
kubeadm init phase addon coredns — it reinstalls just the CoreDNS addon from the cluster configuration
Re-run kubeadm init with --skip-phases=preflight
explain: kubeadm's phased init lets you re-run a single phase, and the coredns addon phase recreates the version-matched manifests. Re-running full init on a live cluster is destructive, a GitHub manifest may mismatch the cluster version, and upgrade apply does not reinstall deleted addons.

q: kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows etcd-cp-1. You run kubectl delete pod etcd-cp-1 to bounce it, and it reappears instantly with the same name. Why can't you delete it this way?
options: It is managed by a hidden DaemonSet that immediately reschedules it
It is a mirror pod for a static pod — the kubelet recreates it from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml; move the manifest away and back to restart it
Static pods can only be deleted by scaling the kubelet deployment to zero
The API server is read-only for kube-system objects
explain: Mirror pods reflect static manifests on the node; the API is read-only for them and the kubelet is the true owner. No DaemonSet is involved, there is no kubelet Deployment to scale, and the API is not read-only for the namespace in general.

q: You want to trend etcd database growth over weeks to predict quota exhaustion before it pages you. Which command gives you the per-member database size?
options: etcdctl endpoint status --cluster -w table — it reports DB SIZE for every member
etcdctl member list — it shows each member's data volume size
du -sh /var/lib/etcd — it isolates exactly the database size
kubectl top pods -n kube-system — it includes etcd storage metrics
explain: endpoint status reports the actual BoltDB size per member, which is what the backend quota applies to. du includes WAL and snap directories (misleading), kubectl top shows CPU/memory only, and member list shows membership, not storage.

q: Your security team mandates the pod network be 172.16.0.0/16. You ran kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=172.16.0.0/16 and now must adapt the stock Calico manifest before applying it. Which field carries the pod CIDR in the Calico manifest?
options: The --cluster-cidr flag in the Calico DaemonSet args — Calico reads the pod CIDR from there
The CoreDNS ConfigMap — the pod CIDR is configured through cluster DNS
No change is needed — Calico auto-discovers the CIDR kubeadm was given
The CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR environment variable (equivalently, the default IPv4 IPPool's cidr) — set it to 172.16.0.0/16 so Calico's pool matches kubeadm's CIDR
explain: Calico's IPAM is driven by its own IPPool (default 192.168.0.0/16, set via CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR in the manifest); it must agree with kubeadm's --pod-network-cidr or allocation and routing disagree. --cluster-cidr belongs to the kube-controller-manager, Calico does not auto-discover the CIDR, and CoreDNS has no role in pod IPAM.

q: You want a manual canary: roll the new image out to start the rollout, freeze it with one new pod running, verify metrics, then continue or abort. Which kubectl sequence does this?
options: Set maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 0 — the rollout pauses itself
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web — it freezes the rollout in place
kubectl rollout pause deployment/web after the rollout begins, then kubectl rollout resume to continue (or rollout undo to abort)
Delete the new ReplicaSet — the rollout pauses waiting for it
explain: rollout pause/resume is the built-in manual gate for staged rollouts. rollout undo reverts rather than pausing, zero surge/unavailable only constrains parallelism, and deleting the ReplicaSet corrupts the rollout instead of pausing it.

q: You need instant cutover between v1 and v2 of an API with instant rollback, and rolling updates are too gradual for this release. Which pattern gives you that?
options: kubectl rollout undo — it cuts traffic over instantly
Change the Service type to LoadBalancer during the release
Run two Deployments (blue and green) and flip the Service's selector from version: blue to version: green to cut traffic over at once
Edit the version label on the running v1 pods so the Service picks up v2
explain: Blue-green keeps both versions live and moves all traffic with one selector edit, and rollback is the reverse edit. Rollout undo is gradual (a rolling update in reverse), editing pod labels directly fights the Deployment controller, and the Service type has nothing to do with version routing.

q: A Job's pod fails and you want the Job controller to create a replacement pod (counted against backoffLimit), not the kubelet restarting the same container. Which pod spec setting gives you that?
options: completions: 0 — it tells the controller to keep creating pods
restartPolicy: Never — the kubelet leaves the failed pod alone and the Job controller creates a fresh pod per retry
restartPolicy: Always — Jobs accept it and it delegates retries to the controller
Set backoffLimit very high — that stops the controller from retrying
explain: Jobs only allow Never or OnFailure; with Never each failure becomes a new pod the controller counts toward backoffLimit. Always is rejected for Job pods, a high backoffLimit increases (not stops) retries, and completions: 0 is invalid.

q: A CronJob runs fine, but finished Job objects accumulate forever. You want to keep only the last 3 successful and the last 1 failed Job for history. Which fields do this?
options: successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3 and failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1 on the CronJob spec
backoffLimit: 1 — it caps the retained failed Jobs
ttlSecondsAfterFinished — it limits how many finished Jobs are kept
activeDeadlineSeconds — it garbage-collects old Jobs
explain: The history-limit fields cap the retained Job object counts by outcome. ttlSecondsAfterFinished deletes by age (a different mechanism), backoffLimit caps retries, and activeDeadlineSeconds caps a single Job's runtime.

q: A pod has a native sidecar (initContainer with restartPolicy: Always, 500m CPU request) and one app container (1000m CPU request). How much CPU does the scheduler reserve for this pod?
options: 500m — only the sidecar counts since it starts first
2000m — the scheduler doubles the app container request for sidecars
1000m — the scheduler takes the max of init and app containers
1500m — a restartable init container's requests are ADDED to the app containers' sum, unlike regular init containers which take the max
explain: Native sidecars change the accounting rule: their requests add to the app sum because they run for the pod's whole life. The max rule applies only to regular (run-to-completion) init containers, and nothing in the scheduler doubles requests.

q: A legacy app requires db.internal to resolve to 10.9.9.9 via /etc/hosts in every pod, but you may not touch CoreDNS or the node hosts files. How do you inject this?
options: Edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap hosts plugin — it is the only cluster-wide way
Set hostNetwork: true — pods then inherit the node's hosts file
Add spec.hostAliases: [{ip: "10.9.9.9", hostnames: ["db.internal"]}] to the pod spec
Add a dnsConfig nameservers entry — it appends hosts entries
explain: hostAliases appends entries to each pod's /etc/hosts without touching cluster DNS. dnsConfig only adjusts resolvers/search domains, CoreDNS was explicitly off-limits, and hostNetwork changes the pod's entire network namespace for a hosts-file need.

q: A node-troubleshooting pod must see the host's process tree (ps aux should show host PIDs) while keeping its own pod IP. Which setting does this?
options: hostNetwork: true — it also shares the host's process tree
shareProcessNamespace: true — it shares processes with the host
privileged: true alone — it implicitly joins the host PID namespace
hostPID: true — the pod joins the host's PID namespace while keeping its own network namespace
explain: hostPID joins the host PID namespace independently of networking. shareProcessNamespace only shares among the pod's own containers, hostNetwork shares networking (not PIDs), and privileged grants capabilities without joining any host namespace.

q: A container has a postStart hook that sleeps 60 seconds. The entrypoint is already serving traffic, yet kubectl shows the container as ContainerCreating and its probes have not started. What is happening?
options: The pod is broken — postStart hooks are not allowed to take longer than a second
Probes start immediately; the ContainerCreating status is a display bug
postStart runs asynchronously relative to the entrypoint, but the kubelet does not mark the container Running until the hook completes — keep hooks fast
postStart always runs before the entrypoint, so the app has not actually started
explain: The documented semantics: hook and entrypoint run side by side, but container state (and therefore probes, readiness, and traffic) waits on the hook. The entrypoint is not gated by the hook, the status is real, and slow hooks are legal but delay Running.

q: Compliance requires every node to run byte-identical images — a retagged mutable tag must never sneak in a different build. How do you pin the image immutably in the pod spec?
options: Use the latest tag — it always resolves to the same digest
Tags are immutable by convention, so nginx:1.27 is sufficient
Reference the digest: image: nginx:1.27@sha256:<digest>
Set imagePullPolicy: Always — it guarantees identical bytes on every node
explain: Only the digest addresses content; tags are mutable pointers a registry can repoint. Always still resolves the tag at pull time (per node, per pull), tags are mutable by default, and latest is the most mutable tag of all.

q: Hardening review: no container in the cluster needs any Linux capabilities. What is the correct baseline to enforce in the pod securityContext?
options: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false — it controls capabilities, not just setuid
runAsNonRoot: true — it implies a full capability drop
privileged: false — it already drops every capability
capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]} — then add back only specifically required capabilities per container
explain: Containers get a default capability set (CHOWN, NET_RAW, etc.) unless explicitly dropped; drop: [ALL] is the baseline. privileged: false is merely the default, runAsNonRoot only gates UID 0, and allowPrivilegeEscalation controls no_new_privs, not the capability bounding set.

q: Cache pods must land on the SAME node as the app pods they serve — a hard requirement, not a preference. Which scheduling rule expresses pod-to-pod co-location?
options: podAntiAffinity — it attracts pods to each other
podAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution, labelSelector app: web, topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
A Service with sessionAffinity — it controls scheduling placement
nodeAffinity on the cache pods — it matches nodes by pod labels
explain: podAffinity (required) forces co-location with matching pods in the same topology domain. podAntiAffinity does the opposite, nodeAffinity matches node labels (not pods), and sessionAffinity only affects traffic stickiness, never placement.

q: You added new nodes, but the old ones stay overloaded — the default scheduler never rebalances already-running pods. Which component fixes this, and what does it actually do?
options: The Descheduler — it evicts pods that violate its policies (e.g., node underutilization) so the scheduler places them fresh
The HPA — it redistributes pods across nodes when scaling
Restart kube-scheduler — it rebalances running pods on startup
Cordon the old nodes — it moves their running pods elsewhere
explain: The scheduler only places new pods; the Descheduler is the component that evicts misplaced running pods for rescheduling. Restarting the scheduler changes nothing about placed pods, cordon only blocks new scheduling, and the HPA changes replica counts, not placement.

q: You want every pod that omits priorityClassName to get priority 5000 automatically. What is the correct object, and what is the constraint?
options: Add defaultPriority: 5000 to the kube-scheduler flags
Set globalDefault: true on several PriorityClasses — the highest value wins
A PriorityClass with value: 5000 and globalDefault: true — only one PriorityClass in the cluster may set globalDefault
Set it via a ResourceQuota — quotas assign default priorities
explain: globalDefault makes the class apply to pods without an explicit priority, and the API rejects a second globalDefault. Multiple globalDefaults are forbidden, the scheduler has no defaultPriority flag, and ResourceQuotas do not assign priorities.

q: A ResourceQuota must count only long-running pods — Jobs and CronJob pods should be exempt from the pod count. How do you scope it?
options: Use a LimitRange — it exempts Jobs automatically
Add scopes: ["BestEffort"] — it excludes batch workloads
Put the Jobs in a separate namespace — quotas cannot scope by workload type
Add scopes: ["NotTerminating"] to the ResourceQuota
explain: The NotTerminating scope counts only pods that are not expected to terminate (excludes Jobs). BestEffort scopes by QoS class, quotas absolutely can scope this way (no namespace split needed), and LimitRange sets per-object defaults rather than exempting anything.

q: An HPA targets 70% CPU and 80% memory. The CPU metric says 6 replicas are needed; memory says 4. How many replicas will the HPA set?
options: 5 — it averages the metric demands
It flaps between 4 and 6 each sync period
4 — it takes the smallest to save resources
6 — the autoscaler evaluates every metric and takes the largest replica count
explain: Multi-metric HPAs take the max across metrics so every target is satisfied. Taking the min would starve the hotter metric, there is no averaging, and the controller is deterministic, not flapping.

q: A pod runs an app container plus a heavy metrics sidecar. You want the HPA to scale on the APP container's CPU only, ignoring the sidecar. Which metric type does this?
options: Custom metrics — container-level scaling requires a custom metrics adapter
type: ContainerResource with container: app — per-container metrics instead of the pod aggregate
type: Resource — it already breaks down per container
type: Pods — it averages the sidecar out
explain: ContainerResource targets a named container's utilization; the classic Resource type uses the pod-level aggregate including the sidecar. Pods-type metrics are per-pod averages, and no custom adapter is needed for this built-in type.

q: To 'save etcd space', someone set revisionHistoryLimit: 0 on all Deployments. Now kubectl rollout undo fails everywhere. Why?
options: Rollout history is stored in annotations, which the limit does not affect
Zero retained revisions means no old ReplicaSets exist to roll back to — keep the limit at 1 or higher
rollout undo works anyway; the failures must be RBAC
Etcd compaction deleted the revisions — raise the etcd quota
explain: revisionHistoryLimit controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept; 0 leaves nothing for undo to target. Etcd compaction is unrelated, history lives in retained ReplicaSets (change-cause annotations aside), and this failure is not RBAC.

q: You want full manual control over a StatefulSet update: change the image now, but have each pod pick it up only when YOU delete that pod. Which update strategy does this?
options: partition: 0 — it pauses all updates until you lower it
updateStrategy: {type: OnDelete}
OnDelete is not a valid StatefulSet update strategy
podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady — it defers updates until manual deletion
explain: OnDelete updates the template but only recreates pods when they are manually deleted. partition belongs to the RollingUpdate strategy (a canary control), podManagementPolicy governs startup/scaling order, and OnDelete is valid for StatefulSets.

q: You try to increase the storage request in a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates; the API rejects the change. What is the rule?
options: Edit the bound PVs directly — the template follows the PV
Scale the StatefulSet to 0 first — then the template becomes editable
volumeClaimTemplates are immutable after creation — you must recreate the StatefulSet (or manage the PVCs outside the template)
Storage expansion applies automatically — the template just needs allowVolumeExpansion
explain: The template is write-once; even scaling to zero does not make it mutable. Per-PVC expansion is a separate operation on the claims themselves, and PVs do not drive the template.

q: A container crashes before its logging framework initializes, so there is nothing useful in the logs — but you need its last stderr lines visible in kubectl describe pod. Which setting captures them?
options: restartPolicy: OnFailure — it preserves the crashed container's logs
A preStop hook — it runs before termination and captures the output
terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError — the kubelet surfaces the tail of container logs as the termination message when the app writes none
terminationMessagePath alone — the default path captures stderr automatically
explain: FallbackToLogsOnError is exactly the 'app wrote no termination message' fallback. The default terminationMessagePath only works if the app writes the file, restartPolicy controls restarts (not log surfacing), and preStop does not run on crashes.

q: You delete and recreate a Service; for about 30 seconds pods get NXDOMAIN for its name even though the Service exists. What is the most likely cause?
options: CoreDNS's cache plugin cached the negative (NXDOMAIN) response — the denial TTL must expire before the new record resolves
CoreDNS only reloads its ConfigMap on pod restart
kube-proxy takes 30 seconds to program endpoints for new Services
The ndots: 5 search-domain walk delays all new DNS records
explain: The cache plugin caches denials too, so a lookup during the gap poisons the cache briefly. kube-proxy programs endpoints (not DNS), ndots affects external names (not this in-cluster record), and the reload plugin picks up ConfigMap changes without restarts.

q: An automation tool needs the cluster DNS IP without querying the API — just from the service CIDR. What is the convention on a kubeadm cluster?
options: The .2 address — CoreDNS always takes the second IP
The .1 address — 10.96.0.1, same as the kubernetes default Service
The 10th IP of the service CIDR — 10.96.0.10 for the default 10.96.0.0/12
The CoreDNS pod IP — it is stable across restarts
explain: kubeadm reserves .1 for the kubernetes Service and assigns .10 to kube-dns/CoreDNS. The .1 is the API Service ClusterIP, .2 is not special, and pod IPs are ephemeral.

q: On a dual-stack cluster you want each Service to get both an IPv4 and an IPv6 ClusterIP when possible, but still work if only one family is available. Which setting does this?
options: ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack — it falls back gracefully
ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack — it assigns both families opportunistically
ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
Just list two entries under ipFamilies — the policy field is optional decoration
explain: PreferDualStack requests both families but tolerates one. RequireDualStack fails provisioning if both are unavailable, SingleStack is one family only, and ipFamilies entries are validated against the policy.

q: Pods using hostPort work on some nodes but not on others. The broken nodes run a minimal CNI. What is the actual requirement for hostPort to function?
options: kube-proxy programs hostPort rules — restart it on the broken nodes
hostPort requires the pod to also set hostNetwork: true
hostPort works with any CNI; the issue must be a NetworkPolicy
The CNI chain must include the portmap meta-plugin — hostPort is implemented by CNI, not by kube-proxy
explain: hostPort mapping is done by the portmap CNI plugin at pod-setup time. kube-proxy does not implement hostPort, NetworkPolicies do not gate host ports, and hostNetwork is a separate (stronger) setting.

q: You annotate pods with kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: 1M, but traffic is not shaped at all. Why is the annotation having no effect?
options: The kubelet enforces bandwidth annotations — check its --v logs
You need a LimitRange — annotations alone cannot shape traffic
The annotation names are wrong — they must be prefixed with pod.
Those annotations need a CNI with traffic-shaping support (e.g., Cilium's bandwidth manager) — most CNIs silently ignore them
explain: Bandwidth shaping happens in the CNI's dataplane; without support the annotations are no-ops. The kubelet does not shape traffic, the annotation names are correct, and LimitRange governs requests/limits, not shaping.

q: An Ingress rule uses path: /api with pathType: Exact. Requests to /api succeed but /api/ returns 404. What is the subtlety?
options: The backend Service strips trailing slashes before matching
Exact matches the literal path only — /api/ is a different string than /api, including the trailing slash
pathType: Prefix would also 404 on /api/
The ingress controller is misconfigured — Exact ignores trailing slashes
explain: Exact is a byte-for-byte (case-sensitive) match, so the trailing slash matters. Prefix would match /api/, the controller is behaving correctly, and path matching happens before the backend is involved.

q: Pods in namespace team-a must reach the database Service that lives in namespace team-b via the short name db, without duplicating the Service object. How?
options: A ClusterIP Service named db in team-a with manually managed Endpoints
A headless Service named db in team-a — it resolves across namespaces automatically
Cross-namespace Service references are impossible in Kubernetes
Create an ExternalName Service named db in team-a pointing to db.team-b.svc.cluster.local
explain: ExternalName is a DNS CNAME, and the target can be any cluster DNS name including another namespace's Service. Manual Endpoints work but duplicate state, cross-namespace aliasing via ExternalName is fully supported, and a headless Service still needs its own endpoints.

q: Security requires the ingress-nginx edge to demand client certificates (mutual TLS) for the /admin Ingress before traffic reaches the backends. How do you configure this?
options: Enforce it with a NetworkPolicy — policies validate client certificates
Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret: <ns>/<ca-secret> (plus auth-tls-verify-client) on the Ingress
Add the CA to the Ingress tls: block — it already handles client certs
Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: HTTPS — it enables mTLS
explain: The auth-tls-* annotations make nginx verify client certificates against the given CA at the edge. The tls: block only configures the server certificate, backend-protocol only changes the upstream scheme, and NetworkPolicies filter packets, not TLS identities.

q: A NetworkPolicy from-entry combines namespaceSelector: {} with podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}. Traffic from api pods in OTHER namespaces is unexpectedly allowed. Why?
options: You also need policyTypes: [Ingress] for selectors to take effect
The policy is invalid — an empty selector can never match
An empty namespaceSelector means the policy's own namespace
namespaceSelector: {} matches ALL namespaces — combined with the podSelector it selects api pods in every namespace
