explain: In label-selector semantics, an empty selector matches everything; omitting namespaceSelector (not emptying it) would scope to the policy's namespace. The policy is valid, and policyTypes defaults are not the issue here.

q: With kube-proxy in IPVS mode, one backend pod holds most long-lived connections while others sit idle. The default scheduler is round-robin. What is the targeted fix?
options: Switch kube-proxy back to iptables mode — it balances long-lived connections better
Set kube-proxy's --ipvs-scheduler to lc (least connection) or another algorithm suited to uneven connections
kube-proxy does not support scheduler algorithms; use a service mesh
Enable sessionAffinity: ClientIP — it evens out connection distribution
explain: IPVS supports multiple schedulers (rr, lc, dh, sh, ...); lc sends new connections to the least-loaded backend. iptables mode has the same distribution behavior, sessionAffinity pins clients (worsening imbalance), and the --ipvs-scheduler flag exists precisely for this.

q: You must proxy raw TCP (not HTTP, not TLS) through Gateway API, routing by listener port to different backends. Which route resource does this?
options: TLSRoute — it works for plaintext TCP via SNI sniffing
TCPRoute — attached to a TCP protocol listener
HTTPRoute — it handles any TCP payload
Ingress — it supports TCP services with an annotation
explain: TCPRoute is the L4 route for raw TCP on TCP listeners. HTTPRoute is L7 HTTP only, TLSRoute needs TLS/SNI, and Ingress is HTTP(S) only.

q: Game servers need UDP load balancing through Gateway API. Which route resource expresses this?
options: A plain NodePort Service — Gateway API cannot do UDP
UDPRoute — attached to a UDP protocol listener
TCPRoute — it covers both TCP and UDP
HTTPRoute with a UDP backendRef
explain: UDPRoute is the dedicated L4 route for UDP listeners. TCPRoute is TCP-only, HTTPRoute cannot carry UDP, and while NodePort works, the question asks for the Gateway API resource.

q: Applying an Ingress on networking.k8s.io/v1 fails with: pathType is required. The manifest was copied from an old extensions/v1beta1 example. What changed?
options: ingressClassName became required in v1
path is now required to start with / — that is the real error
The v1 API made pathType mandatory (Exact, Prefix, or ImplementationSpecific) — the beta allowed omitting it
You used the wrong apiVersion — v1 Ingresses do not need pathType
explain: Promoting Ingress to GA required explicit path-matching semantics, so pathType is now a required field. The apiVersion is correct, the path format is a separate validation, and ingressClassName remains optional.

q: You deployed NodeLocal DNSCache, but pods still send every query to the CoreDNS ClusterIP. What must change so pods actually use the node-local cache?
options: Set dnsPolicy: Default on every pod — that enables the node-local cache
Add a stub domain to the CoreDNS ConfigMap — that redirects queries into the cache
Scale the node-local-dns DaemonSet — pods discover the cache automatically
Point the kubelet's --cluster-dns at the node-local link-local IP 169.254.20.10, which the DNSCache DaemonSet binds on each node
explain: Pods use whatever --cluster-dns the kubelet writes into their resolv.conf; NodeLocal DNSCache works by binding 169.254.20.10 per node and having the kubelet point there. Scaling does not change discovery, stub domains live in CoreDNS (the component being bypassed), and dnsPolicy: Default uses the node's own resolver, not the cache.

q: Your service mesh needs to know which Service ports carry gRPC versus plain HTTP. Port names like grpc- are only a convention. What is the machine-readable field?
options: appProtocol on the Service port — e.g., appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c
targetPort — it declares the application protocol
An annotation like service.beta.kubernetes.io/protocol
The port name — meshes are required to parse it
explain: appProtocol is the first-class, machine-readable protocol hint consumed by meshes and controllers. targetPort is just a port mapping, there is no standard protocol annotation, and name parsing is convention, not contract.

q: An Ingress declares tls: [{hosts: [shop.example.com], secretName: shop-tls}] but its rule host is store.example.com. Browsers show certificate warnings. What is wrong?
options: TLS hosts are cluster-wide and matched by path, not hostname
The tls.hosts entry must match the rule's host — SNI-based selection missed, so the controller served its default/fake certificate
The Secret must be of type kubernetes.io/tls — any other type breaks SNI
One Ingress can only serve one hostname — split them
explain: Certificate selection is by SNI hostname against tls.hosts; a mismatch falls through to the default cert. The Secret type is a separate concern, one Ingress routinely serves many hosts, and matching is by hostname, not path.

q: You edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap (add a stub domain) and within a minute queries reflect it — without restarting CoreDNS. What makes this work?
options: CoreDNS polls the API server for ConfigMaps on every query
The kubelet restarts the CoreDNS pods when their ConfigMap changes
You must always run kubectl rollout restart — the change you saw was cached
The reload plugin watches the ConfigMap and reloads CoreDNS automatically (about every 30 seconds by default)
explain: The reload plugin is enabled by default in the kubeadm CoreDNS Corefile, so config changes apply without restarts. The kubelet does not restart pods on ConfigMap change, no manual restart was needed, and CoreDNS does not consult the API per query.

q: A backend is flaky: you want the Gateway to retry idempotent GETs up to 3 times on 5xx before giving up. Where does this belong in Gateway API?
options: The retry stanza on the HTTPRouteRule — attempts and retry conditions per rule (support varies by implementation)
BackendTLSPolicy — it configures retry budgets
The Deployment's replicas — retries are a workload concern
The RequestMirror filter — it duplicates requests as retries
explain: GEP-1731 defines per-rule retry (attempts/codes) on the HTTPRoute itself. BackendTLSPolicy is for backend TLS, RequestMirror shadows traffic (clients still get the primary response), and replicas do not retry failed requests.

q: A NetworkPolicy must select pods where app is in (web, api) — a set-based requirement matchLabels cannot express. How do you write the selector?
options: matchLabels: {app: "web,api"} — comma-separated values are set expressions
Two separate NetworkPolicies — selectors cannot use operators
podSelector with matchExpressions: [{key: app, operator: In, values: [web, api]}]
namespaceSelector — it supports set-based pod matching
explain: matchExpressions brings In/NotIn/Exists semantics to policy selectors. matchLabels is exact-match only (the comma string would match a literal label value), one policy suffices, and namespaceSelector selects namespaces, not pods.

q: A telecom app needs SCTP through a Kubernetes Service. What do you set, and what is the caveat?
options: protocol: SCTP works everywhere with no prerequisites
SCTP requires hostNetwork on every backend pod
SCTP is not a valid Service protocol — use TCP instead
protocol: SCTP on the Service port — but the CNI and kube-proxy must support SCTP, which many setups do not
explain: SCTP is a valid API protocol value, but dataplane support (CNI, kube-proxy, cloud LBs) is patchy and must be verified. It is not TCP-equivalent, it is not universally supported, and hostNetwork is not the requirement.

q: Two PVs exist: pv-a with no storageClassName, and pv-b with storageClassName: fast. A PVC sets storageClassName: "". Which PV can it bind to?
options: Only pv-b — the empty string is a wildcard matching any class
Only pv-a — the empty-string class binds exclusively to PVs that also have no storage class
Neither — storageClassName: "" is invalid, so the PVC stays Pending
Either — the scheduler picks whichever has more free space
explain: The empty string is a real class value meaning 'no class', and binding requires class equality — so it matches only class-less PVs. It is not a wildcard, the scheduler does not choose by free space, and the empty string is valid: it is precisely how you opt out of dynamic provisioning.

q: A live database volume must move from gp2 to gp3 with higher IOPS — without recreating the PVC or copying data. Which mechanism supports mutating volume attributes in place?
options: Delete and recreate the PVC — the only supported way to change volume type
Edit the PVC's storageClassName — it is mutable for attribute changes
A VolumeAttributesClass referenced by the PVC's spec.volumeAttributesClassName — unlike storageClassName, it is mutable and the driver applies the change
Change the StorageClass parameters — existing volumes pick up the new settings
explain: VolumeAttributesClass is the API for in-place mutable volume attributes (type, IOPS, throughput) via drivers implementing ModifyVolume. storageClassName is immutable, StorageClass edits affect only future volumes, and recreate-and-copy is the disruptive path this feature avoids.

q: You see PVC manifests using dataSource for cloning and newer ones using dataSourceRef. What is the difference?
options: They are identical aliases — the API treats them the same
dataSourceRef is the newer field — it supersedes dataSource and additionally supports cross-namespace data source references
dataSource is the newer field; dataSourceRef is deprecated
Both fields are required together for cloning to work
explain: dataSourceRef is the graduated replacement with namespace support for cross-namespace sources; dataSource is the legacy field. They are not aliases, the direction of deprecation is the reverse, and only one is needed.

q: Containers in a pod must run with group 4000 in their process group list, but you must NOT trigger a recursive ownership change of the already-correct mounted volume. Which field does this?
options: securityContext.runAsGroup: 4000 — it adds a supplemental group
securityContext.supplementalGroups: [4000] — it adds GIDs to the container processes without touching volume ownership
Mount the volume with the group option in volumeMounts
securityContext.fsGroup: 4000 — it only affects processes, never volume ownership
explain: supplementalGroups adds process group membership with no volume side effects, while fsGroup would also chown the volume (the expensive side effect to avoid here). runAsGroup sets the primary GID rather than adding a supplemental one, and volumeMounts have no group option.

q: A statically provisioned NFS PV must be mounted with noatime. The pods only declare PVCs and there is no StorageClass involved. Where do you set the mount option?
options: spec.mountOptions on the PersistentVolume itself
In the StorageClass parameters — mount options only live there
With a kubelet flag — mount options are node-global
On each pod's volumeMounts — they accept mountOptions
explain: Static PVs carry their own mountOptions field; StorageClasses are not in the picture for static provisioning. volumeMounts have no mountOptions field, and there is no such kubelet flag.

q: Your CSI driver needs storage-backend credentials at volume stage/publish time, but you refuse to put secrets in pod specs or StorageClass parameters. Where do the credentials go?
options: The PV's nodeStageSecretRef and nodePublishSecretRef, referencing a Secret in the PV's namespace scope
imagePullSecrets on the pod — they are reused for storage auth
StorageClass parameters — they are the only channel to the driver
Environment variables on the CSI node-driver DaemonSet pods
explain: The CSI PV spec has dedicated secret references for the stage and publish calls, keeping credentials out of workloads. imagePullSecrets are for registries, DaemonSet env vars are node-global (not per-volume), and parameters are non-secret, API-visible strings.

q: You want every individual PVC in namespace team-a constrained between 1Gi and 100Gi — a per-claim floor and ceiling, not a namespace total. Which object does this?
options: A LimitRange with type: PersistentVolumeClaim and min/max storage entries
A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy — the only way to bound PVC sizes
A ResourceQuota with requests.storage — it caps each PVC individually
A StorageClass with min/max parameters — classes enforce claim sizes
explain: LimitRange constrains each object at creation time (per-PVC min/max). ResourceQuota caps namespace aggregates, StorageClasses have no per-claim size bounds, and a VAP would be overkill for a built-in LimitRange feature.

q: You change a StorageClass's reclaimPolicy from Delete to Retain, but the already-provisioned PVs still show Delete. Why, and how do you fix the existing ones?
options: Class changes apply only to subsequently provisioned PVs — patch spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy on each existing PV directly
The change propagates automatically within 10 minutes — just wait
Delete and recreate the StorageClass — that rewrites existing PVs
Restart the kube-controller-manager — it re-renders PVs from their class
explain: The StorageClass is a template for provisioning; each PV carries its own independent reclaimPolicy field. There is no delayed propagation, no controller re-render, and recreating the class does not touch existing PVs.

q: You hand-create a PV for an existing CSI disk (vol-0abc123). The PV stays Available and the PVC never binds, though driver and selectors look right. What is missing?
options: spec.csi.volumeHandle must be set to the driver's volume ID (vol-0abc123) — static CSI PVs identify the asset by handle, not by path
Setting spec.csi.driver alone is enough — the driver discovers the disk
Add a claimRef — static CSI PVs cannot bind without one
Use a hostPath volume with the disk's device path instead
explain: volumeHandle is the required driver-specific identifier for pre-provisioned CSI volumes. The driver name alone does not locate the asset, hostPath is a different volume type, and claimRef is optional (a binding aid, not the identity).

q: A StorageClass sets parameters: {iops-per-gb: "10"} but the driver expects iopsPerGB. Volumes provision fine — as the driver's defaults, ignoring your setting. Why no error?
options: The external-provisioner fails the PVC with an InvalidParameter event
The API server rejects unknown parameter keys at apply time
Parameters are validated against the driver's published schema
StorageClass parameters are passed opaquely to the driver — unknown keys are silently ignored with no API-side validation
explain: Kubernetes treats parameters as an opaque string map; typos fail silently into driver defaults, which is exactly why provisioning 'succeeds' wrongly. There is no admission validation, no provisioner error, and no schema check.

q: A pod uses emptyDir with medium: Memory for a cache. The app's own heap is small, yet the container gets OOMKilled when the cache grows. Why?
options: tmpfs-backed emptyDir counts against the container's memory cgroup — the cache plus the heap together exceeded the memory limit
emptyDir with medium: Memory is free and never counted anywhere
It counts against ephemeral-storage, not memory
sizeLimit on the emptyDir prevents OOMKills — it must be unset
explain: Memory-medium emptyDir is a tmpfs charged to container memory, so a fat cache OOMs the container like any allocation. It is not free, it is not ephemeral-storage, and sizeLimit drives eviction accounting rather than preventing cgroup OOMs.

q: You need a Secret volume to place files at tls/cert.pem and tls/key.pem (with the tls/ subdirectory). How do you express the nested paths?
options: Item paths cannot contain slashes — you need one volume per file
Use subPath: tls/cert.pem on the volumeMount — it creates the directories
items: [{key: tls.crt, path: tls/cert.pem}, ...] — item paths may contain slashes and the subdirectories are created as needed
Mount the whole Secret — nested paths are impossible
explain: The items path field accepts relative paths with directories, which the kubelet creates. Slashes are legal (the 'one volume per file' claim is false), subPath mounts a single file without creating sibling dirs, and whole-secret mounts flatten keys to filenames.

q: A ConfigMap must hold a binary protobuf descriptor file. kubectl create configmap rejects the non-UTF8 bytes in data. What is the correct field?
options: binaryData — it accepts base64-encoded values for non-UTF8 content
ConfigMaps cannot hold binary data at all — use a hostPath file
data with escaped byte sequences — the API accepts them
stringData — it handles binary transparently
explain: binaryData is the ConfigMap field designed for arbitrary bytes (base64-encoded). data requires valid UTF-8, stringData is a Secret write-convenience (and also UTF-8), and ConfigMaps absolutely can carry binary via binaryData.

q: A pod's projected ServiceAccount token must carry audience vault and expire after 10 minutes (not the default lifetime). How do you request that?
options: Create a legacy token Secret — it supports custom audiences
Token audiences are fixed to the API server and cannot be customized
Set automountServiceAccountToken: true — it accepts audience and expiry settings
A projected volume with serviceAccountToken: {path: token, audience: vault, expirationSeconds: 600}
explain: The projected serviceAccountToken source supports audience and expirationSeconds per mount. The auto-mounted default token has no such options, legacy token Secrets are long-lived without audiences, and custom audiences are a core projected-token feature.

q: With nfs-subdir-external-provisioner, every dynamic PVC lands in one flat directory. You want per-namespace, per-claim subdirectories. Where is this configured?
options: The PVC's volumeName — it controls the subdirectory
StorageClass parameters — pathPattern is a standard StorageClass field
One PV per namespace, created by hand
The provisioner's pathPattern setting, e.g. ${.PVC.namespace}/${.PVC.name}
explain: pathPattern is the provisioner's own templating setting for the directory layout. It is not a generic StorageClass field, hand-creating PVs defeats dynamic provisioning, and volumeName is assigned at bind time, not a layout control.

q: The platform team must cap team-a at 100Gi on fast-ssd AND 500Gi on standard — separate ceilings per class in one namespace. Which ResourceQuota entries do this?
options: Two ResourceQuotas each with requests.storage — the API merges them per class
One quota with requests.storage: 600Gi — it splits evenly across classes
fast-ssd.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage: 100Gi and standard.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage: 500Gi
StorageClasses have their own quota fields — set them on the class
explain: Quota supports per-StorageClass keys in the <class>.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/<resource> form. Duplicate requests.storage keys are impossible, a single aggregate cannot split per class, and StorageClasses carry no quota fields.

q: kubectl get pvc shows a claim in STATUS Lost. The underlying PV was deleted out-of-band last night. What does Lost mean and what is next?
options: Lost is a transient phase — the claim will rebind automatically
The bound PV is gone and cannot come back — the data is almost certainly lost; restore from backup and delete the PVC
Recreate a PV with the same name — the data reappears
It means Pending with a typo — check provisioner events
explain: Lost is terminal: the backing asset disappeared outside Kubernetes control. It does not self-heal, it is not a Pending variant, and a same-named PV is a new empty asset, not the old data.

q: A DaemonSet must read the host's /etc/machine-id but must never be able to write to the host filesystem through that mount. How do you enforce read-only?
options: Run the container unprivileged — that makes hostPath mounts read-only
Set hostPath type: File — it implies read-only
Set readOnly on the volume definition — it applies to all mounts
Set readOnly: true on the container's volumeMount for the hostPath volume
explain: readOnly is a per-volumeMount setting, which is exactly the granularity needed. The hostPath type only asserts the path kind, the volume source has no readOnly field, and unprivileged does not make mounts read-only.

q: A namespace has ResourceQuota requests.storage: 100Gi. Developers discover heavy emptyDir usage does not count against it. Is this expected?
options: Yes, but only for emptyDir with medium: Memory
No — the quota controller is broken and must be restarted
No — emptyDir usage is converted to storage requests automatically
Yes — the storage quota counts PVC requests only; emptyDir is node-local scratch and is never part of requests.storage
explain: requests.storage sums PersistentVolumeClaim requests; emptyDir volumes are not claims and never enter the accounting. There is no automatic conversion, the medium does not matter, and the controller is behaving correctly.

q: A Secret volume is mounted writable into a pod, but one container must mount a single key from it read-only via subPath while the others stay writable. How?
options: On that container's volumeMount set subPath: <key> and readOnly: true — readOnly is per mount, not per volume
One volume cannot be both writable and read-only — duplicate the Secret
Set readOnly on the Secret volume source — it applies per container automatically
subPath mounts are always read-only, so no extra field is needed
explain: readOnly lives on the volumeMount, so the same volume can be writable in one container and read-only in another. The volume source has no readOnly field, subPath mounts inherit the mount's writability, and no duplication is needed.

q: In the middle of an incident you want ONLY Warning events across ALL namespaces, newest first, in one command. Which does it?
options: kubectl logs -A --level=warning — it aggregates warning logs
Events are namespaced — there is no way to list them cluster-wide
kubectl describe all -A | grep -i warning — the supported filtering path
kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
explain: get events supports -A plus a field-selector on type, and sort-by orders them. kubectl logs has no level flag or -A aggregation, describe-all piping is slow and lossy, and events absolutely list cluster-wide.

q: API requests are being rejected by an auth issue and the API server logs are too terse. You need verbose API server logs. How do you raise the log level on a kubeadm cluster?
options: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml to add --v=4 — the kubelet restarts the static pod automatically
journalctl -u kube-apiserver -f — the API server logs through systemd
--v only affects kubectl; server verbosity cannot be changed
kubectl logs --v=4 -n kube-system kube-apiserver-cp-1 — it raises verbosity retroactively
explain: Static-pod flags are edited in the manifest; the kubelet notices and restarts the pod. kubectl's --v is client-side only, the API server is a static pod (not a systemd unit), and server verbosity is fully configurable.

q: The API server is down and you need the logs of a CrashLoopBackOff pod from the node it runs on. kubectl is useless right now. What works?
options: Wait for the API server — container logs are only reachable through it
crictl ps -a to find the container ID, then crictl logs <container-id> — node-local, no API server needed
kubectl logs --previous — it reads from the node's local log store
journalctl -u kubelet — it contains the container's stdout
explain: crictl talks to the CRI directly on the node, bypassing the API entirely. kubectl logs needs the API, journalctl shows kubelet logs (not container stdout), and waiting wastes the incident window.

q: From a debug pod you must inspect the HOST's network namespace (its iptables rules) without SSH — but the pod must keep its own pod IP (hostNetwork is not allowed). What works?
options: Run a privileged debug pod and use nsenter -t 1 -n iptables -L — it enters the host's network namespace via PID 1
hostNetwork: true is the only way to see host iptables
kubectl exec into the kube-proxy pod — it shares the host network namespace
chroot /host — it switches the network namespace
explain: nsenter -t 1 -n joins PID 1's network namespace while the pod keeps its own. hostNetwork was ruled out by the premise, kube-proxy pods do not share the host netns, and chroot changes the filesystem view, not namespaces.

q: A ClusterIP works from pods on node-a but not node-b. You suspect kube-proxy on node-b never programmed the NAT rules. What is the direct node-level check?
options: Restart kube-proxy on node-b — that is both diagnosis and fix
kubectl get svc — it shows whether the rules were programmed
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep <cluster-ip> on node-b
Check CoreDNS — DNS is the usual cause of ClusterIP failures
explain: The KUBE-SERVICES chain is where kube-proxy programs ClusterIP rules; its absence on the node proves the dataplane gap. kubectl shows API state (not node datapath), restarting without diagnosing is shotgun debugging, and this is IP-level, not DNS.

q: kube-proxy runs in IPVS mode and you want to confirm the virtual server and its real backends for a Service's ClusterIP. Which command shows this?
options: iptables -t nat -L — IPVS mode still programs everything there
kubectl get endpoints — it shows the IPVS forwarding table
ip route show — it lists the virtual servers
ipvsadm -Ln | grep <cluster-ip> — it lists virtual servers and their real servers
explain: ipvsadm is the IPVS management tool showing virtual/real server state. In IPVS mode the NAT chains are mostly empty, endpoints are API objects (not the forwarding table), and ip route shows routing, not IPVS state.

q: A NodePort Service does not answer on <node>:31080. Before blaming the network, you want to confirm kube-proxy is even listening on that port on the node. Which check?
options: ss -tlnp | grep 31080 on the node — it shows listening sockets and their processes
kubectl get svc — a NodePort value proves the port is listening
Run netstat inside a pod — it shows the node's listening ports
curl the port first — listening checks are unnecessary
explain: ss on the node directly verifies the listen socket (kube-proxy opens NodePorts). A pod's netns does not show node listeners, the API object existing does not prove the dataplane, and curling first skips the cheaper local check.

q: kubectl get nodes shows a node NotReady, but the kubelet process is alive on it. What is the quickest kubelet-local health check that does not need the API server?
options: systemctl is-active kubelet — a running process means a healthy kubelet
kubectl describe node — it queries the kubelet directly
curl -sk https://localhost:10250/healthz — the kubelet's own HTTPS health endpoint
curl https://localhost:6443/healthz — it checks the kubelet
explain: Port 10250 is the kubelet's serving port with /healthz; it answers even when the node cannot reach the API. Port 6443 is the API server, a live process can still be wedged, and describe node goes through the API server.

q: After a config change, the API server logs 'etcdserver: request timed out' on every write, yet etcd itself is healthy and its data is intact. What should you check first?
options: Run etcdctl defrag — fragmentation causes request timeouts
The --etcd-servers flag in the API server static pod manifest — it is likely pointing at wrong or unreachable etcd endpoints
Raise --etcd-compact-interval — it fixes slow etcd writes
Restore etcd from snapshot — the timeouts mean the data is corrupt
explain: Healthy etcd plus API-side timeouts points at the connection between them — the classic cause is a mis-edited --etcd-servers list. The data is fine (no restore needed), defrag addresses quota (not timeouts), and the compact interval is unrelated.

q: New nodes receive podCIDRs from a range that does not match the CNI's configured pod network, so pods get IPs the CNI cannot route. Which component hands out those node CIDRs?
options: kubeadm's --pod-network-cidr at join time — it sets the range on running nodes
kube-controller-manager via its --cluster-cidr flag — it allocates each node's podCIDR from that range
The kube-scheduler — it assigns podCIDRs during scheduling
CoreDNS — it allocates pod CIDRs from its Corefile
explain: The node CIDR allocator lives in the controller-manager and uses --cluster-cidr (seeded by kubeadm's --pod-network-cidr at init). kubeadm does not re-apply it at join, the scheduler never allocates CIDRs, and CoreDNS has no such role.

q: A node drain hangs: a CrashLoopBackOff pod guarded by a PDB blocks eviction, and the app will never become healthy. The PDB uses default settings. What unblocks the drain without deleting the PDB?
options: Raise maxUnavailable — it lets the eviction API skip unhealthy pods
kubectl drain --force — it overrides PDB decisions
Delete the PDB — it is the only way to evict the pod
Set unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow on the PDB — the default IfHealthyBudget protects unhealthy pods of an already-disrupted app
explain: AlwaysAllow treats running-but-unhealthy pods as evictable regardless of the disruption budget; IfHealthyBudget (the default) shields them when the app is already disrupted. Deleting the PDB loses protection, drain has no PDB-overriding --force, and maxUnavailable does not cover unhealthy-pod policy.

q: You must drain only the batch-workload pods from a node for maintenance, leaving monitoring and system pods running there. Which command does this?
options: kubectl drain node-1 --pod-selector=workload=batch --ignore-daemonsets
kubectl delete pods -l workload=batch --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-1 — it cordons first
kubectl cordon node-1 — it evicts only matching pods
kubectl drain always evicts every pod — selective drain is impossible
explain: drain accepts a --pod-selector to filter which pods are evicted (still cordoning the node). The delete command does not cordon, cordon evicts nothing, and selective drain is a supported flag.

q: A taint key spot takes unpredictable values (spot=true, spot=azure, spot=preemptible...). Pods must tolerate the taint regardless of its value. Which toleration does this?
options: operator: Equal with value: "*" — wildcards match any value
tolerations: [{key: spot, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}] — Exists matches any value
Omit the value with operator: Equal — Equal without a value matches everything
Taints cannot be tolerated without specifying their exact value
explain: Exists is the operator for value-agnostic matching. Equal requires an exact value (no wildcards), and omitting value with Equal matches only empty values — not everything.

q: Maintenance is over and you must remove the taint you added earlier: kubectl taint nodes node-1 maintenance=true:NoSchedule. Which command removes it?
options: kubectl taint nodes node-1 maintenance=true:NoSchedule- — the trailing dash deletes the taint
kubectl delete node node-1 — the taint goes away with the node object
kubectl taint nodes node-1 maintenance=:NoSchedule — empty value removes it
kubectl untaint nodes node-1 maintenance
explain: The taint command uses a trailing - to remove (same idiom as label removal). There is no untaint subcommand, re-applying with an empty value adds a taint, and deleting the node is wildly disproportionate.

q: You want the kubelet to start evicting at 85% disk usage with a grace period, but only hard-evict immediately at 95%. Which kubelet settings express the two tiers?
options: Only --eviction-hard exists — soft eviction is not a kubelet feature
A PodDisruptionBudget — it defines the soft and hard disk thresholds
--eviction-soft with --eviction-soft-grace-period for the 85% warning tier, and --eviction-hard for the immediate 95% tier
The OOM score — it provides the two-tier eviction behavior
explain: The kubelet supports soft thresholds (with grace periods) and hard thresholds (immediate) as separate flag sets. Soft eviction is real, PDBs govern voluntary disruptions (not disk pressure), and OOM scores order kills within a cgroup, not disk tiers.

q: A script that lists resources in a tight loop starts getting 429 Too Many Requests from the API server. What does this mean and what is the right response?
options: Restart the API server — it clears the rate limiter permanently
etcd is full — 429 means the backend database rejected writes
Client-side API rate limiting throttled the burst — slow the script down, batch requests, or raise client QPS/Burst; the server is protecting itself
Raise the etcd quota — 429 is a storage-pressure signal
explain: 429 is the API server's client rate limiter (flow control) doing its job; the fix is on the client's request rate. It is not etcd-full (different error), restarts do not change limits, and etcd quota is unrelated.

q: After dropping a second CNI's config into /etc/cni/net.d for testing, all NEW pods lose networking, though the original CNI's DaemonSet is healthy. What happened?
options: Restart the kubelet — it re-discovers the correct CNI automatically
Reinstall the original CNI — its config was overwritten
The runtime uses the alphabetically-first .conflist in /etc/cni/net.d — the new file shadows the working one; remove it
The two CNI versions are incompatible — upgrade the older one
explain: CNI config selection is by sorted filename; an extra file wins or conflicts regardless of DaemonSet health. A restart does not change ordering, version skew is not the mechanism, and the original config was shadowed, not overwritten.

q: The API server is down and you need post-mortem on recently EXITED containers (exit codes and names) from the node. Which command lists them?
options: crictl ps -a — it includes stopped/exited containers, unlike the default running-only view
crictl ps — it shows exited containers by default
kubectl get pods --show-all — it works without the API server
docker ps -a — the standard fallback on any node
explain: The -a flag is what surfaces exited containers with their exit codes, node-locally. Plain crictl ps shows only running containers, Docker is not the runtime here, and kubectl cannot function with the API down.

q: A pod is stuck Terminating and someone proposes kubectl delete pod x --force --grace-period=0. What does this actually do, and when is it acceptable?
options: It restarts the kubelet on the node to clear the stuck pod
It removes the API object immediately without kubelet confirmation — acceptable only when the node is dead/gone; otherwise the kubelet may still be running the container
It is always safe — it cleanly tears down containers first
--force alone is enough; --grace-period=0 is redundant
explain: --force --grace-period=0 bypasses graceful termination and etcd-deletes the object, risking orphaned running containers and endpoint confusion on a live node. It is not a cleanup (it skips cleanup), it does not touch the kubelet, and --force without grace-period=0 still waits.

q: Before trusting a nightly etcd backup, you want a lightweight check that the snapshot file is valid and to see its revision and key count. Which command does this?
options: Only a full test restore proves anything — status checks are meaningless
etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd.db -w table — it verifies integrity and reports hash, revision, total keys, and size
ls -lh the file — size alone proves the snapshot is restorable
etcdctl get --from-file — it queries keys directly from the snapshot
explain: snapshot status validates the file's integrity and surfaces revision/key metadata — the cheap pre-restore sanity check. File size proves nothing about corruption, you cannot query a snapshot file with get, and while test restores are the gold standard, the status check is the meaningful lightweight gate.

q: Before running kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34 on the first control-plane node, you want to preview exactly which static pod manifests will change and how. Which command shows this?
options: kubeadm upgrade apply v1.34 --dry-run, which prints the diff and exits
kubeadm upgrade diff --config kubeadm.yaml, which renders the static pod manifest changes the upgrade would apply, without changing anything
kubeadm upgrade plan v1.34, which prints the manifest diff
kubectl diff -f /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, which previews static pod changes
explain: kubeadm upgrade diff exists precisely for this: it prints the differences the upgrade would write into the static pod manifests. upgrade plan only reports available versions and component config states, kubectl diff works against live API objects rather than manifest files, and upgrade apply has no --dry-run mode.

q: After compaction, etcd's database file is 6 GB but the in-use size is only 900 MB. The cluster is healthy and must stay up. Which command reclaims the fragmented space on the live member?
options: etcdctl defrag --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 (with the etcd PKI certs), because etcdctl defrag operates over the network against a running member
etcdutl defrag --data-dir /var/lib/etcd, which defragments the live member in place
etcdctl compact, because compaction alone reclaims the disk space
Restarting the etcd static pod, because the restart rebuilds the database file
explain: etcdctl talks to a running member over its API, so etcdctl defrag reclaims space online (issued per member). etcdutl operates directly on data files and must only be used while etcd is stopped. Compaction only marks revisions free logically -- the file stays fragmented until defrag -- and a restart does not rewrite the backend file.

q: New worker nodes join fine, but they get no spec.podCIDR and their pods receive IPs the CNI cannot route. Which component and setting is responsible for handing pod CIDRs to nodes?
options: The kube-controller-manager, via --allocate-node-cidrs (default true) and --cluster-cidr: its node IPAM controller assigns each node a podCIDR
The kube-scheduler, via --pod-cidr: the scheduler assigns pod CIDRs during placement
kube-proxy, via --cluster-cidr: it programs the pod CIDR routes
The CNI plugin config in /etc/cni/net.d: the CNI hands out node CIDRs
explain: The kube-controller-manager's node IPAM controller carves per-node blocks out of --cluster-cidr and writes them into each Node's spec.podCIDR. Without that, nodes never get a podCIDR and the CNI has no routable block to allocate from. The scheduler never assigns CIDRs, kube-proxy programs service NAT rather than pod CIDR allocation, and the CNI only assigns pod IPs within the block it is given.

q: You enforce the restricted PodSecurityStandard on every namespace, but kube-system workloads break under it. You refuse to weaken enforcement with per-namespace labels. Where do you carve out the exemption centrally?
options: Label kube-system with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: privileged
Add --disable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity to the API server
Annotate the CoreDNS Deployment with a seccomp bypass
In the PodSecurityConfiguration file's exemptions stanza (exemptions.namespaces: [kube-system]) referenced by the API server's --admission-control-config-file
explain: The admission config file supports a central exemptions list for namespaces, usernames, and runtime classes -- the intended way to exempt system namespaces without touching labels. Labeling kube-system enforce:privileged works but violates the stated no-labels requirement, disabling the plugin removes protection everywhere, and seccomp annotations do not affect PodSecurity admission.

q: Your kubeadm config file uses apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta2 and the new kubeadm binary refuses it with an unknown-apiVersion error. What is the supported fix?
options: Hand-edit the apiVersion string to v1beta3, since field renames are cosmetic
Run kubeadm init --force with the old file, since force overrides version checks
Keep the old kubeadm binary for init and the new one for upgrades
Run kubeadm config migrate --old-config old.yaml --new-config new.yaml to convert it to the current API version
explain: kubeadm config migrate is the supported converter between ClusterConfiguration API versions. Hand-editing the version string ignores renamed and restructured fields, --force does not perform schema conversion, and mixing kubeadm versions across phases is unsupported.

q: Every engineer with a valid cluster credential should be able to list pods and nodes cluster-wide, but nothing more. Which single binding expresses 'all authenticated users'?
options: A ClusterRoleBinding to system:unauthenticated, which covers everyone with credentials
A RoleBinding in every namespace, which grants cluster-wide read
Adding each engineer to the system:masters group in their kubeconfig
A ClusterRoleBinding of a read-only ClusterRole (e.g. view) to the group system:authenticated
explain: system:authenticated is the built-in group containing every authenticated identity, so one ClusterRoleBinding grants the read-only role to all of them. system:unauthenticated covers only anonymous requests (the opposite), RoleBindings are namespaced and cannot reach cluster-scoped resources like nodes, and system:masters grants full cluster-admin.

q: You enabled encryption at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration. Secrets are encrypted in etcd, but an audit finds ConfigMaps still stored in plaintext. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Rotate the encryption key -- the old key only covered Secrets
Only secrets were listed under resources: -- add configmaps to the resources list in the EncryptionConfiguration, then re-write the ConfigMaps so they are stored encrypted
Base64 in etcd means encrypted -- the audit tool misread the encoding
Restarting etcd re-encrypts everything automatically
explain: The provider encrypts only the resource types named under resources:; the stock example lists just secrets, so ConfigMaps stay plaintext until you add them. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; a restart does not rewrite stored objects (you must re-write them to encrypt); and rotation changes keys, not coverage.

q: etcd disk usage is high partly because objects are stored as JSON. Which API server flag switches etcd storage to the more compact binary encoding?
options: --storage-media-type=application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf on kube-apiserver
--storage-backend=protobuf on etcd, which selects its protobuf storage engine
--serialization=protobuf on the kubelet, since kubelets choose the storage encoding
Setting Content-Type: application/protobuf on client requests, since clients control etcd storage
explain: The API server decides how objects are serialized into etcd, and --storage-media-type selects the compact binary form. etcd itself has no such storage-backend flag, kubelets do not control etcd's storage encoding, and per-request content types only affect the wire format.

q: You want etcd to auto-compact keeping only the last hour of revisions, instead of a revision count. Which etcd flags express time-based compaction?
options: A cron job running etcdctl compact hourly, since etcd cannot do time-based compaction natively
--auto-compaction-mode=periodic --auto-compaction-retention=1h on the etcd static pod
--auto-compaction-retention=1000 --compact-every-hour, since retention takes a duration flag
--etcd-compaction-interval=1h on kube-apiserver, since the API server controls compaction retention
explain: etcd natively supports periodic compaction: mode=periodic with a duration retention like 1h. There is no --compact-every-hour flag, the apiserver's --etcd-compaction-interval only controls how often it asks etcd to compact (not the retention window), and a cron job is a clumsy substitute for the built-in mode.

q: You set failSwapOn: false in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, but the kubelet STILL exits with 'running with swap on is not supported'. What is the most likely cause?
options: The node needs a kubeadm rejoin: config changes need rejoin
YAML booleans need quotes: false must be 'false'
The kubelet systemd unit (or drop-in) passes --fail-swap-on=true: command-line flags override the config file
failSwapOn is not a real field: the config is ignored
explain: Kubelet command-line flags beat the config file: if the systemd unit or a drop-in sets --fail-swap-on=true, the config file's false loses. failSwapOn is a genuine KubeletConfiguration field, a restart (not a rejoin) applies config changes, and YAML booleans need no quotes.

q: Nodes keep hitting DiskPressure from gigabytes of unused container images, long before logs or volumes fill up. Which kubelet settings make image garbage collection more aggressive?
options: --image-gc-high-threshold and --image-gc-low-threshold (e.g. 70/60) in the kubelet config: GC starts earlier and cleans more
Raising --eviction-hard imagefs.available, since eviction thresholds trigger image GC
--serialize-image-pulls=false, since parallel pulls reduce disk usage
A cron job running crictl rmi --prune, since the kubelet has no image GC
explain: The kubelet's image GC is driven by the high/low thresholds (defaults 85/80); lowering them reclaims unused images sooner. eviction-hard governs pod eviction rather than image GC tuning, serialize-image-pulls governs pull parallelism, and an external prune cron duplicates -- and can race -- the built-in collector.

q: Your 96-core nodes could host far more pods than the 110-IP CNI limit allows, but small 4-core edge nodes should cap pods by core count too. Which single kubelet setting caps pods per CPU core?
options: --kube-reserved=cpu=..., since reserved CPU limits pod count
--pods-per-core (combined with --max-pods: the effective limit is the smaller of the two)
--max-pods=110 on every node, since per-core caps do not exist
A scheduler policy, since the scheduler enforces per-core pod caps
explain: --pods-per-core multiplies cores by the value and the kubelet enforces the smaller of that and --max-pods, giving big nodes a higher cap and small nodes a lower one automatically. --max-pods alone is flat, the scheduler does not enforce kubelet caps, and kube-reserved only shrinks allocatable CPU.

q: You migrate from stacked to external etcd. The API server still dials the old local endpoint and the cluster cannot write. Which API server flag must now point at the external members?
options: --etcd-servers=https://etcd-1:2379,https://etcd-2:2379,https://etcd-3:2379 on kube-apiserver (plus --etcd-cafile/--etcd-certfile/--etcd-keyfile)
--advertise-client-urls on the etcd members, since members advertise the new endpoints automatically
--etcd-servers on the kubelet, since kubelets proxy etcd traffic
Updating /etc/hosts on the control-plane node, since name resolution is the only change needed
explain: kube-apiserver learns etcd's location solely from --etcd-servers (with the etcd TLS flags); after a migration this must be updated or writes still go to the old member. Member-side advertise URLs do not reconfigure clients, kubelets never contact etcd, and name resolution cannot change a configured endpoint list.

q: Only the apiserver certificate expired (the rest are fine). You want to regenerate just that one certificate without touching the others. Which command does this?
options: Deleting /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt, since the kubelet recreates missing certs
kubeadm certs renew all, since it is the only renewal command
Editing the expired PEM dates with openssl, since certificate fields are editable
kubeadm init phase certs apiserver --config kubeadm.yaml, then restart the API server static pod
explain: kubeadm init phase certs <component> regenerates an individual control-plane certificate from the existing CA. Deleting the file leaves nothing to recreate it, renew-all is the blunt instrument rather than the targeted one, and signed certificate fields cannot be hand-edited without invalidating the signature.

q: Your team wants kubectl apply -k to deploy a shared base straight from Git, with no local clone. Which invocation is valid?
options: Only Helm can install from a Git URL: kustomize needs local files
kubectl apply -k https://github.com/org/repo//k8s/base?ref=v1.2.0, since kustomize supports remote bases over HTTPS
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/org/repo//k8s/base, since -f processes kustomization.yaml remotely
kustomize edit remote add, since remotes must be vendored first
explain: kustomize (and kubectl -k) fetches remote bases over HTTPS, with // separating repo from path and ?ref= pinning the version. kubectl -f never runs a kustomize build, there is no vendoring requirement, and Helm is not involved.

q: kustomize build prints: 'patchesStrategicMerge is deprecated'. What is the current replacement?
options: Keep patchesStrategicMerge, since deprecation warnings never become removals
patchesJson6902 only, since strategic merge is gone entirely
Switch to Helm post-renderers, since kustomize patching is removed
The consolidated patches: field, which accepts strategic-merge, JSON 6902, and inline patches in one list
explain: Kustomize merged patchesStrategicMerge and patchesJson6902 into a single patches: list covering all patch styles. Staying on the deprecated field risks a future break, JSON-6902-only is unnecessarily limiting, and patching was consolidated rather than removed.

q: Each environment's kustomize overlay must prefix every resource name (dev-web, prod-web) without editing the base. Which kustomization field does this?
options: namespace: dev, since the namespace field prefixes names
vars:, since vars rewrite resource names
namePrefix: dev- (or nameSuffix): it prepends (or appends) to all resource names in the build
commonLabels, since labels rename resources
explain: namePrefix/nameSuffix are the kustomize-native way to prefix or suffix every built resource name per overlay. commonLabels only adds labels, the namespace field only sets .metadata.namespace, and vars do value substitution rather than renaming.

q: Kubelet client CSRs (signer kubernetes.io/kube-client) get auto-approved, but kubelet serving-certificate CSRs sit in Pending. Which built-in ClusterRole governs the auto-approved client CSRs, and what follows for serving certs?
options: system:node: nodes approve their own CSRs
system:certificates.k8s.io:certificates-selfnode-server: it auto-approves both client and serving CSRs
system:certificates.k8s.io:certificates-selfnode-client: the CSR approver controller auto-approves node client CSRs bound to it, while serving certs need manual approval or a custom approver
cluster-admin: the approver impersonates cluster-admin to sign CSRs
explain: The built-in kubelet CSR approver auto-approves client CSRs via the certificates-selfnode-client ClusterRole; serving-certificate CSRs are deliberately left for manual approval (or your own approver) because they assert DNS/IP SANs. cluster-admin is not involved, system:node is the requester identity rather than the approver role, and there is no default auto-approve binding for serving certs.

q: You drop a static pod manifest for a node agent into /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, but no pod -- not even a mirror pod -- ever appears in kubectl. Where do you look first?
options: kubectl describe pod <name>, since the API records the parse error
systemctl status kube-apiserver, since the API server watches the manifest directory
journalctl -u kubelet on that node: the kubelet parses the manifest directory, and if it never accepted the file only kubelet logs say why
kubectl get pods -A, since the mirror pod must exist somewhere
explain: Static pods are a kubelet-only mechanism: the kubelet reads the manifest directory and creates mirror pods via the API. If no mirror pod exists, the kubelet rejected the file (bad YAML, invalid spec) and only its logs record why. kubectl cannot show what the API never received, and the API server does not watch that directory.

q: The --certificate-key from this morning's kubeadm init phase upload-certs has expired (2h TTL), and the second control-plane node still is not joined. How do you get a fresh key without re-running full init?
options: Reuse the expired key with --ignore-preflight-errors, since expiry is only a warning
Copy /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.crt to the new node by hand, since certs are all it needs
Re-run kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs on the first control-plane node, then join with the new key
Run kubeadm init again, since upload-certs only runs during init
explain: upload-certs is a re-runnable phase that encrypts the control-plane certs with a fresh key and stores it in the cluster. Re-running full init would rebuild (destroy) the cluster, an expired key cannot decrypt anything regardless of preflight flags, and hand-copying PKI files skips the kubeconfigs and key handling the phase performs.

q: A pod's app container sets requests equal to limits for CPU and memory, but its init container sets no resources at all. What QoS class does the pod get?
options: Guaranteed: only app containers count toward QoS
BestEffort: any missing resource block zeroes the class
Guaranteed once the init container finishes: QoS is re-evaluated at runtime
Burstable: the Guaranteed criteria (every container with requests==limits for CPU and memory) apply to init containers and app containers equally
explain: Kubernetes applies the Guaranteed rule to init and app containers equally, so the resourceless init container drops the pod to Burstable. It is not BestEffort (the app container has resources), and QoS is assigned once at creation -- it is never re-evaluated when init finishes.

q: An indexed Job (completions: 10) has successPolicy.rules: [{succeededIndexes: '0', succeededCount: 1}]. Index 0 succeeds while indexes 1-9 are still running. What happens?
options: Only index 0's pod is deleted: the rest run to completion
The Job is marked SuccessCriteriaMet/Complete and the controller terminates the lingering pods: successPolicy short-circuits the completions count
Nothing until all 10 indexes succeed: successPolicy is advisory
The Job fails: indexes 1-9 never completed
explain: successPolicy (indexed Jobs only) declares the Job succeeded as soon as any rule matches -- here, index 0 succeeding -- and the job controller then terminates remaining pods. It is authoritative rather than advisory, the Job does not fail, and lingering pods are cleaned up rather than left running.

q: An HPA has two scaleUp policies: {type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 60} and {type: Pods, value: 4, periodSeconds: 60}. Both allow an increase. From 3 replicas, how many replicas does the HPA add?
options: 4: with multiple scaleUp policies the HPA applies the one permitting the largest change
3 (100%): percent policies take precedence
7: the policies are additive
Whichever is listed first: order decides
explain: HPA behavior policies are alternatives: each computes an allowed change and the controller picks the largest for scale-up. Percent allows +3, Pods allows +4, so +4 wins. They are never summed, list order is irrelevant, and percent has no precedence.

q: A pod's nodeAffinity has two nodeSelectorTerms: [{disktype In [ssd]}, {disktype In [nvme]}]. A teammate says the pod needs a node that is both ssd AND nvme. Is that right?
options: Only the first term is evaluated
No: nodeSelectorTerms are ORed, so the pod may land on an ssd node or an nvme node (expressions within one term are ANDed)
Yes: all terms must match
The manifest is invalid: duplicate keys across terms are rejected
explain: Node affinity semantics: matchExpressions inside a single term are ANDed, but separate nodeSelectorTerms are ORed. The pod accepts ssd-only or nvme-only nodes -- no node needs both labels -- the manifest is valid, and every term is considered.

q: A Deployment sets topologySpreadConstraints (maxSkew: 1, zone key) plus nodeAffinity requiring disktype=ssd, on nodes where some ssd nodes also carry a NoSchedule taint the pod tolerates. By default, which nodes count toward the skew calculation?
options: Only untainted ssd nodes: both policies default to Honor
Taints are always excluded from skew math
Only nodes matching the nodeAffinity (nodeAffinityPolicy defaults to Honor), but tainted nodes are still counted (nodeTaintsPolicy defaults to Ignore)
All nodes: both policies default to Ignore
explain: The two inclusion policies have asymmetric defaults: nodeAffinityPolicy null behaves as Honor (only affinity-matching nodes count), while nodeTaintsPolicy null behaves as Ignore (taints do not remove nodes from the math). So the skew counts ssd nodes including tainted-but-tolerated ones.

q: You canary with a track: canary label on new pods and want them spread across zones counting ONLY canary pods (stable pods must not affect the math). Which constraint field scopes the counting to the canary label key?
options: matchLabelKeys: [track]: its key-value pairs merge into the counting selector so skew is computed per label value
labelSelector matching app: web: it counts the canary pods
A second topologyKey per track: topology keys split pod groups
podAffinity with the canary label: affinity does skew math
explain: matchLabelKeys merges the pod's own label values (e.g. track: canary) into the counting selector, so each cohort spreads independently. A broad labelSelector would lump stable pods into the count, topologyKey operates on node labels rather than pod groups, and affinity co-locates instead of spreading.

q: A 2-zone cluster runs a Deployment with topologySpreadConstraints {maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: zone, minDomains: 3, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule}. What happens?
options: The scheduler creates a third zone: minDomains provisions domains
Pods stay Pending: minDomains: 3 requires at least 3 eligible domains, but only 2 exist
Pods spread 2-and-1 across the zones: minDomains is a preference
minDomains is ignored without nodeAffinityPolicy
explain: minDomains sets the minimum number of eligible topology domains; with DoNotSchedule and only 2 zones present, the constraint cannot be satisfied and pods pend. It is a hard minimum rather than a preference, it is independent of nodeAffinityPolicy, and the scheduler never provisions topology.

q: Applying a container with requests {cpu: 100m} and limits {cpu: 500m} fails with 'maximum limit/request ratio violated'. No LimitRange max is breached. Which LimitRange field is responsible?
options: max.cpu: the container exceeds the max
ResourceQuota: quotas reject ratio violations
The scheduler: it enforces ratio policy
maxLimitRequestRatio: it caps the limit-to-request ratio per container (here 5 exceeds the allowed ratio)
explain: LimitRange's maxLimitRequestRatio enforces per-container limit/request ceilings at admission; a 5x ratio trips it even when max.cpu is fine. Quotas aggregate usage rather than ratios, the scheduler does no admission validation, and max was not the cited breach.

q: You must confine the app container to a custom AppArmor profile (localhost/k8s-deny-write) on nodes that load it. Where is this declared?
options: securityContext.capabilities, since capabilities select AppArmor profiles
A privileged securityContext, since profiles require privilege
As the pod annotation container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>: localhost/k8s-deny-write
securityContext.seccompProfile, since seccomp and AppArmor are the same mechanism
explain: AppArmor profiles are selected per container via the container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<name> annotation (runtime/default or localhost/<profile>). seccompProfile configures a different LSM, capabilities grant privileges rather than selecting profiles, and privileged mode bypasses confinement instead of applying it.

q: You want to raise a live Deployment's memory requests from 256Mi to 512Mi and have it roll out like any other template change. Which imperative command does this?
options: kubectl top deployment/web --set requests: top applies resource changes
kubectl set resources deployment/web -c app --requests=memory=512Mi: it patches the template and triggers a rolling update
kubectl scale deployment/web --requests=memory=512Mi: scale adjusts resources
kubectl edit is always required: resources cannot change imperatively
explain: kubectl set resources patches the pod template's resource fields, which -- like any template change -- triggers a rolling update. scale touches only replicas, imperative resource changes are supported without editing YAML, and top is read-only metrics.

q: A pod uses image: myapp (no tag). After a registry rebuild, restarted pods unexpectedly run the NEW build. The manifest never changed. Why?
options: No tag means :latest, and the default imagePullPolicy for :latest is Always: every container start re-pulls
The kubelet caches by digest: restarts always pull
A mutating webhook rewrote the tag: webhooks retag images
imagePullSecrets force re-pull: credentials refresh the cache
explain: An untagged image is :latest, and Kubernetes defaults :latest to imagePullPolicy: Always, so each container start pulls whatever the registry currently serves under that tag. The kubelet does not cache by digest, no webhook is implicated, and pull secrets only authenticate.

q: A container has a preStop hook (sleep 20) and terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60. In what order do preStop and SIGTERM run?
options: SIGTERM first, then preStop: the hook runs during the grace period
They run in parallel: total shutdown is max(20, 60)
preStop replaces SIGTERM: the app never gets the signal
preStop runs first and blocks; SIGTERM is sent only after it completes
explain: The kubelet invokes the preStop handler and waits for it before sending SIGTERM, then the grace period applies -- so the hook extends the shutdown timeline rather than overlapping it. SIGTERM does not come first, they are not parallel, and the hook supplements rather than replaces the signal.

q: An app needs its own pod IP in an env var for gossip clustering. Which downward API entry provides it?
options: An init container writing /etc/hosts, since the downward API cannot expose IPs
valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath: status.podIP
fieldPath: status.hostIP, since it is the pod's IP
fieldPath: metadata.name, since names resolve to IPs automatically
explain: status.podIP is the downward API field for the pod's own IP. status.hostIP is the node's address, metadata.name is just the name, and no init container is needed since the field exists.

q: A Deployment uses envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: feature-flags}}] but the feature-flags ConfigMap does not exist in some clusters. New pods block in CreateContainerConfigError. How do you let them start without the flags?
options: configMapRef.optional: true: the whole reference becomes optional and the pods start with no injected vars
envFrom is always optional: the block is a bug
Add each key with optional: true: envFrom needs per-key flags
Use valueFrom instead: envFrom cannot be optional
explain: envFrom with a configMapRef or secretRef blocks pod startup when the object is missing -- unless you set optional: true on the ref, which lets the pod start with nothing injected. envFrom is not optional by default, there are no per-key flags under envFrom, and valueFrom is the per-key alternative rather than the fix.

q: A container needs 45s to flush buffers on SIGTERM, but the pod-wide grace period is short and shared. On a recent cluster, which per-probe field gives this container its own termination grace window?
options: terminationGracePeriodSeconds inside the probe spec: the probe-level grace overrides the pod's for that container's termination
Raising the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds only: probes cannot have their own
periodSeconds: 60 on the probe: probe timing extends shutdown
Disabling the liveness probe: it is the only way
explain: Probe-level terminationGracePeriodSeconds lets a slow-shutdown container get a longer kill window without changing the pod-wide grace for everything else. Pod-level grace is coarser, periodSeconds only spaces probe executions, and dropping the probe sacrifices health checking.

q: You need a pod spec that lands you in an interactive shell (stdin open, TTY allocated) for a debugging base image. Which container fields do this?
options: kubectl exec -it only: interactivity cannot be declared in the spec
privileged: true: privilege allocates the TTY
command: [/bin/sh]: a shell implies stdin/TTY
stdin: true and tty: true on the container: the spec-level equivalents of -i -t
explain: stdin and tty are first-class container fields that request an open stdin and a TTY from the runtime -- what -i -t do at exec time. exec flags cannot pre-declare it, privileged is about host access rather than terminals, and merely running a shell attaches neither input nor a terminal.

q: A Job is halfway through a 2-hour run and you must pause it NOW without losing it, then resume later. Which field does this, and what happens to running pods?
options: Set parallelism: 0: it is the documented pause mechanism
Delete the Job: completed work is remembered
Set spec.suspend: true (it is mutable): the controller deletes active pods; unsetting it later recreates them
kubectl scale job/myjob --replicas=0: jobs scale like deployments
explain: suspend is the mutable pause switch: true stops the controller from creating pods and deletes active ones; flipping it back resumes. Jobs have no replicas field, parallelism: 0 is not the pause mechanism, and deleting the Job destroys its state.

q: A RuntimeClass sets overhead.podFixed: {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi} (sandbox cost). A pod requests cpu: 1. How much CPU does the scheduler reserve for the pod?
options: 1 CPU: overhead is runtime-only and invisible to scheduling
500m: overhead replaces the request
1 CPU plus converted memory: memory overhead becomes CPU
1.5 CPUs: the scheduler adds pod overhead to the container requests when checking node capacity
explain: Pod overhead accounts for the sandbox's own consumption: the scheduler sums container requests plus overhead for admission. It does not replace requests, it is not invisible to scheduling, and memory overhead never converts into CPU.

q: An indexed Job runs backoffLimitPerIndex: 2 with maxFailedIndexes: 3. Index 5 fails twice and index 7 fails once. What happens?
options: The Job keeps running: only the global backoffLimit can fail it
All indexes reset: one index failing resets the others' budgets
The Job fails: 3 failed indexes hit maxFailedIndexes (index 5 alone exhausted its per-index budget but that alone would not fail the Job)
Index 5 is retried a third time: backoffLimitPerIndex is advisory
explain: backoffLimitPerIndex caps retries per index while maxFailedIndexes caps how many distinct indexes may fail before the whole Job is marked Failed -- here 3 failed indexes trip it. Per-index limits are enforced (index 5 stops retrying), maxFailedIndexes is a real failure condition, and budgets are per-index and independent.

q: A script deletes a stuck pod and must block until the object is GONE from the API (or fail after 60s) before continuing. Which command does this?
options: kubectl get pod -w and grep: watch is the blocking primitive
kubectl logs -f: logs block until the object disappears
kubectl wait --for=delete --timeout=60s pod/stuck-pod
kubectl delete --wait=false: it blocks until deletion
explain: --for=delete inverts kubectl wait's logic: it returns when the object disappears, with the timeout as the backstop. --wait=false does the opposite (returns at once), watch-plus-grep is the fragile manual version, and log streaming never signals API deletion.

q: A LoadBalancer Service uses externalTrafficPolicy: Local. The cloud LB needs a health check, but the Service's nodePort carries traffic. Which port does the cloud LB actually probe?
options: 6443: the API server reports service health
The auto-allocated spec.healthCheckNodePort: kube-proxy serves a health endpoint on it reflecting local-endpoint health
The Service's nodePort: health checks reuse the traffic port
targetPort: the LB probes pods directly
explain: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, Kubernetes allocates a second node port (healthCheckNodePort) where kube-proxy answers health checks based on whether local endpoints exist. The traffic nodePort serves the app, cloud LBs cannot address pods directly, and the API server plays no role in LB health checks.

q: You set spec.loadBalancerIP: 203.0.113.10 on a Service, but the cloud controller ignores it and assigns its own IP. Why?
options: The cloud provider lacks the IP: any routable IP works
spec.loadBalancerIP is deprecated and ignored by most implementations: IP selection moved to the LB implementation/IPAM
The IP must be in the pod CIDR: 203.0.113.10 is invalid
You need type: NodePort too: LB IPs require a nodePort
explain: loadBalancerIP was deprecated because implementations manage their own IPAM; setting it is a no-op on most clouds. The IP's range is not the problem, NodePort is unrelated, and no cloud honors the field anymore.

q: Two Ingress rules share host shop.example.com and path /api: one Exact pointing at api-v2, one Prefix pointing at api-v1. A client requests exactly https://shop.example.com/api. Which Service answers?
options: api-v1: Prefix rules outrank Exact
Round-robin between them: identical paths load-balance
The Ingress is rejected: duplicate paths are invalid
api-v2: the Exact rule wins over the Prefix rule for the identical path
explain: ingress-nginx renders Exact as an nginx exact (=) location, tested before prefix locations, so api-v2 serves the request. Prefix does not outrank Exact, rules never load-balance against each other, and the combination is valid.

q: Your Ingress TLS secret holds a wildcard cert for *.example.com, but https://example.com (the bare domain) throws a name-mismatch warning. Why?
options: Wildcards cover the apex: the secret must be corrupt
Ingress requires one cert per host: wildcards are unsupported
TLS passthrough would fix it: termination breaks wildcards
A wildcard *.example.com does not cover the bare apex example.com: the cert needs a SAN for both
explain: Per certificate name-matching rules, *.example.com matches one-level subdomains but never the bare domain -- you need example.com as an additional SAN. The secret is not corrupt, wildcards work fine for subdomains, and passthrough versus termination does not affect name validation.

q: You set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: 'true' on an Ingress, but traffic is still terminated at the controller. What is missing?
options: The controller needs --enable-ssl-passthrough at startup: the annotation is honored only when the feature is enabled on the controller
A backendProtocol: HTTPS annotation: passthrough needs it
The TLS secret must be removed: passthrough cannot reference a secret
ssl-passthrough only works with pathType: Exact: change the paths
explain: ssl-passthrough is opt-in on the ingress-nginx controller via --enable-ssl-passthrough; without it the annotation is silently ignored and TLS terminates normally. backendProtocol governs controller-to-pod re-encryption, the secret reference does not block passthrough, and pathType is irrelevant.

q: You apply a NetworkPolicy with an ingress rule allowing only the frontend, but set policyTypes: [Egress]. Afterwards anyone can still reach the API pods. Why did the ingress rule not isolate them?
options: The policy is invalid: rules and policyTypes must match
Ingress rules need a port: without ports nothing is enforced
The CNI ignores ingress rules: only egress is implemented
policyTypes: [Egress] selects only egress isolation: the ingress rule is stored but never enforced because ingress was not selected
explain: policyTypes chooses which directions a policy isolates; an ingress rule under policyTypes: [Egress] is accepted but never enforced. The manifest is valid (hence the silent footgun), ports are optional in ingress rules, and CNIs enforce both directions.

q: An HTTPRoute shows Accepted: True but Programmed: False in status, and traffic 404s. Where is the problem?
options: The Gateway API implementation has not programmed the route: check the implementation's controller and logs, not the route spec (the spec was accepted)
The route spec is invalid: Accepted would be False otherwise
The Gateway listeners are misconfigured: re-create the Gateway
The backend Service is down: backends affect Programmed
explain: Accepted means the route bound to a Gateway successfully; Programmed: False means the dataplane implementation has not translated it into config -- an implementation-side issue. The spec is not invalid (Accepted says so), the Gateway binding worked, and backend health surfaces under ResolvedRefs/backend conditions rather than Programmed.

q: An HTTPRoute must ensure backends receive exactly one X-Tenant header with the new value, even if the client sent one. Which RequestHeaderModifier action does this, and why not the other?
options: Either: they are aliases
set: it overwrites any existing values, while add would append a second X-Tenant alongside the client's
add: add replaces existing headers
remove then add in two filters: set cannot touch client headers
explain: RequestHeaderModifier's set overwrites all existing values of the header while add appends another value -- so a client-supplied X-Tenant would duplicate under add. set operates on client-supplied headers directly, and the two actions are not aliases.

q: On a single-stack IPv4 cluster you create a Service with ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack. What happens?
options: The Service never gets cluster IPs: RequireDualStack demands both families and the cluster cannot provide IPv6
It works with IPv4 only: RequireDualStack falls back gracefully
The API rejects it: single-stack clusters cannot store the field
It gets an IPv6 IP via NAT64: the cluster synthesizes one
explain: RequireDualStack is a hard requirement: the Service stays without cluster IPs until both families are allocatable. PreferDualStack is the graceful fallback, the API accepts the field, and Kubernetes never invents addresses.

q: You delete a Service with auto-assigned nodePort 31080 and immediately recreate it. It gets 31080 again. Is the port reserved for the old Service?
options: The API server caches allocations for an hour: wait before recreating
Only manually specified nodePorts are released: auto-assigned ones linger
No: deletion releases the nodePort to the pool; reassignment of the same port is coincidence, not reservation
Yes: nodePorts are pinned to the Service name forever
explain: nodePort allocation is a lease held by the Service object; deleting the Service frees the port immediately and the allocator may hand the same one out again. There is no name pinning, no release delay, and no difference between auto and manual ports on deletion.

q: Pods resolve in-cluster names fine but external names fail. The CoreDNS Corefile starts with .:53 { errors health ready kubernetes ... forward . /etc/resolv.conf }. Where do external queries go, and what is the likely break?
options: They are forwarded to the node's /etc/resolv.conf upstreams: check the node's DNS path, not the kubernetes plugin
They are answered by the kubernetes plugin: CoreDNS is misconfigured
They are dropped by the loop plugin: remove loop
External queries need a stub domain: add one
explain: The forward . /etc/resolv.conf line sends every non-cluster query to the node's resolvers, so external failures point at the node DNS path rather than the kubernetes plugin. The plugin only covers cluster.local, the loop plugin detects forwarding cycles (a different symptom), and no stub domain is needed for the default route.

q: Your team needs Service DNS changes to propagate within 5 seconds instead of the default 30. Where do you tune this?
options: The Service's sessionAffinity: affinity controls DNS TTL
kube-proxy --dns-ttl: kube-proxy serves DNS
ndots: 1 on every pod: ndots shortens cache TTL
The CoreDNS Corefile cache plugin (cache 30 becomes cache 5): it sets the maximum TTL CoreDNS caches
explain: CoreDNS's cache plugin caps how long answers are cached (default 30s); lowering it shortens stale-record windows at the cost of more upstream queries. sessionAffinity is about connections, kube-proxy never serves DNS, and ndots only controls the search-domain walk.

q: CoreDNS pods are Running but you want a direct health signal beyond pod phase. Which endpoint does the ready plugin expose, and what uses it?
options: :8181/ready: the ready plugin answers it once all plugins are ready, and the Deployment's readinessProbe hits it
:53/ready: DNS serves health on the query port
:9153/metrics: metrics double as readiness
kubectl get pods is enough: phases are the health signal
explain: CoreDNS's ready plugin serves HTTP /ready on :8181 after every plugin signals ready, and the stock manifests wire the readinessProbe to it. DNS port 53 does not serve health, metrics do not gate readiness, and the Running phase alone does not prove the plugin chain is up.

q: A Service omits internalTrafficPolicy. Traffic from a node hits endpoints on OTHER nodes even when local endpoints exist. Is this a bug?
options: topologyKeys is required: the field was removed
No: the default is Cluster, which load-balances across all endpoints; Local is the opt-in that prefers node-local endpoints
Yes: kube-proxy always prefers local endpoints
The endpoints are misordered: order controls preference
explain: internalTrafficPolicy defaults to Cluster: every node load-balances across all endpoints. Local is the explicit opt-in for node-local preference (with its drop-if-no-local-endpoint semantics). Endpoint order does not matter, and topologyKeys is a separate retired mechanism.

q: On bare metal you set spec.externalIPs: [203.0.113.50] on a Service and it is reachable there -- but your security review flags it. What is the concern?
options: They bypass NetworkPolicy: external IPs skip policy
They require privileged pods: the Service is insecure
externalIPs are not validated: anyone who can create Services can claim arbitrary IPs, enabling traffic interception
The cloud provider assigns them: on-prem they conflict
explain: Kubernetes does not verify you own an externalIP -- kube-proxy will serve traffic for any IP you claim, so RBAC over Services is the only guardrail. There is no cloud allocator on bare metal, NetworkPolicy still applies to the backends, and no privileges are involved.

q: An Ingress rule has host: '' (empty) with a default backend. Which requests does it match?
options: Only the default backend's Service name: host defaults to the Service
All hosts: an empty or omitted host is a wildcard catch-all
None: an empty host is invalid and the rule is ignored
Only requests with no Host header: empty matches empty
explain: In Ingress, an unspecified or empty rule host matches all hosts -- that is how catch-all routing is expressed. It is not invalid, it does not mean an empty Host header, and it has nothing to do with Service names.

q: Compliance demands pods use ONLY the corporate DNS (10.0.0.53): no cluster DNS at all, not even as fallback. Which pod DNS setup does this?
options: dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst plus dnsConfig nameserver 10.0.0.53: the corporate server handles everything
dnsPolicy: Default: it uses only the corporate DNS
hostAliases for every name: it replaces DNS entirely
dnsPolicy: None with a dnsConfig listing the corporate nameserver: None disables all default DNS so only your config applies
explain: dnsPolicy: None strips all default DNS behavior so the pod's resolv.conf comes solely from your dnsConfig -- the only way to guarantee no cluster-DNS fallback. ClusterFirst keeps kube-dns in the path, Default inherits the node's resolvers rather than enforcing yours, and hostAliases only injects static /etc/hosts entries.
