q: With ingress-nginx you want canary traffic sticky by cookie (canary_always) so the same client consistently hits v2. Which annotations do this?
options: canary-weight: '100': weight gives stickiness
rewrite-target: rewrites make routing sticky
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: 'true' plus nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-cookie: canary_always: cookie presence routes to the canary backend
sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service: it pins canary clients
explain: ingress-nginx's canary-by-cookie routes requests carrying the named cookie to the canary Ingress, giving sticky canary sessions. Service sessionAffinity is not canary-aware, weight-based splitting is probabilistic per request rather than sticky, and rewrites only transform paths.

q: A Gateway API HTTPRoute needs a 120s cap on the TOTAL request duration (including retries) for one route, while backend attempts keep a 30s cap. Which timeout fields express this?
options: Only request: 30s: one field does both
Timeouts cannot be per-route: they are Gateway-wide
timeouts.request: 120s (whole-request cap) with timeouts.backendRequest: 30s (per-attempt cap)
Only backendRequest: 120s: it covers retries too
explain: Gateway API splits timeouts: request bounds the entire request including retries, backendRequest bounds each backend attempt. Setting only backendRequest leaves total duration uncapped across retries, request: 30s would kill the slow endpoint outright, and timeouts are attachable per route.

q: A Gateway has web and admin listeners. An HTTPRoute sets parentRefs: [{name: my-gw}] with NO sectionName. Which listeners does it attach to?
options: Only the first listener: order decides
Only port 80: it defaults to HTTP
All listeners whose protocol/hostname it is compatible with: omitting sectionName targets every listener on the Gateway
None: sectionName is required
explain: Without sectionName, a route attaches to every listener on the referenced Gateway that it can bind to (matching protocol/hostname rules) -- that is why sectionName exists for narrowing. It is not required, order does not matter, and there is no implicit port default.

q: A StorageClass uses the default volumeBindingMode and provisions zonal EBS volumes. Pods sometimes schedule in zone b while their volume was provisioned in zone a, then fail to attach. What is the structural fix?
options: Add nodeAffinity to the pod: affinity moves the volume
Use a bigger volume: size affects zone placement
Set volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer: binding waits for scheduling so provisioning happens in the pod's zone
Set volumeBindingMode: Immediate explicitly: it zone-aligns volumes
explain: Immediate (the default) provisions the volume before the scheduler places the pod, so zonal backends may pick a different zone than the pod lands in. WaitForFirstConsumer defers provisioning until after scheduling, letting the provisioner use the chosen node's zone. Re-setting Immediate changes nothing, pod affinity cannot relocate a provisioned disk, and size does not influence zones.

q: You hand-create a static PV for an existing disk and set reclaimPolicy: Retain on the StorageClass, expecting it to apply. The PV still shows Delete. Why?
options: reclaimPolicy on a StorageClass only affects dynamically provisioned volumes: a static PV uses its own spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy (default Delete)
Static PVs cannot use Retain: only dynamic volumes can
The StorageClass must be the default: non-default classes are ignored
ReclaimPolicy is immutable: recreate the disk
explain: A StorageClass's reclaimPolicy is a provisioning-time template for dynamic volumes; hand-created PVs carry their own spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy (defaulting to Delete). Set or patch it on the PV directly. Static PVs fully support Retain, class default-ness does not matter, and the PV field is mutable.

q: You set immutable: true on a Secret, then try to rotate its password with kubectl apply. The API rejects it. What is the rule?
options: immutable only applies to ConfigMaps: Secrets ignore the field
kubectl apply works but pods need a restart: the rejection is a client bug
Only data: is frozen: stringData: stays editable
Immutable Secrets (and ConfigMaps) cannot be updated: delete and recreate the object to change values
explain: immutable: true makes the entire Secret/ConfigMap object unchangeable -- updates are rejected at the API, which also lets kubelets cache them aggressively. It applies to Secrets too, the rejection is server-side, and stringData is just a write convenience over data.

q: You are building a StorageClass for local persistent volumes. Which provisioner and binding mode make local provisioning work?
options: provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer: the local static provisioner creates PVs and binding must wait for scheduling
provisioner: kubernetes.io/local with Immediate: local has its own provisioner
Any CSI provisioner with Immediate: binding mode does not matter for local
No StorageClass needed: local PVs bind without one
explain: Local volumes have no dynamic provisioner -- the convention is provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner (PVs come from the local static provisioner or by hand) with WaitForFirstConsumer so the scheduler places the pod first and the PV's nodeAffinity can be honored. There is no kubernetes.io/local provisioner, Immediate defeats node matching, and the class is part of the documented pattern.

q: A pod uses a generic ephemeral volume, but its auto-created PVC lands on the cluster default StorageClass. The team wants these ephemeral claims on fast-ssd. Where do you set it?
options: You cannot: ephemeral volumes always use the default class
Annotate the namespace: defaults are per-namespace
In the ephemeral volume's volumeClaimTemplate.spec.storageClassName: generic ephemeral volumes accept a full PVC spec
On the pod's storageClassName: pods take a storage class
explain: Generic ephemeral volumes embed a volumeClaimTemplate with a complete PVC spec, including storageClassName -- so you can direct them at any class. Pods have no storageClassName field, the default is not mandatory, and default classes are cluster-scoped.

q: A topology-aware app wants to know which NODE it is running on to prefer same-node caches. Which downward API field exposes the node name to the container?
options: fieldPath: status.hostIP: it is the node name
fieldPath: metadata.name: pods share the node's name
The node name is not exposable: use a DaemonSet
valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath: spec.nodeName
explain: spec.nodeName is a first-class downward API field exposing the node the pod is scheduled on. status.hostIP is the node's IP address, metadata.name is the pod's own name, and no DaemonSet is needed.

q: You restore a 50Gi VolumeSnapshot into a new PVC requesting 20Gi. The manifest applies but the restore never completes. What is the rule?
options: Restores need dataSourceRef: dataSource cannot restore
A restore cannot shrink: the new PVC must request at least the snapshot's size (restoring larger is allowed)
Snapshots restore to exact size only: larger is rejected too
The storage class must match: size is irrelevant
explain: Volume restores can grow but never shrink: the target PVC must request at least the snapshot's source size, since the restore cannot compact the data. Larger restores are fine, the class is independent, and both dataSource and dataSourceRef support snapshot sources.

q: PVCs using your CSI driver's StorageClass stay Pending with no provisioner events. Node plugin pods are healthy. Which object tells you whether the driver actually registered on each node?
options: kubectl get pods -n kube-system: driver pods prove registration
kubectl describe storageclass: it shows node registration
crictl ps on the node: the runtime lists CSI drivers
kubectl get csinode: CSINode objects list the drivers each kubelet reports as installed
explain: CSINode objects are the kubelet's report of installed CSI drivers per node -- if your driver is missing there, registration (not provisioning) is the break. Running pods do not prove registration, StorageClass describe shows config, and the container runtime does not track CSI.

q: A security agent runs as a DaemonSet and must observe new host filesystem mounts (USB drives appearing under /mnt) from inside its container, but its own mounts must never leak to the host. Which mountPropagation mode fits?
options: Mounting / as hostPath: propagation modes do not matter
HostToContainer: the container sees host-side mounts while its own mounts stay private
Bidirectional: it only propagates host to container
None: the container still sees new host mounts
explain: HostToContainer is the one-way mode: mounts created on the host after container start become visible inside, while container-created mounts never leak out. Bidirectional would leak container mounts to the host, None shows only mounts that existed at container start, and a bare hostPath mount without propagation misses later host mounts.

q: A ConfigMap volume's files must all be mode 0400 (compliance), and you do not want to list 40 items: entries. Where do you set the blanket mode?
options: securityContext.runAsUser: the user implies the mode
An init container chmod: there is no volume-level option
defaultMode: 256 (0400) on the configMap volume source: it applies to every file unless an item overrides it
fsGroup: it sets file modes
explain: defaultMode on the volume source sets the permission bits for all files from that source (items[].mode can still override per file). fsGroup controls ownership, runAsUser does not chmod, and no init container is needed.

q: A pod uses hostPath type: DirectoryOrCreate for /data/cache. On fresh nodes the directory appears but the app gets permission denied writing to it. Why?
options: DirectoryOrCreate sets 0777: the app's umask is wrong
hostPath volumes are read-only: use emptyDir
The kubelet cannot create directories: the type is broken
The kubelet creates it as root:root 0755: the app user cannot write, so pre-create it with the right ownership instead
explain: DirectoryOrCreate makes the directory as root with 0755, so a non-root app user cannot write -- pre-creating the path with correct ownership (or running as root) is the fix. It is not 0777, hostPath is not read-only by default, and creation itself succeeds.

q: You create a local PV pointing at /mnt/disks/ssd1 on node-a, but the PV never becomes Available. The directory does not exist on the node. What is wrong?
options: The StorageClass is wrong: local needs a provisioner
nodeAffinity is missing: affinity creates the path
Capacity is unset: zero capacity blocks availability
Local PV paths must already exist: the local volume plugin never creates the backing directory
explain: Unlike hostPath DirectoryOrCreate, local persistent volumes require the path to pre-exist -- the plugin will not create it. The provisioner convention and nodeAffinity are separate concerns, and capacity does not affect path validation.

q: A team uses big emptyDir volumes for scratch 'to avoid storage quota'. Under disk pressure their pods get evicted first. What is the flaw in their reasoning?
options: Quotas cover emptyDir: their quota just was not enforced
emptyDir counts against the container's ephemeral-storage: it is not free, not quota-counted, and shares the node's disk with images and logs
emptyDir is actually persistent: it survives pod deletion
emptyDir bypasses the kubelet: no accounting applies
explain: emptyDir is node-local disk accounted as ephemeral-storage: it does not consume the storage quota but it does push pods toward disk-pressure eviction, and it vanishes with the pod. It is not persistent, the kubelet does account it, and quotas do not cover it.

q: You hand-create a PV for an existing CSI volume. You set csi.driver, csi.volumeHandle, and capacity, but pods fail to mount: the driver needs its controller-publish options. What is missing in the PV?
options: nodeAffinity: affinity carries driver options
claimRef: binding supplies the attributes
csi.volumeAttributes: static CSI PVs pass driver-specific options through volumeAttributes
A StorageClass: static PVs do not need attributes
explain: For statically provisioned CSI PVs, csi.volumeAttributes carries the driver-specific volume context (the parameters a dynamic provisioner would inject). The StorageClass does not supply per-volume options, nodeAffinity only constrains placement, and claimRef only pins the binding.

q: A StatefulSet scales up and down daily, but must NEVER lose PVCs when the StatefulSet itself is deleted during a migration. Which retention policy expresses 'delete PVCs on scale-down, keep them on StatefulSet deletion'?
options: The defaults already do this: no policy needed
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy: {whenScaled: Delete, whenDeleted: Retain}
persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy: {whenScaled: Retain, whenDeleted: Delete}: the fields are interchangeable
reclaimPolicy: Retain on the StorageClass: it controls PVC lifetime
explain: The retention policy has two independent axes: whenScaled governs replica scale-down, whenDeleted governs StatefulSet deletion. Mixing Delete/Retain gives weekend-trim plus migration-safety. The fields are not interchangeable, StorageClass reclaimPolicy acts on the PV after the PVC is gone, and the defaults retain on both axes.

q: You need a quick NFS mount in a pod spec without creating PVs/PVCs or installing a provisioner. Which in-tree volume type does this?
options: The nfs volume (server: plus path:) declared directly in the pod spec: in-tree NFS needs no PV
hostPath: it mounts remote filesystems
emptyDir with medium: NFS: the NFS medium
You must use a PV: direct NFS in pods was removed
explain: The in-tree nfs volume type mounts server/path straight into the pod with no PV/PVC involved -- fine for quick or legacy needs. hostPath cannot reach remote servers, emptyDir has no NFS medium, and direct NFS volumes were never removed.

q: A projected ServiceAccount token has expirationSeconds: 3600. The pod runs for 3 hours and keeps working without a restart. How?
options: The API server extends them: expiry is per-request
The pod restarts hourly: rotation needs a restart
The kubelet proactively rotates projected tokens (around 80% of TTL) and updates the volume file: long-lived pods keep working
Tokens do not expire in volumes: expirationSeconds is advisory
explain: Projected service-account tokens are refreshed by the kubelet before expiry (at roughly 80% of TTL) with the new token written into the volume -- that is the point of the projected-volume mechanism. Expiry is real, the API server does not extend tokens, and no restart is needed.

q: A node dies hard. Its CSI volume is stuck Attached to the dead node and the rescheduled pod cannot mount (Multi-Attach). The node will never return. What releases the volume?
options: Delete the Node object: the attach/detach controller treats node deletion as permanent and force-detaches its volumes
Delete the VolumeAttachment: the controller recreates it
kubectl drain the dead node: drain detaches volumes
Wait: attach times out automatically
explain: The attach/detach controller keys off the Node object: deleting it signals the node is gone for good, triggering force-detach of its volumes. Deleting the VolumeAttachment alone gets re-reconciled, drain requires a live kubelet, and no timeout force-detaches automatically.

q: You try to point an existing (empty) PVC at a VolumeSnapshot by adding dataSource, but the API rejects the change. Why?
options: dataSource is set-once at provisioning: it is immutable afterwards, so you must create a new PVC from the snapshot
Snapshots cannot be data sources: only PVC clones work
The storage class forbids it: classes gate data sources
dataSource needs the snapshot's namespace: cross-namespace is the issue
explain: A PVC's dataSource/dataSourceRef is immutable after creation -- it defines how the volume is provisioned, which only happens once. Snapshots are valid sources, no class gates this, and the rejection applies even for same-namespace restores.

q: Your CSI driver needs xfs instead of its default ext4 on dynamic volumes. Setting fstype: xfs as a top-level StorageClass field does nothing. Where does the driver actually read it from?
options: The driver's DaemonSet args: formatting is node-configured
parameters: {csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: xfs}: fstype is a CSI-standard parameter key, not a StorageClass field
spec.fstype on the PVC: PVCs take filesystem types
mountOptions: [xfs]: mount options set the filesystem
explain: There is no top-level fstype field on StorageClass; CSI drivers read the conventional csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype parameter to choose the mkfs filesystem. PVCs have no fstype field, mountOptions apply at mount time (after formatting), and DaemonSet args do not carry per-class formatting choices.

q: A pod with restartPolicy: Never runs a container that exits 1. What state does the pod settle in?
options: Error, with no further restarts: CrashLoopBackOff only happens when the kubelet is allowed to restart the container
CrashLoopBackOff: any repeated failure backs off
Completed: any exit settles as Completed
Pending: the scheduler re-queues failed pods
explain: CrashLoopBackOff is the kubelet repeatedly restarting a failed container with growing delays -- with restartPolicy: Never there are no restarts, so the pod just sits in Error. Completed is reserved for exit 0, and the pod already ran so it is not Pending.

q: After a disk-pressure storm, kubectl get pods -A shows hundreds of Evicted pods that never disappear, cluttering every query. Why are they still there, and what is the cleanup?
options: The kubelet is stuck: restart it to clear them
They will vanish in seconds: eviction auto-deletes
Delete the nodes: pods follow nodes
Evicted pods are terminal API objects the cluster keeps: delete them with kubectl delete pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed
explain: An evicted pod is a finished API object (phase Failed, reason Evicted) that Kubernetes retains for history -- nothing auto-deletes it promptly. It is not a kubelet problem, it does not self-clean in seconds, and node deletion is wildly disproportionate.

q: etcdctl snapshot restore fails with 'sha256 hash mismatch'. You trust the snapshot source (it came from your own backup job). What is the last-resort option?
options: Retry with --skip-hash-check: it bypasses integrity verification when you are certain of the file's provenance
Use --data-dir to skip verification: data-dir implies trust
Restore anyway with --force: force skips all checks
Edit the snapshot's embedded hash: hashes are metadata
explain: --skip-hash-check exists precisely for this last resort: it skips the integrity verification when you trust the file's origin. --data-dir only sets the output directory, there is no --force that skips hash verification, and the hash is derived from content rather than editable metadata.

q: kubectl fails with 'connection refused' but you suspect your kubeconfig, not the cluster. How do you test the API server directly from the control-plane node, bypassing kubectl entirely?
options: systemctl status kube-apiserver: it is a systemd service
etcdctl endpoint health: etcd health proves the API works
ping the VIP: ICMP proves the API port is up
curl -k https://localhost:6443/healthz: it hits the API server's health endpoint without any client config
explain: curl against localhost:6443/healthz exercises the real API server socket and TLS stack with zero client configuration, isolating server health from kubeconfig problems. The API server is not a systemd service, etcd health is a different component, and ping cannot validate the HTTPS endpoint.

q: Two minutes into an incident you need every non-healthy pod across all namespaces on one screen. Which command does this?
options: kubectl logs -A: logs aggregate cluster-wide
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running: a fast triage sweep, then drill into the interesting ones
kubectl describe pods -A: it is the highest-signal first command
kubectl top pods -A: resource usage finds broken pods
explain: Filtering the all-namespaces pod list for non-Running phases is the fastest cluster-wide health sweep; you then describe the offenders. describe-everything is unreadable, top shows metrics rather than states, and kubectl has no cluster-wide log aggregation.

q: You need a throwaway network-debug pod with a shell, right now, that deletes itself when you exit. Which command creates it?
options: kubectl exec into CoreDNS: system pods have debug tools
SSH to a node: pods cannot run shells
kubectl run debug --image=nicolaka/netshoot -it --rm --restart=Never -- sh
kubectl create deployment debug --image=netshoot, then delete it later
explain: kubectl run with -it --rm --restart=Never gives an interactive pod that vanishes on exit -- the standard ephemeral debug pattern. A deployment needs manual cleanup, exec'ing into system pods risks the cluster, and SSH bypasses the API.

q: Pod-to-pod traffic fails between two nodes; each node reaches its own pods fine. CNI configs look right. What node-level check verifies the pod-CIDR routes?
options: iptables-save: NAT rules carry pod routes
cat /etc/resolv.conf: DNS breaks cross-node traffic
kubectl get nodes -o wide: it shows pod routes
ip route on each node: confirm routes for the peer's podCIDR point at the right next hop and interface
explain: Cross-node pod traffic depends on each node knowing a route to the other's podCIDR (via the CNI's routes or the cloud fabric) -- ip route shows exactly that. iptables handles NAT and policy rather than routing, resolv.conf is DNS-only, and node wide output has no route data.

q: The API server is flapping. You want to see WHICH internal health check is failing (etcd, and others) without reading full logs. Which endpoint gives the per-check breakdown?
options: kubectl get componentstatuses: it is the per-check API
kubectl top: load explains flapping
kubectl get --raw '/readyz?verbose' (or /livez?verbose): it lists each health check with ok or fail
kubectl get --raw /healthz: it breaks down checks
explain: /readyz and /livez with ?verbose enumerate every registered check (etcd, poststarthooks, and more) with individual statuses -- the fastest way to spot the failing subsystem. Bare /healthz is one aggregate word, componentstatuses is deprecated, and top shows load rather than checks.

q: You must idempotently create-or-update RBAC Roles, ClusterRoles, and Bindings from manifests in a script that runs on every deploy. Which kubectl subcommand is purpose-built for this?
options: kubectl create -f rbac.yaml: it updates existing objects
kubectl run: it generates RBAC from flags
kubectl auth reconcile -f rbac.yaml: it creates or updates RBAC resources with RBAC-aware merge semantics
kubectl auth can-i: it applies RBAC manifests
explain: kubectl auth reconcile is the purpose-built tool for bootstrapping RBAC from files: it creates missing objects and updates existing ones idempotently. auth can-i only checks permissions, create fails when objects exist, and run does not generate RBAC.

q: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy rejected your pod in staging last week. Before applying a big change to prod, how do you catch admission rejections WITHOUT creating anything?
options: kubectl apply --dry-run=server: the request runs through admission (including policies) but nothing is persisted
kubectl apply --dry-run=client: client-side catches admission
kubectl auth can-i create pods: authorization implies admission
Apply to a test namespace first: namespaces skip admission
explain: Server-side dry-run sends the real request through the full chain -- auth, admission plugins, webhooks, policies -- without persisting, so it surfaces the exact rejection prod would hit. Client dry-run never leaves your machine, auth can-i only checks RBAC (a different stage), and a test namespace both creates objects and may not match the policy's scope.

q: A node goes NotReady with conditions showing KernelDeadlock: True. Disk, memory, and PIDs look fine. Which component surfaces this condition?
options: The node-problem-detector (DaemonSet): it watches kernel logs and posts conditions like KernelDeadlock and ReadonlyFilesystem
The kubelet: it detects kernel deadlocks natively
The scheduler: it marks nodes with deadlocks
Prometheus: alerting sets node conditions
explain: node-problem-detector tails kernel and system logs and translates patterns into node conditions (KernelDeadlock, ReadonlyFilesystem, FrequentKubeletRestart, and more). The kubelet handles resource-pressure conditions, the scheduler only consumes conditions, and monitoring never writes node status.

q: A pod has no events explaining why it will not schedule, but something is gating it. Which field reveals scheduler-independent gates like SchedulingGated?
options: status.conditions: PodScheduled and readiness gates and their reasons live there even when events are empty
spec.schedulingGates: spec shows the current gate state
metadata.annotations: the scheduler writes gates there
kubectl logs: the scheduler logs gate decisions per pod
explain: status.conditions is the API-native record of pod state, including SchedulingGated and PodScheduled=False with reasons -- visible even when no events were emitted. spec holds the configured gates rather than their live effect, annotations are not used for this, and logs are the slow path.

q: A node is dying and you need the list of pods on it -- fast, via the API, without SSH. Which selector does this?
options: kubectl describe node node-1: it lists all pods
Labels select nodes: pods cannot be selected by node
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-1
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep node-1: it is the API-native way
explain: spec.nodeName is a supported field selector, so the API returns exactly that node's pods -- faster and exact versus client-side grep. describe node buries the list in prose, and the claim that pods cannot be selected by node is simply false.

q: In a noisy namespace you want only the events for pod web-0, newest first. Which command does this without grep?
options: kubectl describe pod web-0: events cannot be field-selected
kubectl logs web-0: logs include events
Events are cluster-scoped: you must use -A
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=web-0 --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n <ns>
explain: get events supports field selectors on involvedObject fields, giving exactly one object's events server-side, sortable by timestamp. describe is the manual path, logs are container output rather than API events, and events are namespaced (no -A needed).

q: The API is sluggish and etcd is the prime suspect, but endpoint health is fine. Which command gives a quick read/write latency verdict on etcd itself?
options: Add an etcd member: more members speed up writes
etcdctl check perf --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379: it runs a synthetic workload and reports throughput and latency percentiles
etcdctl defrag: defrag measures latency
etcdctl endpoint status: it shows latency
explain: check perf is etcd's built-in benchmark: it issues real puts and gets and reports latency percentiles -- the direct verdict on disk- or network-induced slowness. defrag reclaims space, endpoint status shows sizes and raft terms, and adding members hurts write latency because quorum grows.

q: You do not remember the exact fields of a NetworkPolicy ingress rule (is it 'from' with 'podSelector', or something else?). Which command shows the schema without leaving the terminal?
options: grep the API source: schemas are not exposed by kubectl
kubectl explain networkpolicy.spec.ingress: it prints the field schema with descriptions
kubectl api-versions: it lists resource schemas
kubectl describe networkpolicy: it shows schemas for objects that do not exist yet
explain: kubectl explain renders the OpenAPI schema for any resource path -- the exam-safe way to recall exact field names under time pressure. api-versions only lists API groups, describe needs a live object, and schemas are fully exposed client-side.

q: Pods fail ErrImagePull: unauthorized. The imagePullSecret exists in the right namespace, but it was created as a generic Opaque secret holding a .dockerconfigjson key. Why does the kubelet reject it?
options: imagePullSecrets must live in kube-system: the namespace is the problem
imagePullSecrets must be type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson: the kubelet only parses that type for registry credentials
Opaque secrets work: the registry credentials are wrong
The key must be named password: .dockerconfigjson is invalid
explain: The kubelet only interprets Secrets of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson as registry credentials; an Opaque secret with the same key is ignored. The credentials themselves are fine, .dockerconfigjson is the right key name, and the secret belongs in the workload's namespace rather than kube-system.

q: A startupProbe has periodSeconds: 10 and failureThreshold: 30. The app sometimes needs 4 minutes to start. What is the worst-case startup window the probe allows, and is it enough?
options: Unlimited: startupProbes never kill
300s (30 x 10s): yes, it covers the 4-minute startup with a minute to spare
40s (30 + 10): no, the app will be kill-looped
30s: failureThreshold is the total seconds
explain: The worst-case window is failureThreshold multiplied by periodSeconds: 30 failed probes spaced 10s apart gives the app 300s to become ready before the kubelet restarts it. 240s fits inside 300s. Threshold and period do not add, the threshold is a count rather than seconds, and startup probes absolutely do trigger restarts past the threshold.

q: A node reboot for patching kills pods instantly instead of draining them gracefully. Which kubelet feature gives running pods a shutdown grace window on node shutdown?
options: kubectl drain: the kubelet drains itself on reboot
preStop hooks: they run during node shutdown without any kubelet setting
Graceful node shutdown: --shutdown-grace-period (and --shutdown-grace-period-critical-pods) lets the kubelet delay shutdown while pods terminate
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: it applies to node shutdown automatically
explain: Graceful node shutdown makes the kubelet watch for shutdown events and hold the node up while pods terminate within the configured grace periods. Pod-level terminationGracePeriodSeconds only matters when something actually terminates the pod, the kubelet does not self-drain on reboot, and preStop hooks only run if the pod is being terminated in the first place.

q: A legitimate high-throughput controller keeps getting 429s from the API server even after adding client-side backoff. Which API server tuning raises the server's concurrent-request ceiling?
options: Adding etcd members: quorum size raises request throughput
--etcd-compaction-interval: compaction frequency gates requests
Restarting the API server: limits reset higher after restart
--max-requests-inflight and --max-mutating-requests-inflight: they raise the server-side concurrent request limits (alongside API Priority and Fairness configuration)
explain: 429s under sustained legitimate load point at the API server's inflight caps (defaults 400/200); raising them -- with Priority and Fairness shares configured -- increases the ceiling. More etcd members slow quorum writes rather than raising API throughput, compaction interval is unrelated, and restarts do not change configured limits.

q: A worker node join fails with 'the token is invalid or has expired'. The cluster was initialized 3 days ago and you are reusing the join command printed by the original kubeadm init. What is the right fix?
options: Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to the worker; the kubelet will mint its own bootstrap token from it
Generate a fresh token and join command on a control-plane node with kubeadm token create --print-join-command — bootstrap tokens expire after 24 hours by default
Re-run kubeadm init on the worker node; init refreshes expired bootstrap tokens
Append --discovery-token-unsafe-skip-ca-verification to the old join command; the token is only used for CA verification so expiry does not matter
explain: kubeadm bootstrap tokens have a default TTL of 24 hours. After that the saved join command is useless for authentication (the token IS the credential, not just a CA check). kubeadm token create --print-join-command mints a new token and prints a complete fresh join command. Re-running init on a worker is wrong, skipping CA verification does not fix an expired credential, and admin.conf must never leave the control plane.

q: You ran kubeadm init on cp-1 Monday morning. On Wednesday you try to join cp-2 as a second control-plane node with the saved --control-plane join command, and it fails on the certificate key while the bootstrap token is still valid. What happened and what fixes it?
options: The certificate key printed at init expires after 2 hours. Re-upload the control-plane certificates from cp-1 with kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs, then join cp-2 using the newly printed key
Bootstrap tokens cannot be used for control-plane joins at all; you must pass --control-plane to kubeadm token create
etcd requires three members before a second control-plane node may join; add a third node first
Delete /etc/kubernetes/pki on cp-1 and re-run kubeadm init to regenerate the whole PKI
explain: Joining an additional control-plane node needs the --certificate-key to decrypt the uploaded control-plane certs, and that key is only valid for 2 hours after upload. The fix is to re-run the upload phase on an existing control-plane node (kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs), which prints a fresh key, and join with that. The bootstrap token (24h TTL) is a separate credential, etcd bootstraps fine with 2 members, and rebuilding the PKI is destructive and unnecessary.

q: After kubeadm reset on a node you re-run kubeadm init, but pod networking misbehaves: stale routes and an old CNI config from the previous install interfere. What did reset leave behind?
options: reset deletes the CNI binaries in /opt/cni/bin, so the old config points at missing plugins
The Node object must be deleted before re-init; a stale Node object corrupts pod networking
kubeadm reset is best-effort only: it does not clean /etc/cni/net.d, iptables/nftables/IPVS rules, or $HOME/.kube — remove /etc/cni/net.d and flush the stale rules (kube-proxy --cleanup) manually
kubeadm reset --force also wipes etcd snapshots; you must restore a snapshot before re-init
explain: The kubeadm reset reference documents exactly what is NOT cleaned: CNI configuration, iptables/nftables/IPVS rules applied by kube-proxy, and the user's $HOME/.kube directory. The documented recovery is rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d (plus the kube-proxy --cleanup container for the rules) before re-initializing. Binaries are left in place, snapshots are untouched, and the Node object is unrelated to CNI config staleness.

q: kubeadm certs check-expiration shows the kube-apiserver certificate expiring in 9 days. Which sequence renews it correctly?
options: Do nothing; control-plane certificates auto-renew 30 days before expiry
Run kubeadm upgrade apply to the next minor version; upgrades renew all certificates automatically
Delete /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt; the kubelet regenerates control-plane certificates on restart
Run kubeadm certs renew apiserver (or renew all), then restart the kube-apiserver static pod so it loads the new certificate from disk
explain: kubeadm certs renew writes fresh certificates into /etc/kubernetes/pki, but the running API server already loaded the old cert into memory — you must restart the static pod (e.g. kubectl delete pod -n kube-system kube-apiserver-<node>, or touch the manifest) for it to take effect. Only kubelet client certificates auto-rotate; control-plane PKI never renews itself, upgrades do not renew certs, and deleting the cert file just breaks the API server.

q: A node's kubelet client certificate expired and the node went NotReady. The cluster has kubelet client certificate rotation enabled, and kubectl get csr shows a Pending CSR for system:node:worker-3. What is the correct recovery?
options: Delete the Node object; the kubelet re-registers with a fresh certificate automatically
Approve the pending CSR with kubectl certificate approve csr-<name> — the kubelet already requested a rotated certificate and is only waiting for approval
Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to the node as kubelet.conf so the kubelet uses the admin client certificate
Run kubeadm certs renew kubelet-client on a control-plane node; it renews kubelet certificates cluster-wide
explain: With RotateKubeletClientCertificate enabled, an expired kubelet generates a new key and posts a CertificateSigningRequest; nothing proceeds until someone approves it. kubectl certificate approve is the documented recovery. admin.conf would grant cluster-admin to the node (and is the wrong cert type), kubeadm certs renew only touches the local control-plane node's files, and deleting the Node object does not mint certificates.

q: A teammate's runbook uses kubeadm join --discovery-token-unsafe-skip-ca-verification for every worker join 'to avoid hash errors'. What is the actual risk?
options: It skips pinning the cluster CA's public-key hash during bootstrap, so a man-in-the-middle could impersonate the API server and harvest the bootstrap token and cluster credentials
It disables TLS for all subsequent kubelet-to-API-server traffic on the joined node
It makes the bootstrap token permanent instead of expiring after 24 hours
There is no risk; the flag only suppresses a cosmetic warning
explain: The --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash lets the joining node verify it is talking to the real cluster CA before handing over the bootstrap token. --discovery-token-unsafe-skip-ca-verification bypasses that check, exposing bootstrap to MITM on untrusted networks — hence 'unsafe' in the name. It affects only discovery, not later TLS; token TTL is unchanged.

q: Your audit Policy lists rule 1 as level: Metadata (catch-all) and rule 2 as level: RequestResponse for secrets. After a secret leak you find only metadata for the secret access. Why did the specific rule not apply?
options: Secrets are never logged above Metadata level for security; this is expected behavior
Matching rules are merged and the highest level across all matches applies, so rule 1 must have a typo
Audit policy rules are evaluated top-down and the first matching rule wins — the catch-all Metadata rule swallowed the secret requests before rule 2 was reached; specific rules must come first
RequestResponse level requires --audit-log-mode=batch on the API server; the default mode caps at Metadata
explain: The audit policy is first-match-wins, evaluated in listed order. A broad early rule shadows every later, more specific rule — the classic audit-policy ordering trap. The fix is to put narrow rules (secrets at RequestResponse) before the catch-all. There is no --audit-log-mode flag, secrets absolutely can be logged at RequestResponse, and levels are never merged.

q: Compliance requires 90 days of API audit history. The API server runs with --audit-log-maxage=30 --audit-log-maxbackup=10 --audit-log-maxsize=100. What do these flags mean, and what must change?
options: maxsize is days and maxage is megabytes — set --audit-log-maxsize=90
These are etcd compaction settings; audit retention is configured inside the Policy file instead
Audit logs are kept forever by default; these flags only affect the audit webhook backend

maxage is days of retention (30), maxbackup is how many rotated files are kept (10), maxsize is MB per file before rotation (100) — raise --audit-log-maxage to 90 and ensure maxbackup keeps enough files
explain: --audit-log-maxage (days), --audit-log-maxbackup (number of old files), --audit-log-maxsize (megabytes before rotation) control the log-file backend's retention. For 90 days you need maxage=90 (and enough maxbackup files that rotation does not prune younger ones). The names are not interchangeable, they are apiserver flags not etcd settings, and without them the defaults (30/10/100) apply.

q: You install a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration for a security scanner without setting failurePolicy. During a webhook outage, nobody can create or update ANY resource, including in kube-system. What is the root cause and the guard?
options: Webhooks default to Audit mode; the outage must be an etcd problem instead
Set reinvocationPolicy: Never; that makes webhook calls best-effort
Validating webhooks cannot affect kube-system; the real problem is RBAC

failurePolicy defaults to Fail: when the webhook is unreachable the API server rejects the admission requests. Set failurePolicy: Ignore for non-critical webhooks and scope them with namespaceSelector/objectSelector so kube-system stays reachable
explain: The default failurePolicy is Fail — a down webhook becomes a cluster-wide admission outage, exactly what happened. The exam-critical guards: failurePolicy: Ignore for webhooks whose failure is survivable, and namespaceSelector (e.g. exclude kube-system) so platform namespaces keep working. reinvocationPolicy controls re-invocation order, not failure behavior.

q: A mutating admission webhook normally responds in 2s, but under load it takes 12s, and API requests start failing with errors naming the webhook and 'context deadline exceeded'. What is happening?
options: Mutating webhooks are limited to 2s by the admission chain; move the logic into a controller
The audit log maxsize truncated the webhook payload; increase --audit-log-maxsize
The webhook exceeded timeoutSeconds (default 10s) — the API server gave up waiting. Raise timeoutSeconds (max 30s), make the webhook faster, and ensure sideEffects is None or NoneOnDryRun
The API server kills webhooks after a hardcoded 5s --webhook-timeout; raise that apiserver flag
explain: Admission webhooks have timeoutSeconds defaulting to 10 seconds (maximum 30). A 12s response trips the deadline and the request fails per the failurePolicy. The fix is a faster webhook and/or a higher timeoutSeconds. There is no --webhook-timeout apiserver flag, no 2s admission limit, and audit settings are unrelated.

q: A stacked-etcd HA cluster has 3 control-plane nodes. Two suffer simultaneous hardware failure. Pods keep running, but every kubectl command fails. What is the cluster state?
options: etcd lost quorum (2 of 3 members required) so the API is unavailable — running workloads are unaffected, but no reads or writes work until at least two members are restored
The kubelets elect a new leader and the cluster self-heals within minutes
With 1 of 3 members the cluster serves reads; only kubectl create/update/delete fail
The surviving member promotes itself and the cluster continues with the last hour of etcd data lost
explain: Stacked etcd needs a majority: 2 of 3. Losing two members loses quorum, and without quorum the API servers cannot serve reads or writes — kubectl fails entirely. Kubelets keep running existing pods (they are autonomous), but nothing is scheduled or updated. etcd has no leader election that restores quorum from one member, and quorum loss blocks reads too.

q: During an upgrade you notice a kubelet running v1.35 while the API servers are at v1.33, and kubeadm upgrade plan warns about skew. What does the Kubernetes version skew policy say about this?
options: It is unsupported: a kubelet must never be newer than the kube-apiserver. Upgrade the control plane first, then the nodes — never the reverse
Components may differ by any amount as long as kubectl matches the server version
The kubelet auto-downgrades to the API server version on its next restart
Version skew only constrains etcd; kubelet and API server versions are independent
explain: The skew policy's hard rule: no component may be newer than kube-apiserver. The supported upgrade order is control plane first, then kubelets (which may lag behind, never lead). A newer kubelet against an older API server can send requests the server does not understand. Nothing auto-downgrades, and the policy covers all components, not just etcd.

q: You enable encryption at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration (aescbc provider) via --encryption-provider-config and restart the API servers. A week later an etcd snapshot shows secrets created BEFORE the change still in plaintext. Why?
options: Secrets are encrypted by the kubelet; you must restart all nodes
Encryption is applied on write — pre-existing secrets stay plaintext in etcd until they are rewritten; you must read and rewrite every secret after enabling encryption
aescbc only encrypts newly created keys; existing data requires the aesgcm provider
The provider config must be passed to etcd, not the API server
explain: Envelope encryption happens in the API server at write time. Objects already stored are untouched until rewritten — the documented migration is to read all secrets and write them back (kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - style). The provider (aescbc vs aesgcm) does not change this, the flag belongs on kube-apiserver, and kubelets are not involved.

q: An auditor flags that pods mount service account tokens that never expire, sourced from auto-generated secrets of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token. What is the modern replacement?
options: Delete the auto-generated secrets; pods regenerate expiring tokens on their own
Use imagePullSecrets; they double as expiring workload identity tokens
Projected bound tokens via the TokenRequest API — time-limited (expirationSeconds), audience-scoped, and auto-rotated by the kubelet instead of static long-lived secret tokens
Set --service-account-extend-token-expiration=false to enable rotation of the legacy secrets
explain: Legacy auto-generated SA token secrets are static credentials with no expiry. The replacement is projected volume bound tokens: short-lived, audience-bound, refreshed by the kubelet before expiration. There is no flag that retrofits expiry onto legacy secrets, deleting them breaks mounts, and imagePullSecrets are registry credentials, not identity.

q: Pods receive IPs from 10.244.0.0/16 (your CNI configuration), but kube-controller-manager runs with --cluster-cidr=10.200.0.0/16. New nodes never get a podCIDR allocated and stay NotReady. What is wrong?
options: Nodes self-allocate podCIDRs; the flag is informational only
The controller-manager's --cluster-cidr must match the pod network the CNI actually uses — it allocates each node's podCIDR from that range, so the mismatch leaves nodes without podCIDRs
The CNI reads --cluster-cidr directly from the controller-manager; restart the CNI DaemonSet
podCIDRs are allocated by kube-proxy; the flag belongs on kube-proxy, not the controller-manager
explain: kube-controller-manager's node CIDR allocator carves per-node podCIDRs out of --cluster-cidr. If that range does not match the CNI's real pod network, allocation still happens from the wrong range (or the CNI ignores it) and nodes never become Ready for pods. The CNI does not read this flag, kube-proxy does not allocate CIDRs, and nodes do not self-allocate.

q: After adding a second control-plane node, you see two kube-scheduler pods running (one per node). A teammate wants to delete one to avoid a split brain. Is that a problem?
options: Yes - two active schedulers will double-schedule every pod; delete one immediately
Yes - but only if they were started with different --scheduler-name values
No - the schedulers run with leader election: one holds the lease and actively schedules while the other stands by. Deleting it would only remove your HA standby
No - Kubernetes runs schedulers active/active and merges their decisions through etcd
explain: Control-plane components (kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager) use leader election via Lease objects: exactly one instance is active at a time. One scheduler pod per control-plane node is the healthy kubeadm HA state, not a split brain.

q: You run etcdctl snapshot restore --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored successfully and restart the etcd static pod, but the cluster still serves the OLD data. What did you miss?
options: Restore writes to a NEW data directory — the etcd static pod manifest still mounts the old /var/lib/etcd. Update the manifest's hostPath volume to /var/lib/etcd-restored (and fix ownership)
snapshot restore merges into the running member; you must also run snapshot defrag afterwards
Restore requires --experimental-no-snapshot-restore on modern etcd versions
The snapshot must be restored on all members simultaneously or the old data wins
explain: etcdctl snapshot restore is an offline bootstrap into a fresh data-dir; it never touches the live member's directory. The static pod keeps mounting the old dir, so the old data keeps serving. You must point the manifest's etcd-data hostPath at the restored directory (each member restored independently, then the cluster re-forms around the restored data).

q: After changing --service-cluster-ip-range to 172.30.0.0/16, pods resolve cluster.local names but external names fail. kubelet --cluster-dns is still 10.96.0.10. What is wrong?
options: kubelet --cluster-dns is deprecated; DNS now comes from the CNI configuration
--cluster-dns must be the ClusterIP of the kube-dns Service — with the new service range that IP moved (e.g. 172.30.0.10), so pods are pointed at a dead DNS address
CoreDNS always serves on 10.96.0.10 regardless of the service CIDR
External DNS requires --cluster-domain to be changed as well
explain: --cluster-dns tells the kubelet which DNS IP to put in every pod's resolv.conf, and it must equal the kube-dns Service's ClusterIP. kubeadm allocates that as the 10th IP of the service CIDR (10.96.0.10 by default); changing the service range moves it. Pods got a DNS IP with nothing behind it, so external (forwarded) lookups fail while the cluster.local path... actually both would fail — the key point is the stale DNS IP. CoreDNS does not keep a fixed IP, and the CNI does not provide DNS.

q: You enable a beta feature gate with --feature-gates on the API server, but kubelets reject pods using the feature with 'unknown field' errors. What is the rule for feature gates?
options: Gates set on the API server propagate to kubelets automatically through node leases
Gates only need to be set on etcd; components read them from storage
Beta gates are enabled by default, so the error must be a typo in the manifest
Feature gates are per-component: every component that handles the feature (API server, controller-manager, scheduler, kubelet) needs the matching --feature-gates setting, and they must agree
explain: A feature gate is a local per-binary switch, not cluster state. If the API server knows a beta API field but the kubelet's gate is off, the kubelet rejects it as unknown. The documented practice: set the same --feature-gates value on every component that participates in the feature (and in kubeadm's ClusterConfiguration for control-plane components plus the kubelet config).

q: Control-plane nodes are joined through a load balancer DNS name lb.example.com, but kubeadm join fails TLS verification: the API server certificate is not valid for lb.example.com. How do you fix this for the cluster?
options: Use --discovery-token-unsafe-skip-ca-verification on every join; SANs are optional
Add lb.example.com to /etc/hosts on each node; the certificate will then validate
certSANs can only be set at kubeadm init time; the cluster must be rebuilt
Add lb.example.com to apiServer.certSANs in the kubeadm ClusterConfiguration, regenerate the apiserver certificate (kubeadm init phase certs apiserver --config), and restart the API server
explain: The API server certificate must list every name clients use to reach it. Adding the LB DNS name to apiServer.certSANs and regenerating the apiserver cert (kubeadm init phase certs apiserver --config <file>) fixes verification for all joiners. Skipping verification trades away MITM protection, /etc/hosts does not affect certificate validation, and certs can be regenerated without rebuilding.

q: A monitoring pod has priorityClassName: monitoring-critical with preemptionPolicy: Never. During node pressure it is evicted anyway. The team assumed Never means 'never evicted'. What does preemptionPolicy: Never actually do?
options: It only applies to manual kubectl drain, not to node-pressure eviction
It only stops the pod from PREEMPTING lower-priority pods — it gives no protection against being preempted or evicted itself
It is invalid on DaemonSet pods, so the field was silently ignored
It requires globalDefault: true on the PriorityClass to take effect
explain: preemptionPolicy controls one direction only: whether THIS pod may evict others to get scheduled. Never means the pod never preempts anyone; it says nothing about the pod's own evictability. A pod that must survive needs a high priority VALUE (so others cannot preempt it) — the policy field is about its behavior as a preemptor, not its immunity as a victim.

q: kubectl apply of a PriorityClass with value: 1500000000 is rejected, and a class named system-urgent is also rejected. What are the rules?
options: Values above one million require cluster-admin; the system- prefix rule is only a warning
PriorityClass values must be negative to avoid colliding with system classes
The cap is 2,147,483,647 for everyone, system classes included

User PriorityClasses are capped at 1,000,000,000 — larger values are reserved for system classes (system-node-critical is 2000001000, system-cluster-critical is 2000000000) — and names may not use the system- prefix
explain: The API caps user PriorityClass values at one billion and reserves the system- name prefix for Kubernetes' own classes. The two built-in classes sit above the cap (2000001000 and 2000000000), which is why user values cannot reach them — guaranteeing system pods always outrank user workloads.

q: You create a second PriorityClass with globalDefault: true and the API server rejects it. Why?
options: The field becomes immutable once any pod has been created
globalDefault only works for pods in the kube-system namespace
Only one PriorityClass cluster-wide may have globalDefault: true — it becomes the default priority for pods without priorityClassName; remove or patch the existing one first
globalDefault requires value: 0
explain: globalDefault marks the PriorityClass applied to every pod that does not name one explicitly, so the API enforces uniqueness — a second globalDefault is rejected at admission. PriorityClass is cluster-scoped (no namespaces involved), the value can be anything within the cap, and the field is mutable.

q: Pods with runtimeClassName: kata stay Pending with 'no runtime handler registered for kata'. The CRI runtime is containerd. What is wrong?
options: RuntimeClass requires the Kata operator; the handler string itself is irrelevant
runtimeClassName is a pod annotation, not a spec field, so it was ignored
The kubelet needs a --runtime-handler=kata flag to recognize the class
The RuntimeClass handler must exactly match a runtime name registered in containerd's configuration — 'kata' is not registered there, so the kubelet cannot hand the pod to any runtime
explain: runtimeClass.handler is matched verbatim against the runtimes configured in the CRI runtime (containerd's plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes table). A typo or an unregistered name means the kubelet has nowhere to send the pod, hence Pending. There is no kubelet flag for this; the contract is handler string == CRI runtime name.

q: A pod using a VM-isolation RuntimeClass requests 100m CPU and 128Mi memory, but the scheduler accounts more than that against the node. Why?
options: Overhead applies only to Windows nodes
The extra is the pause container, which cannot be configured
The RuntimeClass defines overhead (podOverhead): the scheduler adds it to the pod's requests for placement, and the sum counts toward cgroup limits and eviction decisions
Overhead is informational only; the scheduler ignores podOverhead
explain: VM-based runtimes (Kata, gVisor) consume real memory/CPU for the sandbox. RuntimeClass.overhead lets the runtime declare that cost via podOverhead, and the scheduler treats requests+overhead as the pod's footprint. Ignoring it would let the scheduler overcommit the node.

q: You add an ephemeralContainer section with kubectl edit pod/debug-1, save, and the API server rejects the change. What is the correct way to attach a debugger to the running pod?
options: Ephemeral containers can only be declared at pod creation time
Use kubectl attach; it implicitly creates an ephemeral container
Set shareProcessNamespace: true on the pod first, then kubectl edit will succeed
Use kubectl debug -it debug-1 --image=busybox --target=<container> — ephemeral containers are added through the ephemeralcontainers subresource, not by editing the pod spec
explain: Pods are immutable after creation, and ephemeral containers bypass spec editing entirely: they are injected via the /ephemeralcontainers subresource (which kubectl debug drives). kubectl edit can never add one. --target shares the target container's process namespace for debugging.

q: Your ephemeral debug container manifest sets resources.requests and a livenessProbe. The API server rejects it. Which restrictions apply to ephemeral containers?
options: Ephemeral containers require resources.limits to be set
All container fields are allowed; the rejection must be a YAML indentation error
Ephemeral containers disallow ports, all probes, and resources — they are for inspection only, with no resource guarantees and no automatic restarts
Only probes are disallowed; resource requests are permitted
explain: The documented restrictions: no ports, no liveness/readiness/startup probes, and no resources (pod resource allocations are immutable once the pod exists). They also are never restarted and cannot be changed or removed after injection. They exist to inspect, not to run workloads.

q: You want right-sizing recommendations for a Deployment with zero automatic pod restarts. Which VPA updateMode do you use, and where do you read the recommendation?
options: updateMode: Off — the VPA only writes recommendations to its status (kubectl describe vpa); nothing is applied to running or new pods
updateMode: Manual — recommendations appear as annotations on the pods
updateMode: Initial — it only affects new pods, which is close enough
Delete the VPA admission webhook; Off is not a valid updateMode
explain: VPA updateModes: Off (recommendations only), Initial (apply to new pods), Auto/Recreate (evict and recreate pods with new requests). Off is the safe 'advisor' mode: the recommender still observes via metrics-server and publishes target/lowerBound/upperBound in the VPA status, and the admission controller changes nothing.

q: An HPA scales a Deployment on CPU while a VPA in Auto mode also manages CPU requests. The replica count oscillates wildly. What is the documented conflict?
options: VPA and HPA must not act on the same metric: VPA changes requests (which changes the utilization ratio HPA reads) while HPA changes replicas — they fight. Use VPA for memory and HPA for CPU, or run VPA in Off/Initial
The conflict is metrics-server latency; install Prometheus instead
Set the HPA minReplicas above the VPA maxAllowed to separate them
VPA Auto automatically disables any HPA targeting the same workload
explain: HPA computes utilization as usage/requests. When VPA Auto keeps moving requests, the utilization ratio swings and HPA chases it, causing oscillation. The documented guidance: never have VPA and HPA manage the same resource on the same workload — split by metric (VPA memory, HPA CPU) or keep VPA advisory.

q: The cluster-autoscaler never scales down a node whose pods all look evictable. One pod uses an emptyDir volume. What blocks the scale-down?
options: Cluster-autoscaler cannot scale down nodes running more than one pod
Pods using local storage block scale-down by default (--skip-nodes-with-local-storage=true). Annotate the pod cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: 'true' if its emptyDir data is disposable
emptyDir is network storage, so the blocker must be a PDB instead
Set --scale-down-delay-after-add=0 to force immediate scale-down
explain: emptyDir is local to the node, so evicting the pod destroys its data — the autoscaler conservatively refuses to scale down such nodes. The escape hatch is the safe-to-evict annotation (or a PDB-aware design), declaring the local data disposable. The delay flags do not override the safety check.

q: Your node groups mix cheap spot and expensive on-demand pools. On scale-up the autoscaler should prefer the cheapest node type that fits the pending pods. Which expander does that?
options: Set --expander=cheapest; it is a built-in expander
--expander=least-waste (the default): it prefers the node type with the least wasted resources, which in practice selects the cheapest fitting option
--expander=price: it always picks spot instances regardless of fit
Expanders only affect scale-down decisions, not scale-up
explain: The autoscalers expanders: random, most-pods, least-waste (default), priority, price. least-waste simulates each node group and picks the one with minimal unused capacity — effectively the cheapest fit. price needs cloud pricing data; most-pods optimizes for bin-packing count, not cost.

q: After a node failure, replacement pods pile onto the surviving nodes and the cluster stays lopsided for days. Which component rebalances already-running pods, and how is it typically deployed?
options: The descheduler runs as a DaemonSet on every node

The descheduler: it evicts pods that violate its policy (e.g. RemovePodsViolatingInterPodAntiAffinity) and the scheduler places them better. It typically runs as a CronJob with a policy ConfigMap, not as a continuous controller
The kube-scheduler rebalances running pods every 10 minutes automatically
cluster-autoscaler with --balance-similar-node-groups rebalances pod placement
explain: The scheduler only places new pods; it never moves running ones. The descheduler fills that gap: on its schedule it evicts pods matching strategies (duplicates, anti-affinity violations, too many restarts, node taints), and the scheduler recreates them on better nodes. It is deployed as a Job/CronJob driven by a policy file.

q: A high-priority pod stays Pending on a full cluster even though plenty of lower-priority pods look preemptible. The potential victims are covered by tight PDBs. Why does preemption fail?
options: Scheduler preemption honors PodDisruptionBudgets: if evicting the victim pods would violate their budget, the scheduler will not preempt them, so the high-priority pod stays Pending
Preemption only works within the same namespace as the preemptor pod
The preemptor needs preemptionPolicy: Never to bypass PodDisruptionBudgets
PDBs are ignored during preemption; the real blocker must be a resource quota
explain: Preemption is still a voluntary disruption, so it is constrained by PDBs: the scheduler only preempts victims whose eviction keeps budgets intact. Tight budgets (for example maxUnavailable: 0) can therefore block preemption entirely - priority alone does not override a budget.

q: A VPA in updateMode: Off has been attached to a Deployment for a day, but kubectl describe vpa shows no recommendations - status.recommendation is empty. metrics-server was never installed. What is wrong?
options: updateMode: Off disables the recommender; switch to Auto to get recommendations
The VPA recommender consumes CPU and memory history from metrics-server - without it the recommender has no data and publishes nothing. Install metrics-server
Recommendations only appear after 7 days of observation
The VPA needs a ServiceMonitor; install Prometheus first
explain: The VPA recommender is fed by the metrics API (metrics-server), the same pipeline HPA uses. Off mode still recommends - it just never acts. With no metrics backend, status.recommendation stays empty; Prometheus is a separate, optional pipeline.

q: You kubectl delete the pod kube-apiserver-cp-1 and it reappears within seconds. Why, and how do you actually remove it?
options: A ReplicaSet is recreating it; scale that ReplicaSet to 0
Static pods are immutable; the node must be rebuilt
Use kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0
It is a static pod: the kubelet recreates it from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Remove or move the manifest file out of the manifests directory
explain: Static pods are managed by the kubelet directly from manifest files, not by any controller — the API server only shows a read-only mirror pod. Deleting the mirror changes nothing; the kubelet re-creates the pod from the file. To stop it, delete/move the manifest (the kubelet then terminates the pod).

q: A pod specifies image: registry.example.com/app@sha256:9f86d0... with imagePullPolicy: Never on a fresh node, and fails with ErrImagePull. Why?
options: Never is invalid with digests; the API server should have rejected the pod
The digest changes on every pull, so the reference is stale
Never means 'use only images already cached locally' — the digest-pinned image is not in the node's cache and the kubelet will not pull it. Pre-pull it or use IfNotPresent
Digests bypass imagePullPolicy, so the registry must be down
explain: imagePullPolicy: Never disables all pulls; the kubelet only uses what containerd already has. A digest identifies content precisely but does not fetch it. On a fresh node the image is absent, hence ErrImagePull. IfNotPresent would pull once by digest; Always would pull every time.

q: A pod uses imagePullPolicy: Always with a digest-pinned image. The team assumed the digest lets the kubelet skip the registry when the image is cached. What actually happens on every pod start?
options: The kubelet caches by digest permanently and never contacts the registry again
Always is silently ignored when a digest is present
Digest-pinned images are always resolved to the latest tag
The kubelet contacts the registry on every start — Always means always pull; the digest guarantees WHICH image is used, not WHETHER it is pulled
explain: Pull policy and image reference are orthogonal: Always pulls unconditionally (verifying the digest against the registry), IfNotPresent pulls only when the digest is absent locally, Never never pulls. Pinning a digest gives immutability, not pull avoidance — a common exam trap.

q: Which toleration matches every taint on a node regardless of key, value, or effect?
options: tolerations: [{operator: Exists}] — an empty key with operator Exists matches all taint keys, and omitting effect matches all effects
tolerations: [{operator: Equal, key: '*'}] — the wildcard matches every key
tolerations: [{operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}] — matches everything
tolerations: [{operator: Equal, key: ''}] — empty key with Equal matches all
explain: Per the API semantics, operator Exists with an empty key matches every taint key, and leaving effect unset matches all three effects (NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute). There are no wildcards in tolerations; Equal with an empty key matches only empty keys.

q: A pod sets tolerations: [{key: spot-only, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule, tolerationSeconds: 60}]. When the taint appears the pod is evicted immediately instead of after 60 seconds. Why?
options: tolerationSeconds requires operator: Equal
NoSchedule taints evict after node-monitor-grace-period regardless of tolerations
tolerationSeconds only has meaning with effect: NoExecute — with NoSchedule it does nothing. For delayed eviction the taint effect must be NoExecute
tolerationSeconds is in milliseconds, so 60 meant 60ms
explain: tolerationSeconds defines how long a pod tolerates a NoExecute taint before eviction. NoSchedule only affects scheduling of new pods — it never evicts running ones, so a duration is meaningless there. (Also note: the eviction in the scenario implies the real taint was NoExecute, which the pod did not tolerate at all.)

q: An app must deregister from an external load balancer BEFORE it begins its SIGTERM-driven shutdown. Where do you put the deregistration call?
options: In a preStop lifecycle hook — preStop executes before SIGTERM is sent, and both run inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds, so deregistration completes before the app shuts down
In a postStart hook with a sleep; postStart runs before SIGTERM
Nowhere — SIGTERM is always sent first, then preStop runs during the grace period
In a readiness probe failure handler; probes execute before preStop
explain: Pod termination order: preStop hook runs first, then SIGTERM is delivered to PID 1, then the grace period counts down to SIGKILL. preStop is exactly the mechanism for pre-shutdown cleanup (deregistration, connection draining). postStart runs at container start, unrelated to shutdown.

q: At 5,000 services, iptables-based kube-proxy sync latency is hurting. The team wants to switch to IPVS mode. What is required?
options: Nothing — IPVS has been the default proxy mode since Kubernetes 1.20
Set --proxy-mode=ipvs on the kubelet; it forwards the mode to kube-proxy
IPVS requires replacing kube-dns with CoreDNS first
Set --proxy-mode=ipvs on kube-proxy and ensure the IPVS kernel modules (ip_vs, ip_vs_rr, ip_vs_wrr, ip_vs_sh, nf_conntrack) are loaded on every node
explain: iptables remains the default kube-proxy mode; IPVS is opt-in via --proxy-mode=ipvs and needs its kernel modules present, otherwise kube-proxy fails to start. The flag belongs to kube-proxy (usually via its ConfigMap), not the kubelet, and DNS is unrelated.

q: After switching kube-proxy to IPVS mode, MetalLB-assigned LoadBalancer IPs flap and sometimes answer from the wrong node. Which kube-proxy setting addresses this?
options: Switch back with --proxy-mode=iptables to disable ARP entirely
--ipvs-exclude-cidrs with the MetalLB pool range
--ipvs-strict-arp=true — it makes kube-proxy configure arp_ignore/arp_announce so nodes do not answer ARP for virtual IPs they are not serving
--ipvs-scheduler=sh for sticky ARP resolution
explain: With IPVS, every node may hold the virtual IP, and without strict ARP all nodes answer ARP for it — traffic lands on nodes that then forward or blackhole it. --ipvs-strict-arp=true sets the sysctls so only the serving node answers. The scheduler (rr/wrr/lc/sh) is about connection distribution, not ARP.

q: A Service has 250 ready pods. How many EndpointSlice objects will the EndpointSlice controller maintain for it by default, and how do consumers find them all?
options: One slice — EndpointSlices hold up to 1000 endpoints, so 250 fits in a single object
250 slices, one per pod
Slices are only created once a Service exceeds 1000 endpoints

Three slices — the controller packs about 100 endpoints per slice by default (configurable via --max-endpoints-per-slice); every slice carries the label kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>, so consumers list by that label
explain: The EndpointSlice controller's default max is 100 endpoints per slice (the API allows up to 1000, but the controller splits at 100). 250 pods therefore yield 3 slices. kube-proxy and custom consumers aggregate slices using the kubernetes.io/service-name label — the reason Endpoints scale problems disappeared.

q: An EndpointSlice entry shows conditions ready: false, serving: true, terminating: true. What does this describe?
options: A pod that is terminating but still serving traffic — e.g. inside its preStop hook or termination grace period; ready=false stops NEW connections while serving=true reflects in-flight work
A corrupt slice; ready and serving must always agree
A pod that permanently failed its readiness probe
An endpoint waiting for its first readiness check
explain: The three conditions are independent by design: ready gates new traffic, serving reports actual serving state, terminating marks deletion in progress. A terminating pod that is still draining connections is ready=false (removed from load balancing) but serving=true, terminating=true — the graceful-shutdown state.

q: A StatefulSet needs every replica — including ones not yet Ready — to discover peers via DNS at startup. The headless Service only returns Ready pods. Which field fixes peer discovery?
options: Change the Service type to ExternalName
publishNotReadyAddresses: true on the headless Service — DNS then returns A records for all pods regardless of readiness
Set clusterIP: None twice in the Service spec
Add a readiness probe that always succeeds during startup
explain: By default endpoints (and headless DNS) only include ready addresses. publishNotReadyAddresses: true publishes not-ready pods into DNS/endpoints — the standard trick for stateful peer discovery (Cassandra, Kafka, etcd-style quorum bootstrapping) where members must find each other before anyone is ready.

q: You need pods to reach a Service over both IPv4 and IPv6, and the cluster is dual-stack. What must the Service specify?
options: Create two Services, one per family — a Service can only hold a single clusterIP
ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack with both families listed
Nothing — Services are always dual-stack when the cluster is
ipFamilies: [IPv4, IPv6] with ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack — the Service gets one ClusterIP per family; the cluster itself needs dual-stack CIDRs on the API server and kubelet first
explain: Dual-stack Services explicitly declare ipFamilies and an ipFamilyPolicy (SingleStack, PreferDualStack, RequireDualStack); RequireDualStack allocates a ClusterIP from each family. The cluster must be provisioned dual-stack (--service-cluster-ip-range with two CIDRs, dual pod CIDRs, a dual-stack CNI) or the Service cannot get both addresses.

q: A node has /etc/cni/net.d/10-flannel.conflist and /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist after a botched migration. Which configuration does the kubelet actually use for new pods?
options: The most recently modified file wins; check the timestamps
Both are merged and new pods get two network interfaces
Whichever CNI has a running DaemonSet wins automatically
10-calico.conflist — the kubelet reads /etc/cni/net.d in lexicographic order and uses the first file ('10-calico' sorts before '10-flannel'); the fix is to leave exactly one conflist behind
explain: The kubelet sorts the files in /etc/cni/net.d lexicographically and uses the first .conflist/.conf it finds — '10-calico.conflist' beats '10-flannel.conflist'. There is no merging and no timestamp logic, which is why a botched migration with two leftover files produces surprise networking. The fix is to leave exactly one authoritative file.

q: A pod with hostPort: 8080 starts, but the port is not reachable on the node IP. The CNI chain is calico + bandwidth only. What is missing?
options: The API server's --service-node-port-range must include 8080
hostPort only works with the kubenet network plugin
The portmap CNI plugin — hostPort mappings are implemented by portmap in the CNI chain; without it the field is silently ignored
hostNetwork: true is required for hostPort to work
explain: hostPort is not magic in the kubelet — it is implemented by the portmap CNI plugin, which must be present in the chain (after the main plugin). Calico's default install includes portmap, but a custom chain of calico+bandwidth drops it, and the kubelet logs a warning while the port stays closed. hostNetwork is a separate, stronger setting.

q: An Ingress rule has path: /foo with pathType: Prefix. Which request paths route to its backend: /foo, /foo/bar, /foobar?
options: /foo and /foo/bar — Prefix matches element-wise on '/'-separated path segments, so /foobar (a different final segment) does not match
All three — Prefix is a plain string prefix match
Only /foo — Prefix requires an exact match plus an optional trailing slash
/foo and /foobar — but /foo/bar needs path: /foo/ to match
explain: The Ingress spec defines Prefix as element-wise: the path and request are split on '/', and every element of the rule path must equal the corresponding request element. /foo matches /foo and /foo/bar but NOT /foobar — the single most tested Ingress matching trap. (Note: some controllers historically did string matching, which is why the spec calls this out.)

q: An Ingress defines /api (Prefix) -> svc-a, /api/v2 (Prefix) -> svc-b, and /api/v2/health (Exact) -> svc-c. Where does GET /api/v2/health go?
options: svc-b — Prefix rules are evaluated before Exact rules
svc-a — the first matching rule in the list wins
It is ambiguous; the controller load-balances across all three
svc-c — the longest matching path wins, and at equal length an Exact rule beats a Prefix rule
explain: Ingress path precedence: longest match first; ties broken by Exact over Prefix. /api/v2/health (Exact, length 3 segments) beats /api/v2 (Prefix). Rule order in the YAML is irrelevant — a frequent misconception.

q: HTTPS to your Ingress serves the controller's default fake certificate instead of your domain certificate. The Ingress references secretName: web-tls under spec.tls with hosts: [shop.example.com]. What is the most common cause?
options: The Secret is not of type kubernetes.io/tls, is missing the tls.crt/tls.key keys, or its certificate does not cover shop.example.com — the controller falls back to its default certificate
TLS Secrets must live in the ingress controller's namespace, not the Ingress namespace
spec.tls requires every path to use pathType: Exact
The certificate must be referenced via an annotation instead of spec.tls
explain: For TLS termination the controller needs a kubernetes.io/tls Secret (keys tls.crt and tls.key) in the SAME namespace as the Ingress, and the cert's SANs must cover the hosts listed in spec.tls. Any mismatch — wrong type, missing keys, wrong namespace, uncovered hostname — and the controller serves its default cert. spec.tls is the correct, portable mechanism.

q: A NetworkPolicy allows port 80 to the pods, but the app container actually listens on 8080 behind a Service with port 80 and targetPort 8080. Traffic is still dropped. Why?
options: NetworkPolicy ports refer to the pod's container ports, not Service ports — the policy must allow 8080, the port the container actually listens on
NetworkPolicy cannot reference targetPorts at all; it only works with hostPorts
The policy must use the Service port NAME instead of a port number
Egress rules are also required so the reply traffic can return
explain: NetworkPolicy enforcement happens at the pod, before Service translation — so port numbers in a policy are container ports. Allowing '80' when the container listens on 8080 matches nothing. Reply traffic is handled by conntrack; no egress rule is needed for it.

q: You apply a NetworkPolicy intending to isolate one app, but every pod in the namespace loses connectivity. The policy's podSelector is {}. What happened?
options: An empty podSelector selects nothing, so the policy created a default-deny for the whole namespace
podSelector: {} is invalid and the policy was rejected; the outage is coincidental
An empty podSelector ({}) selects ALL pods in the policy's namespace - the policy applied to everything, not just your app. Scope it with matchLabels
NetworkPolicies always apply namespace-wide regardless of podSelector
explain: In Kubernetes selectors, empty ({}) means 'match everything' - the opposite of the common assumption. A NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} therefore governs every pod in its namespace. To target one application, use podSelector with matchLabels.
