q: You need a NetworkPolicy egress rule that allows all external traffic EXCEPT the private range 10.0.0.0/8. How is that expressed?
options: ipBlock does not support except on egress rules, only on ingress
Use a namespaceSelector with matchLabels set to the CIDR string
egress: [{to: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [10.0.0.0/8]}}]}] — the except list subtracts CIDRs from the allowed block
Two rules: allow 0.0.0.0/0 first, then a deny rule for 10.0.0.0/8 — deny rules take precedence
explain: ipBlock supports an except list on both ingress and egress: traffic to cidr MINUS the exceptions is allowed. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is allow-only — there are no deny rules, so 'allow then deny' does not exist as a construct.

q: A ClusterIP Service fronts pods that run on only 2 of 10 nodes. You set internalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client source IP and skip the extra hop. What is the trade-off?
options: Local disables kube-proxy for the Service entirely
internalTrafficPolicy only affects NodePort and LoadBalancer Services

Traffic is only delivered to node-local endpoints — a node with no local pods drops the traffic, so the Service can be unreachable from some nodes. Only use Local when every node has endpoints or the drops are acceptable
Local is already the default; the change had no effect
explain: internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster (default) load-balances across all endpoints with SNAT hiding the source; Local keeps traffic on the node (preserving source IP, avoiding a hop) but any node without a local endpoint blackholes the traffic. It applies to ClusterIP services' internal traffic.

q: A legacy app needs clients pinned to the same backend pod. You set sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service. How long does the stickiness last by default?
options: Session affinity is per-node, not per-client, so the question is moot
10800 seconds (3 hours) — sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds defaults to 10800, and kube-proxy refreshes the entry while the client keeps connecting
30 seconds; it must be raised for real user sessions
Indefinitely, until the backend pod is deleted
explain: ClientIP session affinity defaults to a 3-hour timeout (10800s), configurable via sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds (max 86400). kube-proxy tracks the client IP -> endpoint mapping and refreshes it on use. It is per client IP, not per node.

q: kubectl get endpoints shows <none> for a Service of type ExternalName, and no kube-proxy rules exist for it. Is the Service broken?
options: No — ExternalName Services have no ClusterIP, no label selector, and no endpoints by design; kube-dns simply returns a CNAME to the externalName. That is the expected state
Yes — ExternalName Services require manually created Endpoints
Yes — the externalName must point to an in-cluster Service
Yes — kube-proxy needs --proxy-mode=userspace to program ExternalName rules
explain: ExternalName is pure DNS: it maps a cluster-local name to an external DNS name via CNAME. There is no virtual IP, no proxying, and no endpoints object — <none> is correct. It is commonly used to give stable in-cluster names to external databases.

q: A headless Service (clusterIP: None) selects a 3-replica StatefulSet named web in namespace default. What DNS names resolve, and to what?
options: Headless Services create no DNS entries at all
web-0.web.default.svc.cluster.local (plus web-1, web-2) each resolve to that pod's own IP via A records — headless Services publish per-pod DNS instead of a virtual IP
A single A record for web.default resolving to all pod IPs round-robin
Only SRV records are created; A records require publishNotReadyAddresses
explain: With clusterIP: None, kube-dns creates A records for each ready pod as <pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local pointing at the pod IP (plus SRV records). That stable per-pod DNS is why StatefulSets pair with headless Services.

q: A pod needs fully custom DNS (corporate resolvers and search domains). You set dnsPolicy: None, but the pod ends up with no nameservers at all. What is required?
options: Nameservers must be set in /etc/resolv.conf on the node instead
dnsPolicy: None requires a dnsConfig block carrying nameservers, searches, and options — with None the kubelet inherits nothing, so an empty dnsConfig means no DNS
dnsPolicy: None is not a valid value; ClusterFirst is the only option
Custom DNS must be configured with a CoreDNS rewrite, not dnsConfig
explain: dnsPolicy: None means 'do not apply any default DNS behavior' — the pod gets exactly what dnsConfig specifies and nothing else. Omit dnsConfig and the pod has zero nameservers. (ClusterFirstWithHostNet and Default inherit from the node; None inherits nothing.)

q: An old manifest sets spec.topologyKeys: ['kubernetes.io/hostname'] on a Service and the API server rejects it. What replaced topologyKeys?
options: Zone-aware routing is no longer supported in Kubernetes
topologyKeys was removed in v1.22 — use internalTrafficPolicy: Local for node-local routing and topology-aware hints for zone-aware routing
topologyKeys moved to an annotation of the same name
It was renamed to spec.topologyLabels
explain: ServiceTopology (topologyKeys) was beta and removed in 1.22. Its two use cases were split: internalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps traffic node-local, and topology-aware routing hints (the service.kubernetes.io/topology-aware-hints annotation, later auto-hints) prefer zone-local endpoints. Old manifests must be migrated.

q: A CSI driver is used only for inline ephemeral volumes. Its CSIDriver object sets attachRequired: true, and pods hang at ContainerCreating. Why?
options: Set volumeLifecycleModes: [Persistent] to fix the hang

attachRequired: true makes Kubernetes create VolumeAttachment objects and wait for controller-side attach — meaningless for inline ephemeral volumes. Set attachRequired: false so the kubelet mounts directly via NodePublishVolume
Inline ephemeral volumes require attachRequired: true; the hang must be a node problem
Ephemeral volumes need attachRequired set on the StorageClass instead
explain: attachRequired tells the attach/detach controller to intervene (ControllerPublish/Unpublish). Inline ephemeral volumes skip the whole PV/PVC/attachment machinery — the kubelet calls NodePublishVolume directly. With attachRequired: true the pod waits forever for an attachment that will never come.

q: A node was hard-deleted without draining. Its EBS volume is stuck attaching to the dead node and the rescheduled pod stays Pending. What unblocks it?
options: Restart kube-controller-manager to clear its attach cache
VolumeAttachments are garbage-collected with the Node object automatically
Delete the stale VolumeAttachment object (kubectl delete volumeattachment <name>) — the external-attacher will then detach the volume and attach it to the new node
Delete the PersistentVolume; it will be reprovisioned automatically
explain: The attach/detach controller tracks attachments in VolumeAttachment objects; when a node vanishes without a clean detach, the object lingers and blocks re-attach (the classic Multi-Attach/force-detach scenario). Deleting the VolumeAttachment tells the driver it is safe to detach and re-attach elsewhere. Deleting the Node object does not clean these up.

q: A CSI driver needs credentials at mount time, during NodePublishVolume. Where do you configure the secret reference so the kubelet can pass it to the driver?
options: Mount the secret into the CSI node DaemonSet; the driver reads credentials from disk
Put the credentials in the PersistentVolume's annotations
CSI drivers cannot receive secrets at publish time; use node-stage secrets only
In the StorageClass parameters: csi.storage.k8s.io/node-publish-secret-name and csi.storage.k8s.io/node-publish-secret-namespace — they are forwarded to the driver's NodePublishVolume call
explain: The CSI external-provisioner translates these well-known StorageClass parameters into the secrets passed at each CSI RPC stage (provision, controller-publish, node-stage, node-publish). node-publish-secret-name/namespace is the documented mount-time variant; baking secrets into the driver DaemonSet would share one credential across all volumes.

q: You expand a PVC from 10Gi to 20Gi (the StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true) while the pod is running. The PVC shows the condition FileSystemResizePending. What happens next?
options: FileSystemResizePending means the StorageClass forbids expansion
Shrink the PVC back; online expansion is not supported

The external-resizer already grew the block volume; the kubelet now calls the driver's NodeExpandVolume and resizes the filesystem online — no pod restart is needed when the driver supports node expansion
You must delete and recreate the pod for the filesystem to grow
explain: Expansion is two-phase: the external-resizer grows the volume (controller side), then the kubelet expands the filesystem in place (node side) for drivers advertising the EXPAND_VOLUME capability — the FileSystemResizePending condition marks the handoff. allowVolumeExpansion gates the whole flow, and shrinking is never allowed.

q: You need to clone a PVC from namespace team-a into namespace team-b. spec.dataSource only permits the same namespace. What enables cross-namespace cloning?
options: Copy the PersistentVolume object and change its namespace field
Add namespace: team-a inside the existing dataSource block
Cross-namespace cloning is impossible; use a backup tool instead
spec.dataSourceRef — the newer field that adds an optional namespace, enabling cross-namespace volume data sources (AnyVolumeDataSource) when the driver and RBAC allow it
explain: dataSource is the legacy same-namespace-only field. dataSourceRef generalizes it with an optional namespace for cross-namespace references (graduated with the AnyVolumeDataSource feature). PersistentVolumes are cluster-scoped and have no namespace to change.

q: A Deployment mounts a Secret with subPath: tls.crt. You update the Secret, but the pod still serves the old certificate a day later — while pods mounting the whole Secret received the update. Why?
options: subPath mounts are a one-time bind of the file: the kubelet does not propagate Secret/ConfigMap updates into subPath volumes. Recreate the pod (or avoid subPath for rotated data)
Secrets never update in running pods, with or without subPath
subPath requires the Secret to be re-applied with --force for updates to flow
The kubelet syncs subPath volumes on a 24-hour period; wait longer
explain: Whole-volume secret/configmap mounts are updated atomically by the kubelet via the projected-volume machinery — but subPath does a single bind-mount of one file at container start and never revisits it. This is the documented rotation trap: use full-volume mounts (or projected volumes) for anything that rotates, and recreate pods that used subPath.

q: Each replica of a StatefulSet must write to its own directory on a shared ReadWriteMany volume, named after the pod. Which volume feature does this?
options: hostPath with the pod name hardcoded per replica
subPathExpr with $(POD_NAME) — e.g. subPathExpr: data/$(POD_NAME). The kubelet expands downward-API variables per pod, unlike static subPath
subPath: $POD_NAME — environment variables expand in subPath
A volumeClaimTemplate per replica is the only way; subPath cannot vary
explain: subPathExpr evaluates a small set of downward-API variables ($(POD_NAME), $(POD_UID), etc.) per pod, giving each replica its own directory on a shared volume. Plain subPath does no expansion — $POD_NAME would be a literal directory name. volumeClaimTemplates are the heavier alternative (one PVC per pod).

q: A pod uses the default projected service-account token, which expires after about an hour. Does the pod need to be restarted when the token expires?
options: No — the kubelet refreshes projected bound tokens before expiry and updates the projected volume automatically; the app should re-read the token file instead of caching it forever
Yes — projected tokens are written once at pod start and never refreshed
No — expirationSeconds on projected tokens is advisory and never enforced
Only if automountServiceAccountToken is false
explain: Projected service-account tokens are bound, audience-scoped, and time-limited (expirationSeconds, default 3600s) precisely so they can rotate: the kubelet proactively refreshes the token (at ~80% of lifetime) and rewrites the volume. Apps must read the file per request (or watch it), not cache the first value.

q: Two pods on different nodes mount the same EBS-backed PVC (accessModes: ReadWriteOnce). The second pod stays Pending with a Multi-Attach error. What is the fix?
options: EBS volumes are ReadWriteOnce: attachable to one node at a time. For writers on multiple nodes you need a ReadWriteMany volume type (EFS, NFS, cloud filestore) — RWO cannot be shared across nodes
Add ReadWriteMany to the existing PVC's accessModes
Change volumeMode to Block; block volumes attach to many nodes
Delete the first pod; Multi-Attach resolves itself after 6 minutes
explain: accessModes describe what the VOLUME supports, and EBS only supports RWO. accessModes are immutable on a bound PVC, and no setting overrides the driver's capability. Multi-node shared writes require a RWX-capable backend (NFS/EFS/etc.). The 6-minute figure is the attach/detach reconciler period, not a fix.

q: A backup sidecar needs mounts created inside the main container to appear on the host and vice versa. You set mountPropagation: Bidirectional, but the pod is rejected at admission. What is required?
options: Use HostToContainer; it is equivalent to Bidirectional
Bidirectional mount propagation requires a privileged container (securityContext.privileged: true) — the API server rejects Bidirectional on non-privileged containers
Bidirectional requires hostPID: true instead of privileged
mountPropagation is set on the volume definition, not on the container's volumeMount
explain: Bidirectional propagation lets container mounts leak onto the host — a privileged operation, so Kubernetes requires privileged: true (HostToContainer only needs no such privilege... actually HostToContainer also has constraints, but Bidirectional is the one gated on privileged). mountPropagation is a per-volumeMount field, and HostToContainer is one-directional.

q: A PVC with storageClassName: '' (empty string) stays Pending even though a suitable PV with storageClassName: fast exists and is Available. Why will it not bind?
options: Empty storageClassName means 'use the default class'; the cluster must be missing its default

storageClassName: '' explicitly disables dynamic provisioning AND restricts binding to PVs with no storage class - it will never bind to the 'fast' PV. Set storageClassName: fast, or omit the field to use the default class
The PV must also set storageClassName: '' to match the claim
Static PVs cannot bind to any PVC that names a class, even an empty one
explain: The empty string is a deliberate opt-out: no dynamic provisioning, and binding only to classless PVs. To consume the 'fast' PV the claim must name that class (or omit the field to fall back to the cluster default). This is the classic static-provisioning mismatch.

q: New volumes must only be provisioned in zones us-east-1a and us-east-1b (1c has no capacity). Where do you enforce this for dynamic provisioning?
options: Pod nodeAffinity; the provisioner follows pod placement automatically
A ValidatingWebhookConfiguration on PersistentVolumes
allowedTopologies on the PVC spec
StorageClass.allowedTopologies with matchLabelExpressions on topology.kubernetes.io/zone — the provisioner only creates volumes in those zones
explain: allowedTopologies is a StorageClass-level constraint evaluated at provisioning time: the external-provisioner filters candidate zones before creating the volume. Pod affinity influences placement only with WaitForFirstConsumer and does not constrain the provisioner directly; the field lives on the StorageClass, not the PVC.

q: You need to make new-sc the default StorageClass instead of old-sc. What is the correct sequence?
options: Set the annotation true on both; the most recently created becomes the default
Delete old-sc; its default status transfers to new-sc automatically
The default is chosen by the provisioner, not by annotations
Set storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=false on old-sc and true on new-sc — only one class should carry the default annotation at a time
explain: The default StorageClass is designated by the storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true annotation. Marking two classes default is allowed by the API but ambiguous for PVCs without storageClassName — the documented procedure is to unset the old before (or as you) set the new. Deleting a class does not transfer anything.

q: Every volume provisioned from a StorageClass must be mounted with the noatime flag for a database workload. Where do you set this once for all dynamic volumes?
options: On each PVC spec
In the pod securityContext; mount flags are a per-pod setting
StorageClass.mountOptions: ['noatime'] — the kubelet applies these mount flags to every volume provisioned from the class
In the CSI driver's DaemonSet arguments
explain: mountOptions is the StorageClass field for mount flags (noatime, nosuid, etc.), applied by the kubelet at mount time for dynamically provisioned volumes. There is no mountOptions field on PVCs, and driver args do not control per-volume mount flags.

q: Pods with EBS volumes stay Pending with 'exceeded maximum number of volumes attached to node'. The node is otherwise healthy. What is the constraint?
options: The EBS CSI driver allows unlimited attaches; restart the driver
Delete the VolumeAttachment objects; they count against the limit
Cloud instance types cap how many volumes attach to one node — spread the pods across more nodes or use fewer volumes per pod; it is a node allocatable limit, not a scheduling bug
Raise --max-pods on the kubelet to lift the volume cap
explain: Every cloud block-storage driver documents per-instance attach limits (the scheduler models them as node allocatable 'attachable-volumes'). --max-pods is unrelated, the driver cannot exceed the cloud API limit, and VolumeAttachments are records of attachments, not the limit itself.

q: A CI job pod needs scratch space that lives exactly as long as the pod, provisioned from the default StorageClass. Which volume type fits, and what happens to the PVC?
options: emptyDir — it provisions from the StorageClass
A normal PVC, deleted manually in a postStop hook
CSI inline ephemeral — it creates a backing PVC automatically
A generic ephemeral volume (volumeClaimTemplate) — Kubernetes auto-creates a PVC for the pod and garbage-collects it when the pod is deleted
explain: Generic ephemeral volumes embed a volumeClaimTemplate in the pod spec: the ephemeral-volume controller creates the PVC (owned by the pod) and deletes it with the pod. emptyDir is node-local disk with no provisioning; CSI inline ephemeral volumes never create PVCs at all.

q: A secrets-store CSI driver documents ephemeral inline volumes. A pod uses csi: {driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io, volumeAttributes: {...}} with no PVC. How does the driver receive its Vault credentials?
options: Via nodePublishSecretRef on the inline volume — the kubelet passes the referenced Secret to the driver's NodePublishVolume call; inline ephemeral volumes never create PV/PVC objects
Credentials go in volumeAttributes in plaintext
Inline volumes cannot use secrets at all; use a projected volume instead
The driver reads the pod's service-account token automatically
explain: CSI inline ephemeral volumes support nodePublishSecretRef, letting the kubelet hand a Secret to NodePublishVolume without any PV/PVC indirection. volumeAttributes are for non-sensitive driver parameters; putting credentials there would expose them in the pod spec.

q: A database pod needs a raw block device and uses volumeDevices, but its PVC was created with volumeMode: Filesystem. The pod fails to start. What is the fix?
options: Change the pod to use volumeMounts; raw block devices work through volume mounts
Patch the PVC's volumeMode in place from Filesystem to Block
Recreate the PVC with volumeMode: Block - volumeMode is immutable, and volumeDevices requires a block-mode volume; a Filesystem volume can only be consumed via volumeMounts
volumeMode is a pod-level field; move it into the container spec
explain: volumeMode (Filesystem vs Block) is set at PVC creation and immutable. Block volumes are consumed via volumeDevices as raw devices with no filesystem; Filesystem volumes via volumeMounts. A mismatch means recreating the claim with the right mode - and the CSI driver must support block volumes.

q: A pod needs a local persistent volume whose PV has nodeAffinity for node-3, but the pod keeps landing on node-1 and stays Pending. What must the pod add?
options: Matching node affinity (or nodeSelector) for node-3 — the scheduler does not infer placement from the PV; the pod's own constraints drive where it can run and, with WaitForFirstConsumer, which PV can bind
Nothing — local PVs attract matching pods automatically via the provisioner
volumeBindingMode: Immediate on the StorageClass so the PV binds before scheduling
Taints on node-1 and node-2 to repel the pod
explain: Local volumes use no provisioner — binding is purely the scheduler matching the pod's node constraints against the PV's nodeAffinity. The scheduler never reads a PV to decide pod placement; the pod must declare node-3 affinity itself (this is also why local storage pairs with WaitForFirstConsumer).

q: A PersistentVolume with reclaimPolicy: Retain sits in Released state after its PVC was deleted. You want a new PVC to use that storage. What must happen first?
options: Delete the PV object; Retain preserves the underlying data for a fresh PV
Clear the PV's spec.claimRef (and clean the data if needed) — a Released PV is not automatically reusable; only as Available can it bind to a new claim
Nothing — Released PVs rebind automatically to the next matching PVC
Change reclaimPolicy to Delete; that recycles the volume for reuse
explain: Retain means 'keep the data and do nothing else': the PV goes to Released with its claimRef still pointing at the deleted claim, and it stays there until an admin clears claimRef (making it Available again) after handling the leftover data. Automatic rebinding is the behavior of dynamic provisioning, not Retain.

q: kube-proxy fails to start after you set --proxy-mode=ipvs: 'can't initialize ipvs: protocol not available'. iptables mode worked on the same nodes. What is missing?
options: IPVS mode requires booting the nodes into a real-time kernel
You must also set --proxy-mode=ipvs on the kubelet; the mode has to match

The IPVS kernel modules (ip_vs, ip_vs_rr, ip_vs_wrr, ip_vs_sh, nf_conntrack) are not loaded - IPVS is a kernel feature and kube-proxy cannot initialize it without the modules. Load them with modprobe on every node
IPVS was removed from kube-proxy; use nftables mode instead
explain: Unlike iptables mode, IPVS needs its kernel modules present. The fix is modprobe ip_vs and friends (persisted via /etc/modules-load.d) on all nodes, then restart kube-proxy. The --proxy-mode flag belongs to kube-proxy, not the kubelet.

q: The kubelet crashloops with 'running with swap on is not supported'. What is the required fix?
options: Set --fail-swap-on=false and continue running with swap enabled
Increase vm.swappiness to 100 so the kernel favors swap
Add more swap; the kubelet needs swap for memory accounting
Disable swap (swapoff -a) and remove it from /etc/fstab — the kubelet's fail-swap-on defaults to true and it refuses to start with swap enabled
explain: kubelet defaults to --fail-swap-on=true: any active swap is a hard startup failure, because swap breaks memory QoS guarantees and eviction accounting. The supported fix is swapoff plus removing the fstab entry so it survives reboot. The flag to ignore swap exists but defeats the safeguard the error is enforcing.

q: A node's /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem expired yesterday, rotation CSRs were never approved, and the node is NotReady. How do you recover it without rebuilding the node?
options: Copy kubelet client certificates from a healthy node
Run kubeadm certs renew kubelet-client on the node
Just restart the kubelet; it self-renews expired certificates without bootstrap credentials
Delete the expired client certificate files and restart the kubelet — it re-bootstraps using /etc/kubernetes/bootstrap-kubelet.conf, generates a new key and CSR, which you then approve
explain: kubeadm nodes keep a bootstrap kubeconfig with a bootstrap token precisely for this: with no valid client cert, the kubelet uses it to request a new certificate via the CSR API. Deleting the expired cert forces that path. Certificates are node-identity-bound (never copy them), kubeadm certs renew only handles control-plane PKI files, and without bootstrap credentials the kubelet cannot authenticate a new CSR.

q: kubectl describe node shows the condition KernelDeadlock: True, reported by node-problem-detector. What is the Node Problem Detector and how does it usually run?
options: Part of kube-proxy; it marks nodes unschedulable on network faults
An API server admission check that validates node health

A privileged DaemonSet that watches kernel logs/journald for problems (deadlocks, read-only filesystems, frequent kubelet/runtime restarts) and reports them as node conditions — it detects, it does not fix
A kubelet plugin that automatically reboots deadlocked nodes
explain: NPD runs as a DaemonSet on every node with host log access, translating kernel and system-log signals into NodeConditions (KernelDeadlock, ReadonlyFilesystem, FrequentKubeletRestart, FrequentContainerdRestart...). Remediation (reboot, drain) is left to external automation — NPD only surfaces the condition.

q: A node hits memory.available<100Mi. Pods are killed instantly: no SIGTERM handling, preStop hooks skipped, PDBs ignored. Is this a bug?
options: Only soft evictions skip grace; hard evictions are always graceful
No — that is a hard eviction threshold: no grace period, the kubelet kills immediately to reclaim the resource, and PDBs and terminationGracePeriodSeconds do not apply to node-pressure eviction
Yes — the kubelet must always honor terminationGracePeriodSeconds
The PDB was misconfigured; fix the PodDisruptionBudget
explain: Hard eviction thresholds exist to save the node: when memory.available<100Mi (the Linux default) trips, the kubelet kills pods immediately with no graceful termination. Node-pressure eviction deliberately bypasses PDBs and pod grace periods — the documented behavior, and the reason soft thresholds (with grace periods) exist as the gentler alternative.

q: You set kubelet eviction-hard to just ['memory.available<1Gi'], and later a disk-full node never evicts any pods. What happened to the other default thresholds?
options: Setting any eviction-hard value drops ALL other defaults to zero unless the kubelet config sets MergeDefaultEvictionSettings: true — you must specify the complete threshold set or enable merging
Disk thresholds are immutable defaults; the custom config was rejected
eviction-hard only accepts percentage quantities
The kubelet always merges custom values with the defaults automatically
explain: The documented gotcha: defaults (memory.available<100Mi, nodefs.available<10%, imagefs.available<15%, inodesFree<5%) apply ONLY if no threshold is customized. Change one without MergeDefaultEvictionSettings: true and the rest become zero — i.e. disabled. Disk pressure then never triggers eviction.

q: A node's image filesystem fills with old unused images until DiskPressure starts evicting pods. Which kubelet mechanism should have reclaimed that space, and at what thresholds?
options: The kubelet never deletes images; a CronJob running crictl rmi is required
Image GC triggers at 95% high / 90% low by default
Images are removed automatically every time their pod is deleted
Image garbage collection: triggered when usage exceeds --image-gc-high-threshold (default 85%), deleting unused images until usage falls to --image-gc-low-threshold (default 80%)
explain: The kubelet's image GC watches disk usage: above the high threshold it deletes images unused for longer than --image-minimum-gc-age until usage drops to the low threshold. If images accumulate to DiskPressure anyway, GC is misconfigured, overwhelmed, or the images are all 'in use'.

q: A CrashLoopBackOff container restarts after 10s, then 20s, 40s, 80s, 160s, then holds at 5 minutes between attempts. Is the backoff broken?
options: No — the kubelet uses exponential backoff capped at 300 seconds: 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, then 300s. The backoff resets after the container runs cleanly for 10 minutes
Yes — backoff should cap at 60 seconds
The cap is 30 seconds; something is stuck
Backoff only applies to liveness-probe failures, not crashes
explain: CrashLoopBackOff delay is exponential (10s doubling) with a 5-minute cap — the lengthening restart interval is the designed behavior, not a bug. It resets once the container stays up for 10 minutes. (ImagePullBackOff uses the same backoff.)

q: A node loses network connectivity. Its pods linger for about 5 minutes before being deleted and rescheduled elsewhere. What causes the 5-minute delay?
options: etcd compaction delays pod deletion by 5 minutes

Kubernetes auto-adds tolerations for node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable with tolerationSeconds: 300 — pods tolerate the NoExecute taint for 5 minutes before the taint-based eviction controller removes them
The kubelet waits out --node-monitor-grace-period, which is 5 minutes
Pods always get exactly 5 minutes of graceful termination
explain: When the node goes NotReady/Unknown, the taint-based eviction controller adds a NoExecute taint. Every pod carries auto-added 300s tolerations for not-ready/unreachable (unless explicitly overridden), so eviction waits 5 minutes — the buffer against transient network blips. DaemonSet pods get these tolerations without any timeout, so they are never evicted this way.

q: You need to inspect a node's host filesystem (e.g. /etc/cni/net.d) but have no SSH access. Which kubectl command gives you a root shell on the node's host?
options: kubectl ssh node/<node-name>
kubectl debug node/<node-name> -it --image=busybox — it starts a privileged debug pod on that node; run chroot /host to access the node's filesystem
kubectl exec into the kubelet's static pod
kubectl debug pod/<pod> --target=node
explain: kubectl debug node creates a privileged pod scheduled to the named node with the host filesystem mounted at /host — chroot /host gives a root shell on the node for CNI, kubelet, and runtime forensics. There is no kubectl ssh, and exec only reaches pod filesystems.

q: On a containerd node, crictl ps shows no containers even though pods are running. crictl is using default settings. What is the most likely cause?
options: crictl cannot communicate with containerd at all
Running containers are hidden from crictl by design
Use docker ps instead of crictl
Wrong containerd namespace or socket: Kubernetes containers live in the k8s.io namespace, and crictl must point at the right runtime endpoint (unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock)
explain: containerd isolates containers by namespace; kubelet uses k8s.io. A default crictl config may query the default namespace or the wrong socket and show nothing. Point crictl at the containerd socket and the k8s.io namespace (crictl --runtime-endpoint ... -n k8s.io, or /etc/crictl.yaml) to see pod containers.

q: Pod A shows a container with exit code 137 and reason OOMKilled. Pod B shows phase Failed with reason Evicted and a message about memory.available. What is the difference?
options: A exceeded its own container memory LIMIT (cgroup OOM killer) — raise the limit or fix the leak. B was killed by the kubelet for NODE memory pressure (an eviction threshold) — the node, not the pod's limit, ran out
Both are node-pressure evictions; 137 is just the numeric eviction code
OOMKilled means the node ran out of memory
Evicted pods restart automatically but OOMKilled pods do not
explain: OOMKilled (137) is the kernel OOM killer enforcing the container's memory limit — a per-container resource problem. Evicted is the kubelet enforcing node-level eviction thresholds — a node capacity problem; the pod's status shows why. Both honor the pod restartPolicy.

q: Your log aggregator needs machine-parseable kubelet logs with severity and timestamp fields. Which kubelet setting produces JSON structured logs?
options: Set --v=6; verbosity level 6 is JSON-encoded
Pipe journalctl through jq on each node
--logging-format=json — switches klog to structured JSON output instead of the default human-readable text format
--log-format=json on the API server only; the kubelet cannot emit JSON
explain: klog supports --logging-format=text (default) or json on all components including kubelet. JSON mode emits structured records with timestamp, severity, message, and key-value fields — what aggregators parse reliably. Verbosity only controls volume, not format.

q: A namespace vanished overnight. The audit policy logs RequestResponse level for delete verbs. How do you identify who deleted it?
options: Search the API server audit log for verb 'delete' with requestURI /api/v1/namespaces/<name> — user.username and sourceIPs identify the caller, and RequestResponse level preserves the requestObject
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Deleted
etcdctl get /registry/namespaces/<name>
Audit logs record the verb but never the user identity
explain: The audit log is the forensics source: each entry carries the requesting user (user.username, groups), source IPs, verb, requestURI, and — at RequestResponse level — the full object. Events do not record actors, and the etcd key is gone with the namespace.

q: Pods resolve cluster.local names fine, but all external names time out. The CoreDNS pods are Running. What is the most likely fault domain?
options: Upstream DNS: CoreDNS's forward plugin (typically . /etc/resolv.conf) points at unreachable upstream resolvers — check the Corefile forward target, node DNS, and CoreDNS logs for dial timeouts
The cluster domain is wrong; external names need a cluster.local suffix
kube-proxy is not proxying DNS traffic; restart kube-proxy
External resolution requires dnsPolicy: Default on every pod
explain: cluster.local working proves CoreDNS itself is healthy; external names go through the forward plugin to the node's upstream resolvers. Timeouts there mean the upstream path is broken (wrong /etc/resolv.conf on nodes, egress firewall, DNS outage) — check CoreDNS logs for 'dial udp ... i/o timeout' to confirm.

q: A new default-deny NetworkPolicy was rolled out, and now app pods log 'dial tcp: lookup auth.example.com: i/o timeout'. Pods in kube-system are unaffected. What is the diagnosis?
options: NetworkPolicy cannot affect DNS; check the pods' ndots setting

The policy blocks egress DNS: the selected pods cannot reach kube-dns on port 53 (UDP/TCP). Add an egress rule to the kube-dns pods on port 53; kube-system pods are unaffected because the policy does not select them
CoreDNS is down; the timeout proves the DNS server is unreachable for everyone
The app only needs an egress rule to auth.example.com on 443
explain: DNS lookup failure is the signature of denied port-53 egress after a default-deny rollout. kube-system pods keep working because the policy's podSelector does not match them. The fix is an egress allow for 53/UDP+TCP to kube-dns — and only then will the 443 egress rule to the auth host matter.

q: kubectl drain node-2 hangs with 'error when evicting pods ... PDB'. kubectl get pdb shows disruptionsAllowed: 0 and most of the app's pods are in CrashLoopBackOff. What are your options?
options: Delete the PDB, drain, and recreate it afterwards
Cordon the node instead; cordon evicts the pods

The PDB (default IfHealthyBudget) is protecting the unhealthy app: fix the crashloop so pods become healthy, or set unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow if evicting broken pods is acceptable. Drain will not override the budget
drain --force overrides PodDisruptionBudgets
explain: disruptionsAllowed: 0 means the budget is exhausted, and under the default IfHealthyBudget policy the Running-but-not-Ready (crashlooping) pods cannot be evicted while the app is disrupted. Either restore health or explicitly opt into AlwaysAllow. --force does not bypass PDBs, and cordon only stops new scheduling.

q: You are investigating yesterday's FailedScheduling warnings, but kubectl get events shows nothing older than about an hour. Why?
options: Events are stored in etcd forever; read them with etcdctl
kubectl get events defaults to --since=1h
FailedScheduling is only written to kubelet logs, never to events
Events expire: the API server garbage-collects events after their TTL (default --event-ttl of 1h). For history you need external event/log aggregation
explain: Events are a short-lived debugging aid with a 1-hour default TTL (configurable via kube-apiserver --event-ttl). Anything older is gone from the API — the reason production clusters ship events to external systems. FailedScheduling IS an event type; it just aged out.

q: A container restarted 5 minutes ago; the current logs show only startup lines. How do you see what it logged BEFORE the crash?
options: Use kubectl attach to replay the old logs
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous — it reads the terminated instance's logs. For init-container failures, address the init container with -c <init-name>
kubectl logs --since=5m shows the previous instance
Previous instances' logs are deleted by the kubelet on restart
explain: --previous targets the last terminated container instance, whose logs the kubelet retains until log rotation/GC removes them. Without it you only see the current (restarted) instance. Init containers are separate -c targets with their own previous instances.

q: An HPA targets 70% CPU but shows <unknown> and never scales, although metrics-server is healthy and kubectl top works. The Deployment's containers set no resources.requests. Why can the HPA not scale?
options: The HPA needs resources.limits, not requests, to compute utilization
metrics-server is healthy so the HPA controller itself must have crashed; restart kube-controller-manager
HPA computes utilization as usage divided by requested CPU - with no requests set there is no denominator, so utilization is <unknown>. Set resources.requests on the containers
<unknown> means the target is already exceeded; lower the target percentage
explain: CPU-utilization HPAs need requests: utilization percent equals actual usage divided by requested CPU. Without requests the ratio is undefined and the HPA cannot act, even with perfect metrics. (Autoscaling on raw metrics via type Pods or External avoids requests, but the standard CPU path needs them.)

q: A custom controller starts getting HTTP 429 errors from the API server under load. The metric apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total shows flow_schema='catch-all' with reason='concurrency-limit'. What does this tell you, and what is the fix?
options: The controller's requests match no custom FlowSchema, so they fall into the built-in catch-all FlowSchema — which has only one concurrency share and no queue, so it rejects excess traffic almost immediately. Create a dedicated FlowSchema (with an appropriate matchingPrecedence) pointing the controller's user or service account at a PriorityLevelConfiguration with real concurrency shares and queueing.
The API server is out of memory; increase its memory limits so it stops shedding load
etcd is overloaded and rejecting writes; add more etcd members to raise write throughput
The controller's RBAC permissions are wrong — 429 is the API server's way of reporting forbidden requests, so widen its ClusterRole
explain: APF classifies every request via FlowSchemas evaluated in increasing matchingPrecedence order; anything unmatched lands in the mandatory catch-all FlowSchema, whose priority level gets a single concurrency share and no queue — by design it 429s quickly to surface misclassification. The fix is classification, not capacity: write a FlowSchema matching the controller's identity and assign it a proper priority level. 429 is throttling, not RBAC (403) or etcd trouble.

q: You run two mutating webhooks. Webhook A injects a logging sidecar container into every pod; webhook B sets imagePullPolicy: Always on every container it sees. Pods end up with the sidecar running imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent while all other containers get Always. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Set failurePolicy: Ignore on webhook B so it retries until it observes the sidecar

Set reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded on webhook A (and make it idempotent). By default (Never) each mutating webhook runs at most once per admission, so B never sees the sidecar that A adds later in the chain; IfNeeded lets A be re-invoked after later plugins mutate the object.
Add a namespaceSelector to webhook A so it only fires in namespaces where B is disabled
Raise timeoutSeconds on both webhooks so B has time to wait for A's sidecar to appear
explain: reinvocationPolicy defaults to Never: a mutating webhook is called at most once per admission evaluation, so mutations made by webhooks ordered after it are invisible to it. IfNeeded re-invokes the webhook when later admission plugins modify the object (the webhook must be idempotent, and re-invocation count is not guaranteed to be exactly one). failurePolicy controls webhook-down behavior, timeoutSeconds bounds call duration — neither changes call ordering.

q: Your CISO asks: with the KMS provider configured, does the external key service see the plaintext of your Secrets, and what does key rotation actually involve?
options: The KMS provider generates the DEKs and stores them alongside the KEK, so rotation only requires deleting the old key version
KMS replaces etcd storage entirely — Secrets live in the key service, so rotation is just a key-service-side operation with no cluster work

No — Kubernetes uses envelope encryption: the API server generates a unique data-encryption key (DEK) per Secret, encrypts the Secret locally with it, and only the DEK is sent to the KMS provider to be encrypted by the key-encryption key (KEK). Rotation means configuring a new keyID in the EncryptionConfiguration, restarting the API servers, and rewriting every Secret so its DEK gets re-encrypted under the new KEK.
Yes — every Secret's plaintext is shipped to the KMS provider for encryption, so rotation is automatic and instant across the cluster
explain: The KMS provider never sees Secret plaintext: encryption is envelope-style, DEKs are generated and used locally by the API server, and only encrypted DEKs are stored in etcd. Because of that, rotating the KEK does not retroactively re-encrypt anything — you must point the config at the new keyID and rewrite all Secrets so each DEK is re-wrapped under the new key.

q: You are adding a fourth member to a healthy 3-member etcd cluster backing Kubernetes. The new member needs time to catch up on a large dataset. Which is the safest way to add it?
options: Add it as a full voting member immediately — a 4-member cluster tolerates 2 failures, so quorum is safer during the catch-up
Stop one existing member, copy its data directory to the new host, and start it with the same member ID
Take a snapshot, restore it on the new host with a fresh cluster token, and let the old members discover it via DNS SRV
Add it as a learner with etcdctl member add <name> --learner, let it replicate the full dataset without voting, then promote it with etcdctl member promote once it is caught up.
explain: A learner replicates data but does not vote and does not count toward quorum, so a slow catch-up cannot stall or break quorum the way adding an uncaught-up voting member can. Promotion is explicit once the learner is current. A 4-member cluster still only tolerates 1 failure (quorum of 4 is 3), so adding a voter gains nothing during catch-up and risks availability; member IDs must be unique per member.

q: Your EncryptionConfiguration lists two entries for secrets: first an aesgcm provider, then an aescbc provider. A teammate claims new Secrets are encrypted with aescbc because it appears last and 'overrides'. Who is right?
options: Neither override theory holds: the API server uses the FIRST provider listed for a resource when encrypting new data — so new Secrets use aesgcm. Order matters exactly like audit policy rules.
The teammate is right — later entries override earlier ones, so new Secrets use aescbc
Both providers encrypt every Secret, layered — reads try aesgcm first, then aescbc
The API server refuses to start with two providers for the same resource and logs a duplicate-provider error
explain: EncryptionConfiguration is an ordered list: the first matching entry supplies the provider used to encrypt newly written data; the remaining entries are only tried, in order, when decrypting (which is what makes provider migration possible). Listing aesgcm before aescbc is precisely the documented migration pattern — new writes use the new provider while old data still decrypts.

q: A node is tainted with maintenance=true:NoExecute. A pod tolerates it with tolerationSeconds: 300. The taint stays on the node. What happens to the pod?
options: The pod is evicted after 300 seconds and automatically rescheduled onto the same node once the taint is removed
The pod keeps running for 300 seconds, then the kubelet evicts it because the taint is still present when the toleration expires.
The pod runs forever — any toleration of a NoExecute taint is permanent once the pod is scheduled
The pod is evicted immediately — tolerationSeconds only applies to NoSchedule taints
explain: tolerationSeconds sets a time-limited tolerance for NoExecute taints: the pod may stay on the tainted node only for that duration, then it is evicted (the 5-minute default you see for the built-in node.kubernetes.io/unreachable and not-ready taints is the same mechanism with an implicit 300s). Eviction does not reschedule the pod itself — its controller creates the replacement, and the replacement cannot land on the still-tainted node without its own toleration.

q: A pod's nodeAffinity lists two required nodeSelectorTerms: term 1 requires label zone=a, term 2 requires label ssd=true. A node is labeled zone=a but has no ssd label. Does the pod schedule on that node?
options: No — every nodeSelectorTerm must be satisfied, so the node fails the ssd=true term
No — required nodeAffinity terms are ANDed across different label keys by design
Yes — nodeSelectorTerms are ORed, so satisfying any single term is enough; the node matches term 1. (Inside one term, multiple matchExpressions are ANDed.)
Yes — but only because zone=a is a well-known label; custom labels in a second term are ignored
explain: The documented rule: multiple terms in nodeSelectorTerms are ORed (one satisfied term suffices); multiple matchExpressions inside a single term are ANDed (all must hold). To demand zone=a AND ssd=true, put both expressions in ONE term. Mixing this up is the classic affinity bug — pods landing on half-matching nodes.

q: A team wants GPU-like scheduling for a custom accelerator without writing a device plugin, using Dynamic Resource Allocation. They put the claim reference under spec.volumes and the pod never starts. What is wrong?
options: The claim needs a StorageClass — DRA reuses the storage provisioning path, so no class means no allocation
DRA claims must be referenced in spec.containers[].resources as example.com/accel: 1, exactly like extended resources
Nothing is wrong — DRA allocates lazily after the pod starts, so they should wait for the first container to request the device

ResourceClaims are not volumes — the pod must reference the claim in spec.resourceClaims (a claim name or an inline ResourceClaimTemplate). The scheduler then waits for the DRA driver to allocate the claim before the pod starts.
explain: With DRA, allocation is decoupled from the container: the pod declares spec.resourceClaims entries pointing at ResourceClaim objects (or embedded ResourceClaimTemplates that get materialized per pod), and the scheduler only places the pod once the DRA driver reports the claim allocated. Stuffing it into spec.volumes is a category error — volumes are mounts, claims are allocations.

q: A DPDK pod requests hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi and mounts an emptyDir with medium: HugePages. It sits Pending with 'Insufficient hugepages-2Mi' on every node, though the nodes have 64Gi RAM free. What is the actual problem?
options: HugePages must be pre-allocated on the node at boot (kernel hugepagesz/hugepages parameters) — free regular RAM is irrelevant. Until the node OS reserves the huge pages, the kubelet reports zero allocatable hugepages-2Mi.
The scheduler cannot see hugepages — you must add a nodeSelector for nodes with the hugepages feature gate enabled
emptyDir with medium: HugePages is deprecated; the pod must use a hostPath mount at /dev/hugepages instead
The pod needs limits, not requests — hugepages are only allocated from the limits field
explain: The kubelet only advertises hugepages the kernel pre-allocated; no boot-time reservation means zero allocatable hugepages-2Mi regardless of free RAM. The pod spec itself is correct — requests plus medium: HugePages is the documented pattern — the fix is node-level: reserve the pages in the kernel and the capacity appears.

q: An inference pod needs its 4 exclusive CPUs and its GPU on the same NUMA node to avoid cross-socket latency. CPU manager static is enabled and the pod is Guaranteed with integer CPUs, but cpuset shows CPUs spread across both sockets. What is missing?
options: Nothing — the static policy already guarantees NUMA alignment; the cpuset output is showing logical, not physical, core IDs

The topology manager policy: set --topology-manager-policy=single-numa-node on the kubelet (it requires the static CPU manager policy). Without it, CPU manager allocates exclusive CPUs without NUMA alignment to the device.
Set --cpu-manager-policy=none — the static policy pins CPUs but ignores topology, while none lets the kernel align them
Add topologySpreadConstraints with topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname — that constrains the pod to one NUMA node
explain: CPU manager static gives exclusive CPUs but, on its own, picks them without regard to NUMA locality of allocated devices. --topology-manager-policy=single-numa-node makes the HintProviders (CPU manager, device manager) agree on one NUMA node, and admission fails if alignment is impossible. topologySpreadConstraints spreads pods across nodes/zones — a different layer entirely.

q: You create an HTTPRoute with correct rules and backendRefs, but no traffic ever arrives and kubectl get httproute shows no status parents. The Gateway exists in another namespace. What is missing?
options: The kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation — Gateway API still routes through the ingress class mechanism
HTTPRoutes only attach to Gateways in the same namespace — cross-namespace routing is not supported

The HTTPRoute's parentRefs — a route binds to a Gateway only through parentRefs naming the Gateway (and optionally listener/port). Without it the route is orphaned; also check the Gateway listener's allowedRoutes permits routes from the route's namespace.
A GatewayClass must be referenced in the HTTPRoute's spec.gatewayClassName field
explain: Gateway API attachment is explicit: parentRefs on the route point at the parent Gateway (cross-namespace is normal — that is the point of parentRefs), and each Gateway listener decides which routes it accepts via allowedRoutes (same-namespace, selector, or all). No parentRefs means the route binds to nothing, which is exactly the empty-status symptom.

q: After deleting an old test Ingress, the team discovers the DNS record for the production app on the same external-dns instance is gone too. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
options: The Ingress controller deletes DNS records on Ingress removal by design — switch to Gateway API, which never touches DNS
CoreDNS cached a negative response — flush the CoreDNS cache and the record returns
The TXT registry record expired — increase --txt-cache-interval so ownership records survive Ingress deletion

external-dns was running with --policy=sync: it mirrors cluster state to DNS, so deleting the Ingress deleted its DNS record. Run with --policy=upsert-only if you want external-dns to only create/update records and never delete them.
explain: external-dns in sync policy treats DNS as a mirror of desired state derived from Services/Ingresses: remove the source object and it removes the record. That is by design for GitOps-style management, but upsert-only is the safer mode when humans also manage the zone — it creates and updates but never deletes.

q: DNS lookups are slow under load and CoreDNS pods are saturated. You deploy NodeLocal DNSCache. Afterwards, what do pods use as their resolver, and where do cache misses go?
options: Pods resolve via the link-local address 169.254.20.10 served by the node-local-dns DaemonSet on their own node; on a cache miss the local instance forwards upstream to the CoreDNS Service (kube-dns). CoreDNS stays the authority — the cache just absorbs the hot path.
The DaemonSet replaces CoreDNS entirely; the CoreDNS Deployment should be scaled to zero after the rollout
Pods use the node's host /etc/resolv.conf nameserver — the cache only accelerates host-network pods
Pods keep using the CoreDNS ClusterIP — NodeLocal DNSCache works by transparently intercepting that IP with iptables on each node
explain: NodeLocal DNSCache binds 169.254.20.10 on every node (pods get it via clusterDNS/dnsConfig), caches aggressively with the local Corefile, and forwards misses to the kube-dns upstream. It is a caching proxy in front of CoreDNS, not a replacement; CoreDNS still answers everything the cache cannot.

q: After a domain migration, clients still query legacy.example.com but the records now live under new.example.com in CoreDNS. Which CoreDNS plugin and directive answers legacy queries with the new records without duplicating zone data?
options: The forward plugin with legacy.example.com in its except list — that keeps the query in-cluster
The rewrite plugin: rewrite name regex legacy.example.com new.example.com — it rewrites the query name before the kubernetes/other plugins answer, so one zone definition serves both names.
The template plugin with an ANY query — it synthesizes answers for arbitrary names
The hosts plugin — add legacy.example.com entries pointing at the same IPs
explain: rewrite name (exact or regex) renames the incoming query before the rest of the plugin chain processes it, so the existing zone/plugin data for new.example.com answers queries for legacy.example.com. hosts is for static exact entries, template synthesizes records from Go templates (overkill here), and forward sends queries upstream — none of which reuses the in-cluster data.

q: As the cluster grows from 10 to 200 nodes, DNS latency climbs even though CoreDNS CPU looks fine per-replica. What is the standard fix, and how is it sized?
options: Switch CoreDNS to the forward-only plugin — removing the kubernetes plugin halves per-query CPU
Increase the CoreDNS cache TTL to 24h — fewer upstream queries means the existing replicas can absorb the growth

Run CoreDNS behind the cluster-proportional autoscaler (dns-autoscaler) in linear mode — replicas scale with nodes and/or cores (e.g. 1 replica per N nodes), which matches DNS load far better than per-replica CPU, since DNS pressure grows with cluster size, not CPU.
Add an HPA on CoreDNS CPU at 50% — the per-replica CPU will drive replicas up as query load grows
explain: DNS query volume correlates with pods/nodes, not with CoreDNS CPU (which stays flat while latency climbs due to queueing). The standard pattern is dns-horizontal-autoscaler with linear mode: coresPerReplica/nodesPerReplica (commonly ~1 replica per 25-50 nodes). CPU-based HPA reacts too late and to the wrong signal.

q: You need dynamic NFS provisioning. The in-tree volume list has no NFS provisioner, so you deploy nfs-subdir-external-provisioner. What provisioner name must the StorageClass use?
options: nfs.csi.k8s.io — the external provisioner registers under the CSI driver name
kubernetes.io/nfs — the in-tree NFS provisioner handles dynamic provisioning once the module is loaded on nodes
Any name works — the provisioner is selected by the reclaimPolicy, not the provisioner field

cluster.local/nfs-subdir-external-provisioner (or whatever PROVISIONER_NAME the deployer set) — the StorageClass provisioner field must exactly match the name the external provisioner registers with; plus server and share parameters for the NFS export.
explain: There is no in-tree dynamic NFS provisioner; dynamic NFS comes from the external nfs-subdir-external-provisioner, and binding works by exact string match between StorageClass.provisioner and the provisioner name it was deployed with (default cluster.local/nfs-subdir-external-provisioner). A mismatch means PVCs sit Pending with 'no provisioner found' events.

q: You try to clone a PVC with dataSource naming a PVC in another namespace. The API server rejects it. Why?
options: Cloning via dataSource only works within the same namespace — the source PVC must live in the target PVC's namespace, with kind: PersistentVolumeClaim and apiGroup: '' (empty). Cross-namespace cloning is not supported by the core API.
Cloning requires the source PV's reclaimPolicy to be Retain — with Delete the API server refuses as a safety measure
The apiGroup must be snapshot.storage.k8s.io — plain PVC-to-PVC cloning requires the snapshot API group
The source PVC must be unbound — you cannot clone from a PVC that is currently mounted
explain: Volume cloning (dataSource/dataSourceRef to PersistentVolumeClaim) is strictly same-namespace in core Kubernetes; the API validates the group/kind and the namespace locality. For cross-namespace copies the supported path is VolumeSnapshots (same-namespace restore) plus external tooling — not a direct dataSource reference.

q: Pods mounting a 500Gi volume take 6+ minutes to start; kubelet logs show a long recursive chown on every mount even though the volume already has the right group. Which setting fixes this, and what is its default?
options: Set fsGroupChangePolicy: Never — the default is OnRootMismatch and it is broken for volumes over 100Gi

Set fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch in the pod securityContext — it skips the recursive ownership change when the volume root already matches. The default is Always, which re-chowns the whole tree on every mount.
Remove fsGroup entirely — fsGroupChangePolicy defaults to Always and cannot be changed per pod
Set runAsGroup instead of fsGroup — runAsGroup implies OnRootMismatch behavior by default
explain: fsGroup triggers a recursive chown/chmod at mount time, and the default policy Always does it unconditionally — brutal on large volumes. OnRootMismatch checks only the volume root and skips the recursion when it already matches, cutting minutes to seconds. (It has no effect on ephemeral volume types like configMap/secret/emptyDir.)

q: You need a new PVC seeded from yesterday's VolumeSnapshot. What does the dataSource block look like?
options: dataSource: name: <snapshot-name>, kind: PersistentVolumeClaim, apiGroup: '' — snapshots are referenced as PVCs
dataSourceRef with kind VolumeSnapshotContent — you reference the content object, not the snapshot
dataSource: name: <snapshot-name>, kind: VolumeSnapshot, apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io — in the same namespace as the snapshot, with a StorageClass whose provisioner supports snapshot restore.
Snapshots can only seed volumes via Velero restores — the core API has no snapshot-to-PVC path
explain: Restoring from a snapshot is a dataSource naming the VolumeSnapshot in the snapshot.storage.k8s.io API group (same namespace for dataSource restores). The CSI external-snapshotter plus provisioner do the actual restore; a provisioner without snapshot support leaves the PVC Pending.

q: A 100Gi PV with no storageClassName sits Available, but a 50Gi PVC requesting storageClassName: fast-ssd stays Pending. Capacity and access modes are compatible. Why no bind?
options: The PV is too large — a PVC only binds a PV within 10% of the requested size
The PV needs nodeAffinity — classless PVs cannot bind without a node pin
The PVC must be in the same namespace as the PV — PVs are namespaced to their creation namespace

StorageClass must match: a PVC that requests a class only binds PVs with that same class (and a classless PV only binds a classless PVC). The PV needs storageClassName: fast-ssd — or the PVC must drop the class request.
explain: Binding is a three-way match: storageClassName equality (including empty-equals-empty), accessMode compatibility, and capacity >= request. Class mismatch is the silent one — describe the PVC and the events spell it out. PVs are cluster-scoped (not namespaced), and larger PVs bind fine to smaller requests.

q: A Running pod intermittently fails to reach a backend Service. Its image has no diagnostic tools and you must not restart it. How do you capture traffic from the pod's network namespace?
options: kubectl debug -it pod/<name> --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- tcpdump -i any — the ephemeral container joins the running pod (same network namespace) with full tooling, no restart and no change to the workload image.
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- tcpdump — exec works even when the binary is absent from the image
Copy the pod with kubectl debug --copy-to and capture there — a copy shares the live pod's network namespace
Run tcpdump on the node — pod traffic never leaves the node, so node-level capture sees the same packets with pod IPs
explain: Ephemeral debug containers share the target pod's namespaces (network always; pid with --target), so netshoot's tcpdump sees the pod's actual traffic — the live namespaces, not a copy's. exec cannot conjure binaries the image lacks, node-level capture loses the pod context, and --copy-to creates new namespaces, which defeats the purpose.

q: A pod is stuck in CreateContainerConfigError. kubectl describe shows: 'secret "app-creds" not found'. The Deployment references it in envFrom. What is the diagnosis and fix?
options: The kubelet's --config is invalid — CreateContainerConfigError refers to the kubelet's own configuration file

The Secret app-creds does not exist in the pod's namespace (typo in the name, wrong namespace, or never created). Create it (or fix the reference) — kubelet cannot even create the container until every referenced config object resolves.
The node's container runtime is out of disk — config errors are a symptom of image pull failures; run crictl rmi to free space
The container image is corrupt — CreateContainerConfigError means the image config JSON failed to parse; repush the image
explain: CreateContainerConfigError is the kubelet telling you container creation failed before the runtime was ever involved — almost always a missing/unresolvable Secret or ConfigMap referenced by env, envFrom, or volumeMounts (including a bad key in secretKeyRef). The container never starts, so image/runtime/node-disk theories do not fit; create the object or correct the reference.

q: A container restarts every few minutes. How do you tell whether the kubelet's liveness probe is killing a healthy-but-slow app versus the app itself crashing?
options: There is no way to distinguish them — both paths produce identical container statuses
Restart count alone decides — more than 5 restarts always means the liveness probe is at fault

Compare events and lastState: liveness kills are preceded by 'Liveness probe failed' events and the old container's logs stop abruptly (often exit 137 from SIGKILL); app crashes show no probe failures but a fatal error in the app's own logs and lastState.terminated with the app's real exit code/reason (e.g. OOMKilled, Error).
Check the scheduler events — probe kills are recorded as FailedScheduling events on the node
explain: The evidence differs: liveness kills are preceded by 'Liveness probe failed: ...' events and the terminated container often shows exit code 137 (SIGKILL from kubelet) with the app logs stopping mid-stream; genuine crashes show the app's own fatal log/exit code (e.g. OOMKilled, exit 1 with a traceback) and no probe-failure events. Read events + lastState + previous logs (--previous) together.

q: kubectl apply of a Deployment fails with: 'exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: cpu=2, used: cpu=7900m, limited: cpu=8'. The cluster has free capacity. What is the fix?
options: Add more nodes — the error means the scheduler cannot find 2 free CPUs anywhere in the cluster
Delete the LimitRange — LimitRanges cap total namespace CPU and this one is set to 8
Set the Deployment's resources to zero — quota only counts pods that declare requests
It is a ResourceQuota ceiling, not a capacity problem: the namespace has used 7.9 of its 8-CPU quota and the new pods need 2 more. Either raise the quota or lower the pods' CPU requests.
explain: ResourceQuota admission rejects the create before scheduling ever happens: used + requested would exceed the quota's hard limit, so the API server says no regardless of free cluster capacity. The math is right in the message (7.9 + 2 > 8). Fix the quota or the requests — adding nodes changes nothing because scheduling was never reached.

q: A developer reports 'Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden: User "dev" cannot list resource "deployments" in namespace "team-a"'. What is the fastest way to check what they CAN do, and what does the error imply?
options: kubectl auth can-i list deployments --as=dev -n team-a (and --list) — it answers authorization directly. The error is RBAC: no Role/ClusterRole grants that verb on that resource in that namespace; fix the binding, not the API server.
Check the audit log for 403s — auth can-i only works for service accounts, not human users
Restart the API server with --authorization-mode=RBAC — Forbidden means authorization is misconfigured globally
kubectl get clusterroles --as=dev — listing cluster roles shows the user's effective permissions
explain: auth can-i evaluates the RBAC graph for any subject (users included, via --as) without guessing: it tells you exactly which verbs are allowed where. A Forbidden on one verb/resource/namespace is a missing or mis-scoped binding — widen the Role or add the binding. The API server is enforcing policy correctly; restarting it changes nothing.

q: On a 1.28 cluster, setting kubelet --dynamic-config-dir fails with 'unknown flag'. A blog says to enable the DynamicKubeletConfig feature gate. What is actually going on?
options: The gate is now called DynamicKubeletConfigV2 — enable it on the API server and the flag reappears
Dynamic kubelet configuration was deprecated in 1.22 and REMOVED in 1.24 — the flag no longer exists and the feature gate is gone. Configure the kubelet via its config file (--config) instead.
The flag moved to the controller-manager — set it there and the kubelet picks it up via the API
It only works on control-plane nodes — workers never supported dynamic config
explain: DynamicKubeletConfig was removed entirely (KEP retired, code deleted in 1.24), not renamed or moved — no gate re-enables it. The supported path is the kubelet config file referenced by --config (dropped in place and kubelet restarted, or managed by your provisioning). Blog posts predating the removal are the trap.

q: Pods using imagePullSecrets pull fine from your private registry, but you want pull-through without per-namespace secrets, so you configure a kubelet credential provider exec plugin. New nodes still get 401s. What did you most likely miss?
options: The plugin must be registered as a MutatingWebhookConfiguration so it can inject credentials into pod specs
Credential providers only work with docker.io — private registries still require imagePullSecrets in each namespace

The plugin binary and its config must exist on every node: the kubelet reads --image-credential-provider-config (matching registry host patterns via matchImages) and executes the plugin binary from --image-credential-provider-bin-dir at pull time. A config applied only to the API server or a missing binary on the node means the kubelet never calls it.
You need to restart the API server — the kubelet reads credential provider config from etcd via the API
explain: Image credential providers are kubelet-local: the kubelet matches the image's registry against matchImages in its provider config file and execs the plugin binary on the node to mint a short-lived token (with caching). Nothing about this flows through the API server or admission — if the binary/config is absent on the node, pulls fall back to anonymous and 401.

q: You are writing a scheduler plugin for gang scheduling (all-or-nothing pod groups). At which extension point can the scheduler park a pod and wait for its gang-mates before binding it to a node?
options: Filter — it can hold the pod in the scheduling queue until the gang is complete
PostBind — it runs after binding and can roll the bind back if the gang is incomplete
Score — a score of zero keeps the pod unassigned until its mates arrive
Permit — it runs after a node is selected (post Reserve) and can approve, deny, or wait with a timeout before the pod proceeds to PreBind/Bind.
explain: The framework order is PreFilter → Filter → PostFilter → PreScore → Score → NormalizeScore → Reserve → Permit → PreBind → Bind → PostBind. Only Permit supports wait: it can pause binding (with timeout) until a condition is met — the exact hook coscheduling plugins use. Filter only accepts/rejects nodes, Score only ranks, and PostBind runs after the bind is done.

q: You want batch jobs bin-packed onto as few nodes as possible so the cluster autoscaler can remove empty nodes. Which kube-scheduler scoring strategy does that, and which does the opposite?
options: MostAllocated packs pods onto the most-utilized nodes (bin-packing); LeastAllocated spreads them onto the emptiest nodes. Set the NodeResourcesFit plugin's scoringStrategy accordingly.
RequestedToCapacityRatio with shape points is the only strategy; LeastAllocated/MostAllocated were removed in 1.24
Scoring strategies only apply to the TaintToleration plugin — NodeResourcesFit is filter-only
LeastAllocated bin-packs; MostAllocated spreads — the names describe the nodes they avoid
explain: NodeResourcesFit scores two ways: LeastAllocated favors nodes with the most free capacity (spread), MostAllocated favors the fullest feasible nodes (pack, which is what you want for scale-down). RequestedToCapacityRatio is a separate scoring plugin for shaped utilization curves, and NodeResourcesFit does both filtering and scoring.

q: A cert-manager Certificate has stayed not-ready for an hour. kubectl describe certificaterequest shows an Order, and the Challenge is pending with 'Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation'. The solver pod is running. What is the most likely cause?
options: Delete the Certificate — cert-manager only processes Certificates created before the Issuer

The self-check is failing: cert-manager's solver pod must reach the challenge URL through your ingress from inside the cluster. If ingress routing, DNS, or a firewall blocks that path, the challenge never completes — check the Challenge events and curl the token URL yourself.
The Certificate's renewBefore is too short — increase it so cert-manager retries the Order sooner
The solver pod needs a valid certificate itself — install the CA into the solver pod's trust store
explain: HTTP-01 requires the CA (via cert-manager's self-check first) to fetch http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token> served through your ingress. The classic failure is reachability: hairpin NAT, wrong ingress class on the solver ingress, or DNS not resolving in-cluster. The Challenge resource's events narrate each check — start there, not with renewBefore or re-creation.

q: You set --cpu-manager-policy=static on the kubelet and it refuses to start, logging that a CPU reservation greater than zero is required. Why?
options: Static policy requires --reserved-cpus to list every CPU on the node — a partial reservation is rejected
Static policy is incompatible with cgroup v2 — the node must be reverted to cgroup v1 first

The static policy manages a shared pool plus exclusive CPUs; the kubelet requires --kube-reserved/--system-reserved (or --reserved-cpus) greater than zero so the shared pool can never be empty — system daemons and non-exclusive pods need somewhere to run.
The error is misleading — it actually means the feature gate CPUManagerPolicyAlpha is not enabled
explain: With static, exclusively-allocated CPUs are carved out of the shared pool; if reservations were zero, the shared pool could drain to nothing and BestEffort/Burstable pods plus system processes would have no CPUs. The kubelet enforces a nonzero reservation up front rather than failing weirdly at runtime. --reserved-cpus pins exact CPUs; kube/system-reserved carve integer CPUs from the pool's low end.

q: A pod requests nvidia.com/gpu: 1 but sets limits nvidia.com/gpu: 2, expecting burst capacity. The API server rejects the pod. Why?
options: The scheduler ignores extended resources in requests — only limits are evaluated, so the request line must be deleted
GPU requests must use the resource name gpu.example.com/v1 — nvidia.com/gpu is only valid in limits
Fractions are allowed for GPUs (e.g. 0.5) — the rejection is because 1 and 2 are integers, which GPUs do not support

Extended resources cannot be overcommitted: request and limit must be equal when both are set, and quantities must be whole numbers. Devices also cannot be shared between containers — the device plugin assigns whole devices.
explain: Device-plugin resources are extended resources: integer-only, no overcommit (request == limit if both present), no sharing between containers. The API server validates the equality — set both to 1 (or just the limit, which the docs use in examples). Fractional GPUs need vGPU/MPS solutions, not plain device plugins.

q: A debugging tool inside a container needs to see host-level /proc entries (like /proc/sysrq-trigger). The pod sets securityContext.procMount: Unmasked. What does this change, and what is the risk?
options: Unmasked lifts the container runtime's masking of sensitive host /proc paths — the container sees the real host proc entries. Risk: it exposes host kernel interfaces; combined with capabilities the container can poke host-level knobs, so reserve it for trusted debug pods.
It enables the pod to write to /proc/sys on the host without any capabilities — equivalent to privileged mode
It mounts the host's /proc at /host/proc — read-only and safe, the standard monitoring pattern
procMount is a kubelet flag, not a pod field — setting it in the pod spec is silently ignored
explain: procMount has two values: Default (runtime masks sensitive host /proc paths like sysrq-trigger and core pattern) and Unmasked (the mask is lifted). It does not remount anything — it just stops hiding. It is not a privilege grant by itself, but combined with capabilities it widens the blast radius, so it belongs on locked-down debug tooling, not app pods.

q: A pod sets sysctls: net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time=600 and fails with 'forbidden sysctl'. The same manifest with kernel.shm_rmid_forced works. What distinguishes them?
options: The pod needs privileged: true — sysctls are ignored unless the container is privileged

kernel.shm* are in the safe sysctl set (namespaced and considered isolated); net.* sysctls are unsafe and disabled by default — the kubelet must explicitly allow them with --allowed-unsafe-sysctls on each node.
net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time does not exist — the kernel renamed it, so the kubelet rejects unknown sysctls
Safe sysctls are set via annotations; the sysctls field only accepts unsafe ones, so kernel.shm_rmid_forced should also fail
explain: Kubernetes splits sysctls into safe (enabled by default: kernel.shm*, kernel.msg*, kernel.sem, etc.) and unsafe (net.*, others) which are off unless the kubelet's --allowed-unsafe-sysctls permits them per node. The pod spec is fine — the node configuration is what forbids it. Privileged is unrelated to the sysctl allowlist.

q: A pod sets spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault, but one container needs a custom localhost profile. How do you configure it, and what wins?
options: Pod-level seccomp always wins — per-container profiles are merged, with the pod's syscalls taking precedence
You must use the deprecated annotation seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod — the field API does not support per-container overrides

Set securityContext.seccompProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: <path>} on that container — container-level seccomp overrides the pod-level setting; other containers inherit RuntimeDefault. (Privileged containers always run Unconfined regardless.)
Set type: Localhost at the pod level — localhostProfile paths are resolved relative to the container image, so one pod-level entry covers all
explain: seccompProfile exists at both pod and container level (plus init/ephemeral containers); the container-level value wins over the pod default, and unset containers inherit the pod's. Localhost profiles live on the node under the kubelet's seccomp root (<root-dir>/seccomp), not in the image. The annotation syntax predates v1.19 and is long retired.

q: A hostNetwork: true monitoring pod sets dnsPolicy: Default so it can resolve the company's internal domains via the node's resolver. Now it cannot resolve ClusterIP Service names. Why, and what is the correct dnsPolicy?
options: The pod needs hostPort 53 — without it, DNS replies cannot route back through the host network namespace
Set dnsPolicy: None with manual nameservers — ClusterFirstWithHostNet is only valid for non-hostNetwork pods
hostNetwork pods cannot use cluster DNS at all — service discovery requires a sidecar proxy on the host

dnsPolicy: Default makes the pod inherit the host's resolv.conf verbatim — no cluster DNS search domains or cluster nameserver. For host-network pods that also need service discovery, use ClusterFirstWithHostNet: cluster DNS first, with host-network semantics.
explain: dnsPolicy: Default = pure host resolv.conf, so cluster.local names are unknown. ClusterFirstWithHostNet exists precisely for host-network pods: kubelet configures the cluster DNS server while keeping host-network semantics (unlike ClusterFirst, which assumes pod networking). None with hand-rolled dnsConfig is the escape hatch when you need full control.

q: A LoadBalancer Service uses externalTrafficPolicy: Local. One node has no pods for the Service, but the cloud LB still sends it traffic. What do clients see, and why?
options: Connection refused/timeouts for traffic hitting that node — with Local, packets are never forwarded cross-node, so traffic arriving at an endpoint-less node is dropped instead of being rerouted. The LB should be health-checking nodes (via healthCheckNodePort, which only answers where endpoints exist) to keep such nodes out of rotation.
The Service stops working entirely — Local requires every node to run at least one endpoint
