Clients are transparently redirected — kube-proxy forwards the packets to a node that has endpoints
Traffic is load-balanced normally — externalTrafficPolicy only affects the source IP, not routing
explain: externalTrafficPolicy: Local disables cross-node forwarding so the client's source IP is preserved; the tradeoff is that a node without local endpoints drops the traffic (there is nothing to forward to). Correct LB health checking (via healthCheckNodePort, which only answers on nodes with endpoints) keeps such nodes out of rotation — when health checks are wrong or missing, blackholing is the symptom.

q: An ingress-nginx setup serves the right certificate for browsers but old clients without SNI get a certificate mismatch error. The Ingresses all specify their own tls secrets. What is missing?
options: A wildcard tls secret on every Ingress — SNI-less clients require the wildcard to be duplicated per host

A default TLS certificate: --default-ssl-certificate on the ingress-nginx controller. Non-SNI clients never send a hostname, so the controller cannot select per-host certs and falls back to the default (a self-signed fake cert unless you configure a real one).
A second Ingress without host rules — the controller picks the first Ingress's certificate for non-SNI clients
The ssl-redirect annotation — without it, non-SNI clients are served over HTTP and the TLS handshake fails
explain: TLS host selection happens via SNI during the handshake; clients that do not send SNI get whatever --default-ssl-certificate points at (default: the controller's bundled fake certificate). Browsers work because they send SNI and match per-Ingress tls blocks. Point the default at a real cert covering your apex/legacy clients.

q: You write a custom controller that creates EndpointSlices for a headless Service directly. Endpoints appear in your slices, but kube-proxy ignores them and DNS has no records. What did you forget?
options: An Endpoints object with the same name — EndpointSlices are only read if a legacy Endpoints object exists
The slice's addressType must be IPv4 — IPv6 or FQDN address types are ignored by kube-proxy

The kubernetes.io/service-name: <svc> label on each EndpointSlice — kube-proxy, CoreDNS, and the endpointslice controller key off that label to associate slices with a Service. Without it your slices are orphans.
The endpointslices.discovery.k8s.io finalizer — without it, kube-proxy garbage-collects the slices immediately
explain: The service-name label is the join key: the built-in endpointslice controller sets it when mirroring, and consumers (kube-proxy, CoreDNS's kubernetes plugin) list slices by it. Manually-created slices without the label are invisible to all of them. Finalizers, legacy Endpoints, and addressType are red herrings — FQDN addressType is valid and legacy Endpoints are not required.

q: Under heavy UDP load (DNS-heavy workloads), dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' and queries intermittently fail, while TCP is fine. What is happening?
options: CoreDNS is rate-limiting — the table-full message is CoreDNS's way of reporting its max-concurrent-queries ceiling
etcd is throttling — DNS failures under load are always an etcd quorum symptom
The CNI ran out of IP addresses — conntrack entries are allocated per pod IP, so add a larger pod CIDR

The conntrack table is exhausted — every UDP 'connection' (including DNS) consumes an entry until its timeout, and kube-proxy in iptables mode relies on conntrack for Service DNAT. Raise nf_conntrack_max (and check kube-proxy's conntrack sizing) or lower the UDP timeout; TCP is unaffected because its entries recycle faster under this pattern.
explain: conntrack tracks every flow for NAT; short-lived UDP bursts (DNS) churn entries faster than the default table/timeouts absorb, and once full the kernel drops new flows — reads as intermittent DNS failure. The fix is kernel-level (nf_conntrack_max, nf_conntrack_udp_timeout) plus kube-proxy's conntrack sizing flags, not CoreDNS or IPAM.

q: A singleton database must guarantee that no second pod ever mounts its data volume — even on the same node — to fence against split-brain after a network partition. Why is ReadWriteOnce insufficient, and what do you use?
options: RWO is single-NODE: multiple pods on the same node can all mount an RWO volume. Use ReadWriteOncePod (CSI drivers only) — it is enforced single-pod, cluster-wide, and cannot be combined with other access modes.
RWO already guarantees single-pod — the second mount attempt fails at the CSI driver with no config change needed
Set the pod's nodeName — pinning the pod to a node is what makes RWO single-pod
Use ReadWriteMany with a file lock — Kubernetes delegates single-writer enforcement to the application's lock file
explain: ReadWriteOnce constrains to one node, not one pod — two pods scheduled on the same node can both mount it. ReadWriteOncePod closes that hole at the Kubernetes layer: exactly one pod cluster-wide may use the volume. That is the fencing primitive for singleton writers; RWO plus wishful thinking is how split-brains happen.

q: A database wants raw block storage (no filesystem) for its data volume. What must the PVC/PV and pod spec declare?
options: Nothing special — any PVC can be used as raw block by opening the mount path with O_DIRECT
volumeMode: Block on the PV/PVC and a volumeDevices entry (devicePath, e.g. /dev/xvda) in the container instead of volumeMounts — the raw device appears at that path with no filesystem formatting.
volumeMode: Filesystem with fstype: raw — the CSI driver skips mkfs when fstype is raw
A volumeMount with mountPropagation: Bidirectional — block devices are exposed through the mount namespace
explain: volumeMode: Block tells Kubernetes not to format or mount a filesystem; the pod consumes it via volumeDevices[].devicePath as a raw device node. volumeMounts always imply a filesystem. The provisioner/driver must support block volumes (most CSI block drivers do).

q: A ConfigMap is mounted with subPath: nginx.conf at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf. After updating the ConfigMap, the file in the pod never changes, while a second plain mount of the same ConfigMap updates within a minute. Why?
options: kubelet syncs subPath mounts on a 10-minute period instead of 1 minute — wait longer and it appears
The ConfigMap update failed validation — subPath mounts pin the resourceVersion, so the API server rejected the edit

subPath mounts are bind-mounts of a single file resolved at container start — kubelet's atomic symlink-swap update mechanism only refreshes whole-directory mounts. subPath (file or dir) never receives updates; recreate the pod to pick up changes.
subPath requires the ConfigMap to be marked immutable — mutable ConfigMaps are silently ignored by subPath
explain: Whole ConfigMap/Secret volume mounts are updated by kubelet swapping a ..data symlink (kubelet sync period ~1m); subPath mounts bypass that mechanism entirely — they bind the resolved file at start and never re-resolve. This is documented and by design: use subPath for stable single files, accept pod recreation (or a reloader sidecar) for changing ones.

q: A pod needs one directory containing: a ConfigMap file, a Secret file, the pod's namespace, and CPU limit info — all under /etc/podinfo. What is the cleanest volume to use?
options: The downwardAPI volume alone — it can project ConfigMaps and Secrets as well as pod fields
An emptyDir populated by an init container that cats the four sources together
Four separate volumes mounted at the same path — Kubernetes merges volume contents at identical mountPaths
A projected volume with four sources (configMap, secret, downwardAPI x2) mounted once at /etc/podinfo — projected volumes merge multiple source types into a single directory.
explain: projected is the union volume: configMap, secret, downwardAPI, and serviceAccountToken sources combined under one mount. Four mounts at one path do not merge (last mount wins/hides), downwardAPI only projects pod fields and container resources, and the init-container copy is unnecessary machinery.

q: A pod is Evicted with 'Usage of EmptyDir volume exceeds the limit'. The container's memory limit was never reached. What happened?
options: The emptyDir declared sizeLimit, and the data written there exceeded it — emptyDir sizeLimit is enforced against ephemeral-storage, and breaching it evicts the pod. Container memory limits are a separate accounting domain.
The kubelet confused emptyDir with memory — emptyDir always counts against the container's memory limit
The image's writable layer filled — emptyDir shares the container's overlay filesystem quota
sizeLimit is advisory — the eviction means the node's disk actually filled up (DiskPressure)
explain: emptyDir.sizeLimit caps that volume's usage against the pod's ephemeral-storage (not RAM, not the container memory limit); exceeding it triggers pod eviction by the kubelet. Without sizeLimit, emptyDir is bounded only by node disk (DiskPressure eviction). The message names the volume, so the fix is raising sizeLimit or writing less.

q: Creating a pod with cpu request 100m fails: 'minimum cpu usage per container is 500m'. No quota is configured. What enforces this?
options: The container runtime — containerd enforces a 500m minimum CPU share per container
The scheduler's NodeResourcesFit plugin — it refuses pods that would fragment CPU allocation
A LimitRange in the namespace with min.cpu=500m — LimitRange admission enforces per-container min/max and can inject defaults. Either raise the request to 500m or adjust the LimitRange.
The default ResourceQuota — every namespace gets an implicit 500m minimum CPU quota
explain: LimitRange is the per-container constraint admission: min/max per container (and per pod), plus default request/limit injection for pods that omit them. The error text is LimitRange's signature. Quotas bound namespace totals, the scheduler never rejects creates, and the runtime has no such minimum.

q: A bad validating webhook (failurePolicy: Fail) now rejects EVERY create/update, including attempts to fix workloads. You fear even kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration broken-hook will be rejected. Can you recover?
options: Use --validate=false on the delete — client-side validation bypasses the webhook
Restart the API server with --disable-admission-plugins=ValidatingAdmissionWebhook to bypass it once
No — with failurePolicy: Fail the cluster is bricked until the webhook's backing service is restored

Yes — ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects are never sent to admission webhooks, so the API server always allows operating on them. The delete succeeds; a broken webhook can never make the cluster unrecoverable this way.
explain: The API server deliberately exempts ValidatingWebhookConfiguration/MutatingWebhookConfiguration from admission webhooks so a broken webhook can never make the cluster unrecoverable — you can always delete or fix the configuration object itself. --validate=false only skips kubectl-side schema validation, and restarting the API server is unnecessary.

q: Writes to the cluster start failing with 'etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded' and etcd raises a NOSPACE alarm. The db file is near 2Gi. What is the fix?
options: Free backend space: run etcdctl defrag (reclaims fragmented space after compaction — compaction alone only marks revisions free, it does not shrink the file), and raise --quota-backend-bytes if the dataset legitimately needs more room. The alarm clears once space is available.
Run an etcd snapshot restore — restoring compacts the database and clears the alarm
Add two more etcd members — more members share the data so each stays under quota
Run compaction only — compacting revision history shrinks the db file immediately
explain: NOSPACE fires at --quota-backend-bytes (default 2Gi): etcd goes read-only for writes. Compaction reclaims revision history logically but does NOT shrink the file — defrag does. Snapshot restore is for quorum loss/corruption, not space; new members copy the same-sized db. Also set auto-compaction retention so history does not balloon again.

q: Pods stop scheduling onto a node that is Ready, and kubectl describe node shows Taints: node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure:NoSchedule. Pods already there keep running. What does this mean?
options: The node is cordoned — uncordon it to allow scheduling again

The kubelet detected disk pressure and tainted the node NoSchedule — new pods avoid it, but existing pods are NOT evicted by a NoSchedule taint (that would need NoExecute). Free disk space (images, logs, emptyDir) to clear the condition.
The disk is full so the kubelet is down — the Ready status is stale and the node needs a reboot
All pods on the node will be evicted within 5 minutes — NoSchedule taints always escalate to eviction
explain: Kubelet node-pressure taints (disk/memory/PID pressure) are NoSchedule: they steer new pods away while leaving running pods alone. Only a NoExecute taint evicts. DiskPressure specifically means image/container/ephemeral-storage disk usage crossed thresholds — clean with crictl rmi, log rotation, or bigger disks; uncordon is for the manual cordon taint, a different thing.

q: A pod fails with ImagePullBackOff; describe shows 401 Unauthorized from the private registry. The imagePullSecret exists — in the default namespace — but the pod runs in team-a. What is the fix?
options: Set the secret's type to kubernetes.io/tls — registry auth requires a TLS-type secret, not dockerconfigjson
Restart the pod — 401s are transient and the backoff will resolve once the registry token refreshes
Copy the Secret into team-a (imagePullSecrets are namespaced) and reference it there — kubelet only looks for pull secrets in the pod's own namespace.
Add imagePullSecrets to the kubelet config — pull secrets are node-scoped, so one copy per node covers all namespaces
explain: imagePullSecrets resolve strictly within the pod's namespace; a same-named secret elsewhere is invisible to the kubelet. (ErrImagePull to ImagePullBackOff is just the backoff progression on repeated failures.) The registry secret type stays kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson with a .dockerconfigjson payload — TLS type is for certs, not registry auth.

q: Your audit webhook backend receives events in bursts every 30 seconds instead of a steady stream. Which audit setting controls this batching delay, and what is the tradeoff of lowering it?
options: The webhook's timeoutSeconds — the API server holds events until the backend's timeout elapses
omitStages — skipping RequestReceived removes the buffering stage entirely

batch-max-wait (with batch-max-size) — it caps how long the API server buffers audit events before flushing. Lowering it delivers events faster but increases request count/load on the webhook backend.
max-batch-before-rotation — it controls log rotation, and lowering it speeds up webhook delivery
explain: Webhook audit mode batches: batch-buffer-size queues events, batch-max-size caps a single request's events, and batch-max-wait caps the delay before a partial batch is sent. The 30s bursts are max-wait in action. Lower it for fresher forensics at the cost of more backend requests; raise it to smooth load. (Batch mode also means a dead backend drops events once the buffer fills rather than blocking the API.)

q: A kubeadm join command generated yesterday now fails with 'the token is expired'. The cluster CA and certs are all valid. What happened and what is the fix?
options: The node was already registered — run kubeadm reset on the worker and the old token reactivates
Join tokens are single-use — every node needs a token created with --usages=single
The cluster certificates expired — run kubeadm certs renew all on the control plane, then retry the join
Bootstrap tokens default to a 24h TTL — the join token expired. On a control-plane node run kubeadm token create --print-join-command to mint a fresh one (and re-fetch the CA hash if needed).
explain: kubeadm bootstrap tokens live 24 hours by default (check with kubeadm token list); expiry is the routine cause of stale join commands. Minting a new token with --print-join-command gives a fresh token plus discovery hash. Certificates last a year and produce different errors; tokens are multi-use until they expire.

q: You seal a Secret for the staging namespace, then apply the SealedSecret in production. The sealed-secrets controller logs a decryption scope error and no Secret appears. Why?
options: Default (strict) scope binds the sealed secret to its name AND namespace — it can only be decrypted into a secret with the same name in the same namespace it was sealed for. Re-seal it for production (or use namespace-wide/cluster-wide scope annotations deliberately).
SealedSecrets are cluster-scoped objects — applying one in a different namespace is silently ignored
The production namespace needs the sealed-secrets controller's public cert as a Secret before any decryption works
The controller's key rotated — sealed secrets can only be decrypted with the key version active at seal time
explain: Strict scope (the default) seals name+namespace into the ciphertext; the controller refuses to materialize it elsewhere — that binding is the theft-protection. namespace-wide scope allows renaming within the namespace; cluster-wide allows any name/namespace (weaker, use sparingly). The fix here is sealing per target namespace, not key management.

q: A custom operator's LIST calls against a huge cluster fail at exactly 60 seconds, but kubectl get --watch sessions stay up for hours. Which API server behavior explains both?
options: Watches bypass --request-timeout only when --watch-cache is enabled — the operator needs watch-cache=true

--request-timeout (default 60s) bounds normal API requests, but long-running requests — watches, exec attach, log streaming, portforward — are exempt. The operator should paginate (limit/continue) instead of one giant LIST.
The API server kills all connections at 60s — kubectl get --watch reconnects transparently, which is why it appears stable
The 60s failures are etcd compaction — raise --etcd-compaction-interval to match the watch duration
explain: request-timeout defaults to 60s for regular requests; the API server deliberately exempts long-running verbs (WATCH, proxy/exec/attach/portforward/logs -f) because they are streams by nature. A giant LIST is a regular request — the correct fix is client-side pagination, not raising the global timeout (which just moves the cliff).

q: You enable a beta feature gate on the kube-apiserver and restart it, but the scheduler still behaves the old way. What did you miss?
options: Feature gates require etcd to be restarted too — the gate state is stored in the cluster, not the binaries
Beta gates cannot be enabled manually — they are locked until the feature graduates to GA

Feature gates are per-component: the gate must be set (and the component restarted) on every binary that implements the feature — typically kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, and kubelet. Setting it on one does nothing for the others.
You must also set it in the EncryptionConfiguration — gates are validated against the encryption providers
explain: A feature gate is a process flag, not cluster state: each component binary reads its own --feature-gates at startup. Scheduler-side behavior needs the gate on kube-scheduler, kubelet-side on kubelet, and so on. Forgetting one component is the classic 'I enabled it but nothing changed' — check every static pod manifest / systemd unit.

q: Three zones hold 2, 2, and 1 matching pods. maxSkew: 1, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone. Where can the next pod schedule?
options: Any zone — maxSkew 1 permits a difference of one, and 3/2/1 has max difference 2 which rounds down
Only the zones with 2 pods — the scheduler fills the fullest zones first to minimize skew
Nowhere — 2/2/1 already violates maxSkew 1, so all scheduling is blocked until a pod is deleted
Only the zone with 1 pod — the global minimum is 1, so placing into a 2-pod zone would make its skew (3-1=2) exceed maxSkew 1. It becomes 2/2/2.
explain: With DoNotSchedule, maxSkew is the max allowed gap between the target zone's count and the global minimum (min over eligible domains, here 1). 2→3 in a full zone gives skew 2 > 1: rejected. Only the zone at the minimum accepts the pod. 2/2/1 does not violate anything — skew is measured per-placement, not as a pre-existing condition.

q: The descheduler's RemovePodsViolatingInterPodAntiAffinity strategy evicts most offending pods but consistently skips one pod that uses an emptyDir volume. Why?
options: The default evictor filter excludes pods with local storage (emptyDir/hostPath) — evicting them destroys their data with no rescheduling safety. Adjust the descheduler profile's evictor filter if you accept the data loss.
Inter-pod anti-affinity violations are only logged, never acted on — the strategy name is aspirational
emptyDir pods are mirror pods — the descheduler can never evict static pod mirrors
The pod has a PodDisruptionBudget — PDBs block all descheduler evictions unconditionally
explain: Descheduler's DefaultEvictor refuses (by default) to evict mirror/static pods, DaemonSet pods, pods with local storage, and pods without controllers — all cases where eviction loses data or the pod cannot come back. emptyDir data dies with the pod, so it is filtered. PDBs are honored too, but the local-storage filter is the specific reason here; the fix is an explicit profile choice, not a PDB change.

q: Cluster-autoscaler manages three identical node groups (one per zone). Under load it scales up only group A, leaving B and C empty, which skews your topologySpread. Which setting fixes this?
options: Set the expander to random — random selection across groups naturally balances them
balance-similar-node-groups: true — it makes the autoscaler treat similar node groups as one pool and keep their sizes balanced instead of piling new nodes into whichever group it picked first.
Add a nodeSelector to the autoscaler Deployment — it then only manages the labeled group
Enable scale-down-unneeded-time — faster scale-down rebalances the groups automatically
explain: By default the autoscaler scales the single 'best' node group per iteration, which concentrates growth. balance-similar-node-groups detects groups with the same instance type/labels and balances new nodes across them — the intended fix for zone-skewed scale-up. The expander picks between DIFFERENT node types for a pending pod; it does not balance identical groups.

q: A high-priority pod shows nominatedNodeName: node-3 in its status but remains Pending for several minutes. What does this mean?
options: The pod was rejected by node-3 — nomination means the node refused it and the scheduler is retrying elsewhere
The scheduler crashed mid-cycle — nominatedNodeName is only set when the scheduler restarts unexpectedly

Preemption is in flight: the scheduler nominated node-3 and is waiting for the lower-priority victim pods to terminate (including their grace periods). The pod binds once they are gone; if it stays Pending, check that the victims are actually terminating.
nominatedNodeName is advisory — the pod will actually schedule to a different node once capacity appears
explain: nominatedNodeName records where the scheduler INTENDS to place the pod after preemption completes — it is set before the victims finish terminating, so a Pending pod with a nomination is mid-preemption, not stuck. Only if victims hang (e.g. very long terminationGracePeriodSeconds or finalizers) does the nomination linger; the scheduler will not re-nominate elsewhere while it waits.

q: A Job runs a main container plus a logging agent as a regular sidecar container. The Job never completes — the agent keeps the pod alive after the main container exits. What is the native fix (1.29+)?
options: Set the pod's restartPolicy: Never — sidecars then exit automatically with the main container
Set activeDeadlineSeconds on the Job — the kubelet then SIGKILLs sidecars when the main container exits
Add a preStop hook to the agent that exits when the main container's PID disappears — the standard sidecar pattern

Move the agent to initContainers with restartPolicy: Always — native sidecars start before app containers, restart on failure, and are terminated after the main containers finish, so the Job can complete.
explain: Regular containers share the pod's lifecycle, so a long-running helper blocks Job completion (the pod never reaches Complete). Native sidecars (init container + restartPolicy: Always, beta on-by-default since 1.29) get proper startup ordering AND shutdown-after-mains semantics — the kubelet tears them down once app containers finish, letting the Job complete. preStop PID-watching is the old hack this replaces.

q: You convert an Ingress with pathType: Prefix path /api to an HTTPRoute with path type PathPrefix /api. After cutover, requests to /apiv2 start hitting the backend, though the Ingress never routed them there. What changed?
options: Prefix semantics differ: Ingress Prefix matches on path ELEMENTS (/api matches /api/v1 but not /apiv2), while Gateway API PathPrefix is a plain string prefix (/api matches /apiv2). The conversion widened the match — use a more specific match or a regex.
HTTPRoute PathPrefix is element-based like Ingress — the /apiv2 traffic is coming from a different route
Nothing changed — both are string prefixes; /apiv2 must have been routed by the Ingress too and nobody noticed
Ingress Prefix requires a trailing slash — /api only matched /api/ before, so the route actually narrowed
explain: This is the documented conversion gotcha: Ingress Prefix splits on '/' and matches whole segments, so /api never matches /apiv2; HTTPRoute PathPrefix is 'request path begins with value' string matching, so it does. Mechanical Ingress-to-Gateway conversions must audit every Prefix path for sibling paths that now collide.

q: A NetworkPolicy needs to allow egress to NodePort-range ports 30000-32767 on cluster nodes. Listing 2,768 ports is absurd. What is the correct field?
options: port: 30000-32767 — port accepts a dash range string directly
ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 30000, endPort: 32767}] — endPort defines an inclusive range starting at port. (endPort must be >= port.)
NetworkPolicies cannot express ranges — you must allow each port with a separate policy object
Use an ipBlock with the node CIDR and omit ports — ipBlock entries allow all ports by default
explain: endPort turns one port entry into an inclusive range — the intended tool for NodePort/ephemeral ranges. The dash-string is not valid syntax, omitting ports from an ipBlock rule allows ALL ports (too broad, and the wrong direction of intent), and separate objects per port is unmanageable.

q: You set allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false on a LoadBalancer Service to save NodePorts. Afterwards the cloud LB marks all nodes unhealthy. Why?
options: The Service lost its ClusterIP — allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false also disables cluster IP allocation
kube-proxy stops programming any rules for the Service — without NodePorts it cannot DNAT load-balancer traffic

Many cloud LB integrations health-check nodes via the auto-allocated healthCheckNodePort — with NodePort allocation disabled there is no health-check port, so the LB's probes fail and nodes look unhealthy. Either keep NodePorts allocated or switch the LB to a working health-check path.
The cloud controller deletes the LB — a LoadBalancer Service without NodePorts is invalid and gets garbage-collected
explain: healthCheckNodePort is carved from the NodePort range on demand; disabling NodePort allocation removes the port the cloud provider's node health check targets. ClusterIP and kube-proxy programming are unaffected — the breakage is specifically the health-check path most cloud LBs default to.

q: kubectl get pods shows 40 pods, but new pods fail with 'no available IP addresses' from the CNI IPAM. Node after node reports its subnet exhausted. What is the likely cause?
options: The podCIDR is too small — 40 pods cannot fit in any default podCIDR, so expand --cluster-cidr
IPAM counts init containers as pods — each init container consumes an additional IP
The CNI allocates one IP per container — a 40-pod cluster with 3 containers each needs 120 IPs

Leaked IPAM allocations: if the CNI DEL fails (or the runtime never calls it, e.g. after unclean kubelet/containerd restarts), IPs stay allocated in the IPAM store while no pod uses them. Reconcile with your CNI's garbage-collection tooling instead of just widening CIDRs.
explain: IP exhaustion with few live pods is the signature of leaked allocations: ADD without a matching DEL leaves the address marked used. Common triggers are crashed runtimes, force-deleted pods, or CNI binary errors on teardown. The fix is CNI-specific reconciliation (IPAM GC), not CIDR expansion — though chronic leaks do warrant checking the CNI's cleanup path.

q: In an IPv6 single-stack cluster, a pod resolves a ClusterIP Service. What record type does it get, and what does the Service's clusterIP look like?
options: AAAA records, and the clusterIP is an IPv6 address from the configured service CIDR. Everything — pod IPs, ClusterIPs, kube-proxy rules — is v6; there are no A records for cluster services.
Both A and AAAA — CoreDNS always answers dual-stack regardless of the cluster's IP family
AAAA records, but the clusterIP stays IPv4 — Services are always IPv4, only pod IPs are IPv6
A records with NAT64-mapped IPv4 — single-stack v6 clusters synthesize A records via the cluster DNS
explain: Single-stack means one family everywhere: service-cluster-ip-range is an IPv6 CIDR, ClusterIPs are IPv6, pods get IPv6, and DNS serves AAAA. There is no NAT64 synthesis in vanilla Kubernetes DNS — clients must be v6-capable. (Dual-stack is the separate mode with ipFamilies/ipFamilyPolicy.)

q: A team deletes a test PVC and the cloud disk vanishes along with the data. They expected the PersistentVolume to linger for inspection. What happened?
options: Kubernetes always deletes backing storage with the PVC — there is no policy to prevent it

Dynamically provisioned volumes default reclaimPolicy to Delete (taken from the StorageClass) — deleting the PVC deletes the PV and the backing storage. Set reclaimPolicy: Retain on the StorageClass for data that must survive the claim.
The PVC was in the default namespace — PVCs elsewhere are protected from storage deletion
The CSI driver malfunctioned — Delete only removes the PV object, never the backing disk
explain: reclaimPolicy governs release behavior: Delete (the dynamic-provisioning default) wipes the PV and the external volume when the PVC is deleted; Retain keeps both for manual handling. The surprise comes from assuming Retain — for anything stateful you care about, set Retain on the class deliberately.

q: You define a PV with an iscsi volume: targetPortal, iqn, and lun. Pods stay in ContainerCreating with 'failed to log in to iSCSI target'. The target is reachable. What node-level prerequisite is commonly missed?
options: iSCSI requires a StorageClass — static iscsi PVs are rejected without one
The PV needs volumeMode: Block — iscsi volumes cannot be used with Filesystem mode

The iSCSI initiator tooling and configuration on the node (iscsid running, initiator name set, CHAP credentials if the target requires them via chapAuthDiscovery/chapAuthSession secrets). Kubernetes does not install or configure open-iscsi for you.
The IQN must match the pod's name — Kubernetes validates initiator IQN against the workload identity
explain: The in-tree iscsi volume just orchestrates login/mount — the node must already have a working initiator stack (iscsid, initiatorname.iscsi, multipath if used). CHAP goes through the referenced secrets; without the daemon running, login fails exactly as described. Filesystem mode is the normal iscsi use; StorageClass is optional for static PVs.

q: A pod sets fsGroup: 2000, but files on its CSI volume stay root-owned and the app gets permission denied. The CSIDriver object for the driver sets fsGroupPolicy: None. What is happening?
options: SELinux is relabeling the files — fsGroupPolicy governs SELinux contexts, not ownership
The pod also needs fsGroupChangePolicy: Always — fsGroupPolicy only takes effect when the change policy is Always
fsGroupPolicy: None is invalid — the CSIDriver object is rejected and the volume never mounts, so the real error is elsewhere

fsGroupPolicy: None tells Kubernetes to skip ALL fsGroup ownership changes for that driver's volumes — the driver opted out, so the kubelet never chowns anything. The application (or an init container) must manage permissions itself; a policy of ReadWriteOnceWithFSType (the default) or File would have applied them.
explain: CSIDriver.spec.fsGroupPolicy lets each driver declare whether Kubernetes should attempt recursive ownership changes: ReadWriteOnceWithFSType (default — apply when it makes sense), File (always attempt), or None (never attempt — e.g. drivers for storage without POSIX ownership). With None, fsGroup/fsGroupChangePolicy on the pod are silently inert for that driver's volumes, so permission setup moves into the image or an init container.

q: You try to shrink a PVC from 20Gi to 10Gi to save cost. The API server rejects the change. Why?
options: Shrinking a PVC is never supported — the API rejects any decrease. Only expansion is allowed, and only when the StorageClass sets allowVolumeExpansion: true (and the new size exceeds the current one).
Shrinking requires reclaimPolicy: Retain — with Delete the API server blocks size decreases as a safety measure
The driver only supports offline expansion — shrinking requires the pod to be deleted first
The PVC shows FileSystemResizePending — you must wait for the pending resize to finish before shrinking
explain: Volume shrinking is not implemented in Kubernetes — period. The API validates that the requested size is greater than the current size whenever allowVolumeExpansion permits changes at all. To use less storage, provision a new smaller PVC and migrate the data.

q: You create local PersistentVolumes for SSDs on specific nodes, but pods keep getting scheduled to nodes without the disk and hang in ContainerCreating. What is missing on the PV?
options: Pods must use nodeName — the scheduler cannot place local volumes without an explicit nodeName

nodeAffinity on the PV pinning it to the node(s) with the disk — local volumes are tied to a node, and without nodeAffinity the scheduler can bind the PVC to a PV whose disk is elsewhere. Pair it with a WaitForFirstConsumer StorageClass so binding waits for scheduling.
A StorageClass with provisioner: kubernetes.io/local — static local PVs require the in-tree local provisioner
The volumeMode must be Block — local volumes only work as raw devices
explain: local PVs must carry nodeAffinity (the local static provisioner generates this; hand-made PVs need it explicitly) — it is the only thing telling the scheduler which node the storage lives on. Without it, binding is node-agnostic and the pod lands wrongly. WaitForFirstConsumer defers binding until the pod is scheduled, letting the scheduler choose a compatible PV.

q: An app needs 3 minutes to warm up. The liveness probe (initialDelaySeconds: 30) kills it mid-startup, causing a crash loop. What is the proper fix?
options: Set successThreshold: 3 on the liveness probe — three successes in a row prove the app is up

Add a startupProbe — while the startup probe runs, liveness and readiness probes are disabled; liveness only starts after startup succeeds. It handles variable startup times that no fixed initialDelaySeconds can cover.
Increase timeoutSeconds on the liveness probe — a longer timeout lets the slow startup finish
Decrease periodSeconds — more frequent checks detect readiness sooner and stop the kills
explain: startupProbe exists for slow-starting containers: it gates the liveness/readiness probes until it succeeds (with its own failureThreshold x periodSeconds budget), so a 3-minute warmup no longer races a fixed initialDelaySeconds. timeoutSeconds/periodSeconds tune a running probe; they do not pause it during startup. successThreshold > 1 is not even allowed on liveness probes.

q: kubectl get events shows a confusing interleaved list from the last hour while debugging a rolling failure. How do you get a clean chronological view, and what is events' retention limit?
options: Events are retained for 24 hours by default — just widen --since to see the full incident
kubectl logs --events — the events subresource streams directly from kubelet journals with full history

kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp (often with -A and --field-selector); the API server only keeps events for about 1 hour (etcd TTL), so older history is gone — check external logging for anything earlier.
kubectl get events --watch --sort-by prints them sorted — watch mode is required for chronological order
explain: Events are etcd objects with a 1-hour TTL (the API server prunes them) — they are a recent-signal tool, not an audit trail. --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp orders them; combine with namespace/all-namespaces and field selectors (involvedObject.name=...) to isolate the incident. For anything older than an hour you need shipped logs or the audit log.

q: After hand-editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, the API server never comes back. kubectl cannot connect. Where do you look first, and what is the likely cause?
options: Check etcd — a bad manifest corrupts the etcd-stored pod object, so restore etcd from snapshot
Run kubeadm init again — a failed static pod means the control plane must be re-bootstrapped
kubectl get pods -n kube-system — the static pod will show CrashLoopBackOff with the parse error in its logs

On the node: journalctl -u kubelet for manifest parse errors — the kubelet refuses to start a static pod with invalid YAML/fields, and there is no API server to report it. Fix the manifest; kubelet picks up the change automatically.
explain: Static pods are files, not API objects: with the API server down there is nothing for kubectl to query. The kubelet logs the manifest error (bad indentation, unknown field, bad volume path) and keeps retrying. Fix the file in place — kubelet watches the directory and restarts the pod. etcd is untouched by manifest edits.

q: A pod defines two init containers; the first completes, the second is stuck in ImagePullBackOff, and the app container was never created — not even attempted. Why?
options: Init containers run sequentially and must ALL complete before any app container starts — the pod is gated on the second init container's image. Fix the image name/tag/registry access for the init container; the app cannot start early.
The pod needs restartPolicy: Always — with the default policy, init failures permanently block app containers
App containers start in parallel with init containers — the app should be running; its absence means the scheduler failed
Delete the init containers — they are optional and the kubelet skips them when their images are unavailable
explain: The init-container barrier is absolute: each init container runs to completion in order, and app containers start only after the last one succeeds. An unpullable init image therefore blocks the entire pod — by design (they often provision config the app needs). The fix is the image/reference, not the restart policy.

q: A ClusterIP Service answers nothing — curl hangs. kubectl get endpoints my-svc shows <none>, but the pods are Running. What is the diagnosis?
options: ClusterIP services need publishNotReadyAddresses: true — otherwise endpoints stay empty until DNS TTL expires

Selector mismatch: the Service's selector labels do not match any pod's labels, so no endpoints were ever programmed. Fix the selector (or the pod labels) — kube-proxy and DNS have nothing to route to.
kube-proxy is down — without it, ClusterIPs are unroutable even with healthy endpoints
The pods are not Ready — endpoints only appear after all containers pass their startup probes
explain: <none> endpoints with Running pods is the textbook selector mismatch — compare kubectl get pods --show-labels against the Service selector. (Not-ready pods are excluded from endpoints by default too, but Running+Ready pods with <none> means the selector matches nothing.) kube-proxy failing would leave endpoints populated but unrouted — different symptom.

q: Two FlowSchemas both match a request: 'team-a-bulk' with matchingPrecedence 5000 and 'default-bulk' with matchingPrecedence 9000. Which classifies the request?
options: Whichever was created first — matchingPrecedence is only a tiebreaker for identical values
default-bulk — higher matchingPrecedence means higher priority, like PriorityClasses
Neither — overlapping FlowSchemas are rejected by the API server as ambiguous

team-a-bulk — FlowSchemas are evaluated in order of INCREASING matchingPrecedence, so the lower number wins. (The built-ins follow the same rule: system schemas at low numbers, catch-all at the highest.)
explain: matchingPrecedence is 'lower wins' — the API server sorts candidate FlowSchemas ascending and takes the first match. That is why the suggested config puts precise system schemas at 100-1000 and the catch-all at the highest number. PriorityClass uses higher-value-wins, which is the exact confusion this question exploits.

q: To 'reduce API server memory', someone sets --watch-cache=false. Afterwards etcd CPU triples and LIST latency spikes. What happened?
options: The watch cache was absorbing LISTs: with it on (the default), the API server serves reads from its in-memory cache; off, every LIST hits etcd directly. The memory saving cost far more in etcd load — re-enable it and size with --watch-cache-sizes if needed.
The flag is a no-op — watch cache cannot be disabled, so the etcd spike is coincidental
Disabling the watch cache also disables etcd compaction — the growing etcd database is what slowed LISTs
LISTs now bypass RBAC caching — each request re-evaluates authorization against etcd, tripling its CPU
explain: Watch cache (default true) lets the API server answer LIST/watch from memory instead of hammering etcd — it exists precisely to protect etcd at scale. Turning it off trades a bounded memory cost for unbounded etcd read load. Per-resource sizing via --watch-cache-sizes tunes the memory side without losing the protection.

q: You ran kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.0 on the control plane; the API server reports 1.30 but kubectl get nodes still shows kubelet 1.28 on every node. Is the upgrade incomplete?
options: The nodes auto-upgrade within 24h — kubelet version follows the control plane via the node lease mechanism

No — kubeadm upgrades control-plane components only; kubelets are upgraded per node with kubeadm upgrade node (then the kubelet package/service restart), followed by kubectl drain/uncordon around it. The version skew is expected mid-upgrade.
Yes — kubeadm upgrade apply was supposed to roll the kubelets too; the upgrade failed silently on the workers
You must run kubeadm init again on each node — kubelets only take their version from a fresh init
explain: kubeadm's upgrade flow is staged: upgrade plan/apply for control-plane components, then per-node kubeadm upgrade node plus package upgrade plus kubelet restart (drain first for workers). kubeadm never touches the kubelet binary remotely — that is the admin's (or the provisioner's) job. 1.28 kubelets under a 1.30 control plane is within supported skew during the rollout.

q: A node has two NICs (public + private). It registers in the cluster with its public IP, but all pod traffic must stay on the private network. Which kubelet setting fixes the registration?
options: A Node object annotation — node IPs can only be changed by annotating the Node after registration
--advertise-address on the kubelet — it tells the kubelet which IP to register with

--node-ip=<private-IP> on the kubelet — it sets the node's primary address used in the Node object and for pod/host communication. (The API server's --advertise-address is the separate control-plane-side setting.)
--cluster-dns with the private IP — DNS resolution determines the node's registered address
explain: The kubelet chooses its node IP automatically (often the default route's IP — here the public one); --node-ip overrides it explicitly, accepting single or dual-stack addresses. --advertise-address belongs to kube-apiserver (which address it advertises to the cluster), not the kubelet. Fix it in the kubelet config/systemd unit and restart.

q: You run etcd externally on three dedicated hosts. Which kube-apiserver flag points at them, and how should it be formatted for HA?
options: --etcd-servers takes a single URL — HA is achieved with a DNS round-robin name instead
External etcd is configured in the kube-controller-manager — the API server always uses stacked etcd
--etcd-endpoints on the kubelet — each kubelet connects to etcd directly for speed

--etcd-servers=https://etcd1:2379,https://etcd2:2379,https://etcd3:2379 — a comma-separated list; the API server load-balances/fails over across them. Pair with --etcd-cafile/--etcd-certfile/--etcd-keyfile for TLS.
explain: --etcd-servers accepts the full comma-separated member list and the API server handles failover across it — no load balancer required (though one works too). TLS flags authenticate the API server to etcd. Kubelets never talk to etcd; only the API server does.

q: A Deployment uses topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1, minDomains: 3, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, but the cluster currently has only 2 zones and 0 matching pods. How many matching pods can each zone hold?
options: One per zone — when eligible domains (2) are fewer than minDomains (3), the global minimum is treated as 0, so each zone may hold at most global-minimum + maxSkew = 1 pod. A third pod stays Pending until a third zone appears.
Three per zone — minDomains: 3 sets the per-zone cap directly, independent of maxSkew
Zero — with fewer zones than minDomains the constraint can never be satisfied, so nothing schedules
Unlimited — minDomains suspends the constraint until at least 3 zones exist
explain: minDomains guards against degenerate spreads: if eligible domains < minDomains, the scheduler treats the global minimum as 0 instead of the min over the existing domains. With maxSkew 1 that caps every zone at 1 pod — the constraint stays meaningful rather than collapsing. It is not a replica minimum and it does not suspend the rule.

q: An image built only for linux/amd64 is deployed to a mixed cluster. Pods on arm64 nodes fail with 'no matching manifest for linux/arm64 in the manifest list entries'. What is the proper fix?
options: Enable the MultiArch feature gate on the kubelet — it emulates amd64 via qemu automatically

Publish a multi-arch image (manifest list/index with per-arch images) and reference that tag — each node then pulls the variant matching its architecture. Alternatively constrain the workload to amd64 nodes with nodeAffinity.
Set imagePullPolicy: Always — the registry will transcode the image to arm64 on pull
Use an image digest instead of a tag — digests are architecture-independent
explain: The error is exact: the manifest list has no arm64 entry. The fix is build-side (docker buildx / multi-arch manifests) so the tag resolves per-arch, or scheduling-side (nodeAffinity keeping the workload on amd64). Pull policy, digests, and emulation do not conjure a missing architecture variant.

q: You want a custom AppArmor profile enforced on one container. Where does the profile live, and how is it referenced?
options: Profiles are stored in etcd as AppArmorProfile objects and referenced in securityContext.appArmorProfile
Set securityContext.appArmor: localhost/<profile> — AppArmor moved to the securityContext API in 1.24

The profile must be loaded on every node (e.g. in /etc/apparmor.d, enforced via apparmor_parser), and the pod references it per container with the annotation container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>: localhost/<profile-name>.
The profile is baked into the container image at /etc/apparmor.d — the runtime loads it from the image automatically
explain: AppArmor is annotation-referenced per container, with localhost/ meaning 'a profile pre-loaded on the node'. Kubernetes does not distribute profiles — if a scheduled node lacks it, the container fails to start — so config management must load the profile on every node. Profiles never come from the image or etcd.

q: A pod sets seLinuxOptions: {level: 's0:c1,c2'} but the container fails to start with an SELinux denial mentioning an invalid context. The nodes run SELinux in enforcing mode. What is the likely problem?
options: The level must be written as s0:c1-c2 — comma syntax is invalid and the runtime rejects it
seLinuxOptions requires privileged: true — SELinux contexts are ignored on unprivileged containers
SELinux options only apply on Windows nodes — Linux nodes ignore seLinuxOptions silently

The MCS category range is not permitted by the node's SELinux policy for containers — the level must fall within the categories the container policy allows; an out-of-policy level is rejected at container creation.
explain: seLinuxOptions sets user/role/type/level on the container processes, but the values must be valid under the host's SELinux policy — container engines expect MCS levels within their allocated category set. A level outside policy fails container creation with a context error. (Comma-separated categories like s0:c1,c2 are valid MCS syntax; the issue is policy permission, not punctuation.)

q: You need a privileged management container on Windows nodes that runs directly on the host (no container isolation). What does the spec require?
options: A Windows node, hostNetwork: true, and securityContext.windowsOptions.hostProcess: true — hostProcess containers are Windows-only and must use the host network namespace.
A privileged init container — hostProcess is implemented as an init-container feature
privileged: true on a Linux container — that is the cross-platform equivalent of hostProcess
hostProcess: true in the pod securityContext — it works on Linux and Windows identically
explain: HostProcess is a Windows-node feature for host-management pods: the container runs as a host process with the host's network namespace (hostNetwork required) and user. It is not a Linux concept — Linux uses privileged/securityContext capabilities instead — and it is set per-container under windowsOptions.

q: A Service uses sessionAffinity: ClientIP for sticky sessions. Users report being 'logged out' of their backend pod roughly every 3 hours. What controls this?
options: CoreDNS TTL on the service record — DNS expiry every 3h breaks the affinity
sessionAffinityConfig.clientIP.timeoutSeconds — it defaults to 10800s (3h) and caps how long a client IP sticks to one endpoint. Raise it (max 86400) if longer stickiness is needed.
The endpoint's readiness probe — probes reset affinity state on each success
The kube-proxy --iptables-min-sync-period — it rebalances ClientIP affinity every 3 hours by default
explain: ClientIP affinity is kube-proxy state with a bounded lifetime: timeoutSeconds (default 10800, max 86400) after which the client may be rebalanced. The ~3h symptom maps exactly to the default. It is unrelated to DNS TTLs or probe intervals.

q: You create a headless Service (clusterIP: None) WITHOUT a selector for an external database, expecting DNS records. nslookup returns nothing. What is missing?
options: Set publishNotReadyAddresses: true — headless DNS only works for not-ready addresses
Headless services require a selector — clusterIP: None is invalid without one and the Service was rejected

Without a selector, Kubernetes creates no endpoints automatically — you must create an Endpoints (or EndpointSlice) object with the same name as the Service listing the external IPs. Then DNS serves the A records.
External IPs need an ExternalName service — headless services cannot point outside the cluster
explain: A selector-less Service (headless or not) gets no automatic endpoints — that is the documented pattern for fronting external systems: you hand-manage the Endpoints object with the same name, and DNS then serves records for it. publishNotReadyAddresses is about readiness gating, not about missing endpoints.

q: An ingress-nginx Ingress routes path /shop/(.*) to a backend that serves paths WITHOUT the /shop prefix. Requests arrive as /shop/items but the app 404s. What is the standard fix?
options: Add a second Ingress for /items — the backend must be reachable under both prefixes
Change pathType to Exact — exact matching strips the longest prefix automatically
Set the backend Service's port name to http-rewrite — port names control URI rewriting
Add the annotation nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2 (with path /shop/(.*)) — the controller rewrites the URI to /items before proxying to the backend.
explain: rewrite-target is ingress-nginx's URI rewrite: with a regex capture path like /shop/(.*), rewrite-target: /$2 proxies /shop/items as /items. pathType only controls matching, never rewriting; the backend stays as-is. (ImplementationSpecific pathType is what allows the regex in the first place.)

q: NodePort Services are reachable on the nodes' public interfaces, which violates policy — they should only bind the internal 10.0.0.0/8 interface. How do you restrict this cluster-wide?
options: Start kube-proxy with --nodeport-addresses=10.0.0.0/8 — it limits which node addresses get NodePort listeners. (Host firewall rules are the complementary control.)
Add a NetworkPolicy blocking the public CIDR — NetworkPolicy filters NodePort traffic at the node edge
Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local — it restricts NodePorts to the pod's host interface
Set service.spec.clusterIPs to the internal range — ClusterIP controls the NodePort bind addresses
explain: --nodeport-addresses is kube-proxy's bind filter for NodePort (and health-check) listeners — the direct fix for 'NodePorts on the wrong interface'. ClusterIP is the virtual IP, NetworkPolicy governs pod traffic (not host-port binding), and externalTrafficPolicy governs forwarding/source-IP, not listener addresses.

q: An app does thousands of short external lookups (e.g. 'db-backup') with frequent 5s stalls. Packet captures show each lookup generating multiple queries against cluster.local search domains first. What is the standard mitigation?
options: Set dnsPolicy: Default — bypassing cluster DNS removes the search list

The ndots:5 default: any name with fewer than 5 dots is tried against every search domain first. Use fully-qualified names with a trailing dot (db-backup.example.com.) or lower ndots via dnsConfig options.
Raise the CoreDNS cache TTL — caching eliminates the search-domain expansion
Increase the resolver timeout — the stalls are just slow upstreams, not search expansion
explain: ndots:5 means 'db-backup' (0 dots < 5) is expanded through default.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local before the real query — each NXDOMAIN costs a round trip, and with many lookups it storms. A trailing dot makes the name absolute (no search), and dnsConfig can set ndots: '1' per pod. Cache TTL does not stop the expansion from happening.

q: You want a secrets-store CSI driver volume mounted directly in the pod spec — no PVC, no provisioning — for short-lived secrets. Which volume type does this?
options: A projected secret volume — it supports arbitrary CSI drivers via the driver field
An emptyDir with medium: Memory — CSI drivers can only attach through PVCs
A CSI ephemeral volume (volumes: [{csi: {driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io, volumeAttributes: {...}}}]) — inline, per-pod, no PVC/PV lifecycle; the volume dies with the pod.
A generic ephemeral volume — it creates a PVC automatically, which is what you want to avoid
explain: CSI ephemeral volumes embed the driver plus volumeAttributes inline in the pod spec — designed for secrets/config-like drivers where a PV/PVC per pod is overkill. Generic ephemeral volumes DO create PVCs (different feature). The volume is pod-scoped: deleted with the pod, never shared.

q: You edit a StorageClass to change mountOptions (e.g. add vers=4.1 for NFS). Existing pods keep mounting with the old options. Why?
options: The kubelet caches StorageClasses for 24h — the new options apply after the cache expires
mountOptions only apply at provision time — they are baked into the PV and can never change
StorageClass fields are immutable — the edit was rejected and the old options remain
StorageClass mountOptions are consumed at mount time — already-mounted volumes keep their options until the pod is recreated and the volume remounted. The class change only affects future mounts.
explain: mountOptions are mount-time flags passed by the kubelet on each mount; there is no re-mount pass over running pods when the class changes. (Most StorageClass fields are effectively immutable, but mountOptions is the mutable exception — and its effect is still mount-time only.)

q: You edit a StorageClass to change parameters (e.g. type: gp2 to type: gp3) so new volumes get the cheaper disk. The API server rejects the edit. Why, and what is the right approach?
options: StorageClass parameters (and provisioner) are immutable — the API rejects changes. Create a new StorageClass with the new parameters and point new PVCs at it; existing volumes are unaffected either way.
Parameters are mutable but type is not — rename the key to diskType and the edit is accepted
Only mountOptions are immutable — parameters can be edited freely, so the error must be a typo
The edit applies only to new PVCs — the rejection means you also need to restart the CSI provisioner
explain: The StorageClass API forbids changing provisioner and parameters after creation (it is the reverse of the common assumption: mountOptions is the mutable exception). The supported evolution path is a new class plus migration. Existing PVs keep the parameters they were provisioned with regardless.

q: A PV was created with reclaimPolicy: Delete but compliance now requires manual review before storage is wiped. Can you change it, and what does the change affect?
options: Change it on the StorageClass — the PV inherits reclaimPolicy dynamically from its class
Yes — patch the PV's persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy to Retain. It only affects what happens when the NEXT release occurs; the currently bound volume is untouched until its PVC is deleted.
Yes, but it applies retroactively — already-Released PVs with Delete are resurrected to Available
No — reclaimPolicy is immutable after the PV is created; you must recreate the PV
explain: persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy is mutable on the PV object; the recycle/delete/retain action runs at release time using the policy then in effect. Changing it mid-life does not disturb the bound volume or resurrect anything already released — it just changes the next release's behavior. (StorageClass reclaimPolicy only sets the default for dynamically provisioned PVs.)

q: A CSI driver supports volume health monitoring. Where do you, as a cluster admin, see 'volume condition abnormal' signals for a PVC?
options: Only in the driver's own logs — Kubernetes has no API surface for volume health
Via kubectl get volumeattachments — the VolumeAttachment status carries the health field
As Events on the PVC — the external-health-monitor sidecar watches volumes and reports abnormal conditions as warning events on the bound PVC object.
In the PV's status.conditions — health is reported on the PersistentVolume like node conditions
explain: The csi-external-health-monitor sidecar translates CSI volume-condition signals into standard Kubernetes Events on the PVC (e.g. 'VolumeConditionAbnormal'). kubectl describe pvc is therefore the admin's first stop — no driver-log spelunking needed for the headline signal. PV conditions and VolumeAttachment status do not carry this.

q: A namespace has been stuck in Terminating for over an hour. Deleting it again changes nothing. What is the most common cause, and how do you unstick it?
options: Use kubectl delete namespace --force --grace-period=0 — force deletion bypasses finalizers on namespaces
The namespace controller is crashed — restart kube-controller-manager to resume termination
Recreate the namespace with the same name — the new object clears the Terminating state of the old one

A resource in the namespace has a finalizer blocking deletion (or an aggregated API the namespace controller needs is unreachable). List all resources (kubectl api-resources --namespaced, then get across types in the namespace), resolve or remove the blocking finalizers, and the namespace controller finishes the job.
explain: Namespaces terminate by deleting every namespaced object first; any object with a pending finalizer (custom controllers, PV protection, etc.) blocks the whole namespace indefinitely. --force does not strip finalizers (you must edit/remove them deliberately), and recreating the name just queues behind the terminating one. Find the stuck resource, handle its finalizer, and termination completes.

q: A node is NotReady and the kubelet will not stay up. kubectl cannot tell you why because the node is not reporting. What is the first log to check, and how?
options: The kubelet's own logs on the node: journalctl -u kubelet (or /var/log/kubelet.log) — kubelet startup failures (bad config, cgroup driver mismatch, expired certs, swap enabled) are logged there, never in the API.
kubectl logs -n kube-system kubelet — the kubelet ships its logs to the API server like any pod
dmesg only — kubelet failures are kernel panics, so only the kernel ring buffer matters
The API server audit log — kubelet registration failures are recorded as 401 audit events
explain: The kubelet is a node daemon, not an API object — when it cannot start, its logs live on the node (journald or file, per install). Swap-on, cgroupfs-vs-systemd mismatch, unparseable --config, and expired client certs are the greatest hits, all visible in the first screen of journalctl -u kubelet. kubectl logs cannot reach a kubelet that never registered.

q: A node's disk is slowly filling with old container images and you want the kubelet to clean them automatically. Which flags control this, and what are the defaults?
options: Image GC cannot be tuned — the kubelet uses hardcoded 90/85 thresholds on every node

--image-gc-high-threshold (default 85): when disk usage exceeds it, the kubelet garbage-collects images until usage drops to --image-gc-low-threshold (default 80). Unused images go first; images younger than --minimum-image-ttl-duration are spared.
--image-pull-progress-deadline — it sets how long the kubelet waits before deleting a slow image pull
--eviction-hard with imagefs.available — image GC is just a special case of node-pressure eviction
explain: Kubelet image GC is threshold-driven on disk usage percent: high threshold trips collection, low threshold stops it, TTL protects fresh images, and in-use images are never removed. It is separate from eviction (which kills pods under disk pressure) — GC is the routine hygiene that should prevent ever reaching eviction.

q: kubectl drain node1 hangs on a pod that is not managed by any controller (a bare pod). The pod has no PDB. Why does drain refuse, and what is the correct flag?
options: The pod must have a PDB — drain cannot proceed on any pod without a disruption budget
Pass --disable-eviction — it makes drain delete pods directly instead of using the eviction API

Drain evicts via the Eviction API and refuses to delete pods not managed by a controller (they would not come back) unless you pass --force. DaemonSet pods are skipped automatically; mirror (static) pods cannot be evicted via the API at all.
Drain never deletes bare pods, even with flags — you must delete the node object instead
explain: kubectl drain's safety rules: DaemonSet pods are ignored (they would return immediately), mirror/static pods error (not API-deletable), and unmanaged bare pods need --force because deletion is destructive. --disable-eviction was removed long ago — drain always uses the eviction API now, which is also why PDBs are honored.

q: Every new pod on node worker-3 fails with 'FailedCreatePodSandBox: failed to set up sandbox container network: plugin type="calico" failed (add): ...'. Pods on other nodes are fine. Where is the fault?
options: The cluster CIDR is exhausted — the IPAM cannot allocate, which surfaces as a plugin ADD failure
The pod images are corrupt — FailedCreatePodSandBox means the sandbox (pause) image failed to pull
The kubelet's client cert expired — sandbox creation requires a fresh API server round-trip per pod

Node-local CNI: the Calico plugin errors during ADD on that node — check /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist validity and that the plugin binary exists in /opt/cni/bin on worker-3. A broken CNI config breaks pod networking node-wide, before any container starts.
explain: FailedCreatePodSandBox with a CNI ADD error is the runtime failing to set up the pod network namespace — it happens before image pulls and container creation, and node-scoped (one bad conflist or missing binary) while the rest of the cluster is healthy. Fix the CNI config/binary on the node; image, cert, and CIDR theories do not match a plugin-ADD failure on a single node.
